The thirteen profiles of arXiv:2608.02759v2 do NOT refute on their own: an explicit quota-feasible allocation at each of the thirteen has no population paradox anywhere among them, in the full sense of Definition 1. The source's closing relabelling paragraph is load-bearing

An unconditional, symmetry-free finite certificate for the four-state impossibility: the 32-input closure of the source's thirteen profiles under the three cyclic permutations of states 1,2,3 refutes as it stands, and so does a 22-input subset of it which omits the source's central profile X = ((1,1,1,6),3) entirely; both use only transfers between states whose populations are unchanged

The 22-input certificate is irreducible: deleting any single one of its 22 inputs leaves a set of 21 that admits a quota-feasible allocation with no population paradox at all (22 explicit witnesses, each checked under the full Definition 1)

The fixed-house variant the source leaves open, measured: at each of the four house sizes 3, 5, 8, 10 that the source's own proof uses, the 256 four-state inputs with populations at most 4 admit a quota-feasible allocation with no population paradox anywhere among them -- so no refuting gadget for the fixed-house variant lives in that box

families.paper_title: Four-state apportionment: quota versus population monotonicity across house sizes, and the finite gadgets that refute it
families.paper_abstract: Varshney (arXiv:2608.02759) proved that no deterministic apportionment solution for four states satisfies both quota and population monotonicity across house sizes, closing the boundary left between the three-state Webster possibility result and the five-state construction of G\"olz, Peters and Procaccia.  The proof is a thirteen-profile gadget analysed conditionally on one quota choice at a central profile, followed by a relabelling step that removes the condition.  We give what is, as far as we can tell, the first machine check of that theorem and of its corollary for relative population monotonicity: a depth-first search over an explicit list of inputs, proved sound once and for all, is evaluated by the Lean~4 kernel (\lean{decide}, no \lean{native\_decide}).  Three facts about the construction are new.  First, the thirteen printed profiles do \emph{not} refute on their own: we exhibit a quota-feasible allocation of all thirteen with no population paradox among them, so the relabelling step is load-bearing.  Second, the closure of the thirteen profiles under the cyclic permutations of states $1,2,3$ --- 32 inputs --- refutes unconditionally and without any symmetry argument, and so does an explicit 22-input subset that omits the central profile entirely; both use only transfers between states whose populations are unchanged.  Third, the 22-input certificate is irreducible: deleting any one input leaves a satisfiable set, with 22 explicit witnesses. Whether a smaller certificate exists is open.  For the fixed-house variant that the source names as open, we record a measurement: on the box of populations at most $4$ at each of the house sizes $3, 5, 8, 10$, a paradox-free quota selector exists, so no refuting gadget lives there, while four natural quota rules all fail at every house size $3 \le h \le 12$.

families.title: chi_A(G_n), the fewest colours partitioning the n x n Euclidean grid into arcs (no 3 collinear points per class)
families.description: `χ_A(G_n)` is the fewest colours needed to partition the `n × n` integer grid so that no colour class contains three collinear points — collinearity inherited from the Euclidean plane, so **every** line counts, arbitrary rational slopes included, not only rows, columns and diagonals. A class with no three collinear points is an *arc* (the no-three-in-line objects), whence the name. The family is indexed by `n`, the side of the grid — one cell per size, `G_n` carrying `n²` points. families.description: Let `Z_m = Z/mZ`. An **arc** (cyclic interval) is a set `W(a, L) = {a, a+1, …, a+L−1} ⊆ Z_m` with `a ∈ Z_m` and `0 ≤ L ≤ m`; its two endpoints are at graph distance `min(L, m−L)` in the cycle `C_m`. An arc **beats** a subset `x ⊆ Z_m` when

statements.label: The cyclic interval lemma holds for EVERY odd m: for x subset of Z_m with x not empty and x not all of Z_m there is an arc W with |W symmdiff x| < min(|W|, m-|W|). This is Conjecture conj:interval of arXiv:2607.07939v1, which the source proves only in its covering-arc regime and verifies by computer for odd m <= 17

The even dichotomy, which the source does not discuss at all: for m = 2h with h >= 1, a set x subset of Z_m is beaten by NO arc if and only if x is invariant under the antipodal rotation i |-> i + h. Both directions proved for every even m

The same sweep for odd 19 <= m <= 31, seven moduli beyond what the source verified: 0 escaping subsets at every one (odd m <= 29 in Check.lean, m = 31 in Check31.lean, and independently m <= 31 in C)

For every even m = 2h with h >= 1 there are exactly 2^h sets that no arc beats -- the antipodally invariant ones -- of which 2^h - 2 are proper and nonempty; and the sweep confirms the counts 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, 126, 254, 510, 1022, 2046, 4094 at every even m <= 24

families.paper_title: The cyclic interval lemma for every odd modulus
families.paper_abstract: Let $\Zm=\ZZ/m\ZZ$ and call $W(a,L)=\{a,a+1,\dots,a+L-1\}$, $0\le L\le m$, an \emph{arc}. An arc $W$ \emph{beats} a set $x\subseteq\Zm$ when $|W\sd x|<\min(|W|,m-|W|)$.  Fokam Souop and Bitjoka, studying the least dimension $k_{\min}(C_m)$ of a binary Cayley graph into which the cycle $C_m$ embeds isometrically, isolated the assertion that for odd $m$ every $x\notin\{\emptyset,\Zm\}$ is beaten by some arc.  They proved it in one regime, verified it by computer for all odd $m\le 17$, and left it as a conjecture; it is the first of the three problems their paper leaves open.  We prove it for every odd $m$.  The argument instantiates the hypothesis ``no arc beats $x$'' at exactly two arc lengths, $d$ and $d+1$ where $m=2d+1$, which squeezes every length-$d$ window of $x$ to the same cardinality, and a single double count then forces $|x|\in\{0,m\}$.  We also settle the case the source does not discuss: for $m=2h$ the sets that no arc beats are \emph{exactly} the sets invariant under the antipodal rotation $i\mapsto i+h$, and there are exactly $2^{h}$ of them, $2^{h}-2$ of them proper and nonempty.  So the parity hypothesis is not an artefact of the proof.  An independent exhaustive search over all $2^{m}-2$ proper nonempty subsets of $\Zm$ confirms the odd statement for every odd $m\le 31$ and the count $2^{h}-2$ for every even $m\le 24$.  Every result below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Evaluating an avoidance number: $A_3(4)=9$, $A_3(5)\ge18$, and two brackets for oriented Ramsey numbers
families.paper_abstract: Duman, G\"on\"ul, Kaya, Saxena and Tamer introduce two finite Ramsey-type quantities as the inputs to a constant in their work on closed Ramsey numbers of small countable ordinals: the directed Ramsey number $R(\Kst{n},L_3)$ and an \emph{avoidance number} $\A(k)$, the least $m$ such that every $3$-colouring of the arcs of $\Kst{m}$ admits a $k$-set $S$ in which every vertex misses a colour on its arcs from $S$.  They evaluate neither.  We first observe that $R(\Kst{m},L_3)$ is the oriented Ramsey number $r(I_m,L_3)$, for which exact values up to $m=5$ and the bound $r(I_m,L_3)\le m^2-m+3$ are in print but are not cited in that paper.  We then determine $\A(4)=9$, the first value of the avoidance number beyond the trivial $\A(3)=3$, against a published bracket whose upper end is the unknown three-colour Ramsey number $R(4,4,4)$.  The proof rests on a symmetry of $\A$ that acts independently at each vertex; we also give the best upper bound we can prove with no search at all, $\A(4)\le17$, from a new obstruction on \emph{pairs} of vertices, and the first nontrivial lower bound at $k=5$, $\A(5)\ge18$.  For the directed function we prove two brackets for which we could find no published counterpart, $29\le r(I_6,L_3)\le 33$ and $21\le r(I_3,L_4)\le 25$; in each the upper end is Ihringer, Rajendraprasad and Weinert's published bound and the lower end is new, the second being the cell they name as the natural next question and where only $r(I_3,L_4)\ge9$ was available.  Every statement below has been machine-checked.

families.title: B-groups of order p^5: which groups of order 243 and 3125 occur as regular subgroups of a uniprimitive permutation group
families.description: A finite group `H` is a **B-group** (Burnside group) when every *primitive* permutation group containing a regular subgroup isomorphic to `H` is 2-transitive. Equivalently: `H` is **not** a B-group exactly when `H` occurs as a regular subgroup of some **uniprimitive** group — primitive but not 2-transitive. Burnside started the subject by asserting that cyclic groups of order `p^a`, `a ≥ 2`, are B-groups; groups of order `p` never are.

families.paper_title: Non-$B$-groups of order $3^5$ and exponent $9$
families.paper_abstract: A finite group $H$ is a \emph{$B$-group} if every primitive permutation group containing a regular subgroup isomorphic to $H$ is $2$-transitive; equivalently, $H$ fails to be a $B$-group exactly when it occurs as a regular subgroup of a uniprimitive group.  Herbig has classified the $B$-groups of order $p^4$ and names the order-$p^5$ classification as the next step, observing that for $p=3$ and $p=5$ the answer is a finite computation over the primitive-groups and small-groups libraries; the outcome of that computation is not reported there.  We carry out part of the case $p=3$ and certify the outcome inside a proof assistant.  From an explicit list of $18$ permutations of a $243$-point set we prove that the group $\Ga$ they generate is uniprimitive --- primitive by a statement quantified over \emph{all} invariant partitions, not $2$-transitive by an exhibited invariant set of $3888$ ordered pairs --- and that $\Ga$ contains three pairwise non-isomorphic regular subgroups of order $243$: one elementary abelian, and two of exponent $9$.  Hence at least two groups of order $3^5$ of exponent $9$ are not $B$-groups.  Externally, GAP identifies $\Ga$ as the affine primitive group $3^5{:}(2^4{:}A_5)$ of order $233280$ and the two subgroups as \texttt{SmallGroup(243,51)} and \texttt{SmallGroup(243,63)}, both nonabelian with centres of order $9$ and $27$.  Since these have order $p^q$ with $q>p$ and exponent $p^2$, they show that the hypothesis $q<p$ in Herbig's Theorem~B cannot be relaxed to $q>p$, and they answer an instance at $p=3$ of his closing question on regular subgroups of $\AGL(5,p)$.  The primitivity, the failure of $2$-transitivity and the three regular subgroups with their invariants are machine-checked in Lean~4; the few steps checked outside the proof assistant are named where they are used. We do not claim the resulting list of non-$B$-groups of order $243$ is complete, and we say precisely which part of the search did not run.

Correction: the ancillary `Tablesc40all.pdf` of arXiv:2602.12312v3 records `X (d)` for row 93, `A_{5,48} B_{2,24}` (`c = 40`, `d₁ = 45`), but the dimension test does **not** exclude it — `m = 41 860 = 88·385 + 4·1995`, and the two conformal-weight-`2` modules of dimensions `385` and `1995` are exhibited

Negative controls for the 90 `c = 40` exclusions: the size obstruction is about size and not emptiness (`B_{7,8}` has exactly three conformal-weight-`2` modules, of dimensions `230 945`, `271 700`, `388 960`, all above `m = 67 030`; `B_{3,100}^2` has one of dimension `419 881` above `m = 40 507`), a too-small claim is refuted, the coin obstruction is one unit wide at row 274 (`m − 1 = 48 489` is representable, `m = 48 490` is not), the level-one correction moves `m` by `1127` at row 1223, and the conformal-weight condition bites

The `c = 40` dimension test as a kernel statement about modules: `RepByModules` and the completeness theorem `mem_wt2DimsSmall`, with a dimension prune, two interchangeable complete per-factor enumerations and deduplication — the engine that turns each of the 94 exclusions into three data (factor list, common denominator, `m`)

families.paper_title: The dimension test for balanced holomorphic vertex operator algebras\\ at central charges $32$ and $40$
families.paper_abstract: Ampagouni, Mason and Mertens single out a class of holomorphic vertex operator algebras $V=\CC\one\oplus V_1\oplus V_2\oplus\cdots$ that they call \emph{balanced}, for which the Virasoro vectors of $V$ and of the subalgebra generated by $V_1$ coincide when the central charge is $32$ or $40$ and $V_1\ne0$, and they enumerate the $449$ semisimple balanced root systems at $c=32$ and the $1277$ at $c=40$.  Three computational tests then try to rule each of them out.  The cheapest is the \emph{dimension test}: the integer $m=\dim V_2-\dim L_{\hg}(k,0)_2$ must be a non-negative integer combination of the top-level dimensions of the conformal-weight-two modules of $\hg$.  At $c=32$ exactly two root systems defeated even this test for want of resources, $A_{1,64}^{3}A_{4,160}$ and $A_{5,64}$; we decide both.  The test \emph{excludes} $A_{5,64}$, by a size obstruction ($m=147519$ while every conformal-weight-two module has top-level dimension at least $3\,845\,961$, a minimum we determine exactly), and it does \emph{not} exclude $A_{1,64}^{3}A_{4,160}$, where $m=147094=6288\cdot23+10\cdot247$ is certified on the three $A_{1,64}$ factors alone.  At $c=40$ the source ran no test in its body, and its ancillary table records a result for $154$ of the $1277$ rows.  We machine-check the census $\#\BRS(40,0)=1277$ (and find $\#\BRS(10,0)=22$ where the source prints $42$), we show that the dimension test excludes $93$ of the $1123$ rows with no recorded result, and we show that one row the ancillary table marks as excluded by the dimension test, $A_{5,48}B_{2,24}$, is in fact not excluded by it.  The $c=40$ exclusions are stated about modules rather than about a computed list, through a completeness theorem for a pruned enumeration of the conformal-weight-two modules.  A non-exclusion is not an existence statement, and an exclusion is an exclusion by this test only.  All numbered statements are machine-checked in Lean~4; a displayed closed form for $m$ in the source is also corrected.

families.title: The onset table for the two-armed Bernoulli bandit: when each algorithm's worst case leaves the deterministic corner, and whether it leaves first-order or by a jump
families.description: **The instances.** Two Bernoulli arms with means `(p, q) ∈ [0,1]²` and a horizon `T`. The expected regret is

statements.label: The corner ladder of the horizon-`T` Bayes-optimal policy (independent `Beta(1,1)` priors, fair coin at exact ties) on two Bernoulli arms is FLAT: the exact expected regret at both deterministic instances `(1,0)` and `(0,1)` is `1/2` at every horizon `T <= 12`. Exact rational forward dynamic programme over posterior states, with the policy itself computed in Lean by backward induction on the Bellman value table.

For every horizon `T <= 2` the deterministic corner is a worst case of the Bayes-optimal policy over the WHOLE square `[0,1]^2`: `R_T(p,q) <= 1/2` at every Bernoulli instance. Two Bernstein certificates per horizon -- one per triangle, for `(p-q)E[N_2]` and for `(q-p)(T-E[N_2])` -- all four at the base multidegree with no subdivision at all.

At horizon `T = 3` the deterministic corner is NOT a worst case of the Bayes-optimal policy: the instance `(99/100, 0)`, at `L^inf`-distance `1/100` from the corner, has `R_3 = 2029401/4000000 > 1/2 = R_3(1,0)`. Two exact rationals.

`T_c = 3` for the horizon-`T` Bayes-optimal policy: `3` is the SMALLEST horizon at which the deterministic corner is not a worst case over `[0,1]^2` -- the two halves BO2 and BO3 in one statement. For Thompson sampling with the same prior the answer is `5` (`ts-worstcase-corner` TW4), so the Bayes-optimal policy leaves the corner two horizons earlier than the heuristic that approximates it.

The EXACT worst case of the horizon-`4` Bayes-optimal policy over the whole square is the rational `2/3`, attained at `(2/3, 0)`. Both halves are exact -- the upper bound is a polynomial inequality on the square (`E[N_2(4)] = 2 + (3/2)q - (3/2)p + pq^2 - p^2 q`, obtained from the state list by `native_decide`, then `nlinarith` on each triangle), the lower bound the exact rational value -- and on the edge `q = 0` the deficit is an exact square, `2/3 - R_4(p,0) = (3/2)(p - 2/3)^2`.

Negative controls for the Bayes-DP column: the `T <= 2` corner bound `1/2` is REFUTED at `T = 3` by an explicit instance; nothing in the square beats `2/3` at `T = 4`, so the exact value cannot be pushed up; the region is inhabited by an instance of strictly positive regret and equal arms give regret exactly `0`.

Reproduction control (the compute-first gate): THIS family's generic dynamic programme, run with the Thompson-sampling decision rule instead of a counts-based one, reproduces the certified corner ladder `1/2, 5/6, 25/24, 281/240, 2007/1600, 1983559/1512000` of the landed family `ts-worstcase-corner` (its row TW1) and its certified corner-derivative ladder `1/2, 2/3, 13/24, 31/120, -847/14400, -131167/378000` (row TW11, sign flip at `T_c = 5` included); run with the explore-then-commit rule it reproduces that family's exact `ETC(1)` worst case `T^2/(8(T-2))` at `T = 5, 6, 7` (rows TW8/TW9), attained at `p - q = T/(2(T-2))`.

The corner ladder of regularised greedy `RG(alpha,beta)` is FLAT at `1`: for every `(alpha,beta)` in `{(0,0),(1,2),(2,4)}` and every horizon `T <= 12` the exact expected regret at the deterministic instance `(0,1)` is `1`, and at `(1,0)` it is `1` for every `T >= 2` and `0` at `T = 1`. The `T = 1` asymmetry is the initialisation order of arXiv:2607.29375's Algorithm 1 (`A_t = t`), and it is why every bound in this family is taken over the whole square rather than a triangle.

For every horizon strictly below its onset horizon the deterministic corner is a worst case of `RG(alpha,beta)` over the WHOLE square: `R_T <= 1` for `T <= 6` at `(0,0)`, for `T <= 9` at `(1,2)` and for `T <= 10` at `(2,4)`. Two Bernstein certificates per horizon (one per triangle) in the plain square coordinates, 50 certificates in all; no subdivision at all below `T = 6, 7, 7` respectively, and at most a 15-node subdivision tree anywhere.

At its onset horizon each `RG(alpha,beta)` is beaten by an interior instance that is strictly worse than EVERY instance of the boundary of the square: at `T = 7` the regret of `RG(0,0)` is at most `1` on all four edges (eight Bernstein certificates, every one at the base multidegree) while `(7/50, 17/20)` has regret `> 1`; at `T = 10` the same for `RG(1,2)` with the instance `(27/100, 19/25)`; at `T = 11` the regret of `RG(2,4)` is at most `1011/1000` on the boundary while `(29/100, 37/50)` exceeds it.

The onset horizons of regularised greedy are `T_c = T_e = 7, 10, 11` for `(alpha,beta) = (0,0), (1,2), (2,4)`: at every smaller horizon the deterministic corner is a worst case (hence the worst case is on the boundary), and at the onset horizon a single interior instance is strictly worse than every boundary instance. Corner departure and edge departure coincide for all three policies -- unlike Thompson sampling, where they are `5` and `18` (`ts-worstcase-corner` TW4, TW14).

Regularisation strictly delays the departure: `T_c(0,0) = 7 < T_c(1,2) = 10 < T_c(2,4) = 11`, stated as the four certified facts that pin the two strict inequalities (the corner is still a worst case of `RG(1,2)` at `T = 7`, where it has already failed for `RG(0,0)`, and still a worst case of `RG(2,4)` at `T = 10`, where it has already failed for `RG(1,2)`).

Negative controls for the regularised-greedy column: the corner bound `1` is REFUTED at the onset horizon for all three policies; the `1011/1000` boundary bound of `RG(2,4)` at `T = 11` is not removable slack -- the boundary itself already carries more than the corner value there, witnessed by the explicit edge instance `(417785/1000000, 0)` -- while for `RG(0,0)` no boundary instance at all beats the corner at `T = 7`; and the hypotheses are non-vacuous (strictly positive regret at the corner, exactly `0` on the diagonal).

The corner edge-derivative ladders. Along the edge `q = 0` the regret is a one-variable polynomial in `p` and its derivative at `p = 1` is an exact rational: `1/2, 0, -3/4, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1, -3/2, -3/2` for the Bayes-optimal policy at `T = 1..12`; `2^{2-T}` for pure greedy and `1` then `1/2` for `RG(1,2)` and `RG(2,4)` at every `2 <= T <= 14`; and, as the control, `1/2, 2/3, 13/24, 31/120, -847/14400, -131167/378000` for Thompson sampling, which is `ts-worstcase-corner`'s certified row TW11. The derivative is a Mathlib `HasDerivAt` statement, not a formal-derivative convention.

The mechanism is algorithm-dependent, and the corner derivative separates the two classes. FIRST-ORDER for the Bayes-optimal policy: the edge derivative at the corner is exactly `0` at `T = 2`, the last horizon at which the corner is a worst case, and `-3/4 < 0` at `T = 3 = T_c`, so the corner is not even a local maximiser along the edge there. ZEROTH-ORDER for regularised greedy: the same derivative is STRICTLY POSITIVE at every horizon `2 <= T <= 14` for all three `(alpha,beta)` -- `1/32` at `T = 6` and `1/64` at `T = 7` for pure greedy -- with no sign change anywhere near `T_c = 7, 10, 11`, so the corner remains a strict local maximiser along the edge at and past its own departure horizon and no first-order test at the corner can detect the departure.

Negative controls for the derivative rows: the Bayes-DP ladder does not stay at `-1` (it is `-3/2` at `T = 11`), the pure-greedy derivative at the departure horizon is not `0` (so the zeroth-order statement is not the vacuous 'the derivative vanishes'), and it is not constant across the departure either.

MEASUREMENT (float, unbound). UCB1 with the index `S_i/N_i + sqrt(2 ln n / N_i)`, `n` the number of plays already made, arm 1 pulled first, fair coin at exact ties: the worst case over `[0,1]^2` at `T = 1..12` is `1, 1, 1, 1, 1.208876, 1.294452, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2.015427, 2.072208`, so its corner-worst set is NOT an initial segment -- `T_c = 5`, but the corner is a worst case again at `T = 7,...,10`. The reason is exact: at `(1,0)` the trajectory is deterministic and the regret is the number of re-explorations of the dead arm, which happen at rounds `2, 7, 16, 31, 54, 87, 135, 205, 307, 455, 670, 983, 1441, 2117` (so `R_T(1,0)` is `1` on `2 <= T <= 6`, `2` on `7 <= T <= 15`, `3` on `16 <= T <= 30`, ...). That integer sequence is not in OEIS (queried 2026-09-07).

MEASUREMENT (float, unbound). KL-UCB with exploration function `ln t` (`t` the current round, no log-log term), arm 1 pulled first, fair coin at exact ties: the worst case over `[0,1]^2` at `T = 1..12` is `1` for `T <= 7` and then `1.042075, 1.108734, 1.140842, 1.178284, 1.230835`, so `T_c = 8` -- and, unlike regularised greedy, the corner is beaten by a BOUNDARY instance there (`(0, 0.5523)`), with the worst case leaving the boundary only at `T_e = 10` (maximiser `(0.0270, 0.5467)`). The horizon-`T` Bayes-optimal policy's own worst case over the square runs `1/2, 1/2, .598076, 2/3, .716877, .764695, .816951, .847054, .900656, .937890, .983479, 1.018754` for `T = 1..12`, attained in the interior of the square from `T = 8` on -- so `T_e(Bayes-DP) = 8`, ten horizons before its analogue for Thompson sampling but five after its own `T_c`.

families.paper_title: Where the worst case leaves the corner:\\ the Bayes-optimal and regularised greedy policies\\ on two Bernoulli arms at small horizons
families.paper_abstract: For a policy on two Bernoulli arms whose decisions are comparisons of rational numbers, the expected regret at horizon $T$ on the instance with means $(p,q)$ is a piecewise polynomial $\Reg_T(p,q)$ with rational coefficients, so its worst case over the instance square $[0,1]^2$ is a well-defined number.  Three finite invariants of such a policy were introduced for Thompson sampling in a companion paper: the corner-departure horizon $\Tc$, the smallest horizon at which a deterministic instance is no longer a worst case; the edge-departure horizon $\Te$, the smallest horizon at which the worst case leaves the boundary of the square; and the mechanism of the departure, read off the sign of the regret's derivative at the corner along an edge.  We compute them, exactly and with machine-checked proofs, for two further policies: the horizon-$T$ Bayes-optimal policy under independent uniform priors (Bellman's dynamic programme), and the regularised greedy rule $\RG(\alpha,\beta)$ of Zhou, Li and Wang at $(\alpha,\beta)=(0,0),(1,2),(2,4)$. (i)~The Bayes-optimal policy has corner regret exactly $1/2$ at every horizon $T\le 12$ and $\Tc=3$, two horizons before the Thompson-sampling value $5$; at $T=4$ its exact worst case is the rational $2/3$, attained at $(2/3,0)$, with $2/3-\Reg_4(p,0)=\tfrac32(p-\tfrac23)^2$ along the edge. (ii)~Regularised greedy has corner regret exactly $1$ at $(0,1)$ at every horizon $T\le 12$, and $\Tc=\Te=7,\,10,\,11$ for the three parameter pairs: corner departure and edge departure coincide, whereas for Thompson sampling they are $5$ and $18$.  In particular regularisation strictly delays the departure, $7<10<11$. (iii)~The mechanism separates the two classes.  For the Bayes-optimal policy the edge derivative at the corner is $0$ at $T=2$ and $-3/4$ at $T=3$, so the departure is first-order, as for Thompson sampling; for regularised greedy the same derivative, at every $2\le T\le 14$, is $2^{2-T}$ for pure greedy and, for the two regularised rules, $1$ at $T=2$ and $1/2$ thereafter --- strictly positive throughout, so the corner remains a strict local maximiser along the edge at and past its own departure horizon and no first-order test at the corner can detect it: the worst case jumps to an interior instance. Every upper bound is a Bernstein certificate of polynomial nonnegativity on the square or on one of its edges, except the $T=4$ bound, which is a polynomial inequality proved from the explicit degree-four regret; every lower bound is an exact rational evaluation; the derivatives are derivatives of the real polynomial; and every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4.  UCB1 and KL-UCB, whose decisions compare transcendental indices, are measured in floating point only and appear as labelled computations outside the formal development.

families.title: The exact Bayes-optimal (E[tau], probability-of-error) frontier of fixed-confidence best-arm identification for two Bernoulli arms under the uniform prior: four exact linear pieces on delta in [3337/13860, 1/2] with breakpoints lambda = 6, 20, 49/2, 55/2, certified for the infinite-horizon problem by a collapsing rational bracket
families.description: Jang–Komiyama–Yamazaki, *Fixed Confidence Best Arm Identification in the Bayesian Setting* (**arXiv:2402.10429v2**, `[stat.ML]`, NeurIPS 2024), ask for an algorithm that minimises the expected number of samples `E_{μ∼H}[τ]` subject to the *Bayesian* correctness constraint `PoE(π; H) = E_{μ∼H}[P(J ≠ i*(μ))] ≤ δ` (their Definition 1, arXiv PDF p. 4). They give a lower bound `Ω(L(H)²/δ)` (Theorem 4, p. 6) and a matching upper bound `O((L(H)²/δ) log(L(H)/δ))` (Theorem 6, p. 8), and their Remark 2 (p. 8) says the two are "tight up to a `log(L(H)/δ)` factor". Their Section 7 (p. 10) lists as future

statements.label: The exact Beta-comparison posterior probability w(s) = P[mu_1 > mu_2 | s] on posterior states (a1,b1,a2,b2) of two Bernoulli arms under independent Uniform[0,1] priors, its first values (err = 1/2, 1/3, 1/4), and its two structural identities over all 495 states of depth <= 8: w is a martingale under the posterior predictive on either arm, and w(a1,b1,a2,b2) + w(a2,b2,a1,b1) = 1

24 exact rational values of the infinite-horizon Bayes value V(lambda) = inf_pi (E[tau] + lambda*PoE) for fixed-confidence best-arm identification with two Bernoulli arms under the uniform prior, lambda in {4,5,6,7,8,10,12,14,16,18,19,20,21,22,24,49/2,25,26,27,55/2,28,29,30,31}, each certified by a collapsing horizon bracket lowerV N lambda = upperV N lambda (free-exit relaxation = forced-stop policy value), e.g. V(6) = 3, V(20) = 23/3, V(49/2) = 133/15, V(55/2) = 1007/105, V(31) = 205793/19800

The exact Bayes-optimal (E[tau], PoE) frontier for two Bernoulli arms under the uniform prior on delta in [3337/13860, 1/2]: four linear pieces, E[tau] = 3 - 6*delta on [1/3,1/2], 23/3 - 20*delta on [4/15,1/3], 133/15 - (49/2)*delta on [76/315,4/15] and 1007/105 - (55/2)*delta on [3337/13860,76/315], with certified breakpoints lambda = 6, 20, 49/2, 55/2 and the check that consecutive vertices lie on the common supporting line at each breakpoint

The five frontier vertices (E[tau], PoE) = (0, 1/2), (1, 1/3), (7/3, 4/15), (133/45, 76/315), (1069/360, 3337/13860), each obtained by exact forward evaluation of the optimal policy at a horizon where the bracket has collapsed (so the horizon-N policy is optimal for the untruncated problem), together with the Lagrangian identity E[tau] + lambda*PoE = V(lambda) at three of them

Negative controls: V(20) is strictly between 7 and 8 (the lower half witnessed by the free-exit RELAXATION, so no policy whatsoever attains 7); neither the second nor the third linear piece extends past its certified breakpoint (V(21) < 1 + 21/3 and V(8) < 7/3 + 4*8/15); the bracket does not collapse automatically (at N=12, lambda=32 it is [14503/1575, 5733341/540540]); lowerV <= upperV always; lowerV increases and upperV decreases in the horizon; and err is a genuine risk (0 <= err <= 1/2 at every state of depth <= 8, and = 1/2 at every exchangeable state a1 = a2, b1 = b2 -- the proved direction only; the converse is FALSE, 12 of the 27 states of depth <= 8 with err = 1/2 are not exchangeable, namely those with a1 = b1 and a2 = b2) [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was = 1/2 exactly on the exchangeable states]

The source's Definition 2 and Lemma 1 (arXiv:2402.10429v2, arXiv PDF p. 4) in this model, exactly: for k = 2 Bernoulli arms with independent Uniform[0,1] priors, L_12(H) = L_21(H) = 1 so L(H) = 2, and L(H, Delta) = P[|mu_1 - mu_2| <= Delta]/Delta = 2 - Delta for every Delta in (0,1], so the volume lemma holds with an exact linear correction and its interval conclusion L(H,Delta) in (L/2, 2L) holds on the whole range rather than below a threshold

The Bernoulli analogue of the source's Theorem 2 (arXiv PDF p. 5): for delta in (0, 1/2) and any FREQUENTIST delta-correct algorithm, E_{mu ~ H}[tau] = +infinity under the uniform prior on [0,1]^2, by the transportation lemma (their Lemma 5, p. 6) plus d(a,b) <= (a-b)^2/(b(1-b)) <= (16/3)(a-b)^2 on [1/4,3/4]^2 and the divergence of the double integral of (mu_1-mu_2)^{-2}

E[tau*]*delta along the exact frontier is strictly increasing as delta DECREASES along it (i.e. from vertex A to vertex E; it is strictly decreasing in delta) (0 < 1/3 < 28/45 < 1444/2025 < 3567253/4989600, with the five vertices strictly ordered in both coordinates so none dominates another), so on delta in [0.2408, 1/2] the Bayes optimum is not of the constant-E[tau]*delta shape that Theorem 4 of arXiv:2402.10429v2 gives; and the printed constants of Theorem 4 (N_V = L^2 sigma_min^2 ln2/(16 e^4 delta)) and Theorem 6 (C sigma_max^2 (L^2/delta) log(L/delta), C = 320(pi^2/3+1) = 1372.7578), formally substituted with sigma^2 = 1/4 and L(H) = 2, sit about 420-900x below (that ratio is under the sigma_min^2 := variance reading of Theorem 4, the reading the source's own proof establishes; under the literal sigma_min^2 = (variance)^2 reading the ratios are 1680-3604x) and about 4100-7400x above (4065x exactly at the last vertex) the exact optimum at delta = 1/3, 4/15, 3337/13860 [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was strictly increasing over the certified range ... sit about 420-900x below and 4400-7400x above]

families.paper_title: The exact Bayes-optimal sample-size / error frontier of fixed-confidence best-arm identification for two Bernoulli arms under the uniform prior, on $\delta \in [3337/13860,\ 1/2]$
families.paper_abstract: Jang, Komiyama and Yamazaki (arXiv:2402.10429) study fixed-confidence best-arm identification when the bandit instance is drawn from a known prior $H$: minimise the expected number of samples $\E_{\mu\sim H}[\tau]$ subject to the Bayesian error constraint $\PoE(\pi;H) \le \delta$.  For Gaussian arms with Gaussian priors they prove a lower bound of order $L(H)^2/\delta$ and an upper bound of order $(L(H)^2/\delta)\log(L(H)/\delta)$, and list the extension from Gaussian instances to general exponential families as future work.  We compute the object those bounds bracket, exactly, in the smallest non-Gaussian instance: two Bernoulli arms whose means are independent and uniform on $[0,1]$.  For the Lagrangian value $V(\lambda) = \inf_\pi(\E[\tau] + \lambda\,\PoE)$ we certify $24$ exact rational values, at $24$ multipliers $\lambda$ between $4$ and $31$, each for the infinite-horizon problem, by a collapsing horizon bracket: forced stopping at depth $N$ is an admissible policy and bounds $V$ from above, free exit at depth $N$ relaxes every policy and bounds it from below, and when the two rational values coincide the untruncated value is pinned. The optimal frontier $\delta \mapsto \min\{\E[\tau] : \PoE \le \delta\}$ is then exact on $\delta \in [3337/13860, 1/2]$: four linear pieces $3 - 6\delta$, $23/3 - 20\delta$, $133/15 - \tfrac{49}{2}\delta$, $1007/105 - \tfrac{55}{2}\delta$ with breakpoints $\lambda = 6, 20, 49/2, 55/2$ and vertices $(0,\tfrac12)$, $(1,\tfrac13)$, $(\tfrac73,\tfrac4{15})$, $(\tfrac{133}{45},\tfrac{76}{315})$, $(\tfrac{1069}{360},\tfrac{3337}{13860})$, the last three obtained by exact forward evaluation of the optimal policy.  Along this range the product $\E[\tau^\ast]\cdot\delta$ increases strictly as $\delta$ decreases, and the source's Theorem~2 (every frequentist $\delta$-correct algorithm has infinite Bayesian expected sample size) transfers to the Bernoulli model for $\delta < 1/2$, by a proof on paper.  Every rational computation behind these statements is checked in Lean~4 without Mathlib: all $25$ theorems are closed by \lean{native\_decide}, each depending on \lean{propext}, \lean{Classical.choice}, \lean{Quot.sound} and its own per-theorem \lean{native\_decide} axiom, and on nothing else.  The passage from those computations to statements about the untruncated problem, and the integrals that evaluate the source's own quantities in this model, are proved on paper and are labelled as such throughout.

families.title: Worst-case demand-aware weak direct throughput on three nodes: theta*(3) = 13/15 exactly, attained by the uniform demand matrix -- strictly inside the source's printed bracket [17/20, 18/20], with the improved rounding lemma that settles its odd-n conjecture
families.description: Founded 2026-09-07 from arXiv:2605.04699v1 (cs.NI), Bentert–Avin–Schmid, *A Separation Between Optimal Demand-Oblivious and Demand-Aware Network Throughput*. This is the repository's first cs.NI family.

statements.label: Lower bound: every doubly stochastic 3 x 3 demand matrix is a yes-instance of Demand-Aware Weak Direct Throughput at kappa = 13/15, improving the source's Theorem 6 value (7n-4)/(8n-4) = 17/20 at n = 3
Upper bound: the uniform demand matrix (1/3)J has weak direct throughput exactly 13/15 -- no kappa > 13/15 is achievable for it, and 13/15 is attained by the circulant 2J - P
Compute-first gate: the source's own odd-n witness M_3 has weak direct throughput exactly 9/10 = (7n-3)/(8n-4), reproducing the printed cell of its Table 1
The source's printed upper bound (7n-3)/(8n-4) is not tight at n = 3: an explicit doubly stochastic matrix refuses every kappa > 13/15 < 9/10
Negative controls: a too-large claim (kappa = 7/8 is refused by an explicit doubly stochastic matrix) and a non-vacuity control (the hypothesis class is inhabited and Yes is not identically true)

Improved rounding lemma at n = 3: for a 3 x 3 real matrix with entries in [0,1] whose integer row sums r_i and column sums c_j are all at most 2, some 0/1 matrix with those margins picks up at least X - 2 of the mass, where X = r_0+r_1+r_2 (the source's Lemma 1 gives only X^2/9)

Exact value: theta*(3) = 13/15 -- 13/15 is achievable for every doubly stochastic 3 x 3 demand matrix and no larger kappa is, so the worst-case demand-aware weak direct throughput on three nodes is exactly 13/15, strictly inside the source's printed bracket [17/20, 18/20]

PROSE: for every odd n, theta*(n) >= (7n^2-4n+1)/(8n^2-4n) = (7n-4)/(8n-4) + 1/(4n(2n-1)), which settles the source's conjecture that its lower bound can be improved for all odd n >= 3 (and re-derives the source's bound, tight, for even n)

MEASUREMENT: a 212-line Lean file with no search in it went from killed at 21 minutes / 16 GB RSS to 18 seconds by (a) replacing every bare linarith by linarith only, and decisively (b) keeping truncated NATURAL SUBTRACTION out of the context of omega calls -- introduce the difference as a variable with an addition equation instead

families.paper_title: The worst-case demand-aware weak direct throughput\\ on three nodes is exactly $13/15$
families.paper_abstract: Bentert, Avin and Schmid (arXiv:2605.04699) introduce the \emph{weak direct throughput} of a network with respect to a demand matrix and study its demand-aware, worst-case value $\theta^*(n)$ over doubly stochastic $n\times n$ matrices when the network is a directed $(2n-1)$-regular multigraph chosen after the matrix is known. Their Observation~4 reduces the quantity to a finite optimisation, $\theta^*(n)=\frac{1}{(2n-1)n}\min_{M}\max_{N}\sum_{i,j}\min\{(2n-1)M_{ij},N_{ij}\}$, the maximum over non-negative integer matrices with all line sums $2n-1$; their Table~1 prints $\frac{7n-4}{8n-4}\le\theta^*(n)\le\frac{7n-3}{8n-4}$ for odd $n$, states that the bounds are tight for $n=1$ and all even $n$, and conjectures that the lower bound can be improved for odd $n\ge3$.  We show that $\theta^*(3)=13/15$ exactly.  The value is attained by the uniform matrix $\frac13J$, whose best network is the circulant $2J-P$; it lies strictly inside the printed bracket $[17/20,18/20]=[51/60,54/60]$ (it is $52/60$), so at $n=3$ the printed upper bound is not tight either, and the source's own witness matrix $M_3$ has weak direct throughput exactly $9/10$.  The lower bound rests on a rounding lemma sharper than the source's Lemma~1 at $n=3$: a $3\times3$ matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ and integer margins at most $2$ can be rounded to a $0/1$ matrix with the same margins capturing at least $X-2$ of its mass $X$, against the source's $X^2/9$; the two differ exactly at $X\in\{4,5\}$, where the source's bound is weakest.  The same replacement --- Cauchy--Schwarz per row instead of globally, together with the integrality of the row sums of the fractional part --- gives, on paper, $\theta^*(n)\ge\frac{7n^2-4n+1}{8n^2-4n}$ for every odd $n$, exactly $\frac{1}{4n(2n-1)}$ above the source's bound, which settles the conjecture for all odd $n$; the general-$n$ statement is not formalised.  Every theorem stated here about $n=3$ is kernel-checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib, proved by finite case analysis and linear arithmetic, without native evaluation.

families.paper_title: A $2$-adic obstruction for Bessel quadrature formulas\\ with nodes in $\Qi\cap S^{1}$
families.paper_abstract: Let $w(z)=-e^{-2/z}/(4\pi i)$ be the weight on the unit circle for which the Bessel polynomials are orthogonal, and let $\Circ=\Qi\cap S^{1}$ be the set of rational points of the circle.  Matsumura asks, in part~(2) of his Problem~1.2, whether for a given $r$ there is a quadrature formula of degree $r+1$ for $w$ whose $r+1$ nodes all lie in $\Circ$.  He answers \emph{no} for $r=1$ and for $r=2$, the latter by exhibiting a genus-one curve of Mordell--Weil rank $0$, and writes: ``It seems hard to extend the proof of Theorem~1.4 to $r\ge3$.'' We settle $r=3$, in the negative, and the nodes are not assumed distinct.  The proof is a count at the prime $1+i$ of $\Zi$.  Writing each node as $\zeta/\bar\zeta$ with $\zeta=n+mi$ primitive and clearing denominators turns the degree-$4$ moment criterion into the single equation $F(\zeta)=0$ in $\Zi$, where \[ F=128\textstyle\prod n_j-32\prod m_j+13\prod\zeta_j +(8-10i)\prod(n_j-m_j)+(8+10i)\prod(n_j+m_j), \] and the valuation of $F$ at $1+i$ equals the number of $j$ with $n_j,m_j$ both odd, hence is at most $4$; so $F\ne0$.  The same count re-proves the two published cases $r=1$ and $r=2$ with no elliptic curve and no computer algebra.  We also record an explicit degree-$4$ formula with four distinct \emph{rational} nodes, so that the obstruction is caused by the circle condition and not by the degree, and we measure, outside the formal development, exactly how far the obstruction reaches: it is confined to $r\le3$.  Every theorem and proposition below has been formally verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}, with the four exceptions that the closing section lists; no statement rests on an exhaustive search.

families.paper_title: Homology profiles and graded Betti tables\\ of squarefree monomial ideals in five and six variables
families.paper_abstract: Ripke and Yoon recently determined that exactly $134$ distinct graded Betti tables occur among the $208$ nonzero proper squarefree monomial ideals in five variables up to relabelling of the variables, and closed their paper with several questions, two of which we answer here: whether those $134$ types are classified by the homology profiles of induced subcomplexes, and how many distinct graded Betti tables occur for general $n$.  The homology profile --- the multiset, for each cardinality $j$, of the reduced homology dimension vectors of the induced subcomplexes on $j$ vertices --- is a strictly finer invariant than the graded Betti table and a strictly coarser one than the relabelling class: in five variables the $208$ classes realize exactly $189$ profiles and $134$ tables, so of the $74$ coincidences of Betti tables the loss of positional information named by Ripke and Yoon accounts for $19$ and the summation for the remaining $55$.  Exactly $97$ of the $134$ table types come from a single profile.  In six variables, the first open cell of the enumerative question, the $16\,351$ nonzero proper classes realize exactly $8233$ homology profiles and exactly $1604$ graded Betti tables, over every field; the enumeration is certified by orbit counting against the Dedekind number $M(6)=7\,828\,354$, itself computed rather than quoted.  Every count stated here is machine-checked in Lean~4, with Hochster's formula quoted from the literature and one further step, named where it is used, argued rather than formalized.

families.title: The B-Free Graphs Conjecture: the finite exclusion of arXiv:2608.22537, certified and stripped of its corona hypotheses
families.description: Litjens, Polak and Sivaraman call a graph `G` **sum-perfect** when every induced subgraph `H` satisfies `α(H) + ω(H) ≥ n(H)`, and characterise the class by twenty-seven forbidden induced subgraphs (*Sum-perfect graphs*, arXiv:1710.07546, Discrete Applied Mathematics **259** (2019) 232–239). Twenty-four of the twenty-seven — their `H₂, …, H₂₅` — are
families.paper_abstract: Litjens, Polak and Sivaraman call a graph sum-perfect when every induced subgraph $H$ satisfies $\al(H)+\om(H)\ge |V(H)|$, characterise the class by twenty-seven forbidden induced subgraphs, and conjecture that dropping three of them --- leaving the class $\B$ of the twelve six-vertex bipartite graphs with a perfect matching together with their twelve complements --- gives $\al(G)+\om(G)\ge |V(G)|-1$ for every $\B$-free $G$.  A recent preprint of Frijio reduces the conjecture, by structural arguments, to a finite exclusion: twelve parameter triples $(n,a,w)$ with $n=a+w+2\le 14$, each of which must be shown not to occur. That exclusion is the whole computational core of the proof, and the evidence offered for it is a floating-point mixed-integer model and a bespoke solver that print \texttt{UNSAT} without a certificate.  We prove the exclusion from strictly weaker hypotheses.  For each of the twelve triples we show that no $\B$-free graph on $n$ vertices has $\al=a$ and $\om=w$, using none of the corona constraints that the reduction supplies and covering both values of the intersection parameter $t=|S\cap K|$, where the source's table forms only twenty-one of the twenty-four cases.  That the corona constraints are dispensable was measured, not assumed: each remaining hypothesis is shown load-bearing by an explicit seven-vertex graph.  We also certify the encoding step the source reports but does not check --- on all $2^{15}$ labelled six-vertex graphs, the inequality form of $\B$-membership agrees with ``bipartite with a perfect matching or the complement of one'' --- and refine the resulting count $4400$ into $2200+2200$ with the two halves disjoint.  Finally we record the conjecture itself as a consequence of the twelve exclusions and one named hypothesis, the structural reduction, which is stated but not proved here.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4; the twenty-four infeasibility claims are discharged against stored LRAT certificates by a checker that is itself verified in Lean, so no property of the SAT solver is assumed.

families.description: Aygul Azatovna Galimova, *Independent Trivariate Bicycle Codes* ([arXiv:2603.17703](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17703), v1, announced 2026-03-18, quant-ph primary with a cs.IT cross-list) fixes a torus

statements.label: The model is checked, not assumed: CSS orthogonality H_X H_Z^T = 0 entrywise on all eight codes of the source's Table 1; the literal check-matrix k = 2N - rank H_X - rank H_Z agrees with 2 dim F_2[G]/(A,B), and rank H_X = rank H_Z, on all 196196 normalised weight-3 pairs of eight tori; and normalising both A and B to contain the identity preserves the whole k-value set, against the full unnormalised sweep on five tori (396202 pairs)

The exhaustive weight-3 census of 30 finite abelian groups up to N = 56: for each group the exact set of attained k > 0, over all 9959476 normalised pairs (standing for 2770442265 unnormalised ones), with the exponent column checked against lcm(dims)

On all 30 swept groups: k = 6 occurs only where 7 | exp G and k = 4 only where 3 | exp G, and k = 2 occurs nowhere; both converses are FALSE, on exactly one group each -- Z_2 x Z_2 x Z_2 x Z_7 is seven-divisible and attains no k = 6 while Z_2 x Z_4 x Z_7 and Z_8 x Z_7 of the same order 56 do, and Z_2 x Z_2 x Z_6 is three-divisible and attains no k = 4. The finite core of the general abelian argument, replacing Artinian structure theory by enumeration: over all commutative unital associative F_2-algebra structures on F_2^d with a distinguished basis starting at 1 (1, 4 and 64 of them for d = 1, 2, 3), those admitting no F_2-algebra homomorphism to F_2 number 0, 1 and 8; the one at d = 2 has every element other than 0 and 1 of multiplicative order exactly 3, and each of the eight at d = 3 has order exactly 7

For every finite abelian G and all A, B in F_2[G] with A of odd weight, the bicycle code H_X = (A | B), H_Z = (B^T | A^T) satisfies: k != 2; k = 4 forces 3 | exp G; and k = 6 forces 7 | exp G. The last is the sentence arXiv:2603.17703v1 prints as unproven, for every abelian G and every odd weight rather than weight-3 pairs on a 3-torus

families.paper_title: Odd weight and the dimension of an abelian bicycle code: $k\neq 2$, $k=4$ forces $3\mid\Exp G$, and $k=6$ forces $7\mid\Exp G$
families.paper_abstract: For a finite abelian group $G$ and $A,B\in\FF_2[G]$, the bicycle code of the pair $(A,B)$ is the CSS code on $n=2|G|$ qubits with check matrices $H_X=(A\;B)$ and $H_Z=(B^{\mathsf T}\;A^{\mathsf T})$.  Surveying more than $170$ three-factor tori with weight-$3$ polynomials, Galimova observed that $k=6$ occurs only when $7$ divides the exponent of the group, gave a partial explanation, and wrote that ``what remains unproven is whether other algebraic mechanisms \dots\ can also yield $k=6$''.  We prove the statement, in a form that mentions neither weight $3$, nor the number of cyclic factors, nor any bound on $|G|$: if one of $A,B$ has odd weight, then $k\neq 2$, $k=4$ forces $3\mid\Exp G$, and $k=6$ forces $7\mid\Exp G$.  The first of the three was reported by Lin and Pryadko as an unexplained empirical absence, and is proved here. The mechanism is the parity of the weight. Odd weight makes the augmentation of $A$ equal to $1$, so the quotient algebra $Q=\FF_2[G]/(A,B)$, whose dimension is $k/2$, admits no $\FF_2$-algebra homomorphism to $\FF_2$; and a commutative unital $\FF_2$-algebra with no such homomorphism is never $1$-dimensional, is $\FF_4$ in dimension $2$ and $\FF_8$ in dimension $3$ --- a statement about $1$, $4$ and $64$ multiplication tables that we settle by enumeration in place of Artinian structure theory.  Reading the conclusion back through the images of $G$ produces an element of order $3$ or $7$.  For cyclic $G$ the same three conclusions are obtained along a second, independent route, over the published dimension formula $k=2\deg\gcd(a,b,x^{\ell}-1)$ of Panteleev and Kalachev, and are machine-checked for all $\ell$ at once.  We accompany the theorem with an exhaustive census of weight-$3$ pairs over $30$ presentations of abelian groups of order at most $56$ --- $9\,959\,476$ normalised pairs standing for $2\,770\,442\,265$ unnormalised ones --- which shows that neither divisibility implication reverses: $\ZZ_2^3\times\ZZ_7$ is seven-divisible and carries no $k=6$ weight-$3$ code, while $\ZZ_2\times\ZZ_4\times\ZZ_7$ and $\ZZ_8\times\ZZ_7$ of the same order do, and $\ZZ_2^2\times\ZZ_6$ is three-divisible and carries no $k=4$ one.

families.paper_title: Centrally symmetric Bier spheres on twelve vertices,\\ and the Bokowski--Ewald--Kleinschmidt sphere
families.paper_abstract: The Bier sphere of a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on $[n]$ is the deleted join of $\Delta$ with its combinatorial Alexander dual, a simplicial $(n-2)$-sphere on at most $2n$ vertices. Holleben and Yang recently gave a purely combinatorial criterion on $\Delta$ forcing $\Bier(\Delta)$ to be centrally symmetric, polytopal, and yet not realizable by any centrally symmetric polytope, and exhibited one complex on $[6]$ satisfying it.  We classify the whole case: the complexes on $[6]$ whose Bier spheres are the centrally symmetric neighborly $4$-spheres on $12$ vertices are exactly $1024$ in number, they form $13$ orbits under relabelling and Alexander duality, exactly $692$ of them --- exactly $7$ of the orbits --- satisfy the criterion, and the example of Holleben and Yang, read literally, is a family of $64$ complexes realizing precisely those $7$ orbits.  All $13$ orbits are polytopal, from explicit integer coordinates, so the $7$ are polytopal but not centrally symmetric polytopal and the remaining $6$ are the cases the criterion does not decide.  We also settle the status of the sphere $\Cx$ of Bokowski, Ewald and Kleinschmidt, previously --- up to two-point suspension --- the only recorded simplicial sphere that is polytopal but not centrally symmetric polytopal: $\Cx$ is not the Bier sphere of any simplicial complex.  Every statement this paper proves is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Where the substitution method stops on the short product over $\Ftwo$
families.paper_abstract: Let $T_N$ be the structure tensor of the short (truncated) product $\Ftwo[x]/x^N$, whose rank $\Rk(T_N)$ is the number of coefficient multiplications a bilinear algorithm for that product needs.  The value $\Rk(T_5)$ sits at the boundary of what exhaustive search reaches: the bound $\Rk(T_5)\ge 10$ is classical, the matching $\Rk(T_5)\ge 11$ rests on a single covering-sets computation reported in a summary table, and no independent verification of it exists.  We show that the substitution method, in the form of the explicit one-level ladder it yields for $T_{N+1}$, provably cannot supply the missing unit.  Restated on subspaces of matrices, the ladder reduces $\Rk(T_5)\ge 3+m$ to the minimum $m$ of a rank functional over a family of $4$-dimensional subspaces of $\Ftwo^{4\times 4}$ indexed by $4096$ parameter triples.  We prove that this minimum is \emph{exactly} $7$: one member is contained in the span of seven rank-one matrices -- and exactly seven rank-one matrices lie in that span, so the witness is complete -- while no member at all is contained in the span of six, a statement certified by exhausting $103{,}643{,}136$ candidate subspaces.  Since the slice space of $T_4$ needs eight, the comparison is exact and the ladder yields $\Rk(T_5)\ge 10$, never $11$.  The same machinery produces certificates, checked by the Lean~4 kernel, for the exact values $\Rk(T_3)=5$ and $\Rk(T_4)=8$ in both directions, and for the exact symmetric ranks of $\Ftwo[x]/x^N$ for $N\le 5$ and of $\Ftwo[x]/(x^N-1)$ for $N\in\{3,5,6\}$, together with $\Rsym(T_6)\in\{13,14\}$.  Those values are published; the certificates are new.

families.paper_title: Maximal-determinant records at orders 51, 107 and 115,\\ and an adjugate obstruction at order 7
families.paper_abstract: Let $D(n)$ be the largest $|\det X|$ over $X\in\{-1,+1\}^{n\times n}$ and $a(n)$ the largest $|\det M|$ over $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ (OEIS A003432).  Butbaia et al.\ recently announced new record lower bounds for $D(n)$ at $n=51,107,115$, publishing for each order two $\pm1$ seed strings, a block layout in two circulants, and the value $|\det X|/2^{\,n-1}$.  We turn those three announcements into theorems.  The matrices are rebuilt from the published seeds and nothing else; the determinants are then obtained from a triangular certificate --- a lower triangular $L$ with $L\cdot(X\text{ row-permuted})$ upper triangular --- which replaces the $n!$-term Leibniz sum by about $n^3/2$ integer multiply--adds, so that a $115\times115$ determinant with a $119$-digit value is confirmed in $29$ seconds.  A classical bordering identity, proved here for every $n$ and every matrix, carries the three values to $a(50),a(106),a(114)$, three orders that A003432's b-file does not reach.  We also record the complete multiset of entries of $XX^{\mathsf T}$ for each record matrix, data the announcement does not print, and observe that exactly one of the three constructions is normal.  In a second part we prove that a matrix with constant row sum $k$ satisfies $k\,g=n\det M$, where $g$ is the grand sum of $\adj M$; the coprimality hypothesis of a conjecture of Baghel, Ravsky and Segal-Halevi then forces $\det M\mid k$, which shows that conjecture can never certify a maximal determinant at an order $4t-1$ carrying a Hadamard matrix of order $4t$.  At $n=7$, where a determinant of $\pm32$ classically forces row sum $4$, the grand sum is then always $\pm56$ and never coprime to $32$.  Every numbered statement below is formally verified in Lean~4.

families.title: When is the Asgarli-Ghioca-Yip power-residue curve blocking? The r = 4 belief of Remark 6.4 of arXiv:2208.13299 is false at q = 41, its r = 5 belief is true, and the exact range of validity of both Theorem 6.3 and Corollary 2.2 for r <= 5
families.description: Founded 2026-09-02/03. A **correction** family: a belief stated in a remark of a published paper is false at exactly one prime power, and the same machinery then determines the exact range of validity of the theorem the belief is about, with no residual gap.

statements.label: Corollary 2.2's conclusion at `(q,m)` implies that the curve `−(ky+z)x^m + zy^m + kyz^m = 0` of Theorem 6.3 of arXiv:2208.13299v2 is blocking, for every `k` and with no hypothesis on `m` — the source's Proposition 6.1 with `q > r⁴` replaced by the statement it is used to reach

At `q = 41`, `r = 4`, `k = 2` the `F_41`-line `x + y + z = 0` carries none of the 104 `F_41`-points of the curve of Theorem 6.3, so that curve is not blocking — although 41 is prime, `41 ≥ 37`, `41 ≡ 1 (mod 4)` and `41 ∤ 15`
The `r = 4` belief of Remark 6.4 of arXiv:2208.13299v2, "We believe that the conclusion holds for all `q ≥ 37`", is false: its consequence for prime `q` fails at `q = 41`

The source's own datum reproduced: at `q = 29`, `r = 4`, `k = 1` (admissible, `−1` not a fourth power mod 29) the line `x + y + z = 0` misses the curve, so the conclusion of Theorem 6.3 fails at `q = 29`

Controls: `[1:1:1]` lies on the curve for every `q, m, k`; the line `x + y + 2z = 0` does meet `C_2` over `F_41`; exactly 30 of the 41 values of `k` are admissible at `q = 41`; the line `x + y + z = 0` does *not* miss the curve for the admissible `k = 11`; and none of `x + y + cz = 0`, `c ∈ {1,4,10}`, misses the curve at the source's positive data point `q = 37`

The coset reduction: `PowerPairs q m` (the conclusion of Corollary 2.2 of the source, in its equivalent `m`-th-root-of-unity form) follows from a covering check on `r` coset representatives plus the `r²` representative pairs — `~q·r·m` steps instead of `~q³`
Corollary 2.2 of arXiv:2208.13299v2 itself fails at `q = 41`, `r = 4`: there are no fourth powers `y, z` of `F_41^*` with `y + z = −1`

The positive half of the classification: at every prime `q ≡ 1 (mod 4)` with `37 ≤ q ≤ 256` other than `q = 41`, the curve of Theorem 6.3 at `r = 4` is blocking for every `k` — so `q = 41` is the only prime counterexample to the belief, and there is no residual gap, `q > 256` being Theorem 6.3 itself
Control above the theorem's own threshold: at `q = 257, 269, 277, 281, 293` — all `> 4⁴ = 256`, where Theorem 6.3 is proved — the model also says the curve is blocking for every `k`

At `q = 41`, `r = 4` the curve of Theorem 6.3 is blocking for **no** admissible `k`: one of the three lines `x + y + z = 0`, `x + y + 4z = 0`, `x + y + 10z = 0` misses it for each of the 30 admissible values

The **other** belief of Remark 6.4 is true: at `r = 5`, for every prime `q ≡ 1 (mod 5)` with `131 ≤ q ≤ 625` the curve of Theorem 6.3 is blocking for every `k`; above `625` the conclusion is Theorem 6.3 itself, so the belief "the conclusion holds for all `q ≥ 131`" holds over its whole declared range

The exact range of validity of Corollary 2.2 of arXiv:2208.13299v2 over **all** prime powers, for `r = 2, 3, 4, 5`: it fails exactly at `q = 3, 5` (`r=2`); `q = 4, 7, 13, 16 (referee 2026-09-03: P(4,3) fails -- mu_1 = {1}, b + c = 1 fails at b = c = 1; q = 4 was omitted)` (`r=3`); `q = 5, 9, 13, 17, 25, 29, 41` (`r=4`); `q = 11, 16, 31, 41, 61, 71, 101` (`r=5`) — complete, because each search range passes `r⁴`, above which the source proves it

families.paper_title: When is the Asgarli--Ghioca--Yip curve blocking? A sharpness belief that fails at $q=41$, and the exact ranges for $r\le 5$
families.paper_abstract: Let $r\ge 2$, let $q\equiv 1\pmod r$ be a prime power with $p\nmid(r^{2}-1)$, put $m=(q-1)/r$, and let $k\in\Fs$ be such that $-k$ is not an $r$-th power.  Asgarli, Ghioca and Yip proved that the plane curve $-(ky+z)x^{m}+zy^{m}+kyz^{m}=0$ is smooth and nontrivially blocking as soon as $q>r^{4}$, and remarked on the sharpness of that hypothesis: for $r=4$ they wrote that they believe the conclusion holds for all $q\ge 37$, and for $r=5$ that they believe it holds for all $q\ge 131$.  We show that the first belief is false and the second is true.  At $q=41$ --- a prime with $41\ge 37$, $41\equiv 1\pmod 4$ and $41\nmid 15$ --- the line $x+y+z=0$ carries none of the $104$ points of the curve with $k=2$, and in fact the curve is blocking for no admissible $k$; $q=41$ is the only prime power of the range $37\le q\le 256$ admitted by the remaining hypotheses where this happens, so the sharp threshold at $r=4$ is $q\ge 49$ and not $q\ge 37$.  At $r=5$ the conclusion does hold at every admitted prime power of the declared range $131\le q\le 625$, and indeed already from $q\ge 121$.  The mechanism is classical: the hypothesis $q>r^{4}$ enters the proof only through a corollary asserting that $-1$ is a sum $by+cz$ of prescribed power residues, and the failure of that corollary is the vanishing of a cyclotomic number; for $r=4$ the classical formula $16(0,0)_{4}=p-11-6a$ leaves exactly $p=17$ and $p=41$.  We determine the exact set of prime powers where the corollary fails for every $r\le 5$.  Every theorem and proposition below is machine-checked in Lean~4, with the scope limitation recorded in Remark~\ref{rem:scope}; the computations outside that development are labelled where they appear.

families.title: The discrete Colonel Blotto game on the band Dziubinski leaves open
families.description: Marcin Dziubiński, *Non-symmetric discrete Colonel Blotto game*, **arXiv:2511.10827** (econ.TH; v1, 13 November 2025; the only version — checked against the arXiv API on 2026-09-07). Read from the arXiv e-print source `blotto13112025.tex`.
families.paper_title: Exact values of the discrete Colonel Blotto game on the band Dziubi\'nski leaves open
families.paper_abstract: In the discrete Colonel Blotto game $\Bl(A,B;K)$ two players distribute $A>B\ge 1$ indivisible units over $K$ battlefields, and the stronger player is paid the average, over the battlefields, of the sign of his surplus.  Dziubi\'nski (arXiv:2511.10827) solves the game for $K\ge 3$ when $2(\ce{A/K}-1)\le B\le K\fl{A/K}$ (with six excepted cells at $K=3$) and when $B\le\fl{A/K}$, and marks the intermediate band $\fl{A/K}+1\le B\le 2(\ce{A/K}-1)-1$ as open, for the value and for the optimal strategies alike.  We determine the value at fifty-seven cells of that band: every cell with $K=3$ and $A\le 20$ (thirty-six values), and twenty-one cells with $K\in\{4,5,6\}$.  Along the diagonal $B=(A-1)/2$, $K=3$, the value is $5/9$ for every odd $A$ with $7\le A\le 41$, and the upper bound $5/9$ holds for every odd $A\ge 5$ by a uniform argument.  We also determine the six excepted cells.  Five of the values agree with numbers that appear in a commented-out appendix of the arXiv \LaTeX{} source of the paper (they are not in its compiled text); the sixth corrects that appendix: $\val(19,15;3)=47/225$, not $8211/103788$, and the appendix's own printed strategies already exclude the printed number.  Every value is established by an explicit pair of optimal mixed strategies with integer weights, checked against every pure strategy of the opponent; all certificates are verified in Lean~4, and none of the results depends on a minimax theorem.  Hart's bounds for the non-symmetric discrete game determine none of these cells.

families.paper_title: Power sums of the zeros of the BLZ polynomials: a proof of the second-power-sum conjecture of Masoero and Ruzza, a closed formula for the third power sum, and the membership half of their Question~3.7
families.paper_abstract: For a partition $\lambda$ and a parameter $\beta$, Masoero and Ruzza (arXiv:2605.24563v2) attach to the Laguerre Wronskian $\Phi^{(\beta)}_{\lambda,\lambda'}$ a monic polynomial $\mathcal P^{(\beta)}_\lambda$ of degree $|\lambda|$ --- the BLZ polynomial whose zeros $z_i^{(\beta)}(\lambda)$ are the poles of the monster potentials of Bazhanov--Lukyanov--Zamolodchikov at the free-fermion point --- and prove that the sum of the zeros is the shifted symmetric function $2\p4-2\p2^2+3\beta\p3+\beta^2\p2+\tfrac12\p2$ of $\lambda$ (their Proposition~3.6).  For the sum of the squares they conjecture a degree-six shifted symmetric expression (their Eq.~(3.8)), ``verified for all $\lambda\in\mathbb P$ with $|\lambda|\le15$'', and they ask (Question~3.7) whether the $k$-th power sum lies in $\Lam[\beta]_{\le 2k+2}$ for every $k$.  We prove the conjecture for every partition and every $\beta$.  In the reversed Wronskian matrix the coefficient polynomial $G_p(X)=(-1)^p\,\ff{(X/2)}{p}\,\ff{(X/2-\beta)}{p}/p!$ attached to a column is literally the same for the two kinds of Laguerre column, so the determinant is alternating in the nodes, the Vandermonde divides it, and the $k$-th subleading coefficient is a symmetric polynomial in the nodes of total degree at most $2k$. This places the difference of the two sides of Eq.~(3.8) in $\Lam[\beta]_{\le16}$, a space pinned down by the partitions of size at most $16$: a rank-$231$ certificate and the exact verification of Eq.~(3.8), as an identity of polynomials in $\beta$, for every partition of size at most $16$ finish the proof.  The proof itself is on paper; what is machine-checked is exactly its two finite ingredients --- the rank certificate and Eq.~(3.8) for $|\lambda|\le16$ --- together with Eq.~(3.8) for $|\lambda|\le17$ and, at five values of $\beta$ that decide it, for $|\lambda|\le21$.  The same lemma settles, again on paper, the membership half of Question~3.7, $\sum_i (z_i^{(\beta)})^k\in\Lam[\beta]_{\le 8k}$ for every $k$; only the sharp bound $2k+2$ remains open.  We also give a closed formula for the third power sum, an element of $\Lam[\beta]_{\le8}$ that the source does not have, found by exact fitting on $|\lambda|\le10$, verified on all $369$ partitions of size $11$ to $14$ before being written down, and machine-checked for $|\lambda|\le14$; and we record that the top-degree layer of the $k$-th power sum is row $2k$ of OEIS A088617 reversed, with the Catalan number $C_{2k}$ in front of $\p{2k+2}$, for $k=0,1,2,3$.
