families.paper_title: How far a conic of $\PG(2,q)$ extends to an $(n,3)$-arc: the exact maximum for $q=3,5,7,11,13,17,19$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\Oc$ be a conic of $\PG(2,q)$, $q$ odd, and let $m(q)$ be the largest $m$ for which some $m$ points off $\Oc$ can be added to it so that the union is a $(q+1+m,3)$-arc, i.e.\ meets every line in at most three points.  D\"onmez, Akp{\i}nar and Pelen (arXiv:2608.18192) ask for $m(q)$ as a function of $q$; they prove $m(q)\ge5$ for every odd prime power $q$ and $m(q)\ge6$ for every odd prime power $q\ge11$, and report from the literature that $m(7)=m(9)=7$ and from a randomized search that $m(13)\ge8$.  We determine \[ m(3)=5,\quad m(5)=5,\quad m(7)=7,\quad m(11)=7,\quad m(13)=8,\quad m(17)=9,\quad m(19)=10 . \] Each value is a pair of machine-checked statements: an explicit witness set, verified by evaluating the arc condition inside the Lean~4 kernel, and an upper bound obtained from one exhaustive depth-first packing search over the $q^2$ points off the conic ($257\,437$, $1\,105\,078$, $18\,657\,443$ and $55\,313\,459$ search nodes at $q=11,13,17,19$), whose completeness is a proved lemma and whose run is a single compiled evaluation; no certificate is stored.  Outside the formal development the same search gives $m(9)=7$ and $m(23)=11$. Consequences: $q=11$ is the first odd $q$ at which a conic does not extend to an $(n,3)$-arc of the largest size $\mth$ of its plane ($19<21$ and $22<23$); the five-point construction of the source is of maximum size exactly at $q=3,5$ and its six-point construction at none of $q=11,13,17,19$; and $m(q)/q$ decreases from $1.00$ at $q=7$ to $0.48$ at $q=23$, so that $m(q)=\lfloor (q+1)/2\rfloor$, which fits $q=17,19$, fails at $q=23$.  No growth law is claimed.

families.title: The pairwise independent correlation gap: the open case n = 4 of the 4/3 conjecture of Ramachandra-Natarajan, and the tightest bound for n >= 5 (arXiv:2606.19663)
families.description: Ground set `N = [n]`. A set function `f : 2^N → ℝ₊` is in the class when it is **nonnegative, nondecreasing and submodular**. For a marginal vector `x ∈ [0,1]^n`:
families.paper_title: The pairwise independent correlation gap: an exact worst case $4/3$ at $n=4$ outside the known regions, and a lower bound $416/311$ at $n=5$
families.paper_abstract: For a nonnegative nondecreasing submodular set function $f$ on $n$ elements and a marginal vector $\bx\in[0,1]^n$, let $\fp(\bx)$ be the largest expectation of $f$ over all distributions on subsets with marginals $\bx$, and $\fpp(\bx)$ the same maximum over pairwise independent distributions.  Ramachandra and Natarajan conjectured that $\fp(\bx)\le\tfrac43\fpp(\bx)$ always; the bound is known for $n\le 3$ and, by their work, for all $n$ when the marginals are all small or all large, and in June 2026 they refuted it at $n=5$ with a coverage function whose gap is at least $640/479$, leaving $n=4$ open and asking for the tightest bound when $n\ge 5$.  We prove that at $n=4$ and $\bx_0=(\tfrac12,\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac16)$ -- a marginal vector outside every region where the bound was known -- the inequality $\fp(\bx_0)\le\tfrac43\fpp(\bx_0)$ holds for every function in the class and is attained by $f(S)=\min(|S|,1)$, so the worst-case gap there is exactly $4/3$.  The proof is a two-part certificate: a modular majorant of $f$ and one explicit pairwise independent distribution with a Farkas multiplier.  At $n=5$ we show that the counterexample function of Ramachandra and Natarajan, at the marginals $(\tfrac{9}{26},\tfrac{5}{13},\tfrac{5}{13},\tfrac{7}{26},\tfrac{7}{26})$, has $\fp=4$ and $\fpp=311/104$ exactly, so its gap is $416/311>640/479$; this improves their lower bound at $n=5$, the only one we know of, and padding with zero marginals carries it to every $n\ge5$.  We also show that $\fpp=479/160$ exactly at their original instance.  Every theorem is verified in Lean~4 with Mathlib, with all data in exact rational arithmetic.  An exhaustive search over the combinatorial part of the $n=4$ problem, reported separately from the formal development, finds no gap above $4/3$.

families.title: The rank dichotomy of the n = 48 coset-2BGA family of arXiv:2608.09115: when does rank H_Z exceed rank H_X for Q_G^H(a,b) with G = SmallGroup(72,30), H = C_3, m = 24, w_a = w_b = 4?
families.description: Aydin, Tamo and Barg (*Breaking the bicycle frame: Coset-based quantum LDPC codes*, arXiv:2606.17268, Construction 1) generalise two-block group algebra codes by replacing the regular action of a group with its action on the cosets of a subgroup. Fix a finite group `G`, a subgroup `H ≤ G` of index `m`, and let `N = N_G(H)`. On the `m` left cosets `G/H`, `G` acts on the left (`L(g) : xH ↦ gxH`) and `N` acts on the right (`R(g) : xH ↦ xgH`); the two actions commute. For `a ∈ F_2[G]` and `b ∈ F_2[N]` the code `Q_G^H(a,b)` is the CSS code on `n = 2m` qubits with

statements.label: The coset model is checked, not assumed: all 84 stored maps are permutations of the 24 cosets with the identity in each block's slot 0, the left G-action and the right N_G(H)-action commute (so H_X H_Z^T = 0 and every pair of the family is CSS), G is transitive on the 24 cosets, and N_G(H) has exactly two orbits

The full joint (rank H_X, rank H_Z) census of the family: over all 9430575 normalised support pairs, 29 cells are occupied, the rank defect is nonzero for 157464 pairs, splits evenly 78732/78732 by sign, takes the value 3 as well as 1, and k takes 23 distinct values from 2 to 36 -- with k = 10 on 2.47% of the family and k = 9 on 1.51%

The hypothesis of Conjecture 17 of arXiv:2608.09115 is unsatisfiable in its own family: F_2[G/H] has exactly one codimension-1 G-submodule and exactly three codimension-1 N_G(H)-submodules, and for every one of the 495 supports b the vector v_b and the whole image of R(b) lie inside every one of them, so the clause '<b> not contained in U' can never hold -- while the a-half of the same condition is satisfiable

Explicit members refuting the conjecture's dichotomy and the rank-degeneracy theorem's closing clause: a regular weight-8 code with rank H_X = 19 < 20 = rank H_Z, k = 9 and d = 2 (not the asserted d = 5); its mirror with the ranks exchanged; a code with rank defect 3, k = 27; and a code with a rank defect and d = 6, against 'rank loss is tied to distance exactly 5'

The family contains [[48,10,6]] codes with regular weight-8 checks -- the parameter set Aydin-Tamo-Barg report for SmallGroup(72,30) -- exhibited with both side distances exactly 6; and their printed support indices do not transfer across GAP versions, the same indices giving a [[48,8,4]] code with irregular row weights under GAP 4.11.1

Negative controls: 'every code of the family has rank H_X = rank H_Z' and 'the rank defect is at most 1' are both refuted, as are 'no code has distance 6' and 'every code has k <= 10'; the regular-weight-8 hypothesis is non-vacuous (it holds for the defect witness and fails for the pair carrying the Aydin-Tamo-Barg indices), and the distance cap is shown not to truncate

The exact distance distribution of the whole rank-defect stratum: of the 142176 normalised pairs with {rank H_X, rank H_Z} = {19,20} and k = 9, exactly 126048 have d <= 4, 14592 have d = 5 and 1536 have d >= 6

families.paper_title: Rank defect in coset-2BGA codes at $n=48$: an exhaustive census, and a module criterion that cannot hold
families.paper_abstract: Coset-based two-block group algebra (coset-2BGA) codes replace the regular action of a group by its action on the cosets of a subgroup $H\le G$; when $H$ is not normal the two CSS parity checks of $Q_G^H(a,b)$ can have different ranks, and this \emph{rank defect} is what controls the dimension.  Lu, Guo, Liu and Yang (arXiv:2608.09115) study one instance --- $G=\mathrm{SmallGroup}(72,30)$, $H\cong C_3$, $[G{:}H]=24$, $n=48$, $w_a=w_b=4$ --- announce a census of it, and conjecture that the defect is detected by a codimension-one submodule of $\F_2[G/H]$ containing $\langle a\rangle$ but not $\langle b\rangle$.  We compute the joint rank distribution of the whole family: over all $9\,430\,575$ normalised support pairs, $29$ cells occur, $157\,464$ pairs have a rank defect, the defect takes the value $3$ as well as $1$, and the dimension $k$ takes $23$ distinct values from $2$ to $36$ rather than the two values the conjecture allows.  We then show the conjecture's criterion cannot be satisfied: $\F_2[G/H]$ has exactly one codimension-one $G$-submodule and exactly three codimension-one $N_G(H)$-submodules, and every one of them contains every admissible $\langle b\rangle$, because $w_b=4$ is even and $b$ lives in a single orbit.  Finally we give the distance distribution of the rank-defect stratum: of its $142\,176$ normalised pairs, $126\,048$ have $d\le4$, $14\,592$ have $d=5$ and $1536$ have $d\ge6$.  Every numerical statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.title: Is the simplex code the minimiser of the expected DNA coverage depth?
families.description: A DNA data-storage archive holds `n` synthesised strands. Sequencing returns *reads* drawn at random, so the natural cost of full recovery is the expected number of reads needed before the whole file can be decoded. When the file is encoded by a linear code this becomes a purely algebraic question.
families.paper_title: The simplex code and the expected DNA coverage depth: the two smallest open cells, a strict local minimum, and the random-access comparison
families.paper_abstract: Bertuzzo, Ravagnani and Yaakobi (arXiv:2603.06489) ask for the code $C \subseteq \F_q^n$ of dimension $k$ minimising the expected number $E[C]$ of uniformly drawn generator-matrix columns needed before the drawn columns span $\F_q^k$, the \emph{expected DNA coverage depth}, and conjecture (their Conjecture~3.2) that at $n = (q^k-1)/(q-1)$ the $q$-ary simplex code is optimal.  For $k \ge 3$ only the cell $(q,k) = (2,3)$ was known.  We settle the two next cells by exhaustive search over all $10\,400\,600$ and $155\,117\,520$ column multisets: $\Eopt[13,3]_3 = 127/36$ and $\Eopt[15,4]_2 = 291/56$, in both cases with the simplex code as the unique minimiser, and with runner-up values $14219/3960$ and $18233/3432$ (the two full enumerations are a C computation outside the formal development; the runner-up values and the strict minimality of the simplex code within two column exchanges are machine-checked).  Independently of any length, the simplex code is a strict local minimum of the continuous relaxation $E(w) = \sum_{W} c_W/(1-w(W))$ of the functional on the probability simplex over the points of $\PG(k-1,q)$, for $(q,k) = (2,3), (3,3), (2,4)$: the Hessian on the tangent space has positive Gaussian pivots in exact rationals.  We also compute $\Eopt[n,3]_2$ for $6 \le n \le 14$ and find it is not monotone in $n$, with the minimum $47/12$ taken exactly at $n = 7$ and $n = 14$.  Finally, Table~I of Wang and Yaakobi (arXiv:2601.07053) prints non-uniform optimal column distributions at $(q,n,k) = (2,7,3)$; we show this is no counterexample: the two functionals that table minimises are single-strand hitting times, and at that cell the two optimisation problems have disjoint optimal sets, with exact values $271/60$ and $67/15$ against $47/12$, and $3$ against $43/15$.  The exact rational statements are verified in Lean~4 by \lean{native\_decide}, that is, by compiled evaluation rather than by the kernel alone.

families.title: K_q(n,R): the nine 2026 record covering codes, kernel-certified, plus four classical exact values
families.description: `K_q(n,R)` is the **minimum size of a code `C ⊆ Z_q^n` such that every word of `Z_q^n` is within Hamming distance `R` of some codeword** — the covering-code analogue of `A_q(n,d)`. `K_2(n,1)` is the domination number of the hypercube; `K_3(n,1)` is the football pool problem.

families.paper_abstract: A covering system is \emph{distinct} when its moduli are pairwise different.  Dalton and Jones proved that for every integer $m\ge 3$ no distinct covering system has all its moduli in the interval $[m,10m]$, and asked the same question for $[n,12n]$ with $n\ge 4$ and for $[n,15n]$ with $n\ge 5$.  Their proof filters the interval by Krukenberg's discard lemma and then applies the density condition; for twenty-three exceptional values of $m$ it runs a bespoke argument, one ingredient of which is to recount the surviving moduli after a reduction and reduce again.  We turn that recount into a uniform, machine-checkable certificate: a list of prime-power steps, each licensed by a count taken inside the set the earlier steps left, together with an integer test on the reciprocal sum of the survivors.  A single step of the certificate closes twenty cells with $k>10$, namely $[m,km]$ for $k=11$ and $m\in\{13,30,85\}$, for $k=12$ and $m\in\{12,28,78,79,127,128,129,154,155,156,169,170,171,173,174,175\}$, and for $k=13$ and $m=145$; no cell with $k>10$ appears to have been recorded before.  We also compute the one-pass filter tables for $11\le k\le 15$, note five values of $m$ that are missing from the exceptional list of Dalton and Jones, and prove a fixpoint theorem which shows that no certificate at all exists for four named cells, among them the interval $[6,167]$ behind a conjecture of Klein.  All statements are formally verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Exact $(2,0)$-partition numbers for two binary covering codes of covering radius two
families.paper_abstract: Let $\HH$ be a parity-check matrix of a binary linear code of covering radius $2$.  A \emph{$(2,0)$-partition} of its column set is a partition into nonempty blocks such that every syndrome, the zero syndrome included, is a sum of at most two columns lying in distinct blocks.  The number of blocks of such a partition governs the $q^{m}$-concatenating constructions that produce infinite families of covering codes from a single short seed, and the quantity has been named in the literature since 2009; it has only ever been bounded above, by exhibiting a partition.  We determine it exactly, for the two codimension-$10$ matrices that currently seed the covering-radius-$2$ families: the $10\times 50$ matrix $\HH$ of arXiv:2608.27494v1, and the $10\times 51$ Kaikkonen--Rosendahl matrix $\HKR$ of 2003.  In both cases the minimum number of blocks is exactly $10$.  For $\HH$ this shows that the published ten-block partition is of minimum size, which its source leaves open in so many words; for $\HKR$ it produces a ten-block partition where the published one has eleven, and shows that ten cannot be improved.  A consequence is negative and is the point of having a lower bound at all: neither matrix admits a partition into $2^{3}=8$ blocks, so the hypothesis $n_{0}\ge 2^{m}\ge p(\HH_{0})$ of Construction $\mathrm{QM}_2^2$ fails at $m=3$ for both seeds, and the route that would have given a length-$407$ (respectively length-$415$) code at codimension $16$, against the standing $431$, is closed --- not by a search that failed, but by an impossibility.  Both impossibility halves are refutations of propositional formulas, replayed inside Lean~4 by a formally verified checker against formulas that are built, not read from a file; the soundness of the symmetry breaking used to make the refutations affordable is itself a theorem, with no appeal to compiled code.

families.paper_abstract: A covering system of $\F_q[x]$ is a finite family of congruence classes $f\equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$, the $m_i$ monic and non-constant, whose union is all of $\F_q[x]$; it is \emph{distinct} when the moduli are pairwise different.  Recent work of B.~Wang shows that no such system exists for $q>73$, and Li, Wang, Wang and Yi ask for an explicit example in the range that is left; the only examples we have found in print are Azlin's, all of them over $\F_2$.  We introduce the quantity $\Lam(q,d)$, the least degree of the least common multiple of a distinct covering system of $\F_q[x]$ all of whose moduli have degree at least $d$, and determine or bound it in five cases.  Our main result is an explicit distinct covering system of $\F_3[x]$ with eleven congruences and least common multiple $x^2(x-1)(x-2)$, together with the proof that no distinct covering system of $\F_3[x]$ has a least common multiple of smaller degree: $\Lam(3,1)=4$.  We also show $\Lam(2,1)=2$ and $\Lam(2,2)=4$ --- so that Azlin's two systems are optimal for their minimum modulus degree --- prove $7\le\Lam(2,3)\le 8$ by exhibiting a system of $25$ congruences with all moduli of degree at least $3$, prove $\Lam(3,2)\ge 6$, and give the first lower bound for the $\F_q[x]$ analogue of the Erd\H{o}s--Selfridge odd covering problem: over $\F_2$, no distinct covering system has its moduli dividing a common multiple of degree less than $11$ that is divisible by no linear polynomial.  All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Lower bounds for the minimal least common multiple of a distinct covering system with minimum modulus $m\ge 8$
families.paper_abstract: A covering system is \emph{distinct} when its moduli are pairwise different, and $\Lmin(m)$ denotes the least value of the least common multiple of the moduli over all distinct covering systems of $\ZZ$ whose smallest modulus is $m$.  The values $\Lmin(3)=120$, $\Lmin(4)=360$, $\Lmin(5)=1440$ and $\Lmin(6)=5040$ are known, and $\Lmin(7)=10080$ has recently been claimed; above $m=7$ the literature records only upper bounds, and the case $m=8$ has been posed as a problem for which integer programming is ``currently not computationally feasible''.  We prove \[ \Lmin(8)\ge 7200,\ \ \Lmin(9)\ge 7920,\ \ \Lmin(10)\ge 10080,\ \ \Lmin(11)\ge 27720,\ \ \Lmin(12)\ge 25200, \] which together with Krukenberg's construction sandwiches $\Lmin(8)$ between $7200$ and $50400$.  Every published value that a bound consumes is carried as an explicit hypothesis.  The engine is an exclusion certificate in exact integer arithmetic: a recursive sharpening of the reciprocal-sum bound along coprime splittings of the period, with no solver anywhere.  The same certificate excludes twelve of the eighteen candidates for $\Lmin(7)$ without an integer program, and shows that every covering of $\ZZ$ by distinct odd moduli greater than $1$ has least common multiple at least $45045$, closing three cells left open by the previously certified bound of $10^4$.  All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_abstract: \crim{} is the impartial game whose positions are integer partitions and whose moves delete one row or one column of the Young diagram, the surviving cells reattaching into a partition again.  Ba\v{s}i\'c, Gottlieb and Krnc determined the Sprague--Grundy values of several families of positions and closed with nine conjectures.  We show that one of them is false, and false on the paper's own terms.  The conjecture predicts $\sg(R^k_{r,r-1})$ for $r\ge 7$; on the line $k=r-2$ the rectair $R^{r-2}_{r,r-1}$ \emph{is} the padded staircase $\PS_{r-1}$, an identity recorded in the source itself, so that conjecture and the source's conjecture on padded staircases speak about the same positions and predict different values at every $r\ge7$.  Computation decides between them: $\sg(\PS_6)=1$, $\sg(\PS_7)=3$ and $\sg(\PS_8)=1$, where the first conjecture predicts $3$, $1$ and $3$.  Its parity condition is inverted.  We record four further failures at degenerate parameters, one of them a genuine counterexample to a published theorem: the characterisation of losing three-part partitions fails at $[1,1,1]$, which the statement places in $\PP$ although the single column may be removed at once.  We then verify finite instances of the remaining conjectures, among them the main conjecture (every losing partition has even Dyson rank) for all $18\,460$ partitions of size at most $28$.  All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Critical permutations of the symmetric group: a local test for the first degree, and the first-degree counts at $n=8$ and $n=9$
families.paper_abstract: For $\tau$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ let $\Lam(\tau)=\{\sigma:\sigma\le\tau\}$ be its principal ideal in the Bruhat order and let $\lambda_j(\tau)$ be the number of elements of $\Lam(\tau)$ of Coxeter length $j$.  Following Pu\v{c}inskait\.{e}, $\tau$ is \emph{critical of degree $i$} when $i$ is the least index with $\lambda_i(\tau)\neq\lambda_{\ell(\tau)-i}(\tau)$, and \emph{critical} when such an $i$ exists; equivalently, when the rank generating function of the lower Bruhat interval $[\id,\tau]$ is not palindromic.  The set $\CC_n$ of critical permutations is identified in that paper with $\{q\in S_n:[M(\id_n):L(q)]\ge 2\}$ in the principal block of $\mathcal{O}(\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb{C}))$, and its table of $|\CC_n|$ stops at $n=7$.  We prove that criticality \emph{of the first degree} is decided by a condition local to $\tau$: the two quantities the criterion compares are the number of smaller neighbours of $\tau$ and the number of indices $j$ with $\tau(\{1,\dots,j\})\neq\{1,\dots,j\}$, so no principal ideal need be built.  This yields the number of permutations critical of degree $1$ at $n=8$ and at $n=9$, namely $32\,915$ and $329\,513$; the second is out of reach of the ideal-based route. The set $\CC_n$ itself is classical --- palindromicity of that rank generating function is the Carrell--Peterson criterion for rational smoothness, so by Lakshmibai--Sandhya $\CC_n$ is the set of permutations containing $3412$ or $4231$, and $|\CC_n|$ is $n!$ less a known sequence --- but that description is silent about the \emph{degree}, and neither count above follows from it.  We also adjudicate an internal inconsistency in the source, which prints both $354$ and $345$ for $|\CC_6|$: the value is $354$, as the source's own arithmetic and the classical count both show.  Every theorem, proposition, lemma and corollary below is machine-checked in Lean~4; the few numerical remarks that are not are flagged where they occur.

families.paper_title: The maximum number of once-crossed edges\\ in a rectilinear drawing of $K_n$
families.paper_abstract: For a drawing $\Dr$ of a graph, $e_k(\Dr)$ is the number of edges involved in exactly $k$ crossings, and the sequence $(e_0(\Dr),e_1(\Dr),\dots)$ is the \emph{crossing profile} of $\Dr$.  Chen and Sol\'e-Pi, who introduced the profile, determined $\mb e_0(K_n)=2n-2$ and asked, as their Problem~1, for the value of $\mb e_1(K_n)$, the maximum of $e_1$ over rectilinear drawings of $K_n$; for $n \ge 8$ they could only place it between $\lceil 3n/2\rceil-7$ and $2n+\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor+7$.  We determine $\mb e_1(K_n)$ exactly for $4 \le n \le 11$, where its values are $2,2,6,7,10,12,14,14$, and we prove $16 \le \mb e_1(K_{12}) \le 17$.  In particular the pattern $\mb e_1(K_n)=2n-6$, which holds at $n=8,9,10$, fails at $n=11$, so this route yields no candidate answer to the limit half of Problem~1.  We also exhibit drawings giving $\mb e_1(K_n) \ge 17,19,19,21$ for $n=13,\dots,16$, each above the published lower bound. The upper bounds come from an exhaustion over uniform rank-$3$ chirotopes rather than over order types --- dropping realizability enlarges the search space and so preserves an upper bound --- made finite by a deletion bound that lets an $n$-element search be driven by the $(n-1)$- or $(n-2)$-element objects with large $e_1$.  The supporting statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.
