families.paper_title: Which gamma laws are freely infinitely divisible,\\ and strict enlargement of the Hankel hierarchy of free cumulants
families.paper_abstract: For a probability measure with all moments finite, free infinite divisibility forces every shifted free-cumulant Hankel matrix $H_N=(\kappa_{i+j+2})_{i,j=0}^{N}$ to be positive semidefinite.  A single vector on which one of those matrices is negative therefore certifies that the measure is \emph{not} freely infinitely divisible, and the point of this paper is that one such vector can be held fixed while a parameter of the law moves.  For the classical gamma law $\gam_p$ the moments $m_n=(p)_n$ are integer polynomials in the shape $p$, hence so are the free cumulants, so the quadratic form $Q(p)=u^{\mathsf T}H_N(\gam_p)u$ of a fixed integer vector $u$ is one polynomial of degree at most $N+1$, whose sign on a closed rational interval is decided by a Bernstein certificate.  One vector at order $20$ gives $H_{20}(\gam_p)\not\succeq0$ for every real $p\in[\frac23,\frac43]$; since Hasebe's set $\I$ covers $(\frac12,\frac23)\cup(\frac43,\frac32)$, this settles part~(3) of his 2014 conjecture --- $\gam_p$ is not freely infinitely divisible for any $p\in(\frac12,\frac32)$ --- and, with the positive half of his Corollary~1.3(1), completes the classification: $\gam_p$ is freely infinitely divisible exactly for $p\in(0,\frac12]\cup[\frac32,\infty)$.  A second vector, at order $13$ on $[\frac{49}{50},\frac65]$, gives the same conclusion with no appeal to compiled evaluation, and already covers infinitely many of the intervals $\I$ omits, where the exponential law was the only shape previously known.  The rest of the paper studies the hierarchy $\{H_N\succeq0\}_{N\ge0}$ itself, which is where the witness vectors come from.  Yu exhibited, for the beta laws $\bet_{p,q}$, exact rational parameters at which the $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ test is the first to fire, for $2\le N\le11$, and asked whether the hierarchy keeps enlarging at higher orders.  It does, at infinitely many orders, by a completeness statement --- for a measure whose moment sequence is determinate, positive semidefiniteness of \emph{every} $H_N$ is not merely necessary for free infinite divisibility but sufficient --- together with the fact that no test fires at $p=\frac12$. That argument assembles published theorems and is the one part of this paper that is not machine-checked; it is labelled as such throughout, as is the observation that the second half of Yu's open sentence --- that every non-freely-infinitely-divisible beta law is eventually separated by a finite Hankel matrix --- is the contrapositive of the criterion Yu's paper itself cites.  The computational content: the witness ladder continued from $N=11$ to $N=20$ with exact rational parameters and bracketed thresholds; the \emph{gamma ceiling} $\nu(p)$, the first order at which the hierarchy of $\gam_p$ fails, computed at $36$ rational shapes and shown to take every value from $13$ to $25$; a Schur reduction of the whole hierarchy to the sign of one scalar $\Phi_N$, non-increasing in $N$ wherever the trailing Hankel matrices are positive definite, so that the exclusion never un-fires there; and the first negative Hankel determinant of the free cumulants of the exponential law, of size $14\times14$, sharper than the $16\times16$ one on record and certified together with it.  Everything computational is verified in Lean~4 by exact integer arithmetic --- $159$ theorems, no floating point anywhere --- and all of it but the order-$20$ certificate is evaluated by the proof kernel itself.

families.title: The quasipolynomial of OEIS A195806: the erratum in Conjecture 11 of Kauers-Koutschan, and a finite proof of the corrected closed form
families.description: Take the triangular array of side 5: entries `c_{i,j}` for `1 ≤ j ≤ i ≤ 5`, arranged so that row `i` has `i` of them. It has three corners (`c_{1,1}`, `c_{5,1}`, `c_{5,5}`) and three families of parallel lines — the rows (`i` fixed), the left diagonals (`j` fixed), the right diagonals (`i − j` fixed). For each `k = 1, …, 5` there is exactly one line of length `k` in each family.
families.paper_title: The quasipolynomial of OEIS A195806:\\ an erratum to Conjecture~11 of Kauers and Koutschan,\\ and the corrected closed form from forty-two values
families.paper_abstract: OEIS A195806 (R.~H. Hardin, 2011) counts the fillings of the twelve non-corner cells of a triangular array of side five by integers from $\{0,\dots,n\}$ in which all lines of equal length have equal sums.  Kauers and Koutschan (arXiv:2303.02793, \emph{J.\ Integer Seq.}\ 26 (2023), Article 23.4.5) observe that the count is a quasipolynomial in $n$, report that their partition-analysis computation of it ``did not complete in a reasonable amount of time'', and print a guessed degree-six, period-six quasipolynomial as their Conjecture~11; the six constituents they contributed to the OEIS entry are still labelled there as conjectured.  We show that Conjecture~11 as printed is false at every $n\equiv5\pmod 6$: its numerator over $1296$ is congruent to $27$, so the printed value is $1/48$ away from an integer and is a term of the sequence at no index whatever.  A single digit transposition in the constant of that branch, $19496\to19469$, repairs it, and no other value of that constant does; after the repair the formula agrees identically with the OEIS closed form, at the shifted index $a(n+1)$.  We then prove the closed form itself.  The count is the number of lattice points of the $n$-th dilate of an explicit rational polytope in $\R^6$; all $924$ maximal minors of its $12\times6$ constraint matrix lie in $\{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3\}$, so by Ehrhart's theorem the count is a quasipolynomial of degree six whose period divides six; such a quasipolynomial is determined by $42$ consecutive values, $41$ do not suffice, and the first $42$ values, computed from the definition, are those of the closed form.  Everything except Ehrhart's theorem itself---the erratum and its uniqueness, the reduction of the count to a rank-six system, the minor bound, the $42$ values, the rigidity and its sharpness, and the closed form conditional on quasipolynomiality---is verified in Lean~4. The conjectured order-14 recurrence of the OEIS entry follows.

families.title: Sign of the discrete Hardy coefficients b_k(alpha)
families.description: Shubham Gupta, *Discrete weighted Hardy Inequality in 1-D*, **arXiv:2108.01500v2** (2022-05-19; v1 2021-08-03). Primary category `math.FA`, cross-list `math.SP`; MSC 39B62, 26D15. The version read for this family is **v2**, taken from the local mirror `/backup/arxiv-src/papers/2108/2108.01500.gz` (file `discrete_hardy.tex`, mtime 2022-05-19 13:41, matching the v2 submission stamp) and confirmed to be the **latest** version against the live abs page (`[v1] [v2]` only).
families.paper_title: The sign of the coefficients in the improved discrete weighted Hardy inequality
families.paper_abstract: For a real parameter $\alpha$ put \[ b_k(\alpha) \;=\; \binom{\alpha}{k} - (-1)^k\binom{(1-\alpha)/2}{k} - \binom{(1+\alpha)/2}{k}, \qquad k \ge 0 . \] These are the coefficients of the infinite tail of lower-order terms that upgrades the discrete weighted Hardy inequality with power weight $n^{\alpha}$ to the improved inequality of Gupta, and the upgrade is available exactly where they are all non-negative.  Gupta proved $b_k(\alpha)\ge 0$ for $\alpha\in[1/3,1)\cup\{0\}$ and conjectured a converse: for every $\alpha\in(0,1/3)\cup[5,\infty)$ some $b_k(\alpha)$ is negative.  Towards it he reached only the odd integers $\alpha=2m+1$.  We prove the conjecture in full, and more: some $b_k(\alpha)$ is negative for every real $\alpha\in(0,1/3)$ and for every real $\alpha>1$, so that the only real parameters at which the whole sequence stays non-negative are those of $[1/3,1)\cup\{0,1\}$.  The proof is elementary and uniform --- one algebraic identity, whose requirement that a certain coefficient vanish identically is what produces the constant $1/3$, together with a decay estimate for $\prod_j\bigl(1-\tfrac{c}{2j}\bigr)$ that needs nothing beyond Bernoulli's inequality.  We also correct Gupta's partial result at the odd integers: its strict inequality fails at the first index it asserts, where the true value is $0$, and we prove the corrected form of that strict half.  All results are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Harmonic index tuples: complete classifications in $A_5$ and $C_2\times S_4$, and the group orders that admit a counterexample
families.paper_abstract: A tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of positive integers is \emph{$G$-harmonic} if the group $G$ has subgroups $U_1,\dots,U_n$ with $[G:U_i]=a_i$ whose left cosets can be translated so as to be pairwise disjoint, and \emph{$\ZZ$-harmonic} if there are integers $r_1,\dots,r_n$ with $r_i\not\equiv r_j \pmod{\gcd(a_i,a_j)}$ for $i\neq j$.  Ginosar asked whether every $G$-harmonic tuple is $\ZZ$-harmonic; Margolis and Schnabel proved that it is for $n\le 4$, and a recent preprint of Menon answers the question negatively at $n=5$ by exhibiting five harmonic $5$-tuples that are not $\ZZ$-harmonic: three in the alternating group $A_5$ and two in a group of order $48$ isomorphic to $C_2\times S_4$.  We settle the question completely in both of those groups: an $A_5$-harmonic tuple of length at most $5$ is $\ZZ$-harmonic unless its index multiset is $\{6,6,6,10,15\}$, $\{6,6,6,15,20\}$ or $\{6,6,10,12,15\}$, and a $C_2\times S_4$-harmonic one unless its index multiset is $\{4,6,6,6,6\}$ or $\{6,6,6,6,16\}$, so Menon's five families are all of them; being statements about whole subgroup lattices, these also yield twelve index multisets that the two groups do not realise at all, of a kind neither source states.  We then leave the two groups and ask how small a counterexample can be.  The answer is exactly $12$: no group of order less than $12$ carries a $G$-harmonic tuple that fails to be $\ZZ$-harmonic, at any length, while $C_2\times S_3$ carries Menon's own multiset $(4,6,6,6,6)$ --- four times smaller than the smallest order he reports.  A refined count against a subgroup of index $2$ and odd order then shows that no group of order $18$ carries one either, by proof rather than by search; the same count, carried out on paper, settles every order $2p^k$ with $p$ an odd prime, and every group order below $48$ except $42$ is decided, by theorem or by exhaustive computation.  We further extend Menon's four remaining families, and the order-$12$ counterexample, to genuine coset partitions.  Every theorem below is machine-checked in Lean~4, apart from two that are marked where they are stated as proved on paper and verified by machine only outside the kernel, and one minimality clause marked where it is proved.

families.title: ħ-perfect graphs: exact certificates for simultaneous Pauli-variance violations, and three errata

families.paper_title: $\hbar$-perfect graphs: exact certificates for\\ simultaneous Pauli-variance violations, and three errata
families.paper_abstract: Let $S_1,\dots,S_n$ be Pauli strings on $m$ qubits and let $G$ be their frustration graph, whose edges record the anticommuting pairs.  Xu, Wang, Ye, Ko\ss{}mann, Schwonnek and Winter attach to $G$ and a weight $w\in\RR^n_+$ the \emph{weighted beta number} $\beta(G,w)=\sup_\rho\sum_iw_i\langle S_i\rangle_\rho^2$, call $G$ \emph{$\hbar$-perfect} when $\beta(G,w)=\alpha(G,w)$ for every $w\ge0$, and classify all graphs on at most nine vertices up to $78$ undetermined ones.  The only upper bound on an anti-cycle beta number available there, or in the companion paper of Xu, Schwonnek and Winter, is $\beta(\Cbar{n},\mathbf 1)\le\vartheta(\Cbar{n})=1+1/\cos(\pi/n)$ for odd $n$; the sharper value $\beta(\Cbar7,\mathbf 1)=(9+4\sqrt2)/7=2.0938363\ldots$ that the companion records is established there only from below, by one explicit state.  We prove the exact rational upper bound $\beta(\Cbar7,\mathbf 1)\le\frac{421}{200}=2.105$, strictly below $\vartheta(\Cbar7)=2.1099162642\ldots$, together with $\beta(\Cbar5,\mathbf 1)\le\frac{1029}{500}$; combined with an explicit Gaussian-integer state this brackets $2.0937171893\ldots\le\beta(\Cbar7,\mathbf 1)\le2.105$ by machine. The certificate is the second level of a sum-of-squares hierarchy, made computable by an exact symmetry reduction: its $448\times448$ Gram matrix is shown to equal $\hat O(Z\otimes\Id)\hat O$ for an explicit orthogonal signed permutation $\hat O$ and a $28\times28$ Hermitian $Z$, so only $28\times28$ is ever factored.  We also give exact rational witnesses of $\hbar$-imperfectness for six graphs, four of which the source determines only numerically, two of them at weighted facets that no uniform-weight search can see; and we record three errata in the source's tables and appendix.  Every numbered statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4, apart from the two elementary hand steps that \S\ref{ssec:caveat} isolates.

families.paper_title: The diameter of $\U(3,\Z/m\Z)$ with respect to the fundamental roots\\ is $2\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ for every $m\ge 8$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\U(3,\Z/m\Z)$ be the group of upper unitriangular $3\times 3$ matrices over $\Z/m\Z$, and let its Cayley graph be taken with respect to the four fundamental-root generators $I\pm E_{12}$, $I\pm E_{23}$.  The CayleyPy collaboration (arXiv:2509.19162) computed the diameter of this graph for $m=8,\dots,50$, found it to be $2\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ throughout that range, and conjectured (their Conjecture~8) that, for the undirected Cayley graph on the fundamental roots, the diameter of $\U(n,\Z/m\Z)$ equals $(n-1)\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ for all large enough $m$, without naming a threshold.  We prove the case $n=3$ of that conjecture for every $m\ge 8$: every element of $\U(3,\Z/m\Z)$ is a product of at most $2\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ generators, and the element $(\lfloor m/2\rfloor,\lfloor m/2\rfloor,0)$ needs that many.  The upper bound is an explicit lattice-path construction --- one horizontal excursion carrying a prescribed number of up- and down-steps --- together with a three-case arithmetic inequality; it involves no computation over $m$.  The threshold $8$ is sharp: at $m=7$ the element $(0,0,3)$ is not a product of six generators, which is checked by enumerating all $5461$ words of length at most six.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4 over Mathlib, with the standard axioms only.

families.paper_title: How far down does Karapetrovi\'c's beta formula for the Hilbert matrix fail?\\ A certified exponent $4.58$ times below the printed threshold
families.paper_abstract: Let $A^p_\alpha$ be the weighted Bergman space of the unit disk and $\Hc$ the Hilbert matrix operator.  Karapetrovi\'c's beta formula asserts $\|\Hc\|_{A^p_\alpha\to A^p_\alpha} = \Bt(a,1-a) = \pi/\sin(\pi a)$ with $a = (\alpha+2)/p$.  Wulan, Zhou and Zhu (arXiv:2607.23540) disprove it along the ray $a_0 = 800001/1000000$, $\alpha_p = a_0p-2$, for every real $p \ge 1100000$, using the test function $f_{4/5}(z) = (1-z^2)^{-4/5}$ evaluated at $r = 999/1000$, and write that $1100000$ ``is only a convenient rigorous threshold'' and that the least real, or even, failing exponent is unknown.  We show that their own lower bound --- the same test function, the same radius, their own hypergeometric evaluation of $\delta^{4/5}(\Hc f_{4/5})(r)$ --- exceeds the beta value along the nearby ray $a_1 = 4/5 + 1/200000$ at every real $p \ge 240000$, in particular at the even exponent $p = 240000$ ($m = 120000$), a factor $4.583$ below the printed threshold.  The obstruction on the source's own ray is structural: with $a_0 - 4/5 = 10^{-6}$ its own subcritical lemma has its pole at $p = 10^6$, so no arithmetic on that ray can go below $10^6$; enlarging $a-b$ to $5\cdot10^{-6}$ moves the pole to $2\cdot10^5$ at the cost of a slightly larger beta value.  Every inequality of the scalar certificate is checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib under the standard axioms \lean{propext}, \lean{Classical.choice}, \lean{Quot.sound} only, with exactly one imported hypothesis: the source's Gauss-connection identity (its display (24)); the passage from that certificate to the operator norm is the source's own Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, on paper.  The source's printed enclosure $5.3454065393010 < \Phi < 5.3454065393012$ is not assumed but proved from the three positive series it prints, with explicit tails.  Two controls bracket the claim on the same ray: the bound is vacuous at the pole $p = 200000$ and strictly below the beta value at $p = 210000$.  The number $240000$ is an upper bound on the least failing exponent along this ray; no lower bound is claimed, and the least exponent remains open.

families.paper_title: The unresolved case $p = 12$ for the Hilbert matrix on Bergman spaces:\\ the fixed Schur certificate settles $\alpha = 6, 7, 8$ and provably fails at $\alpha = 9$
families.paper_abstract: Let $A^p_\alpha$ be the weighted Bergman space of the unit disk and $\Hc$ the Hilbert matrix operator.  Karapetrovi\'c's beta formula predicts $\|\Hc\|_{A^p_\alpha\to A^p_\alpha} = \Bt(a,1-a) = \pi/\sin(\pi a)$ with $a = (\alpha+2)/p$.  Wulan, Zhou and Zhu (arXiv:2607.23540) prove it for every even exponent $p = 2m$ when $a \le m/(2m-1)$, and for $p = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10$ on the whole admissible range; they call $p = 12$ ``the unresolved case''.  Their proof for $p = 4, \dots, 10$ uses the fixed Schur vector $h_j = (m)_j/j!$ and a one-sign-change argument which, as they remark, is uniform in $m$: only one scalar inequality, their base moment (21), depends on $m$, and they do not evaluate it at $m = 6$. We rewrite the base moment at $m = 6$ as $\Bt(6,a)\sum_{n\ge0} c_n\,\Bt(A+n,\beta) \le \Bt(a,1-a)\,\Bt(6,\beta)$ with $c_n$ decreasing and an exactly telescoping tail, which makes it a decidable inequality between explicit rationals and $\pi$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ whenever $\beta = 12a-6$ is an integer.  It holds at $\alpha = 6, 7, 8$; through the source's own chain this gives $\|\Hc\|_{A^{12}_6} = 2\pi/\sqrt3$, $\|\Hc\|_{A^{12}_7} = \pi\sqrt2$ and $\|\Hc\|_{A^{12}_8} = 2\pi$, three weights above every published range at $p = 12$ (the best being $\alpha \le 5.7511\ldots$).  At $\alpha = 9$ the base moment is strictly violated, so the fixed certificate does not settle all of $p = 12$; this refutes the certificate, not the formula.  A high-precision measurement, outside the formal development, locates the two sign changes of the base moment at $a_1 = 0.906114\ldots$ and $a_2 = 0.981054\ldots$, so the fixed certificate covers $\alpha \in (50/11,\,8.8733] \cup [9.7727,\,10)$ and the open part of $p = 12$ shrinks from width $5.45$ to width $0.90$.  The five inequalities are machine-checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib.
