families.paper_title: Values of $v(k)$, the smallest denominator missing from a $k$-term unit fraction decomposition of $1$
families.paper_abstract: For a positive integer $k$ let $D_k$ be the set of integers that occur as a denominator in some identity $1=1/n_1+\cdots+1/n_k$ with $1\le n_1<\cdots<n_k$, and let $v(k)$ be the smallest integer larger than $1$ not in $D_k$.  Erd\H{o}s and Graham introduced $v(k)$ in 1980 and asked how fast it grows; van Doorn and Tang have recently proved the first lower bound, $v(k)\ge e^{ck^2}$, and their paper prints no value of $v(k)$ beyond $D_2=\emptyset$ and $D_3=\{2,3,6\}$.  We determine $v(k)$ for every $k\le 8$, namely $2,2,4,11,17,103,733,27539$.  We have found no source that states $v(6)=103$, though a $2020$ comment on the OEIS sequence A330808 already implies its non-membership half; $v(7)=733$ and $v(8)=27539$ are the seventh and eighth terms of the OEIS sequence A097048, which records data on the neighbouring problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham on the length $N(a,b)$ of Egyptian fraction expansions.  All eight values are proved here rather than quoted.  We also compute $|D_k|$ for $k\le 6$, namely $1,0,3,15,77,1152$, show that $D_k$ is finite for every $k$, and prove the upper bound $v(k)\le|D_k|+2$ in general.  Everything rests on a bounded depth-first search that is proved \emph{exactly} correct --- its output is the set of decompositions, not merely a subset of it --- so that an empty search is a non-existence theorem.  The proofs are machine-checked in Lean~4; Section~\ref{sec:verif} records the scope of the formalisation and which statements are checked by the proof kernel alone.

families.title: Modes of the Kabata-Matsumoto-Okuno seven-mode Gaussian mixture
families.description: A `d`-variate `k`-component Gaussian mixture density can have more modes (local maxima) than components. Améndola, Engström and Haase (arXiv:1702.05066, Inf. Inference 2020) conjectured that the maximum is `m(d,k) = C(d+k-1, d)`, which is **6** for `(d,k) = (2,3)`.
families.paper_title: Critical points and modes of the Kabata--Matsumoto--Okuno seven-mode Gaussian mixture
families.paper_abstract: Kabata, Matsumoto and Okuno (arXiv:2608.01776) constructed an equally weighted three-component bivariate Gaussian mixture $p_{r,M}$ with at least seven modes for $r\in[97/100,99/100]$ and $M\ge 10^4$, refuting the conjectured maximum $\binom{d+k-1}{d}=6$ recorded by Am\'endola, Engstr\"om and Haase, and explicitly declined to say whether the seven modes are all of them. We settle two parts of that question. First, no mode lies on the three long ridges of the mixture: for $r\in[97/100,99/100]$ and $1000\le M\le 10^6$, no point $x$ with $|n_j\cdot x-r|\le 1/2$ and $16\le t_j\cdot x\le M-1$ is a local maximum. Second, for $r=97/100$ and \emph{every} $M\ge 10^4$, the mixture has exactly seven critical points in the rhombus $\Om=\{|n_1\cdot x|\le 2,\ |n_2\cdot x|\le 2\}$, which contains the closed disc of radius $2$ and hence the central triangle bounded by the three major axes; exactly four of them are modes (the origin and one near each pairwise intersection of the major axes), and the other three are saddle points. The count is uniform in $M$ because a change of coordinates makes the gradient system rational in $(n_1\cdot x,\,n_2\cdot x,\,1/(\sqrt3M))$; the certificate is an exclusion covering by $1451$ boxes under a preconditioned (Krawczyk) test, together with $7\times 4$ Krawczyk existence-and-uniqueness certificates. Every statement, including the seven-mode existence theorem itself (re-proved by a derivative-free argument valid from $M\ge 1000$), is verified in Lean~4 with Mathlib. The mode count on the whole plane, and the count at other values of $r$, remain open; a numerical Newton census, reported but not proved, finds thirteen critical points in the plane---seven maxima and six saddles---for every tested $r\in[0.9,0.99]$.

families.title: Correlation immunity order of the Boolean functions built from families of mutually orthogonal cellular automata (k-MOCA): the exhaustive classification for local rules of diameter d <= 6 and every k
families.description: A **bipermutive** local rule of diameter `d` over `F_2` is

statements.label: Definition fidelity against the source: every bipermutive local rule of diameter 3, 4, 5 induces a Latin square of order 2^(d-1); the source's Figure 1 data (all eight coupled de Bruijn labels of rules 90 and 150 at d = 3, and their orthogonality) is reproduced exactly; and the number of orthogonal pairs of bipermutive CA of diameter 3, 4, 5 (4, 36, 852 unordered) reproduces Table 2 of the source's own reference Mariot-Formenti-Leporati 2017 (1, 9, 213) under that paper's stated convention of dividing by 8

Diameters 3 and 4: there is no 3-MOCA of diameter 3 (though 4 orthogonal pairs exist among the 4 bipermutive rules); at diameter 4 there are 16 bipermutive rules, 36 orthogonal pairs and exactly 16 sets of 3-MOCA, listed explicitly, which is 2 under the source's own divide-by-8 convention (equivalently 2 complementation orbits, all of size 8); and there is no 4-MOCA of diameter 4, so 3 is the maximum family size at that diameter

Diameter 4 correlation immunity: every one of the 16 sets of 3-MOCA has 64 pairwise distinct rows, so its Boolean function has n = 9 variables and Hamming weight 64, and its correlation immunity order is exactly 3 -- never 2, and never 4

Diameter 5, k = 3: among the 256 bipermutive rules there are 852 orthogonal pairs and exactly 264 sets of 3-MOCA, each giving a 12-variable Boolean function of Hamming weight 256 with 256 pairwise distinct rows; 264 is 33 under the source's own divide-by-8 convention (equivalently 33 complementation orbits, all of size 8), where Table 1 of the source prints 36

Diameter 5, k = 3, the exact correlation immunity distribution: of the 264 sets of 3-MOCA exactly 192 give a function of correlation immunity order exactly 3 and exactly 72 give order exactly 4, and no other order occurs; under the source's divide-by-8 convention that is 24 and 9, where Table 1 of the published source prints 27 and 9 (and arXiv v1 prints 27 and 6)

The source's open question, answered exhaustively at diameter 5: no 3-MOCA of diameter 5 gives a function that is only second-order correlation immune -- all 264 have order at least 3, so Theorem 1's bound is attained by nothing; the maximum order attained is 4, and both 3 and 4 occur

Diameter 5 beyond k = 3, a cell the source never enters: there are exactly 224 sets of 4-MOCA and exactly 96 sets of 5-MOCA of diameter 5 and no 6-MOCA, so the maximum family size is 5; every one of the 320 gives a Boolean function of Hamming weight 256 on n = 16 respectively n = 20 variables whose correlation immunity order is exactly 3; and every one of the 852 sets of 2-MOCA has all 256 rows distinct, so its support is the whole of F_2^8 and it defines the constant function, whose order is the maximum 8

Diameter 6, certified witnesses for the column the arXiv table's caption promises and its body omits: named 3-MOCA families of diameter 6 with correlation immunity order exactly 5, exactly 4 and exactly 3 (so the maximum order at d = 6 is at least 5, strictly above the maximum 4 at d = 5); a 4-MOCA of diameter 6 of order exactly 4 (impossible at d = 5); and an 8-MOCA of diameter 6, giving a 40-variable third-order correlation immune function of Hamming weight 1024

The complete diameter-6 classification, computed but not certified: 65536 bipermutive rules, 266740 orthogonal pairs (66685 under the source's divide-by-8 convention, reproducing the published d = 6 entry of Mariot-Formenti-Leporati Table 2), 5808 sets of 3-MOCA (726 reduced) on n = 15 variables of weight 1024 with correlation immunity orders 3, 4, 5 in 4576, 960, 272 families (572, 120, 34 reduced), and 6160, 11392, 13504, 8960, 2560 families at k = 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 with no 9-MOCA -- every one of order exactly 3 except 416 of the 4-MOCA, which have order 4. The minimum order over every family of every k at diameter 6 is 3

Negative controls and definition fidelity: the linear function x_1 xor ... xor x_6 is recovered as correlation immune of order exactly 5 by both routes; the indicator of a single point of F_2^4 is rejected as not correlation immune at all; the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform agrees with the source's Eq. (3) written out over the whole input space in all 512 coefficients of a d = 4 family; orthogonality is neither always true nor always false; the 16 rule encodings give 16 distinct Latin squares; dropping pairwise orthogonality collapses the strength to 1 while leaving the rows distinct; complementing the local rules permutes the diameter-4 families and preserves their correlation immunity order; and the too-large claim 'order at least 4 at d = 4' and the too-small claim 'order at most 2 at d = 4' are both refuted

The Min w_H column of the source's Table 1 is wrong in its last row: for n = 12 variables and correlation immunity order 4 it prints 24, which is a duplicate of the order-3 entry, whereas the minimum Hamming weight of a 4th-order correlation immune Boolean function in 12 variables is 128; consequently the source's own conclusion that 'for n = 12 variables the gap is even greater' overstates the order-4 gap by a factor of more than 5 (the true gap is 256/128 = 2). Separately, the printed 20 for (n, t) = (9, 3) cannot be the minimum weight, because the weight of a t-th order correlation immune function is divisible by 2^t and the Rao bound already forces at least 18, hence at least 24

families.paper_title: Correlation immunity of the Boolean functions built from mutually orthogonal cellular automata:\\ the exhaustive classification for local rules of diameter at most six
families.paper_abstract: A bipermutive local rule of diameter $d$ over $\F_2$ induces a Latin square of order $2^{d-1}$; $k$ rules whose squares are pairwise orthogonal form a set of $k$ mutually orthogonal cellular automata ($k$-MOCA), and Mariot and Manzoni (arXiv:2207.08280; AUTOMATA 2023) proved that the $2^{2(d-1)}\times k(d-1)$ binary array obtained by juxtaposing the $k$ output tables is the support of a Boolean function that is correlation immune of order at least $2$.  Their exhaustive search for $k=3$ and $d\in\{4,5\}$ found only orders $3$ and $4$, and they ask whether the bound $2$ is ever attained.  We classify the construction completely for $d\le5$ and every $k$: there are $16$ sets of $3$-MOCA at $d=4$, and $264$, $224$ and $96$ sets of $3$-, $4$- and $5$-MOCA at $d=5$, with no larger family at either diameter; the correlation immunity order is exactly $3$ for every one of them except $72$ of the $264$, whose order is exactly $4$.  At $d=6$ we compute the whole table ($65\,536$ rules, $266\,740$ orthogonal pairs, $5\,808$ sets of $3$-MOCA of orders $3$, $4$, $5$ in $4\,576$, $960$, $272$ cases, families of every size up to $8$ and none of size $9$) and certify named families of orders $5$, $4$ and $3$, a $4$-MOCA of order $4$, and an $8$-MOCA giving a $40$-variable function of weight $1\,024$ and order $3$.  Hence, in all $48\,984$ families with $k\ge3$ and $d\le6$, the order is never $2$; the largest order is $3,4,5$ at $d=4,5,6$ and collapses to exactly $3$ once $k\ge5$.  Under the counting convention of the source's own reference (families divided by $8$), which its $d=4$ entry obeys exactly, its Table~1 at $d=5$ should read $33=24+9$ rather than $36=27+9$ (the arXiv version prints $27+6$), and its minimum-weight entry $24$ at $(n,t)=(12,4)$ contradicts the published value $128$ of Kiss and Nagy.  The maximum family sizes $3,5,8$ coincide with the maxima for linear rules proved by Mariot, Gadouleau, Formenti and Leporati; no family of general bipermutive rules exceeds them for $d\le6$.  Every statement about $d\le5$ and every named $d=6$ family is verified in Lean~4 by compiled evaluation from the source's definitions.

families.title: Can nonlinear cellular automata make a larger family of mutually orthogonal CA? The clique number of the orthogonality graph of binary bipermutive rules, omega(Gamma_d) = 2, 3, 5, 8 for d = 3..6
families.description: Fix an alphabet `F_2` and a diameter `d`. A **no-boundary CA** (NBCA) of diameter `d` with local rule `f : F_2^d -> F_2` on `n` cells is

statements.label: omega(Gamma_3) = 2: two orthogonal bipermutive CA of diameter 3 exist (the linear pair, Wolfram rules 90 and 150) and no three of the four bipermutive rules of diameter 3 are pairwise orthogonal. Lower bound by the explicit pair, upper bound by a two-element witness cover (native_decide on 4 rules).

omega(Gamma_4) = 3: three pairwise orthogonal bipermutive CA of diameter 4 exist, all three linear, and no four of the 16 bipermutive rules of diameter 4 are pairwise orthogonal -- so nonlinear rules do not beat the linear maximum N_3 = 3. Upper bound by a three-element witness cover.

omega(Gamma_5) = 5: five pairwise orthogonal bipermutive CA of diameter 5 exist, all five linear, and no six of the 256 bipermutive rules of diameter 5 -- nonlinear rules allowed -- are pairwise orthogonal. So the answer to the source's question at d = 5 is NO, and the linear maximum N_4 = 5 is the true maximum. Upper bound from a greedy 5-colouring of Gamma_5 with a collision witness for each of the 14116 same-coloured pairs, all checked from the definition.

8 <= omega(Gamma_6) <= 13: eight pairwise orthogonal bipermutive CA of diameter 6 exist, all eight linear (attaining the linear maximum N_5 = 8, each of the 28 pairs verified from the definition on all 1024 configurations), and no family of pairwise orthogonal bipermutive rules of diameter 6 -- 65536 rules, nonlinear allowed -- has more than thirteen members. The upper bound is a thirteen-element witness cover whose kernel check is linear, not quadratic, in the number of rules.

The census of orthogonal pairs of binary bipermutive CA recomputed in the kernel from the source's definitions: 4, 36 and 852 unordered pairs at d = 3, 4, 5 (i.e. 8, 72 and 1704 ordered pairs), on 4, 16 and 256 rules with 16, 64 and 256 configurations.

All 240 nonlinear (non-affine) bipermutive rules of diameter 5 have at least one orthogonal partner: nonlinear orthogonal PAIRS are abundant even though no family containing a nonlinear rule beats the linear maximum.

Negative controls at d <= 5: no MOCA family of diameter 5 has six members (too-large refutation); prefixing rule 1 to the exhibited five-element family destroys pairwise orthogonality, so the IsMoca hypothesis is not vacuous; and the exhibited maximum family really uses five distinct colours, so the colouring bound is not proving 5 by accident.

Negative controls at d = 6: no MOCA family of diameter 6 has fourteen members, and rules 1 and 0 of diameter 6 are provably not orthogonal (non-vacuity of the pairwise hypothesis on 1024 configurations).

The full orthogonality graph of diameter 6: 65536 bipermutive rules, 266740 edges (= the published 533480 ordered pairs), maximum degree 30, degeneracy 16, chromatic number 8 by greedy in degeneracy order, and clique number omega(Gamma_6) = 8 -- exactly the linear maximum N_5. So the answer to the source's question is NO for every d <= 6.

Every maximum MOCA family of diameter d <= 6 is affine: there are exactly 4, 16, 96 and 2560 maximum cliques of Gamma_d for d = 3, 4, 5, 6 and every one consists of affine rules only. Moreover the largest family containing at least one NONLINEAR rule has 0, 2, 3 and 4 members for d = 3, 4, 5, 6 -- half the linear maximum at d = 6 -- while all 65504 nonlinear rules of diameter 6 have an orthogonal partner.

families.paper_title: Can nonlinear cellular automata make larger families of mutually orthogonal cellular automata?\\ The clique number of the orthogonality graph of binary bipermutive rules for diameters at most six
families.paper_abstract: A bipermutive local rule $f=x_1\oplus g(x_2,\dots,x_{d-1})\oplus x_d$ of diameter $d$ over $\F_2$ defines a no-boundary cellular automaton $F\colon\F_2^{2(d-1)}\to\F_2^{d-1}$ whose Cayley table is a Latin square of order $2^{d-1}$; rules whose squares are pairwise orthogonal form a family of mutually orthogonal cellular automata (MOCA).  Mariot, Gadouleau, Formenti and Leporati (Des.\ Codes Cryptogr.\ 2020) determined the largest such family among \emph{linear} rules: $N_{d-1}=2,3,5,8$ for $d=3,4,5,6$.  Mariot, Mazzone, Manzoni and Leporati (arXiv:2604.11362) ask whether nonlinear rules can do better.  We phrase the question as the clique number $\omega(\G_d)$ of the orthogonality graph on all $2^{2^{d-2}}$ bipermutive rules and answer it for $d\le6$: $\omega(\G_5)=5=N_4$ over all $256$ rules of diameter $5$, and $8\le\omega(\G_6)\le13$ over all $65\,536$ rules of diameter $6$, both machine-checked; the exact value $\omega(\G_6)=8=N_5$ is computed and reported as data, together with the facts that every maximum family of diameter $d\le6$ consists of affine rules only and that a family containing even one nonlinear rule has at most $0,2,3,4$ members for $d=3,4,5,6$.  So at every diameter now reachable nonlinearity buys nothing, although nonlinear rules are not orthogonality-poor: all $240$ nonlinear rules of diameter $5$ have an orthogonal partner.  The upper bounds come from a certificate rather than a search: two rules that identify a common pair of configurations are never orthogonal, the set of rules identifying a given pair is an affine subspace of the space of generating functions, and a cover of the rule set by such subspaces bounds every family by the number of subspaces at a cost linear in the number of rules.  The machine-checked statements are verified in Lean~4 from the source's definitions; the published pair census $8,72,1\,704$ is recovered inside the same development.

statements.label: Lattice weak duality: a dual polynomial for the tail functional need only be nonnegative AT THE INTEGERS, and both certificates used here are negative somewhere on R
The sharp one-sided Chebyshev constant for integer-valued X: sup P(X >= t) = 1/(t(t+1)) for every integer t >= 1 with E X = 0 and E X^2 = 1, against Cantelli's 1/(1+t^2)

The binding regime of the lattice four-moment map: V1^Z(t,kappa) = (kappa-1)/(t^2(t^2-1)) for every integer t >= 2 and every 1 <= kappa <= t^2-t+1, extremal law on {-1,0,1,t}, certificate x^2(x^2-1)/(t^2(t^2-1))

The lattice constant is strictly below Cantelli's for every integer t >= 2, and equal to it at t = 1
Negative controls: a too-large and a too-small claim refuted at (t,kappa) = (2,2), and each of the three regime hypotheses (t >= 2, kappa <= t^2-t+1, kappa >= 1) shown not to be decoration

The map at every real threshold: an integer-valued law has P(X >= t) = P(X >= ceil t), so V1^Z(.,kappa) is a STEP function in t, constant on each (n-1,n], and the two closed forms of M3/M4 determine V1^Z on all of (0,infinity) x [1,infinity)

The exact comparison with Cantelli: the identity (v + a(a+1))(v+s^2) - v(s+a)(s+a+1) = (v-as)(v-(a+1)s), hence the lattice constant is at most Cantelli's v/(v+s^2) with equality if and only if s divides v, plus the uniform envelope v/(v+s^2) - V^Z(s,v) <= 1/(4(v+s^2))

Grid refinement: the sharp constant on (1/k)Z at every real threshold; monotone along divisibility chains but NOT in the mesh (V on half-Z at t=2 is 1/5, strictly above V on third-Z which is 11/56); equal to Cantelli's 1/(1+T^2) exactly when T divides k; and a gap at most 1/(4k^2(1+T^2)) at integer thresholds T

The step ratio in closed form: on each step (n-1,n] the lattice map is constant and the continuous map of arXiv:2607.05226 restricted to t >= 1 is min(1/(1+t^2), (kappa-1)/((t^2-1)^2+kappa-1)), continuous and strictly decreasing; the supremum of their ratio over the step is the three-branch closed form R_n(kappa) at the excluded left endpoint and is NOT attained; the minimum rho_n at t = n is attained; R_n(kappa) < (n^2-1)/(n-2)^2 for every kappa > 1 and n >= 3, while R_2(kappa) = 6/(kappa-1) on 1 < kappa <= 3 is unbounded

families.paper_title: The sharp one-sided tail bound for integer-valued random variables under a fourth-moment constraint
families.paper_abstract: For a real random variable $X$ with $\EE X=0$, $\EE X^2=1$ and $\EE X^4\le\kappa$, the exact value of $\sup\PP(X\ge t)$ is a classical Chebyshev-type extremal problem, solved in closed form on most of its parameter range by Li, Han, Jiang and Gao.  We impose one further hypothesis --- that $X$ is \emph{integer-valued} --- and determine the resulting map $V_1^{\ZZ}(t,\kappa)$ completely.  For every integer $t\ge2$ it has exactly two regimes, separated by the threshold $\kappa=t^2-t+1$: below the threshold $V_1^{\ZZ}(t,\kappa)=(\kappa-1)/\bigl(t^2(t^2-1)\bigr)$, attained on $\{-1,0,1,t\}$; at and above it $V_1^{\ZZ}(t,\kappa)=1/\bigl(t(t+1)\bigr)$, attained on $\{-1,0,t\}$, and the fourth-moment constraint is inactive.  The threshold is exactly the fourth moment of the two-moment extremal law $\{-1,0,t\}$, an integer polynomial in $t$; the corresponding boundary of the real-support map is the fourth moment of Cantelli's two-atom law, $t^2-1+t^{-2}$, which is not.  Both branches are affine in $\kappa$ where the real-support value is strictly concave in $\kappa$, and both are constant in $t$ on each interval $(n-1,n]$, so $V_1^{\ZZ}(\cdot,\kappa)$ is a step function where the real-support map is smooth.  The mechanism is a pair of dual polynomials, $x(x+1)$ and $x^2(x^2-1)$, that are nonnegative at every integer and negative on the real line; neither is a sum of squares, so neither is admissible in the real-support problem, and the sum-of-squares duality used there cannot reach these bounds.  We also record the two-moment case $\sup\PP(X\ge t)=1/\bigl(t(t+1)\bigr)$, against Cantelli's $1/(1+t^2)$, which we present as an anticipated value rather than a new one --- it is a two-line substitution into a closed form of Boros and Pr\'ekopa --- and we say precisely why.  Every theorem, proposition, lemma and corollary below is formally verified in Lean~4, and we state exactly what lies outside that guarantee.

families.title: How nonlinear can a monotone Boolean function be? (exact maximum nonlinearity over the monotone and the balanced monotone Boolean functions of n variables, n = 5 and n = 6, against the best-found values of Carlet-Cupic-Durasevic-Jakobovic-Mariot-Picek arXiv:2604.17342v1 Table 2 and Carlet's 2017 upper bound)
families.description: A Boolean function is a map `f : F_2^n → F_2`. Equip `F_2^n` with the coordinatewise partial order `u ⪯ v ⟺ u_i ≤ v_i for all i`; `f` is **monotone increasing** when `u ⪯ v ⟹ f(u) ≤ f(v)`. The **Walsh–Hadamard transform** of `f` is the integer function
families.paper_title: The exact maximum nonlinearity of monotone Boolean functions\\ of five and six variables
families.paper_abstract: A Boolean function $f\colon\F_2^n\to\F_2$ is monotone if $u\preceq v$ coordinatewise implies $f(u)\le f(v)$, and its nonlinearity $\nl_f$ is its Hamming distance to the nearest affine function.  Carlet, \v{C}upi\'c, \DJ{}urasevi\'c, Jakobovi\'c, Mariot and Picek (arXiv:2604.17342) evolve monotone functions of high nonlinearity for $5\le n\le14$ and report the best values their search found; at $n=5$ and $n=6$ these are $11$ and $23$, and $10$ and $22$ under the additional constraint of balancedness, against Carlet's upper bound for the class, which evaluates to $12$ and $27$.  They leave open whether the gap ``may reflect limitations of the search process'' or ``may also indicate that the current upper bound is not tight''.  We settle both dimensions by exhaustion over the whole class --- all $7\,581$ monotone functions of five variables and all $7\,828\,354$ of six: the exact maxima are $11$ (attained by $24$ functions) and $23$ (attained by $390$), and over the balanced monotone functions $10$ (attained by $31$, among them the majority function $\MAJ_5$) and $22$ (attained by $1\,044$).  So the evolutionary search was optimal in both dimensions and both settings, and Carlet's bound is not attained, with slack $1$ at $n=5$ and $4$ at $n=6$.  We also give the full distribution of the nonlinearity over the monotone and the balanced monotone functions of five variables.  Everything is verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}: the enumeration of the class is proved complete and repetition-free, the six-variable census is reduced by a proved Walsh identity to a pass over pairs of five-variable spectra, the finite arithmetic is evaluated by compiled evaluation confined to a single module, and the bound values $12$ and $27$ are recomputed from Carlet's formula inside the kernel without any axiom.  In this second version we add the threshold subclass.  A threshold function (a halfspace) is $f(x)=[\,w\cdot x\ge t\,]$ with real weights $w$ and a real threshold $t$, and the monotone ones are those with non-negative weights.  Carlet and M\'eaux gave the nonlinearity of the \emph{symmetric} threshold functions $T_{d,n}=[\wt(x)\ge d]$ in closed form, and the source treats only these; the maximum of that closed form is $10$ at $n=5$ and $22$ at $n=6$.  We prove that these are the maxima over \emph{all} positive threshold functions of five and of six variables --- classes of $3\,287$ and $244\,158$ functions (OEIS A002078) --- attained by $\MAJ_5$ and by $T_{4,6}$, so that unequal weights never help at $n\le6$; that the maxima over the balanced positive threshold functions are $10$ and $20$; and that none of the $24$ (respectively $390$) monotone functions of maximal nonlinearity is a threshold function for any real weights of either sign, each carrying an explicit $2$-summability certificate that is checked against its truth table.  So the nonlinearity-optimal monotone functions found by the evolutionary search lie strictly outside the halfspace class, and the monotone-to-threshold gap is exactly $1$ in both dimensions.  The upper bounds never enumerate the threshold functions: they run over the monotone census of the first version and refute thresholdness one function at a time.

The unmatched simplices are **critical**, and `W` is **optimal** when the number of critical simplices is minimal, equivalently when `|W|` is maximal. *How many optimal matchings does a given complex hav

families.paper_title: Counting optimal discrete Morse matchings:\\ the six-vertex projective plane has exactly $428\,400$
families.paper_abstract: A matching $W$ on the Hasse diagram of a finite simplicial complex $K$ is a \emph{discrete Morse matching} when reversing its edges leaves no directed cycle; the unmatched simplices are \emph{critical}, and $W$ is \emph{optimal} when their number is minimal.  How many optimal matchings does a complex have?  For the simplex the answer is a published sequence with four terms, $f(1),\dots,f(4)=2,\,9,\,256,\,380\,125$, the last of them a cluster computation; at $n=5$ even the $f$-vector that would contain the next term is called computationally infeasible.  Every count we could find in the literature is a count for a simplex or for the boundary of one.  We compute an exact count for a complex that is neither: the $6$-vertex triangulation $\RP^2_6$ of the real projective plane has exactly $428\,400$ optimal discrete Morse matchings, and every one of them has Morse vector $(1,1,1)$.  In the notation of Zheng's Morse ensemble polynomial this says $p_{\FF_2}(\RP^2_6)=428\,400$ and $p_{\QQ}(\RP^2_6)=0$: a complex with optimal matchings in abundance and no rationally perfect one, which is where Zheng's ``perfect'' and Scoville's ``optimal'' part company.  It is a new data point above dimension one for Zheng's second open problem, ``Perfect Morse counts in higher dimensions'', whose only such datum is $[z_0z_2]\ME_{\partial\Dl^3}=256$.  The proof is an exhaustive enumeration of the $1\,698\,480$ matchings of size $14$ and the $70\,144$ matchings of size $15$ on the $31$-cell Hasse diagram, testing acyclicity at every leaf and pruning by acyclicity nowhere.  It is machine-checked in Lean~4, as are reproductions of every published number the paper leans on: the Chari--Joswig values $f(1),f(2),f(3)$, Scoville's two $f$-vectors and his $f(4)=380\,125$, three of Zheng's Morse ensemble polynomials, Zheng's identity $p(G)=n\,\tau(G)$ for connected graphs, and the optimum values $c=3$ that Joswig--Pfetsch obtain by branch and cut for the projective plane and for the dunce hat.  Counts for the $7$-vertex torus and the dunce hat, $59\,523\,534$ and $63\,617\,968$, are reported as measurements outside the formal development and are labelled as such wherever they appear.

families.title: Mourre bands for the Molchanov-Vainberg Laplacian
families.description: The **Molchanov–Vainberg Laplacian** on `ℓ²(ℤ^d)` is `D = ∏_{i=1}^d Δ_i` with `Δ_i = (S_i + S_i*)/2`; its spectrum is `[-1,1]`. For a long-range potential `V` with `n_i(V - τ_i^κ V)(n) = O(ln^{-q}|n|)`, `q > 2`, a limiting absorption principle for `D + V` — hence absence of singular continuous spectrum — follows from a **strict Mourre estimate** for `D` with respect to a conjugate operator `𝔸 = Σ_j ρ_{jκ} A_{jκ}`.
families.paper_title: Two rigorous Mourre bands for the Molchanov--Vainberg Laplacian in dimension two
families.paper_abstract: Let $D=\Delta_1\Delta_2$ be the Molchanov--Vainberg Laplacian on $\ell^2(\Z^2)$, with $\Delta_i=(S_i+S_i^{*})/2$. For a conjugate operator $\A=\sum_j\rho_{j\kappa}A_{j\kappa}$ built from the dilation-type generators $A_{j\kappa}$, a strict Mourre estimate for $D$ at an energy $E$ is equivalent to strict positivity, on the constant-energy surface $S_E=\{x\in[-1,1]^2:x_1x_2=E\}$, of the explicit Chebyshev combination $G_\kappa=\sum_j\rho_{j\kappa}g_{j\kappa}$, $g_{j\kappa}(x_1,x_2)=x_2(1-x_1^2)U_{j\kappa-1}(x_1) +x_1(1-x_2^2)U_{j\kappa-1}(x_2)$. Mandich (arXiv:2201.00410) determines the coefficients $\rho_{j\kappa}$ band by band, by interpolation at threshold energies, and then supplies \emph{plots} of $G_\kappa$; he states plainly that he was not able to prove a Mourre estimate on any new interval, and that the new bands of absolutely continuous spectrum are ``justified mainly by graphical evidence''.  We turn the first two of those plots, at $\kappa=4$ and $d=2$, into theorems with explicit constants. For the first band $(\E_1,\E_0)=\bigl((\sqrt5-1)/2,\cos(\pi/4)\bigr)$ and the author's own coefficient $\rho_8=(17+8\sqrt5)/62$, we prove $G_4(x_1,x_2)\ge\frac1{25}\bigl(E^2-\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2\bigr)\bigl(1-2E^2\bigr)$, $E=x_1x_2$, on the whole \emph{closed} band, the right-hand side vanishing exactly at the two thresholds. For the second band $(\E_2,\E_1)=(1/\sqrt3,(\sqrt5-1)/2)$ and the author's exact interpolation coefficients in $\Q(\sqrt5)$, we prove $G_4(x_1,x_2)\ge\frac1{500}(3E^2-1)\bigl(\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2-E^2\bigr)$ for $29/50\le E\le 309/500$, which is $93.40\ band, an \emph{attained interior} zero of $G_4$ on a threshold surface that the interpolation system forces but does not impose; these zeros are what limits every subdivision-based certificate, and the device that removes the first of them --- a fold onto $x_1\ge x_2$ combined with an exact one-parameter deformation of the algebraic threshold --- is what closes the first band. All positivity claims rest on the nonnegativity of explicit finite integer Bernstein coefficient arrays; every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4. The passage from these polynomial inequalities to the Mourre estimate for $D$ itself is the source's functional calculus, quoted rather than reproved.

families.title: Real roots of the massive Thirring model's principal polynomials p-hat_N: the N-real-roots conjecture of arXiv:2603.28544v1 verified exactly to N = 16, with the lower half kernel-bound to N = 16 and a correction to the paper's eq. (4.2)
families.description: Founded 2026-09-07 from arXiv:2603.28544v1, *Rational solutions for algebraic solitons in the massive Thirring model*, Zhen Zhao, Cheng He, Baofeng Feng, Dmitry E. Pelinovsky (nlin.SI primary; v1 only, checked live 2026-09-07). The repository's first `nlin.SI` family.
families.paper_title: Real roots of the principal polynomials of the algebraic multi-solitons of the massive Thirring model: the $N$-real-roots conjecture verified exactly to $N=16$, a bilinear recursion, and a correction
families.paper_abstract: Zhao, He, Feng and Pelinovsky (arXiv:2603.28544) construct a hierarchy of rational solutions of the massive Thirring model describing $N$ algebraic solitons, and reduce their slow dynamics and the mass quantization $\mathcal M_N = 4\pi N$ to a single conjecture: the real polynomial $\ph N$ of degree $N^2$ obtained from the principal part of the denominator polynomial has exactly $N$ real roots.  They check it numerically for $N\le 6$.  We verify it exactly, in rational arithmetic with no floating point, for $N=1,\dots,16$: $\ph N$ is squarefree and has exactly $N$ distinct real roots.  The lower bound (at least $N$ distinct real roots) is proved inside the Lean~4 proof assistant for every $N\le 16$ from explicit sign-change certificates at small rationals; the upper bound rests on Sturm sequences over $\QQ$ outside the formal development.  We find a bilinear recursion in $N$ that the source does not contain, $N^2\ph{N+1}\ph{N-1} = N^2\ups^2\ph N^2 + 4N^2(\ph N\ph N'' - \ph N'^2) + \ph N'^2$, proved in Lean for $N\le 12$ and by exact computer algebra for $N\le 15$; it is built from the same two blocks as the Yablonskii--Vorob'ev recursion on which Roffelsen's proof of the analogous real-root count runs, and it implies that $\ph{N+1}$ and $\ph{N-1}$ have opposite signs at every real root of $\ph N$.  Finally we show that the determinant formula (4.2) of the source, read as printed, does not reproduce the source's own $p_4$, and give the corrected formula, which reproduces every polynomial the source prints.

families.paper_title: Sprague--Grundy values of unpinning avoidance games on multiloops
families.paper_abstract: Seo, Simon and Stucky attach to every multiloop $\gamma$ in a surface an impartial game, the \emph{unpinning avoidance game}: a pin sits in each region of the complement, a move removes one pin provided the remaining pins still form a pinning set, and the player without a move loses.  Their Question~0.16 (arXiv:2602.07344) asks what the Sprague--Grundy values of these games are, whether they can grow fast with the number of double points, and what the restriction to simple multiloops changes; the paper computes no value.  We compute the value and the outcome class of every one of the $1096$ multiloops of the LooPindex census (irreducible, indecomposable multiloops in the sphere with at most $12$ regions, whose pinning data is published): the values $0,1,2,3,4,5$ occur with multiplicities $428,446,97,122,2,1$, the maximum $5$ is attained by exactly one multiloop, the loop $12^1_{105}$, and over the $65$ simple multiloops of the census the value $2$ never occurs and the maximum is $3$.  Two statements hold in general.  A multiloop with a unique minimal pinning set has value $(\#\Reg-\pin)\bmod 2$, where $\#\Reg$ is the number of regions and $\pin$ the pinning number; combined with the source's own observation that a simple two-strand multiloop has a unique minimal pinning set, this decides the game for every simple multiloop with at most two strands in every orientable surface.  The value never exceeds $\#\Reg-\pin$, hence is at most $c+2$ for a multiloop in the sphere with connected image and $c$ double points.  Abstract clause systems already reach the value $7$ on nine regions while the census stops at $5$, so the open half of the question is which pinning ideals are realised by multiloops.  The source's Figure~7 example is identified with the census entry $12^3_{57}$ and has value $1$.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Two questions of Huguin on the multiplier polynomials of $z^{d}+c$, answered at twenty-five pairs $(d,n)$
families.paper_abstract: For $d \geq 2$ let $f_{c}(z) = z^{d}+c$, let $M_{n} \in \Z[c,\lambda]$ be the $n$-th multiplier polynomial of this family and let $\Delta_{n} = \disc_{\lambda} M_{n} \in \Z[c]$. Huguin factors $\Delta_{n} = a_{n} Q_{n} R_{n}^{2}$ with $a_{n}$ a squarefree integer, the roots of $Q_{n}$ being the parameters at which $f_{c}$ has a cycle of period $n$ and multiplier $1$, and the roots of $R_{n}$ the parameters at which $f_{c}$ has two distinct cycles of period $n$ with the same multiplier; he asks whether $Q_{n}$ and $R_{n}$ ever share a root, and whether $a_{n} = \pm 1$ for all $n$.  Both questions survive only in the e-print of \emph{Unicritical polynomial maps with rational multipliers} and in his thesis: the subsection carrying them was removed from the published version.  We answer both questions at twenty-five pairs $(d,n)$ with $2 \leq d \leq 10$, namely all $n \leq 6$ for $d = 2$, all $n \leq 4$ for $d = 3$, all $n \leq 3$ for $d = 4$ and $n \leq 2$ for $5 \leq d \leq 10$.  In every one of them $Q_{n}$ and $R_{n}$ have no common root in $\C$, and $a_{n} = \pm 1$; twelve of these pairs lie beyond the range in which the first question was previously settled or the data displayed, and ten beyond the range in which the second one was.  The answers are certified by exact Bézout identities $u Q_{n} + v R_{n} = m$ over $\Z[c]$ with $m$ a nonzero integer of up to $9465$ decimal digits, together with explicit identities $\Delta_{n} = a_{n} Q_{n} R_{n}^{2}$; we record the polynomials $R_{n}$, which do not seem to have appeared in print for any $n \geq 2$, and the resulting sign data, in which $a_{2} = +1$ occurs exactly at $d = 4$ and $d = 8$ in the computed range.  All identities are checked by the Lean~4 kernel.

families.paper_title: Graphs attaining $\dm(G)=n(G)$ at orders $12$ and $13$, with certified multiset dimensions of king grids
families.paper_abstract: The \emph{multiset dimension} $\dm(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the least size of a landmark set $S\subseteq V(G)$ for which the multiset of distances from a vertex to $S$ --- the landmark labels forgotten --- determines the vertex, and $\infty$ when no landmark set does. Simanjuntak, Siagian and Vetr\'ik conjectured that the trivial bound $\dm(G)\le n(G)$ is never attained.  Allikvere refuted the conjecture by an exhaustive scan through order $11$, which produced exactly eight extremal graphs, all of order $11$; he then asked whether an extremal graph exists for every $n\ge 11$, reporting that his own one-vertex extension search at order $12$ found none.  We answer that question affirmatively at $n=12$ and at $n=13$, by two explicit graphs of $30$ and $35$ edges and diameter $3$ in which the full vertex set is the \emph{only} multiset resolving set.  They were found by extending seeds that the earlier search discarded: the order-$12$ witness descends from an order-$11$ graph whose own full vertex set does not resolve.  Alongside, we certify individual cells of Allikvere's king-grid theorems and the non-monotonicity of the height-four row $\dm(P_4\boxtimes P_{n})$, and we bound by $7$ four cells that his table leaves as $>6$ and that an exhaustive search outside the verified development puts at exactly $7$.  Every value we certify is a witness together with an exhaustion of all smaller landmark sets, and every statement of the paper is formally verified in Lean~4; the few numbers that come from the unverified search are marked as such where they appear.

families.title: Dimension-independence of the Mourre positivity set for the Molchanov-Vainberg Laplacian
families.description: Two of the ingredients below are **published and are not claimed here**, and one is **classical**.
families.paper_title: Multiplicative superadditivity and dimension-free Mourre bands for the Molchanov--Vainberg Laplacian
families.paper_abstract: Let $D=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\Delta_i$ be the Molchanov--Vainberg Laplacian on $\ell^2(\Z^d)$, $\Delta_i=(S_i+S_i^{*})/2$. For the conjugate operators $\A=\sum_j\rho_{j\kappa}A_{j\kappa}$ used by Gol\'enia and Mandich, a strict Mourre estimate at an energy $E$ is equivalent to strict positivity of an explicit Chebyshev polynomial $G_\kappa$ on the constant-energy surface $S_E=\{x\in[-1,1]^d:\prod_lx_l=E\}$. Gol\'enia and Mandich proved that $G_\kappa|_{S_E}$ is \emph{separable} --- $G_\kappa|_{S_E}(x)=E\sum_{i}P(x_i^2)$ for a single-variable $P$ with $P(1)=0$ --- and deduced from it that raising the dimension can only shrink the set of good energies. Nothing was known about the converse, and Mandich, who treats $d=2$ throughout, re-runs his $d=3$ numerics with the two-dimensional coefficients and conjectures that they still work, calling the phenomenon ``quite mysterious and surprising''.  We isolate the property that governs the converse: $P$ is \emph{multiplicatively superadditive} on a region, $P(uv)\le P(u)+P(v)$. When it holds, the minimum of $\sum_iP(u_i)$ under $\prod_iu_i=z$ equals $P(z)$ in every dimension, and is attained at $(z,1,\dots,1)$. For $\kappa=4$ and Mandich's first band --- $\Sigma=\{4,8\}$, $\rho_8=(17+8\sqrt5)/62$ --- we prove multiplicative superadditivity on $[1/10,1]$ and conclude, for every $d\ge1$ and every $E\in(0,1]$ with $E^2\ge1/10$, that $\min_{S_E}G_4=E\,P(E^2)$, a number in which $d$ does not appear. Hence $G_4|_{S_E}>0$ holds in one dimension if and only if it holds in every other; inside that range the positivity set is exactly $(\E_1,\cos(\pi/4))\cup(\sqrt{\E_1},1)$, $\E_1=(\sqrt5-1)/2$, in all dimensions at once. In particular the $n=1$ case of Mandich's Conjecture~1.15 holds in every dimension, at the level of strict positivity to which his own equivalence reduces it, with a sharp and attained constant.  The same works for his \emph{second} band, $\Sigma=\{4,8,12,28\}$, whose coefficients he gives exactly in $\Q(\sqrt5)$: its degree-$14$ polynomial $P_2$ is multiplicatively superadditive on $[1/3,1]$, so $\min_{S_E}G^{(2)}_4=E\,P_2(E^2)$ whenever $E^2\ge1/3$, in every dimension, $G^{(2)}_4$ being the combination those coefficients build. The $n=2$ case of the conjecture follows in the same sense, and at $d=2$ that band, certified until now on $93.40\ identity dividing out the double zero forced by $P(1)=0$, followed by exact decompositions over $\Z[\E_1]$ at the interior zeros of the kernel --- one for the first band, two for the second --- and integer Bernstein certificates. The \emph{two-sided} band set is genuinely dimension-dependent, so the results are stated --- as in Mandich --- for strict positivity. All polynomial statements are machine-checked in Lean~4; the passage from them to the Mourre estimate itself is the sources' functional calculus, quoted rather than reproved.

families.paper_title: The minimax reciprocal approximation to $x$ on $[0,1]$ behind MINBERR: exact values for $k \le 4$, certified enclosures for $k \le 10$, and the constant in the $3/(k^2-1)$ bound
families.paper_abstract: Dereziński, Nakatsukasa and Rebrova (arXiv:2604.16075) prove that their backward-error minimising Krylov method MINBERR satisfies $\berr_{A,b}(x_k) \le 3/(k^2-1)$ for every positive semidefinite $A$ and every $k \ge 2$, and remark that numerical evidence suggests the optimal constant is $2$.  Their proof reduces to a scalar extremal problem, $E_k = \min_{p \in \Pk{k-1}} \max_{x \in [0,1]} |x - 1/p(x)|$ over real polynomials of degree at most $k-1$, of which no value is printed.  We determine $E_k$ exactly for $k \le 4$: $E_1 = 1/2$, $E_2 = (\sqrt2-1)/2$ with extremal polynomial $(2\sqrt2+2) - 4x$, $E_3$ is the unique root of $16x^4 - 8x^2 - 8x + 1$ in $[0.112635213, 0.112646477]$, and $E_4$ is the unique root of $64x^6 - 64x^5 - 112x^4 + 32x^3 + 28x^2 + 12x - 1$ in $[0.070898841, 0.070905932]$; both polynomials are irreducible over $\Q$, so $E_3$ and $E_4$ are algebraic of degrees exactly four and six.  For $2 \le k \le 10$ we give two-sided rational enclosures of relative width below $2\cdot 10^{-4}$, with explicit rational polynomials as upper certificates and exact linear-programming duals on the alternation nodes as lower certificates.  Consequently $(k^2-1)E_k < 1.42$ for $2 \le k \le 10$, so the constant $3$ can be more than halved on that range, and $(k^2-1)E_k$ is strictly increasing there, so a limiting constant $2$, if correct, is approached from below and is still far from visible at $k = 10$; a floating-point extrapolation from $k = 8, 9, 10$ points to about $1.71$ rather than $2$.  Every value and every bound of $E_k$ stated here is machine-checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib.

families.paper_title: Exact windows in the adjacent weight ratio for the linear first-derivative bound of rational B\'ezier curves: the degree-$8$ threshold $\sqrt7$, a bounded degree-$7$ window, and four corrections to a published degree-$7$ illustration
families.paper_abstract: For a rational B\'ezier curve of degree $n$ with positive weights $\omega_i$, control vectors $\Delta_i$ and maximal adjacent weight ratio $\Omega=\max_i\max(\omega_{i+1}/\omega_i,\omega_i/\omega_{i+1})$, Li, Deng, Jin and Zhao conjectured the linear bound $\norm{\mathbf R'(t)}\le n\Omega\max_i\norm{\Delta_i}$ at every degree.  It holds for $n\le6$ and fails from $n=7$ on (Shi).  Shi's proof for $n=6$ (arXiv:2607.10425) reduces the bound at degree $n$ to the inequality $q_n(u;\rr)\le\Omega$ for an explicit variance-like function $q_n$ on the box $[\Omega^{-1},\Omega]^n$ of adjacent ratios, shows that the maximum of $q_n$ over the box lies on a vertex or an edge, defines the sharp constant $K(\Omega)=\sup q_n$, and asserts for $n=7$ that $K(\Omega)>\Omega$ for \emph{every} $\Omega>1$, illustrated by an edge configuration at $\Omega=2$.  We show that on the slice that carries the maximum the failure is confined to a window in $\Omega$, and we compute the window exactly.  Along the ``V-shaped'' vertex $\omega_i=\Omega^{\abs{i-m}}$ of the box, $q_n$ at the midpoint $u=1$ is an explicit rational function of $\Omega$, and for $\Omega>1$ the violation $q_n>\Omega$ holds exactly when $\Omega^2<7$ ($n=8$), $\Omega^3<18\Omega+42$ ($n=10$), $\Omega^4<33\Omega^2+132\Omega+198$ ($n=12$), and never ($n=6$).  So the linear bound fails at degree $8$ for every rational $1<\Omega<\sqrt7$; a floating-point sweep of all vertices and edges puts the threshold of the full degree-$8$ problem at $2.645751311$, which is $\sqrt7$ to the precision of the sweep.  At degree $7$, on the same slice at $u=7/9$, the violation holds exactly when an explicit integer polynomial $H_7(\Omega)$ of degree $7$ is positive; it is positive at $\Omega=21/20$, $11/10$ (Shi's published counterexample, made exact), $5/4$ and $313/250=1.252$, and not at $1253/1000$, $2$ or $3$.  Finally, in exact rational arithmetic from the source's own formulas, four corrections to Section~6 of arXiv:2607.10425v1: the interior critical point of its $\Omega=2$ edge is $x_*=2031250/17792841\approx0.114<\tfrac12$ and therefore inadmissible; its printed value $q_{\max}\approx2.18$ is exactly $28561/13440\approx2.125$; the two endpoints of the edge carry $q\approx1.689$ and $169/128$, so the edge exhibits no violation; and its assertion that $K(\Omega)>\Omega$ for every $\Omega>1$ is unsupported --- on the V-shaped slice there is no violation at $\Omega=2$ or $3$, and an exhaustive floating-point sweep of all vertices and edges finds none at $\Omega=3/2,2,3,5,10$.  The source's qualitative claim that the bound can fail at degree $7$ is right; its witness and its printed value are not, and its uniformity in $\Omega$ is unsupported. Every theorem is verified in Lean~4 over the rationals, by rational-function identities and exact arithmetic only, with no numerical or decision-procedure axioms.

The setup, kernel-checked at all ten cells: the nodes are the n+1 extremal points of Mathlib's Polynomial.Chebyshev.T R n in decreasing order with T_n(x_j) = (-1)^j, the Lagrange basis satisfies l_j(x_i) = delta_ij, each cube vertex interpolates its sign vector, and T_n^(k) is computed explicitly

families.paper_title: The Bojanov--Naidenov extremal problem for the $k$-th derivative\\ of algebraic polynomials: the finite cube-vertex check,\\ settled in every degree $n\le 6$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\pi_n^{\circ}$ be the real polynomials of degree at most $n$ bounded by $1$ on $[-1,1]$ and $T_n$ the Chebyshev polynomial.  Bojanov's problem, as recorded by Naidenov, asks whether $\int_{-1}^{1}\varphi(|P^{(k)}|)<\int_{-1}^{1}\varphi(|T_n^{(k)}|)$ for every strictly increasing convex $\varphi$, every $P\in\pi_n^{\circ}\setminus\{\pm T_n\}$ and every $2\le k\le n-1$.  Inside that range only $(n,k)=(4,2)$ was settled, by Zavalani (arXiv:2606.23020), who interpolates at the $n+1$ extremal points of $T_n$, passes by convexity to the cube of nodal values, and checks the $2^{n+1}$ vertices.  We run that reduction in exact arithmetic over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt D)$ at all ten pairs $3\le n\le 6$, $2\le k\le n-1$: at every vertex $y\in\{-1,1\}^{n+1}$ the integrated tails $\int(|P_y^{(k)}|-t)_+$ are dominated by those of $T_n^{(k)}$ at every level $t\ge0$, the bound is attained at $\pm T_n$, and the extremal sup norm is $T_n^{(k)}(1)$ ($24,80,192,200,840,1920,420,2688,10368,23040$).  Combined with the elementary convexity and tail-to-convex-order lemmas of the source, this gives the Bojanov--Naidenov inequality in its non-strict form --- for every nondecreasing convex $\varphi$ --- at the nine previously open pairs, and under the weaker Duffin--Schaeffer hypothesis $|P(\cos(j\pi/n))|\le1$, $j=0,\dots,n$; we point out that the sup-norm content of every such statement is Duffin and Schaeffer's Theorem~III of 1941, which the source proves at $(4,2)$, under the stronger hypothesis $\norm{P}_{C[-1,1]}\le1$, without citing it. A second finding concerns the method: the pointwise level-set domination through which the source proves its vertex bound is false at nine of the ten pairs, $(4,2)$ being the only one where it holds --- certified at six pairs by explicit vertex witnesses whose $k$-th derivative stays away from zero on $[-1,1]$, and found by external computation at the other three.  Each vertex is certified by a transport between two uniform partitions with degree-four Bernstein enclosures, whose only data per vertex is a pair of partition sizes; the certificates, the setup and the witnesses are verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}.

families.paper_title: The Goreinov--Tyrtyshnikov--Zamarashkin hypothesis at complementary column counts
families.paper_abstract: The Goreinov--Tyrtyshnikov--Zamarashkin hypothesis states that every real $n\times k$ matrix with orthonormal columns has a $k\times k$ row-submatrix whose smallest singular value is at least $1/\sqrt n$.  Sengupta and Pautov (arXiv:2604.05944) proved it for $k=2$ and every $n$, and their abstract lists the range $1<k<n-1$ as otherwise open.  We point out that the hypothesis at column count $k$ and at column count $n-k$ is one and the same statement: if $[\,U\mid V\,]$ is orthogonal, the smallest singular value of the $k\times k$ submatrix of $U$ on the rows $S$ equals that of the $(n-k)\times(n-k)$ submatrix of $V$ on the complementary rows.  The identity is not new -- Nesterenko states it, without proof, in arXiv:2511.02387 -- but we give an elementary proof from two Gram identities, Cauchy--Schwarz and one dimension count (no CS decomposition, no spectral theorem), and we draw the consequence that no paper in this literature draws: the $k=2$ theorem settles $k=n-2$ for every $n$, in particular the case $(n,k)=(5,3)$, so that the open range is $2<k<n-2$ and its first cell is $(6,3)$.  Complementing the Sengupta--Pautov extremal example shows, unconditionally, that $1/\sqrt n$ cannot be raised at $k=n-2$ for any $n\ge 3$; with the $k=2$ theorem this determines the best constant at every $k=n-2$ cell.  Every statement is checked in Lean~4 against Mathlib.

families.paper_title: Certified separation ratios for the Lyapunov operator on symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices at orders seven and nine, and the status of order six
families.paper_abstract:
For $A\in\R^{n	imes n}$ the Lyapunov operator $\Lop_A(X)=AX+XA^{	op}$ preserves the symmetric matrices $\Sn n$ and the skew-symmetric matrices $\Kn n$, and the symmetric-maximizer conjecture of Byers and Nash asserts that $
rm{\Lop_A|_{\Kn n}}\le
rm{\Lop_A|_{\Sn n}}$ for the norms induced by the Frobenius norm.  The conjecture holds for $n\le5$ (Chen and Tian) and fails for every $n\ge7$ (Kressner and Vandereycken, 2026, by an explicit integer matrix of order seven found with a numerical search and certified in exact arithmetic); order six is open.  We study the separation ratio $ho_n:=\sup_A
rm{\Lop_A|_{\Kn n}}^2/
rm{\Lop_A|_{\Sn n}}^2$ and give exact lower bounds for it: an explicit $7	imes7$ integer matrix with $ho_7>180190/179888>1.0016$, and an explicit $9	imes9$ integer matrix with $ho_9>156637/154311>1.0150$.  The two inequalities that Kressner and Vandereycken display in their proof already give $ho_7>1+1.46\cdot10^{-6}$ on division; the excess over $1$ certified here is about $1150$ times larger at order seven and about $10^4$ times larger at order nine.  The order-seven matrix of Kressner and Vandereycken itself achieves the ratio $1.00036$, and only in floating point.  Each bound is a pair of exact certificates: a rational $LDL^{	op}$ elimination written out as a sum-of-squares identity in the free entries of a symmetric matrix bounds the symmetric side from above, and an integer skew-symmetric witness bounds the skew side from below. The same method encloses both restricted norms of the original counterexample in exact brackets, $1195.5316\ldots\le
rm{\Lop_A|_{\Sn7}}^2<1196$ and $1196.0017\ldots\le

families.paper_title: Hurwitz minors with nonnegative coefficients:\\ the split-step Pad\'e denominators of $\exp(\iu t(\sqrt{1+z}-1))$ through order nine
families.paper_abstract: Walsken, Ehrhardt and Petrov (arXiv:2607.03521) integrate a one-way Helmholtz equation by the split-step Pad\'e scheme, whose marching step inverts the denominator $Q_P$ of the $[P/P]$ Pad\'e approximant at $z=0$ of the propagator symbol $f(z)=\exp(\iu t(\sqrt{1+z}-1))$, $t=k_0h>0$.  Their Conjecture~3.1 asserts that for every $t$ and $P$ all zeros of $Q_P$ lie strictly below the real axis; they prove it for $P\le4$ with a computer algebra system and give numerical evidence at $P=5$ and $P=9$.  We observe that with $u=\iu t$ every Pad\'e coefficient is a polynomial in $u$ with integer coefficients, and that after the rotation $z=\iu w$ and multiplication by the conjugate polynomial the question at each order is whether a real polynomial $N_P$ of degree $2P$ is a Hurwitz polynomial---an equivalence we prove in both directions.  For $P=5,6,7,8,9$ we compute the $2P$ leading principal minors of the Hurwitz matrix of $N_P$ exactly, by fraction-free elimination over $\Z[t]$, and find that every one of them is a polynomial in $t$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, not all zero, hence strictly positive for every $t>0$; the leading coefficient of $N_P$ is positive for every $t>0$ as well.  These computations are certified in Lean~4.  The classical Routh--Hurwitz criterion for real polynomials, which we cite and do not formalise, then gives Conjecture~3.1 for $P\le9$ and every $t>0$.  The coefficientwise sign pattern is a separate and stronger fact: we certify it for all leading principal minors at $P\le9$ and for every minor of the $2P\times2P$ Hurwitz matrix at $P\le4$ ($12\,869$ minors at $P=4$), so that, as far as computed, the Hurwitz matrix of $N_P$ is totally nonnegative over $\Z[t]$ in the coefficientwise order.  This is not the theorem of Asner, Kemperman and Holtz, which derives pointwise total nonnegativity from stability: here stability is what is in question, and the nonnegativity is in the parameter.

families.title: exact radix kernels for truncated Neumann series -- the minimum number of matrix products mu_m evaluating T_m(B) = I + B + ... + B^{m-1}: exact radix-15 kernels with four products do not exist, mu_15 = 5, and radix 9 is optimal among exact radix kernels below radix 17
families.description: For a square matrix `A` with `ρ(A) < 1`, the truncated Neumann series `S_k(A) = I + A + ⋯ + A^{k-1}` approximates `(I - A)^{-1}`. On dense problems the cost is counted in matrix-matrix products (GEMMs); additions and scalar multiples are free.
families.paper_title: Exact radix kernels for truncated Neumann series:\\ no four-product radix-15 kernel exists, and $\mu_{15}=5$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\Tm{m}(B) = I + B + \cdots + B^{m-1}$ be the radix-$m$ kernel of the truncated Neumann series and let $\mu_m$ be the least number of matrix products with which a straight-line program (products of linear combinations, starting from $I$ and $B$; additions and scalings free) evaluates $\Tm{m}$.  Sao (arXiv:2602.11843) gives an exact three-product radix-9 kernel, an approximate four-product radix-15 kernel whose output leaks $0.185\,B^{15} + 0.458\,B^{16}$, and asks whether exact radix-15 kernels exist.  We prove that they do not, over every field: a four-product program outputs a polynomial of degree exactly $16$ or of degree at most $12$; degrees $13$, $14$ and $15$ are impossible.  The proof is a degree-parity argument --- both factors of the last product are forced to have the same degree, so $\deg P_4$ is even, and $\deg P_4 = 14$ would force $\deg P_3 = 7$, itself twice a degree.  Consequently $\mu_{14},\mu_{15},\mu_{16} \ge 5$, the degree-16 spillover that Sao observes numerically is forced, and with the five-product construction $\Tm{15}(B) = \Tm{3}(B)\,\Tm{5}(B^3)$ of Dimitrov and Coelho one gets $\mu_{15} = 5$ exactly.  The exact radix-15 update therefore costs $7/\log_2 15 \approx 1.79$ products per doubling of the series length, worse than radix 9's $5/\log_2 9 \approx 1.58$; more precisely, radix 9 strictly beats every exact radix-$m$ kernel with $2 \le m \le 16$, and radix 17 is the first radix the argument leaves open.  Two attributions in the source are corrected: the quinary kernel $\mu_5 = 2$ is not in the paper it is credited to, and the ``degree 15 in 4 products'' scheme it cites is a degree-16 polynomial.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4 with no computational reflection and no axiom beyond the three standard ones.

families.title: the '?' cells of the associative-truncated-product table: an ATP on P_K is the quotient R[x]/(omega), the zero product (omega = phi_1 phi_K) is hyperbolic iff the mean of w is not a K-point Gauss node, and it is positive definite iff the mean and the Gauss nodes lie in Xi
families.description: Intrusive stochastic Galerkin (SG) discretisations of a nonlinear conservation law need a *discrete multiplication* on the finite-dimensional space `P_K(Ξ)` of polynomials of degree `≤ K` in the random variable `ξ ~ w`. Meghaichi and Xing (arXiv:2606.12632v3, math.NA) call a bilinear commutative map `∗ : P_K × P_K → P_K` a **truncated product** when it is *consistent* — `p ∗ q = p q` whenever `deg(pq) ≤ K` — and study the ones that are in addition **associative** (ATPs), because associativity is what makes the flux Jacobian blocks commute and the SG system hyperbolic.
families.paper_title: The zero truncated product on $P_K$ is hyperbolic exactly when\\ the mean is not a Gauss node: the `?' cells of the\\ associative-truncated-product table
families.paper_abstract: Meghaichi and Xing (arXiv:2606.12632) discretise nonlinear conservation laws with uncertainty by replacing the multiplication on the space $P_K$ of polynomials of degree at most $K$ in the random variable by an \emph{associative truncated product} (ATP), and they tabulate five such products against four properties; three cells of their table are printed `?'.  We observe that every ATP on $P_K$ is the quotient product $p\ast q=pq \bmod \omega$ for a unique monic $\omega$ of degree $K+1$, with $\omega=\phi_1\phi_K-\phi_1\ast\phi_K$ up to a scalar, so that hyperbolicity, symmetry and positive definiteness become statements about the roots of one polynomial.  For the \emph{zero product}, $\omega=\pi_1\pi_K$, the two `?' cells are settled exactly: it is hyperbolic if and only if $\pi_K(\mu)\neq0$, that is, iff the mean $\mu$ of the weight is not a node of its $K$-point Gauss rule --- a repeated root of $\omega$ always produces a Jordan chain --- and it is positive definite whenever $\mu$ and the Gauss nodes lie in $\Xi$, whether or not it is hyperbolic, because the eigenvalues of every multiplication operator are the values of the multiplier at the roots of $\omega$ with no diagonalisability assumption.  Consequently $K=1$ is never hyperbolic and $K=2$ always ($\pi_2(\mu)=-\Var w$), for a symmetric weight hyperbolicity is equivalent to $K$ even, and the two cells are independent: the Legendre weight at $K=3$ is defective but positive definite, while the uniform weight on $[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]$ at $K=2$ and an explicit four-point weight at $K=3$ (an odd $K$ that is hyperbolic) are hyperbolic but not positive definite.  The third `?' cell follows from the same dictionary and a lemma of the source: the collocation product at $K+1$ distinct nodes is symmetric iff the nodes are the zeros of $\pi_{K+1}+t\,\pi_K$ for some real $t$.  The two criteria, the cells and the controls are verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}, without compiled evaluation.

families.paper_title: Minimax regret against an adversarial experiment:\\ certified values for three to eight binary signals\\ and the two-point support of Nature's optimal mixture
families.paper_abstract: A decision-maker who will observe $n$ i.i.d.\ binary signals of unknown precision $\pi\in[\tfrac12,1]$ commits in advance to a belief $a_k$ for every count $k$ of high signals; an adversarial Nature mixes over $\pi$; the payoff is the mean-squared-error regret against an oracle who knows $\pi$, under a uniform prior on the binary state.  Che, Li and Luo (arXiv:2602.15246) solve this game for $n\le 3$ --- Nature mixes the two endpoint experiments $\{\tfrac12,1\}$ for $n\le2$ and $\{\tfrac12,\pi^*\}$ with an interior $\pi^*$ at $n=3$ --- state that a closed-form characterisation for $n>3$ is intractable by their approach, conjecture the two-point structure $\{\tfrac12,\pi_n^*\}$ for every $n$, and plot the values that the conjecture predicts for $3\le n\le18$.  We prove, without assuming anything about the structure of Nature's strategy, rational brackets $L_n\le \val_n\le U_n$ on the minimax regret for $n=3,\dots,8$, of width at most $2.1\cdot10^{-11}$: $L_n$ is what an explicit rational two-point mixture guarantees against every belief rule, and $U_n$ is what an explicit rational belief rule guarantees against every precision, proved by a Bernstein subdivision certificate.  The numbers agree with the source's conjecture-based numerics; what is new is that they are bounds.  A second certificate, with a margin vanishing exactly at the two conjectured atoms, shows that every finitely supported mixture guaranteeing $L_n$ --- in particular every finitely supported optimal one --- satisfies $\sum_i w_i\,(2p_i-1)^2(2p_i-1-\hat d_n)^2\le 8.4\cdot10^{-11}$, which localises Nature's optimal support at the two conjectured atoms with an explicit error bar; at $n=4$ at most $5.25\cdot10^{-4}$ of the mass lies further than $1/100$ from both.  Alongside, the game in which Nature is confined to $\{\tfrac12,1\}$ has the closed-form value $1/(4(1+2^{(n-1)/2})^2)$ for every $n$, which reproduces the source's $n\le2$ strategies and is strictly worse for Nature from $n=3$ on, by a factor that grows from below $2$ to above $21$; and $\val_3>\val_4>\dots>\val_8$.  Every statement is verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}.

families.paper_title: How small can a counterexample to the\\ Non-Cancelling-Intersections conjecture be?
families.paper_abstract: Wilhelm has refuted the Non-Cancelling-Intersections conjecture of Amarilli, Monet and Suciu by showing that for every prime $p\ge 10^{5}$ some marking $\mm$ of the lines of $\FF_p^2$ makes the lattice $\Pm$, of $p^3+2p^2+2$ elements, admit no winning dot-algebra tree; the smallest lattice his argument produces has $1\,000\,110\,003\,900\,047$ elements, and he asks how small a counterexample can be.  We answer with exact integer arithmetic on his own first moment.  First, his chain of inequalities, evaluated instead of simplified, already closes at $p=5273$, and $5273$ is the least such prime; the threshold $10^5$ comes from a single lossy step.  The chain is moreover not monotone in $p$: it fails again at $p=5309$, exactly where $\lceil\sqrt{2p}\,\rceil$ jumps.  Second, the same first moment used to its full strength --- the exact hypergeometric hit probability, a sharper Cauchy--Schwarz count of lines, and linear-programming duality over the trace profile --- closes at $p=59$, giving a lattice of $212\,343$ elements with no winning dot-algebra tree, smaller by a factor $4\,709\,879\,788.36\ldots$.  Here $59$ is least, and again the bound is not monotone: it fails at $61$ and closes again at $67$.  From below, every lattice with at most $8$ elements admits a winning dot-algebra tree, so the smallest counterexample has between $9$ and $212\,343$ elements.  All the statements above are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.title: Non-clashing teaching dimension against VC dimension, exhaustively: the full (VCD, NCTD) census of every concept class on at most five points (4,294,967,295 of them, none with NCTD > VCD), the exact values NCTD(2^[n]) = ceil(n/2) for n <= 5 with the hypercube-edge lower bound n <= 2*NCTD(2^[n]), the planar closed-neighbourhood census to 10 vertices (max NCTD = 2 against arXiv:2602.00657's bound of 5), and Warmuth's class as a kernel-checked counterexample to Lemma 2 of the withdrawn arXiv:2603.23561
families.description: For a finite concept class `C` over a domain `X` (a concept is a subset of `X`), a *teacher mapping* sends each `C ∈ C` to a set of examples consistent with `C`; since the labels are forced by `C`, a teaching set is just a subset `T(C) ⊆ X`. Kirkpatrick–Simon–Zilles (ALT 2019) and Fallat–Kirkpatrick–Simon–Soltani–Zilles (JMLR 24 (2023) 40:1–40:33) call `T` **non-clashing** when no two distinct concepts are each consistent with the other's teaching set; unfolded, that is the pairwise condition

families.paper_title: Non-clashing teaching on small domains:\\ a complete five-point census, a planar\\ closed-neighbourhood census, and the class\\ where a withdrawn proof fails
families.paper_abstract: For a finite concept class $\Cc$ over a finite domain, Kirkpatrick, Simon and Zilles and Fallat, Kirkpatrick, Simon, Soltani and Zilles ask whether $\NCTD(\Cc)>\VCD(\Cc)$ is possible; the only search they report is over ``those classes for which $\PBTD>\VCD$ is known from the literature''.  We report an exhaustive computation over all $4\,294\,967\,295$ concept classes on a five-point domain --- the joint distributions of $(\VCD,\NCTD)$ and of $(\VCD,\NCTDp)$ --- which finds $\NCTD\le\VCD$ throughout, so on domains of at most five points the question is settled, by enumeration.  We then show that Warmuth's class --- the class both of the sources above print when they pose the question --- has VC dimension $2$ and no two-element fragment of frequency $1$, so it is a counterexample to Lemma~2 of a preprint that claimed $\NCTD\le\VCD$ in general and was withdrawn by its authors with the comment ``The proof of Lemma 2 is wrong''; the remaining step of that argument is correct, so the whole claim rested on that lemma.  For the closed neighbourhoods of a planar graph Bhore, Khazaliya and Mc~Inerney prove $\NCTD\le5$ and ask whether the bound is tight: we exhibit the smallest graph on which the value $2$ is attained and report an exhaustive census showing that $2$ is the true maximum up to ten vertices.  Around these we give a formal development, in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}, of the small-domain values $\NCTD(2^{X})=\lceil n/2\rceil$ for $n\le5$ with explicit witnesses, and of the hypercube case of the degree lower bound; both are theorems of Kirkpatrick, Simon and Zilles for every $n$, and are recorded here as verified, not as new.  The census computations are external to the formal development and are labelled as such wherever they are used.

families.paper_title: The maximum nonlinearity of negabent Boolean functions\\ in three, five and seven variables
families.paper_abstract: A Boolean function $f\colon\F_2^n\to\F_2$ is \emph{negabent} when its nega-Hadamard transform $\Neg_f(a)=\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)\oplus a\cdot x}\,i^{\wt(x)}$ has constant modulus $2^{n/2}$.  For even $n$ the negabent functions are the bent functions shifted by $\sigma_2=\bigoplus_{i<j}x_ix_j$, so the largest nonlinearity in the class is the bent value $2^{n-1}-2^{n/2-1}$ whenever a bent-negabent function exists.  For odd $n$ we found no value of the class maximum in the literature: Carlet, \DJ{}urasevi\'c, Franch, Jakobovi\'c, Mariot and Picek (arXiv:2602.00843) quote the range $[\,2^{n-1}-2^{(n-1)/2},\ 2\lfloor 2^{n-2}-2^{n/2-2}\rfloor\,]$ of the unrestricted odd-$n$ problem and state that it ``will also represent the nonlinearity range for negabent functions in an odd number of variables'', and Su, Pott and Tang's characterisation of the class yields that $f\oplus\sigma_2$ is semibent, which says nothing about $\nl_f$ itself.  We determine the class maximum for $n=3,5,7$: it is $2$, $12$ and $56$ respectively, in each case the maximum nonlinearity over \emph{all} Boolean functions of that many variables; in particular the upper endpoint $58$ of the quoted range at $n=7$ is attained by no negabent function.  At $n=3$ the class is enumerated from the definition: $64$ functions, the $16$ affine ones of nonlinearity $0$ and $48$ of nonlinearity $2$.  At $n=5$ and $n=7$ the lower bounds are explicit quadratic witnesses of the form $u(x')\oplus\sigma_2(x')\oplus x_n\sigma_1(x')$ with $u$ bent-negabent in $n-1$ variables; the $896$ functions of this form at $n=5$, $u$ ranging over the bent functions of four variables, are pairwise distinct, all negabent, and split $128:768$ between nonlinearity $8$ and $12$. The census of the whole class at $n=5$ --- $802\,816$ functions, the maximum $12$ attained $205\,056$ times --- is reported as a computation outside the formal development.  Every theorem is checked in Lean~4 by compiled evaluation of the definitions themselves.

families.title: The greedy heuristic for the l_0-constrained feature-based newsvendor has no approximation guarantee: an explicit D = 3, d = 2, n = 4 instance whose loss ratio G(S_greedy)/G(S_opt) is at least gamma/2 for every gamma >= 8 (unbounded), whose greedy gain falls strictly below the submodular 1 - 1/e bound, and whose seven exact values at gamma = 8 give the ratio exactly 6 -- answering the open question of arXiv:2609.01544v1 in the negative
families.description: **The greedy heuristic for the `ℓ₀`-constrained feature-based newsvendor has no approximation guarantee.** Founded 2026-09-03 from arXiv:2609.01544v1 (Yuan–Wang, *Variable Selection for Feature-Based Newsvendor*, primary `stat.ML`, cross `cs.LG`, v1 only).
families.paper_title: The greedy heuristic for the $\ell_0$-constrained feature-based newsvendor has no approximation guarantee
families.paper_abstract: Yuan and Wang (arXiv:2609.01544) select features for a linear newsvendor decision rule by minimising the empirical newsvendor (pinball) loss plus a ridge term under a hard sparsity constraint $\|\omega\|_0\le d$, and propose a greedy heuristic for the resulting support-selection problem $\min_{|S|\le d}G(S)$.  They leave the approximation quality of the greedy iterate as an open question, noting that $G$ is not submodular.  We answer the question in the negative.  On an explicit instance with three features, four samples, budget $d=2$ and unit costs, every greedy run, under every tie-breaking rule, ends at a support of value at least $\tfrac12$ while the optimal support has value at most $1/\gamma$, for every ridge parameter $\gamma\ge 8$; the loss ratio is therefore at least $\gamma/2$ and no constant-factor guarantee exists.  The same instance breaks the guarantee in the gain form used by the weak-submodularity literature: the greedy gain is strictly below $1-1/e$ times the optimal gain for every $\gamma\ge 8$, and $G$ has increasing marginal returns.  At $\gamma=8$ all seven values of $G$ are determined exactly, each by a matching primal--dual pair, and the ratio is exactly $6$.  We also explain why the question was genuinely open: the standard lower bound on the submodularity ratio requires a differentiable loss with a finite restricted-smoothness constant, and the pinball loss has none.  Every value certificate rests on a weak-duality inequality proved from first principles; strong duality is never assumed.  All theorems are verified in Lean~4 with Mathlib.

families.paper_title: Exact versus unique nondeterministic automatic complexity: the missing length-16 automaton, explicit witnesses at lengths 15 and 16, and complete censuses at lengths 14 and 15
families.paper_abstract: For a word $x$ over a finite alphabet, $\ANe(x)$ is the least number of states of a nondeterministic finite automaton that accepts $x$ and no other word of length $|x|$, and $\AN(x)$ is the least number of states of one that in addition accepts $x$ along a single computation; always $\ANe(x) \le \AN(x)$.  Kjos-Hanssen and Rivera Petit have recently shown that the inequality can be strict, that $13$ is the least length at which it can be, and that up to renaming of letters the separating words of length $13$ are exactly the $365$ letter-mergings of $\texttt{0123444445126}$.  They also print a table of the pairs $(\ANe, \AN)$ at lengths $13$ through $17$, but leave the rows for lengths $15$ and $16$ without a witness of any kind: their length-15 automaton diagram carries no letters on any arrow, and there is no length-16 diagram at all.  (At lengths $13$, $14$ and $17$ a word is printed, or recoverable from a labelled diagram.)  We supply the missing witnesses and certify them.  The word $\wsix = \texttt{0123}\,\texttt{4}^8\,\texttt{5126}$ --- their length-13 witness with its run of fours lengthened from five to eight --- satisfies $\ANe = 8 < 9 = \AN$, with an explicit eight-state exactly accepting automaton and an explicit nine-state uniquely accepting one; deleting its last letter leaves a length-15 word with $\ANe = 7 < 8 = \AN$.  Two further separating words of length $16$ and the reversal of the length-15 one are certified in the same way.  We also carry the census two lengths further: at length $14$ exactly $20$ words separate the two measures, all letter-mergings of $\texttt{01233333333401}$, all with $(\ANe, \AN) = (6,7)$, and each of the twenty is certified individually; at length $15$ exactly $74$ do, forming $37$ reversal pairs, all with $(\ANe, \AN) = (7,8)$, and none of them binary, although lengths $13$ and $14$ both carry binary witnesses.  The Hyde--Kjos-Hanssen bound $\AN(x) \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ is verified for all $190{,}899{,}322$ canonical words of length $14$, one length beyond the published verification.  Every value stated below is machine-checked in Lean~4 except where it is explicitly labelled otherwise: the two censuses, the bound verification and a handful of auxiliary counts are computations outside the formal development.

families.paper_title: How many nice bases does a direct sum of Heisenberg algebras have? A binary-partition lower bound
families.paper_abstract:
A basis of a Lie algebra is \emph{nice} when each bracket of two basis vectors is a multiple of a single basis vector and, for a fixed basis vector, the pairs whose bracket is a nonzero multiple of it are pairwise disjoint.  Two nice bases are \emph{equivalent} when an automorphism carries one to multiples of the other, and $
u_\g$ counts the classes.  Der'e and Gantois record that $
u$ of the direct sum of $2k$ copies of the Heisenberg algebra $\h_3$ is at least $k+1$ (Gorbatsevich) and that the exact number is unknown.  We prove $
u_{\hm m}\ge b(m)$, where $b(m)$ is the number of partitions of $m$ into powers of two (OEIS A018819): for $p=2^d$ the complete bipartite graph $K_{p,p}$, edge-coloured by the regular action of $(\Z/2)^d$, is the bracket graph of a nice basis of $\hm p$ with $p^2$ nonzero brackets --- the Sylvester--Hadamard character table is the change of basis --- and concatenating blocks over a binary partition of $m$ gives $b(m)$ nice bases, pairwise inequivalent because the bracket graph of a nice basis is an invariant of its equivalence class, a slight strengthening of Gorbatsevich's observation that the number of nonzero brackets is such an invariant.  The bound exceeds $k+1$ from four summands on: $4$, $6$ and $10$ against $3$, $4$ and $5$ at $m=4,6,8$.  For $m\le8$ every one of the $35$ bases is certified in Lean~4 by exhaustive evaluation of the definition, with no axioms, and for $m\le6$ so is the pairwise inequivalence.  A computation over Conti and Rossi's classification of nice nilpotent Lie algebras of dimension $9$ gives $
u_{\hm3}=2=b(3)$, outside the range of the published determinations, and we conjecture $
u_{\hm m}=b(m)$ for every $m$.

families.paper_title: Nice grid diagrams for the twelve fibered knots of at most thirteen crossings left open by Itzlinger's census
families.paper_abstract: A grid diagram is \emph{nice} (Itzlinger, arXiv:2602.02642, Definition~2.6) if it has a unique grid state realising the winding-matrix upper bound $A'(x) \le \min\{\rn,\cn\}$ for the Alexander function; by the Ghiggini--Ni theorem a knot with a nice grid diagram is fibered, and Itzlinger asks whether every fibered knot has one (his Question~2.7, a strengthening of Open Problem~17.1.5 of Ozsv\'ath--Stipsicz--Szab\'o).  His search found nice diagrams for $5385$ of the $5397$ fibered prime knots of crossing number at most $13$ and printed the twelve knots it could not settle: $12n_{79}$, $12n_{168}$, $13n_{282}$, $13n_{917}$, $13n_{1279}$, $13n_{1281}$, $13n_{1413}$, $13n_{1826}$, $13n_{2915}$, $13n_{3089}$, $13n_{3904}$ and $13n_{3932}$.  We show that all twelve admit a nice grid diagram.  For each knot we give an explicit grid of size $13$ or $14$, reached from KnotInfo's minimal grid diagram of the knot by commutations, a single $X$-NW stabilisation, further commutations and, for four of them, an orientation reversal, together with its unique perfect grid state; the Alexander grading of that state equals the Seifert genus in every case.  Uniqueness of the perfect state and the legality of every move are checked in the Lean~4 kernel.  Along the way we record the soundness of Itzlinger's elimination test, a two-line lemma (row-perfect and column-perfect states coincide when $\rn = \cn$) that his decision procedure silently relies on, and an off-by-one discrepancy between the count in his abstract ($5385$) and the one in his closing section ($5384$).  Consequently every fibered prime knot of crossing number at most $13$ in the KnotInfo census admits a nice grid diagram.
