families.paper_title: Circles of radii $1,2,\dots,n$ around a central circle: the exact minimal polynomials of $R^{\ast}(4)$ and $R_{\dagger}(4)$, and the closure and seam equations made algebraic
families.paper_abstract: Falconi (arXiv:2607.28654) studies circles of radii $1,2,\dots,n$, all externally tangent to a central circle of radius $R$ and pairwise non-overlapping, and asks how small $R$ can be.  For a cyclic order $\sigma$ the necklace of consecutive tangencies closes at the unique root $\Rchain(\sigma)$ of the transcendental equation $\sum_i \theta_R(\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1}) = 2\pi$, where $\theta_R(a,b) = 2\arcsin\sqrt{ab/((R+a)(R+b))}$; the optimal order is a fixed Supnick tour $\sigstar$, and the optimum $R^{\ast}(n)$ equals $\Rchain(\sigstar)$ as long as the necklace is geometrically realizable, which the source certifies for $n \le 7$.  The source prints its optima as decimals, with an exact form only for $n = 3$.  We show that $R^{\ast}(4)$ is the unique positive root of the irreducible quartic $383x^4 + 3840x^3 + 9408x^2 - 9216$, and that the radius-maximising necklace value $R_{\dagger}(4)$ of the source's Proposition~8 is the unique positive root of $125x^4 + 1280x^3 + 2880x^2 - 3072$; the roots agree with the printed decimals $0.844453589560855604\ldots$ and $0.867281640255$.  Both come from a general statement: for four circles of radii $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order the closure equation is equivalent to an explicit two-radical identity and forces the quartic $[(a-c)^2(b-d)^2 - 16abcd]R^4 - 16abcd(a+b+c+d)R^3 - 8abcd[(a+c)(b+d)+2ac+2bd]R^2 + 16a^2b^2c^2d^2 = 0$, whose curvature form is, term for term, the four-petal case of the generalised Descartes theorem of Mathews and Zymaris (arXiv:2310.11701)---a paper the source cites; we re-derive it by elementary elimination and record the equivalence.  On the realizability side we give an exact polynomial criterion for one circle failing to separate two others, prove that for every real $n \ge 8$ and every $R \ge 21/4$ the unit circle fails to separate the circles of radii $n$ and $n-1$, and deduce the source's Proposition~9 on its whole certified range $8 \le n \le 13$ from the closure equation alone; the seam mathematics is already in the source author's public repository as a post-publication theorem, and is included here as a kernel-checked account of it.  Two printed decimals of the source do not reproduce ($\theta_R(13,12) = 0.83470$, not $0.83488$; the $n = 10$ chain bound is $9.7216$, not $\approx 9.90$); neither affects any stated conclusion.  Every theorem is checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib on the three standard axioms, with no numerical enclosure of $\arcsin$ anywhere: the transcendental equations are eliminated, not approximated.

families.title: The first-order lattice ladder for the affine Bernstein basis on a q-quadratic lattice: Conjecture conj:ladder of arXiv:2608.04802v1, settled uniformly in n
families.description: **The first-order lattice ladder for the affine Bernstein basis on a `q`-quadratic lattice — Conjecture `conj:ladder` of arXiv:2608.04802v1, settled.**

statements.label: Conjecture conj:ladder of arXiv:2608.04802v1, settled and sharpened: for every n >= 3 (the source asks n >= 4), every 0 <= k <= n and every q in (0,1), the first-order lattice ladder sigma * D_x B^n_k = tau * S_x B^n_k with deg sigma <= 2 and deg tau <= 1 forces sigma = tau = 0. Proved uniformly in n from the norm identity QB4 and the coprimality QB5, computing no determinant. Both the mu form (ladder_trivial) and the q form (conj_ladder_q) are bound here.

The conjugate-pair representation that justifies the definitions: for every real x and every d with d^2 = (mu^2-1)(x^2-1), B^n_k(mu*x + d) = (S_x B^n_k)(x) + d (D_x B^n_k)(x), and likewise with -d. This pins Sp and Dp as the two components of the half-step value in the quadratic extension R[x][d]/(d^2 - (mu^2-1)(x^2-1)).

The lattice bridge: on the q-quadratic lattice x(s) = (q^s + q^-s)/2 with Q = q^(1/2), mu = (Q+Q^-1)/2, the two half-step abscissae satisfy x(s+1/2) + x(s-1/2) = 2 mu x(s) and ((x(s+1/2)-x(s-1/2))/2)^2 = (mu^2-1)(x(s)^2-1); consequently the polynomials Sp, Dp evaluated at x(s) are exactly the source's S_x B^n_k and D_x B^n_k.

The norm identity: (S_x B^n_k)^2 - (mu^2-1)(x^2-1) (D_x B^n_k)^2 = (C(n,k)/2^n)^2 (x+mu)^{2k} (x-mu)^{2(n-k)} for every n and every k <= n. Equivalently, the product of the two half-step values of the affine Bernstein element factors completely, with the only roots x = +-mu.

S_x B^n_k and D_x B^n_k are coprime in R[x], for every n, every k <= n and every q in (0,1) -- the rank statement the source says is unavailable for n >= 4. Proved by a constructive Bezout chain: (S_x B^n_k)(mu) and (S_x B^n_k)(-mu) are nonzero, so S is coprime to (x-mu) and (x+mu), hence to the right-hand side of the norm identity, hence to D.

Sharpness of QB1 in n: for n <= 2, every k <= n and every q in (0,1), (sigma, tau) = (S_x B^n_k, D_x B^n_k) is a nonzero solution of eq:ladder with deg sigma <= 2 and deg tau <= 1. With QB1 this gives the exact dichotomy: eq:ladder has a nonzero solution if and only if n <= 2.
mu = (q^(1/2) + q^(-1/2))/2 > 1 for every q in (0,1), so the q form of the conjecture (conj_ladder_q) follows from the mu form.

Negative controls. (i) Non-vacuity: D_x B^n_k is not the zero polynomial for n >= 3 and mu > 1, so eq:ladder is a genuine constraint. (ii) Too-small control: the degree bounds deg sigma <= 2, deg tau <= 1 cannot be dropped -- without them (S_x B^n_k, D_x B^n_k) is a nonzero solution for every n. (iii) The hypothesis on mu is not decoration: at mu = 1 (that is q = 1) the classical ladder (1-x^2) D_x B^3_0 = (-3-3x) S_x B^3_0 is a nonzero solution; at mu = -1 so is (1-x^2, -3+3x); at mu = 0 one has S_x B^3_1 = -D_x B^3_1, so (1,-1) solves.

Reproduction of the source's four displayed degree-three polynomials, from the definitions, in the kernel: 8 D_x B^3_0 = (mu^2-4) + 6 mu x - (4 mu^2-1) x^2; 8 S_x B^3_0 = (4-3mu^2) + 3mu(mu^2-2)x + 3(2mu^2-1)x^2 - mu(4mu^2-3)x^3; (8/3) D_x B^3_1 = -mu^2 - 2 mu x + (4mu^2-1)x^2; (8/3) S_x B^3_1 = mu^2 - mu(3mu^2-2)x - (2mu^2-1)x^2 + mu(4mu^2-3)x^3.

The source's eq:ladderdet reproduced exactly: with 8 M_{3,0} and (8/3) M_{3,1} the coefficient matrices the source displays (columns = the coefficient vectors of D_x B^3_k, x D_x B^3_k, x^2 D_x B^3_k, -S_x B^3_k, -x S_x B^3_k), det(8 M_{3,0}) = 64 (mu^2-1)^6 and det((8/3) M_{3,1}) = -64 mu^8 (mu^2-1)^2, i.e. det M_{3,0} = (mu^2-1)^6/512 and det M_{3,1} = -243 mu^8 (mu^2-1)^2/512 as printed, and det M_{3,2} = -det M_{3,1}, det M_{3,3} = -det M_{3,0}.

The exact degenerate locus of the ladder. For every n >= 3, every k <= n and every REAL mu with mu != 0 and mu^2 != 1, eq:ladder admits only the trivial solution -- equivalently the (n+2) x 5 coefficient matrix M_{n,k} has full column rank 5. Together with QB8(iii), which exhibits a nonzero degree-three solution at each of mu = 0, 1, -1, the rank of M_{n,k} drops exactly on {mu = 0, 1, -1}. q in (0,1) is the special case mu > 1.

Computed 5th determinantal divisor of the ladder matrix M_{n,k} (the gcd of all C(n+2,5) maximal minors, whose roots are the rank-drop points), for 3 <= n <= 7 and every k: always c * mu^{a(n,k)} (mu^2-1)^{b(n,k)} with c a nonzero rational, b(n,k) = 6 for k in {0,n} and 2 otherwise, and a(n,k) = (0,8,8,0) for n=3, (0,5,9,5,0) for n=4, (0,0,8,8,0,0) for n=5, (0,0,5,9,5,0,0) for n=6, (0,0,0,8,8,0,0,0) for n=7.

families.paper_title: The affine Bernstein basis on the $q$-quadratic lattice\\ admits no first-order lattice ladder beyond degree two
families.paper_abstract: On the $q$-quadratic (Askey--Wilson) lattice, Area (arXiv:2608.04802) introduced the affine Bernstein basis $\Bs^n_k(x)=\binom nk\bigl(\frac{1+x}{2}\bigr)^k\bigl(\frac{1-x}{2}\bigr)^{n-k}$ and asked whether it satisfies a first-order lattice ladder $\sigma\,\Dx\Bs^n_k=\tau\,\Sx\Bs^n_k$ with $\deg\sigma\le2$ and $\deg\tau\le1$, where $\Dx$ and $\Sx$ are the divided-difference and averaging operators of the lattice.  He proved that a nonzero solution exists for $n\le2$ and that only the trivial one does for $n=3$, by an explicitly factorised $5\times5$ determinant, and conjectured the same for every $n\ge4$ and every $q\in(0,1)$, noting that no general determinant or rank formula was available.  We prove the conjecture, for every $n\ge3$, every $0\le k\le n$ and every $q\in(0,1)$, computing no determinant.  The engine is a norm identity: with $\mu=(q^{1/2}+q^{-1/2})/2$, the two half-step values of $\Bs^n_k$ are conjugate in the quadratic extension $\R[x][d]/(d^2-(\mu^2-1)(x^2-1))$, and their product is $\bigl(\binom nk/2^n\bigr)^2(x+\mu)^{2k}(x-\mu)^{2(n-k)}$.  Hence $\Sx\Bs^n_k$ and $\Dx\Bs^n_k$ are coprime for every $n$, which is the missing rank statement, and a degree count finishes the proof.  With the $n\le2$ half this is an exact dichotomy: the ladder has a nonzero solution if and only if $n\le2$.  The argument sees $q$ only through $\mu$ and works for every real $\mu\notin\{0,1,-1\}$; each of the three excluded values carries a nonzero solution already in degree three, so this is the exact degenerate locus.  Every result is machine-checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib.

families.title: Both halves of Guo-Zudilin's Problem 1 (arXiv:1812.11322v2, JMAA 475 (2019) 1636-1646): the q-congruence sum_{k=0}^{(n-1)/2} (q;q^2)_k^2 (q^2;q^4)_k / ((q^2;q^2)_k^2 (q^4;q^4)_k) (-q)^k = 0 mod Phi_n(q) for n = 7 mod 8, and the closed form it asks to be found for n = 3 mod 8 -- proved for all n by a Jackson q-Clausen split at a = q^{-3n}, and kernel-checked at 25 values of n through an import-free integer-coefficient-array layer (Polynomial.cyclotomic being noncomputable in Mathlib)
families.description: **Source.** Victor J. W. Guo and Wadim Zudilin, *On a `q`-deformation of modular forms*, arXiv:1812.11322 (v2, 2019-03-21 — the latest version), J. Math. Anal. Appl. **475** (2019) 1636–1646, DOI `10.1016/j.jmaa.2019.03.035`. arXiv primary category math.NT; MSC 11F33.

statements.label: Problem 1(a) of arXiv:1812.11322v2 (Guo-Zudilin, JMAA 475 (2019) 1636-1646), kernel-checked: Phi_n(q) divides the cleared numerator N_n of S(n) = sum_{k=0}^{(n-1)/2} (q;q^2)_k^2 (q^2;q^4)_k / ((q^2;q^2)_k^2 (q^4;q^4)_k) (-q)^k, i.e. S(n) = 0 (mod Phi_n(q)), at all 14 values n = 7, 15, 23, 31, 39, 47, 55, 63, 71, 79, 87, 95, 103, 111 (n = 7 mod 8), seven of them composite; deg N_111 = 12320 with coefficients to 31 decimal digits

The q-congruence Problem 1 of arXiv:1812.11322v2 asks to be FOUND for n = 3 mod 8: S(n) = (q,q^2;q^4)_{(3n-1)/8}^2 (-q;q)_{(n-1)/2} q^{-(1-n)^2/4} / (q^4;q^4)_{(3n-1)/4}^2 (mod Phi_n(q)) -- the source's own Theorem 5 formula with (n-1)/8 -> (3n-1)/8 and (n-1)/4 -> (3n-1)/4, everything else unchanged; kernel-checked as Phi_n | E_n at all 11 values n = 3, 11, 19, 27, 35, 43, 51, 59, 67, 75, 83 (deg E_83 = 24193) and verified exactly in Z[q] to n = 107

Proof of BOTH halves of Problem 1, for all n: Jackson's q-Clausen identity at a = q^{-3n}, z = -q (which terminates exactly when n = 3 mod 4, where the source's own a = q^{-n} does not) gives sum_{k=0}^{(3n-1)/2} T'_k = A' B'; modulo Phi_n(q) the head is S(n), the middle block (n+1)/2 <= k <= n-1 has Phi_n-valuation 3 and vanishes, and the tail satisfies T'_{n+i} = T'_n T_i with regularised value T'_n = 1, so the left side is 2 S(n); then B' = 0 by the source's Theorem 3 gives S(n) = 0 for n = 7 mod 8, and A', B' evaluated by the source's Theorems 4 and 3 give the QM2 closed form for n = 3 mod 8 after two elementary Pochhammer reflections

Sharpness, uniform over all four residue classes mod 8: the source's Theorem 2 shows the SAME summand with weight q^{2k} vanishes modulo Phi_n(q)^2 for every n = 3 mod 4, but with weight (-q)^k the Phi_n-valuation is EXACTLY 1 everywhere -- Phi_n(q)^2 does not divide N_n for n = 7 mod 8 (n = 7..55) nor for n = 5 mod 8 (n = 5..37), nor E_n for n = 3 mod 8 (n = 3..35, the QM2 closed form) nor for n = 1 mod 8 (n = 9..33, the source's Theorem 5), nor the Theorem 3 numerator T3(n) for n = 5, 7 mod 8 (n = 5..23)

Engine controls on the import-free Array Int layer: Phi_1, Phi_2, Phi_7, Phi_12, Phi_15 against their textbook coefficient vectors; Phi_105 of degree 48 with exactly two coefficients -2 and every other in {0, +-1} (the classical first cyclotomic polynomial with a coefficient outside {0, +-1}); Phi_n monic on 12 values; deg N_n = n^2 - 1 on 14 values; and q^n = 1 (mod Phi_n) as the e+n shift of the QM2 exponent

Compute-first gate, kernel-checked: the source's Theorem 5 in both published cases (n = 5 mod 8 zero at n = 5, 13, 21, 29, 37, 45; n = 1 mod 8 closed form at n = 9, 17, 25, 33, 41) through exactly the code path rows QM1 and QM2 use, and its Theorem 3 vanishing at n = 5, 7 mod 8 (n = 5..31) together with its failure at n = 1, 3 mod 8

Thirteen refuted claim shapes, false at all 91 (n, claim) pairs checked: Phi_n(q)^2 divides none of N_n (n = 5, 7 mod 8), E_n (n = 1, 3 mod 8) or the Theorem 3 numerator T3(n) (n = 5, 7 mod 8) -- 27 pairs; S(n) is not 0 mod Phi_n(q) for n = 1 mod 8 (n = 9..41) or n = 3 mod 8 (n = 3..43), and T3(n) is not 0 for n = 1, 3 mod 8 (n = 3..27) -- 18 pairs, wrong class; and the QM2 closed form with j-1, with j+1, with the source's denominator index (n-1)/4, and with exponent e+1 is false at every one of n = 3, 11, 19, 27, 35 -- 20 pairs; plus the 26 non-vacuity pairs of row QC4

Non-vacuity: Phi_n(q) divides neither the cleared denominator D_n = (q^2;q^2)_{(n-1)/2}^2 (q^4;q^4)_{(n-1)/2} (14 values of n) nor the closed form's denominator (q^4;q^4)_{(3n-1)/4}^2 (12 values), so both are units modulo Phi_n(q) and the polynomial divisibilities of QM1 and QM2 really are the stated q-congruences

families.paper_title: Both halves of Guo--Zudilin's Problem~1: the $q$-congruence for $n\equiv7\pmod 8$ and the closed form for $n\equiv3\pmod 8$
families.paper_abstract: For odd $n$ put $S_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{(q;q^2)_k^2(q^2;q^4)_k}{(q^2;q^2)_k^2(q^4;q^4)_k}(-q)^k$. Guo and Zudilin evaluated $S_n$ modulo the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n(q)$ for $n\equiv1\pmod4$ and left the two remaining residue classes as the only open problem of their paper: to show that $S_n\equiv0\pmod{\Phi_n(q)}$ for $n\equiv7\pmod8$, and to find a related $q$-congruence for $n\equiv3\pmod8$.  We settle both.  The vanishing holds for every positive $n\equiv7\pmod8$, and for every positive $n\equiv3\pmod8$ \[ S_n\;\equiv\;\frac{(q,q^2;q^4)_{(3n-1)/8}^2\,(-q;q)_{(n-1)/2}} {(q^4;q^4)_{(3n-1)/4}^2}\,q^{-(1-n)^2/4} \pmod{\Phi_n(q)}, \] which is the $n\equiv1\pmod8$ formula of Guo and Zudilin with the two indices $(n-1)/8$ and $(n-1)/4$ replaced by $(3n-1)/8$ and $(3n-1)/4$ --- exactly the substitution their own auxiliary theorems make when they pass from $n\equiv1$ to $n\equiv3\pmod8$, and, in an equivalent normalisation, the substitution $n\mapsto3n$ applied to every index at once.  Together with their result this evaluates $S_n$ modulo $\Phi_n(q)$ in all four residue classes of odd $n$ modulo $8$. The proof specialises Jackson's $q$-analogue of Clausen's identity at $a=q^{-3n}$ rather than at $a=q^{-n}$: this is the specialisation that terminates precisely when $n\equiv3\pmod4$, and the extra length of the resulting sum is absorbed by a tail identity that returns a second copy of $S_n$.  We also show, by exact computation, that neither congruence survives a squaring of the modulus, in contrast with the $q^{2k}$-weighted companion sum, which Guo and Zudilin evaluate modulo $\Phi_n(q)^2$.  Twenty-five instances of the two congruences, at $n$ up to $111$, together with the published cases and thirteen refuted variants, have been verified by the Lean~4 kernel in exact integer arithmetic.

families.title: The secret-sharing level of a finite group: which collaborations of parties can read a message stored in an extreme point of the decohered quantum double D(G), for the invariant arXiv:2506.04221v2 TABLE II tabulates on three groups and asks about in general
families.description: Derived from **arXiv:2506.04221v2** (Tai-Hsuan Yang, Bowen Shi, Jong Yeon Lee, *Topological Mixed States: Phases of Matter from Axiomatic Approaches*), Section VI B "Secret sharing models", p. 19-20 of the arXiv PDF: Eq. (55)-(58), Fig. 15(b), TABLE II, and the printed question **"Do all non-Abelian quantum doubles have this property?"**, together with Proposition 14 and Eq. (44) of Section VI A "Non-Abelian quantum double" (p. 18).

statements.label: The three two-party marginals are equivalent, so the source's TABLE II is a three-valued invariant: for every finite group G, the pair of conjugacy classes (C_g, C_h) determines the simultaneous class C_{g,h} of a commuting pair if and only if (C_g, C_{gh}) does, if and only if (C_h, C_{gh}) does -- there is no group in which one pair of parties can read the stored message and another pair cannot
Every finite abelian group is level 1: two parties can read the stored message (TABLE II, row 'Abelian')

The general criterion for failing level 1: if some element g of a finite group commutes with a conjugate x g x^{-1} different from itself, then the commuting pairs (g, g) and (g, x g x^{-1}) have the same pair of conjugacy classes and lie in different simultaneous classes, so no two parties can read the stored message
A finite group with a normal abelian subgroup that is not central is not level 1
A non-abelian finite group of nilpotency class at most 2 -- every commutator central -- is not level 1

The level is inherited by direct factors: if G is level 3 then G x H is level 3 for every finite H, and if no two parties can read G's message then none can read (G x H)'s -- so level-3 groups exist in every order divisible by 12

TABLE II row 'S3' reproduced from the group-theoretic definition: the symmetric group on three letters is level 2 -- no two parties can read the stored message, the three two-party marginals together can

The source's own A4 computation verified: Eq. (57)-(58) hold for alpha = (12)(34), beta = (13)(24), gamma = (14)(23), and its printed 'One can check' sentence C_{alpha,beta} = {(alpha,beta),(beta,gamma),(gamma,alpha)}, C_{alpha,gamma} = {(alpha,gamma),(beta,alpha),(gamma,beta)} is exact, so (alpha, beta, gamma) satisfies every clause of Eq. (56)
TABLE II row 'A4' reproduced: the alternating group on four letters is level 3 -- not even the three two-party marginals determine the stored message

The level is not monotone under subgroups: S4 is level 2 although it contains A4, which is level 3 -- so 'contains a level-3 subgroup' is not the criterion, and the classification cannot be read off small subgroups

The exhaustive census: of the 213 non-abelian groups of order at most 63, not one is level 1, exactly 175 are level 2 and exactly 38 are level 3; with the abelian theorem this settles the level of all 319 groups of order at most 63

The orders of the 38 level-3 groups of order at most 63, in order: 12, 20, 21, 24, 27, 27, 32 x5, 36 x3, 39, 40, 40, 42, 42, 48 x4, 52, 54 x5, 55, 56, 57, 60 x4, 63, 63 -- the smallest is A4 at order 12, the source's own example, and it is the only level-3 group of order 12 (by the classical list of the five groups of order 12: the census covers the three non-abelian ones -- C3 : C4, A4 and the dihedral group of order 12 -- of which only A4 is level 3, and the two abelian ones are level 1) [corrected 2026-09-08, hygiene 11c: was 'and it is the only level-3 group of order 12', which the census alone does not give]

Negative controls: a non-abelian group need not be level 3 (S3 refutes the too-large reading of the source's question), the level is not always at most 2 (A4), all three values are attained, the criterion of QS3 has a non-vacuous hypothesis, the commuting pairs are non-empty, and the third datum C_{gh} of the triple does real work (in S3 the pairs (c,c) and (c,c^{-1}) are separated by the class of the product and by nothing else)

PROSE: level 1 characterises the abelian groups -- every non-abelian finite group has an element g and an x with x g x^{-1} != g and [g, x g x^{-1}] = 1, hence is not level 1. Proof: if some Sylow p-subgroup P is non-abelian take g in Z_2(P) \ Z(P) and x in P with [x,g] != 1, so that g^x = [x,g] g commutes with g; otherwise every Sylow subgroup is abelian, and if some N_G(P) != C_G(P) an x in N_G(P) not centralising P gives the witness inside the abelian P, while N_G(P) = C_G(P) for every Sylow P forces a normal p-complement for every p (Burnside's normal p-complement theorem), hence G nilpotent, hence the direct product of its abelian Sylow subgroups, hence abelian

MEASUREMENT (GAP, not kernel-checked): the level of the named families -- level 2 for Dic_n (n = 2..10), Q8, D8, Q16, SD16, M16, S3, S4, SL(2,3), GL(2,3) and both extraspecial groups of order 32 (the dihedral groups are row QS16, a theorem); level 3 for A_n (n = 4,5,6,7), S_n (n = 5,6), PSL(2,7), the two non-abelian groups of order 27, the two extraspecial groups of order 125, and the Frobenius group C_p : C_q exactly when q >= 3 (14 cases against 5 cases at q = 2); and, over orders 64..127 excluding 64 and 96, 343 non-abelian groups with 0 at level 1, 246 at level 2 and 97 at level 3

Every dihedral group is level 2: for every n >= 3 the three two-party marginals of D_n together determine the stored message and no two of them do -- an infinite family on the middle row of TABLE II, where the source evaluates only S3 = D_3

An infinite family at level 3: the affine group AGL(1,p) of the line over ZMod p needs a three-party marginal for every prime p >= 5 -- level-3 groups at the orders p(p-1) = 20, 42, 110, 156, 272, ... -- and the bound is sharp, AGL(1,3) = S3 being level 2

Every non-abelian finite nilpotent group fails level 1 -- in particular every non-abelian p-group and every direct product of them -- via the normaliser criterion: if x normalises C_G(g) without centralising g then x g x^{-1} commutes with g and differs from it
Every dicyclic (generalised quaternion) group Dic_n = Q_{4n} is level 2 for n >= 2 -- a second infinite family on the middle row of TABLE II, containing the quaternion group Q8 = Dic_2

Level 1 characterises the abelian groups: for every finite group G, two parties can read the message stored in an extreme point of the decohered quantum double D(G) if and only if G is abelian -- the exact converse of the source's own abelian remark, so the first row of TABLE II is a characterisation and not an example

Two named groups the census cannot name: the alternating group A5 (the (60,5) entry of the census, but there only a multiplication table) and the symmetric group S5 (order 120, past the census range) are both level 3 -- so S5 is the smallest symmetric group that is not level 2

A structural criterion for level 3: if a finite group G has an abelian subgroup A which is the centraliser of each of its non-identity elements, whose non-identity elements are all G-conjugate, and with |A| >= 4, then G is level 3 -- one mechanism covering both the source's own A4 (A = the Klein four-group) and the affine groups AGL(1,p) (A = the translations), and giving a kernel-clean proof of TABLE II's A4 row

The whole scale of Frobenius groups C_p : H at level 3: for a prime p and any subgroup H of (ZMod p)^* containing a multiplier other than +-1, the group of affine maps x -> a x + b with a in H needs a three-party marginal -- so C_p : C_q is level 3 for every q >= 3 dividing p - 1, and the hypothesis is sharp (H = {1} is C_p, level 1; H = {1,-1} is D_p, level 2)
The Frobenius group C7 : C3 of order 21 is level 3, as a named group: its multiplier group is the group of cube roots of unity {1,2,4} in (ZMod 7)^*, of order 3, and the group has order 21

Every finite non-abelian group whose derived subgroup is central of order 2 is level 2 -- in particular every extraspecial 2-group, so both groups of order 32, i.e. every central product of copies of the ORDER-8 dihedral group D4 and the order-8 quaternion group Q8, and the modular groups M_{2^k}; the criterion does NOT reach D_{2^k} or SD_{2^k} for k >= 4 (already D_8 and SD_16, of order 16, have |G'| = 4) [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was and every central product of dihedral and quaternion 2-groups]

The other half of the extraspecial dichotomy: if a central z <> 1 has g conjugate to gz and g^2 conjugate to g^2 z then the group is level 3, so every extraspecial p-group with p odd is level 3 -- in particular the Heisenberg group over ZMod p (order p^3) for every odd prime p, at the orders 27, 125, 343, ... -- while the same construction at p = 2 gives D4, which is level 2

Both extraspecial groups of order 32 are level 2, as explicit groups rather than as census tables: the central extensions of (ZMod 2)^4 by ZMod 2 given by the hyperbolic form and by its Arf-twisted form, which have 19 and 11 involutions respectively and so are not isomorphic
SL(2,3) and GL(2,3) are level 2, inside Mathlib's own Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) (ZMod 3) and Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup (Fin 2) (ZMod 3), of orders 24 and 48

The level of a direct product is the maximum of the levels of its factors: level (G x H) = max (level G) (level H) for all finite groups, so with the level-1 classification a direct product is level 1 exactly when both factors are abelian, level 3 exactly when some factor is level 3, and level 2 otherwise

families.paper_title: The secret-sharing level of a finite group:\\ level one characterises the abelian groups,\\ and the census of the groups of order at most $63$
families.paper_abstract: Yang, Shi and Lee (arXiv:2506.04221) store a logical message in an extreme point of the information convex set of the charge-decohered quantum double of a finite group $G$ on a torus cut into four patches, and ask which collaborations of parties can read it.  By their Proposition~14 the extreme points are labelled by the simultaneous conjugacy classes $\Cl{g,h}$ of commuting pairs, and each pair of parties learns one of the three conjugacy classes $\Cl{g}$, $\Cl{h}$, $\Cl{gh}$.  Their Table~II evaluates the answer on three groups --- abelian, $S_3$, $A_4$ --- and asks whether every non-abelian group behaves like $A_4$. We study the resulting invariant of a finite group, its \emph{level}: $1$ if the pair $(\Cl{g},\Cl{h})$ determines $\Cl{g,h}$, $2$ if only the triple $(\Cl{g},\Cl{h},\Cl{gh})$ does, and $3$ otherwise.  We prove that the three two-party data are equivalent, so that the level is well defined; that level $1$ characterises the abelian groups --- the converse of the source's own remark, which rests on the fact that every non-abelian finite group contains an element commuting with a distinct conjugate of itself, proved by a Sylow split and Burnside's transfer; that every dihedral group $D_n$ ($n\ge3$) and every dicyclic group $\Dic_n$ ($n\ge2$) has level $2$; that the affine groups $\AGL(1,p)$ have level $3$ for every prime $p\ge5$, while $\AGL(1,3)\cong S_3$ has level $2$; and a structural criterion for level $3$ that covers $A_4$ and $\AGL(1,p)$ by one mechanism.  Level $3$ is inherited by direct products, but the level is not monotone under subgroups: $A_4\le S_4$ have levels $3$ and $2$.  An exhaustive census of the $213$ non-abelian groups of order at most $63$ finds none at level $1$, $175$ at level $2$ and $38$ at level $3$; the smallest level-$3$ group is $A_4$.  So the answer to the printed question is no, and both answers occur along infinite families.  Every theorem and every census entry is verified in Lean~4 over Mathlib, except that the minimality of $A_4$ also uses the classical list of the groups of order at most $12$; the completeness of the census list is that of the SmallGroups library. \par This second version adds five results.  Every finite non-abelian group whose derived subgroup is central of order $2$ has level $2$, with the conjugating element written down explicitly --- so every extraspecial $2$-group has level $2$, both groups of order $32$ being certified as explicit central extensions; a central $z\ne1$ with $g$ conjugate to $gz$ and $g^2$ conjugate to $g^2z$ forces level $3$, so the Heisenberg group of order $p^3$ has level $3$ for every odd prime $p$ while the same construction at $p=2$ gives $D_4$ at level $2$: for extraspecial groups the row of Table~II is the parity of $p$.  The affine group $C_p\rtimes H$ of the line over $\Z/p$ with multipliers in a subgroup $H\le(\Z/p)^\times$ has level $3$ as soon as $H$ contains an element other than $\pm1$, for every prime $p$; this contains $\AGL(1,p)$ and settles $C_p\rtimes C_q$ at level $3$ for every $q\ge3$ dividing $p-1$, the smallest case beyond $\AGL(1,p)$ itself --- that is, with $H$ a proper subgroup of $(\Z/p)^\times$ --- being $C_7\rtimes C_3$ of order $21$. $SL(2,3)$ and $GL(2,3)$ have level $2$ inside Mathlib's own matrix groups.  Finally $\lev(G\times H)=\max(\lev G,\lev H)$ for all finite $G$, $H$.  The values that the first version could only measure in GAP for these groups are now theorems; what is still measured only is listed.  The theorems of this version are verified in Lean~4 as well, with the exceptions flagged in the text and listed in Section~\ref{sec:verif}: the passage from the criterion to all extraspecial groups of odd order, two elementary steps, and three classical identifications.

families.title: The quantum extension property for full-support stabilizer codes: the minimal lengths at stabilizer dimension k = 4 and k = 5, a distance-3 counterexample on the perfect five-qubit code, and a positive answer for CSS codes
families.description: Founded 2026-08-30 from [arXiv:2607.26214](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26214) v1 (Ali Assem Mahmoud, *Minimal Counterexamples of the MacWilliams Extension Theorem for Stabilizer Codes*, announced 2026-07-28), on rows R1–R3 of `journal/2026-08-30-scout-qec.md`. The family answers three of that paper's seven numbered open problems.

statements.label: open problem 4 at k = 4: the minimal full-support lengths are 4 (for a non-extendable isometry) and 5 (for a monomially inequivalent pair) -- the gap persists, with the same values the source proves for k = 3
open problem 4 at k = 5: the minimal full-support non-extendable isometry length is 5, i.e. the floor n = k, so the answer stops being 4 and becomes k

open problem 3, answered negatively: distance > 2 does NOT restore the extension property -- the perfect [[5,1,3]] code has a weight-preserving automorphism implemented by no local Clifford circuit and qubit permutation

open problem 6, answered positively for the CSS subclass: the class incidence matrix is invertible over Q, so the weight vector determines the multiset of coordinate kernels and every CSS-preserving weight-preserving isometry extends

the CSS positive answer at every length and dimension: for all kX, kZ, n, a weight-preserving CSS-preserving isometry between CSS stabilizer codes on a common splitting extends to a monomial transformation
the compute-first control: the source's own k = 3 census reproduced from its definitions, and the finite content of its kernel reduction at k = 3, 4, 5
negative controls: the model, the monomial-extension test, each hypothesis, and each search are all non-vacuous in both directions
the census beyond Lean's reach: exact GL(k,2)-orbit counts by union-find under the elementary transvections, and the cost of the whole search

open problem 4 at k = 5, the pair half: the minimal full-support length carrying a monomially inequivalent weight-isometric pair of stabilizer dimension 5 is exactly 6, so the gap between the two minimal lengths persists at k = 5 and the answer there is (5, 6) against (4, 5) at k = 3 and k = 4

open problem 3 with the vacuity escape closed: a [[6,1,3]] stabilizer code and a second of distance >= 3, with a weight-preserving isometry that extends to no monomial transformation and whose weight vector is NOT constant, so weight preservation is a real hypothesis -- distance > 2 does not restore the extension property even then

the k = 5, n = 6 census: 63082768 full-support data, 43278108 weight vectors, 14436204 counterexample classes, exactly 937440 of them monomially inequivalent, and 13516 all of whose codes have stabilizer distance >= 3

open problem 6 with the `CSS-preserving` hypothesis dropped: the extension property **fails** for CSS codes, and at the unrestricted minimal lengths -- `4` for a non-extendable weight-preserving isometry between two CSS stabilizer codes, `5` for a monomially inequivalent weight-isometric CSS pair -- so the CSS restriction on its own buys nothing and the whole of `QF4`/`QF5`'s positive answer rests on `CSS-preserving`

the monomially-inequivalent column of the CSS filter: how many counterexample weight classes contain two codes in different `GL(k,2)` orbits, with and without the CSS restriction, at `k = 3, 4` and `n <= 6`

open problem 6, the graph-code sub-question, answered negatively at the isometry level: the four-qubit linear cluster state `C_{P_4}` has a weight-preserving automorphism of its stabilizer group -- transpose the two leaf generators -- implemented by no local Clifford circuit and qubit permutation; minimal length `4`; and the published counterexample of Gluesing-Luerssen--Pllaha is checked here to BE that cluster state

families.paper_title: The quantum extension property for full-support stabilizer codes: the minimal lengths at stabilizer dimensions $4$ and $5$, distance-$3$ counterexamples, and a positive answer for CSS codes
families.paper_abstract: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails over the label alphabet $\Al=\FF_2^2$ of qubit Pauli operators, and Mahmoud has recently located the smallest scales at which it fails for \emph{stabilizer} codes.  Writing $k$ for the $\FF_2$-dimension of the stabilizer, he determines, for $k\le 3$, the minimal length of a full-support non-extendable weight-preserving isometry (it is $4$) and the minimal length of a full-support weight-isometric pair of codes that are not even monomially equivalent (it is $5$), and asks for $k\ge 4$.  We answer that question at $k=4$ and $k=5$: the two minimal lengths are $(4,5)$ at $k=4$ and $(5,6)$ at $k=5$, so over the four stabilizer dimensions now known the isometry length is $\max(4,k)$, the pair length is $\max(5,k+1)$, and the gap of one between them persists.  We answer a second question of his negatively: distance $>2$ does not restore the extension property.  The perfect $[[5,1,3]]$ code carries a weight-preserving automorphism of its stabilizer group implemented by no local Clifford circuit together with a qubit permutation; since every nonzero element of that stabilizer has weight $4$, weight preservation is a vacuous hypothesis there, and we therefore also exhibit a pair of $[[6,1]]$ codes of stabilizer distance at least $3$ with a non-extendable weight-preserving isometry whose weight vector takes four distinct values, so that the hypothesis is doing work.  A third question we answer positively: for CSS codes with CSS-preserving isometries the extension property holds, at every length, because the class incidence matrix is invertible over $\QQ$ --- certified by an explicit integral matrix carrying it to a nonzero multiple of the identity, at $k=3$ and $k=4$.  Every existence statement below is machine-checked against the definitions themselves, the failure of extension being tested against all $6^n\,n!$ monomial transformations, $33\,592\,320$ of them at $n=6$; the matching lower bounds at $k=5$ rest on an exhaustive orbit census over $63\,082\,768$ parameterized data and are labelled throughout as computations rather than as formal proofs.

families.title: How few vertices can a quantum isomorphic, non-isomorphic pair of graphs have? The published bracket [6, 24], moved to [10, 24] by a planar homomorphism-count census of every graph on at most nine vertices
families.description: Two finite graphs `G` and `H` are **quantum isomorphic**, `G ≅_qc H`, when the `(G,H)`-isomorphism game has a perfect strategy in the commuting-operator model. Quantum isomorphism is strictly weaker than isomorphism: Atserias, Mančinska, Roberson, Šámal, Severini and Varvitsiotis (*Quantum and non-signalling graph isomorphisms*, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B **136** (2019) 289–328; arXiv:1611.09837v3, Theorem 6.4) turn the Mermin magic square into a pair of quantum isomorphic, non-isomorphic graphs on **24** vertices.

statements.label: The least number of vertices of a pair of quantum isomorphic but non-isomorphic graphs is at least 10; the published bracket is [6, 24]
Six explicit connected planar graphs on at most six vertices separate all 288248 graphs on 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 vertices by homomorphism counts
All 129 connected planar graphs on at most six vertices, each certified planar in the kernel by an explicit integer straight-line plane drawing

Negative controls: the four connected patterns on at most three vertices fail to separate at n = 5, 6 and 7; the thirty connected planar patterns on at most five vertices separate at n = 7 and fail at n = 8; planarOK rejects the crossing drawing of K4

The homomorphism counter is pinned by four textbook identities over all 1044 graphs on seven vertices, the fast and transparent searches agree on all 129 x 1044 pattern/graph pairs, and the five census lengths are A000088 at n = 5..9

Cost of pushing the census sweep to n = 10: 41 CPU-min in C for one pass (measured on a 1/64 geng slice), about 24 CPU-h kernel-bound, and the six-pattern set does not even separate at n = 10 -- over the cap, parked

families.paper_title: A quantum isomorphic pair of non-isomorphic graphs\\ needs at least ten vertices
families.paper_abstract: Two graphs are \emph{quantum isomorphic} when the isomorphism game between them has a perfect quantum-commuting strategy.  Such a pair need not be isomorphic: Atserias, Man\v{c}inska, Roberson, \v{S}\'amal, Severini and Varvitsiotis turned the Mermin magic square into a quantum isomorphic, non-isomorphic pair of graphs on $24$ vertices.  How small can such a pair be?  Writing $N$ for the least order of one, the published bracket is $6\le N\le 24$, and it is restated in that form by an expert paper of October 2025.  We prove $N\ge 10$. The proof exhibits six connected planar graphs on at most six vertices --- the bull, the path $P_6$, one further tree and three unicyclic graphs --- whose homomorphism counts take pairwise distinct values on the $288\,248$ isomorphism classes of graphs on $5,6,7,8$ and $9$ vertices, and then applies the forward direction of Man\v{c}inska and Roberson's theorem that quantum isomorphism is exactly equality of homomorphism counts from planar graphs.  The two halves are logically separate, and we keep them separate.  The combinatorial half --- that these six graphs separate every pair of non-isomorphic graphs on five to nine vertices --- is proved outright here, modulo one imported fact, that \texttt{nauty}'s catalogues of small graphs are complete; the planarity of each of the six is certified by an explicit integer straight-line drawing rather than cited.  The transfer to quantum isomorphism is the one ingredient we do not prove, and it appears as an explicit hypothesis of the theorem rather than in a remark.  Everything below except a handful of elementary steps, each named where it occurs, is machine-checked in Lean~4, in a development that uses neither the axiom of choice nor \texttt{sorry}.  The bracket becomes $10\le N\le 24$; nothing here says anything about $10$ itself.

families.title: The Butson reach of the quantum-Latin-square spectrum: the sumset sizes |S+T| over BH(n,m) column-class sets, and the order-seven cardinality 45
families.description: A **quantum Latin square** `QLS(n)` is an `n × n` array of unit vectors in `ℂⁿ` whose every row and every column is an orthonormal basis (Musto–Vicary 2016). Its **cardinality** is the number of entries counted up to a global phase — the number of distinct *rays*. `n` means classical, `n²` means as quantum as possible, and the open question is which values in between occur at each order. Zhang–Lv–Cao (arXiv:2607.19969v2, 2026-07-22) survey the state of that question in their Table 6, whose order-seven row reads verbatim

statements.label: The reach layer: the mixed-Schur collision relation, the COMPLETE Butson column criterion at q = 6, the bridge from a reachable value to a quantum Latin square, and the bracket n <= k <= n^2
The symmetric ceiling: the Butson construction with K = H reaches at most n(n+1)/2 ray classes, at every order and modulus, and the ceiling is attained at order seven
A quantum Latin square of order seven with cardinality 45, from an explicit pair of BH(7,6) matrices -- a cell the most recent survey prints as uncertain
Negative controls: the cardinality 45 is pinned from both sides on the witness, and both family-level bounds refute
The measured reach axis: Reach(n,m) computed exhaustively at seven cells, and what each one does to Table 6
A machine-checked correction to this repository's own prose: the prime-order argument in QuantumLatin/ButsonGeneral.lean concludes too much

families.paper_title: Reachable cardinalities of the Butson mixed Schur construction, and a quantum Latin square of order seven with cardinality~$45$
families.paper_abstract: A \emph{quantum Latin square} of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array of unit vectors of $\CC^n$ every row and every column of which is an orthonormal basis; its \emph{cardinality} is the number of entries once vectors differing by a global phase are identified.  Zhang, Lv and Cao tabulate, at the orders their determination of the spectrum leaves open, which cardinalities are known to occur and which are uncertain; the order-seven row of that table prints $45$ as uncertain.  We exhibit a quantum Latin square of order seven whose cardinality is exactly $45$. The witness is a mixed Schur product $\Phi(H,K)_{ij}=7^{-1/2}(h_i\odot k_j)$ of two Butson Hadamard matrices $H,K\in\BH(7,6)$, presented by explicit exponent matrices over $\ZZ/6$, and the certificate is exact and integral: for a Butson pair the cardinality is the size of a sumset $|S+T|$ of two $n$-element subsets of $(\ZZ/m)^n$ modulo constants, and at $m=6$ the Butson condition is \emph{equivalent} to two integer equations on each column difference profile.  The sufficient shift criterion previously used to assemble such witnesses certifies none of the $84$ ordered pairs of distinct columns of ours, and it is the equivalence that replaces it.  We also record, general in $n$ and $m$, the ceiling $\card\Phi(H,H)\le n(n+1)/2$ for the symmetric construction --- sharp at $n=7$, where it gives the value $28$ that the same table lists as attainable and isolated --- and the bracket $n\le\card\Phi(H,K)\le n^2$.  In particular the dichotomy $|S+T|\in\{p,p^2\}$, which holds at a prime order $p$ for matrices monomially equivalent to the Fourier matrix $F_p$, fails once the modulus is allowed to differ from the order.  Every theorem below is machine-checked in Lean~4; the exhaustive enumerations reported alongside them are stated as measurements and are marked as such.

families.title: Q_p-weighted zero-sum constants D_{Q_p,1}(p)
families.description: Fix an odd prime `p`, write `Z_p = ℤ/pℤ`, `U(p)` for its units,

statements.label: `D_{Q_p,1}(p) = 4` for every prime `p = 1 mod 4`
every length-4 sequence in `Z_p`, `p = 1 mod 4`, has a `(Q_p,1)`-weighted zero-sum subsequence

`D_{U(p),1}(p) = 3` -- control, a different weight set gives a different value

`p = 5`: `(1,2,0)` has no `(Q_5,1)`-weighted zero-sum subsequence -- control, three terms are not enough

`(1,1,0,0)` is bad at `p = 7` and good at `p = 5` -- control, the hypothesis `p = 1 mod 4` is not vacuous
exhaustive check of `D_{Q_p,1}(p)` at all 168 odd primes `p <= 1009`

families.paper_title: A Paley colouring settles $D_{Q_p,\one}$:\\ the quadratic-residue weighted Davenport\\ constant is $4$ for every prime $p\equiv 1 \pmod 4$
families.paper_abstract: For an odd prime $p$ let $Q_p$ be the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$ and let $\one=\{1\}$.  A sequence $(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ in $\Zn{p}=\ZZ/p\ZZ$ is a $(Q_p,\one)$-weighted zero-sum sequence if there are $a_1,\dots,a_k\in Q_p$ with $a_1x_1+\dots+a_kx_k=0$ and $a_1+\dots+a_k=0$, and $D_{Q_p,\one}(p)$ is the least $k$ such that every length-$k$ sequence in $\Zn{p}$ has such a subsequence.  Paul and Paul, who introduced this doubly-weighted constant, proved $D_{Q_p,\one}\in\{4,5\}$ for every odd $p$ and $D_{Q_p,\one}=5$ for $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$, and wrote of the remaining case: ``we believe that $D_{Q_p,\one}=4$ \dots\ However, despite our best efforts, we have been unable to show this''.  We prove it.  The mechanism is that for $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ the element $-1$ is a square, so the quadratic character $\chi(x-y)$ is a well-defined $2$-colouring of the edges of the complete graph on $\Zn{p}$ --- the Paley colouring --- and each of three configurations forces a weighted zero-sum subsequence: a repeated term, a monochromatic triangle, and a monochromatic perfect matching, the last through the weight vector $(1,-1,-u,u)$.  Since every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_4$ contains a monochromatic triangle or a monochromatic perfect matching, four terms always suffice. With the authors' own theorem for $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ the value of $D_{Q_p,\one}(p)$ is now known at every odd prime, and their conditional consequence becomes unconditional: $D_{Q_p,B}(p)=4$ for $p\equiv 1\pmod4$ and every nonempty $B$ with $0\notin B$.  Every theorem below is machine-checked in Lean~4; \S\ref{sec:verif} says exactly what the machine checks.  An independent exhaustive computation, outside the formal development, confirms the value at all $168$ odd primes $p\le 1009$.

families.title: Orbit lengths of q-discrete Painleve one over finite fields: the Hasse bound and the bin structure verified past the published range, and the maximum made exact

The kernel band: Conjectures 1.2.A and 1.2.B for every orbit over F_2, F_3, F_5, F_7 with no native_decide axiom, plus a cross-check that the array engine and the array-free kernel engine return the same maxima

What the integer checks mean, and two facts at every q: hasseOK is equivalent to #(gamma)/r <= q + 2 sqrt q + 1, inBin is exactly the integer test (mL-(q+1))^2 <= 4q and that test is membership in B_m, consecutive bins below M_q are disjoint, and ord(s) divides the period of any state with nonzero time over an arbitrary field

The source's Magma verification re-run from scratch: Conjectures 1.2.A and 1.2.B for every orbit at all 45 prime powers q <= 131 (44 in one sweep, q = 128 separately), 3 327 974 orbits, on an independent implementation

q-Painleve I over F_1009, more than twice the source's range: Conjectures 1.2.A and 1.2.B hold for all 5 756 256 orbits with s among the twelve smallest elements of F_1009^*, M_q = 8, maximum reduced orbit length 1073 = hasseStrictMax 1009

Conjecture 1.2.B is an equality for prime q: the set of realised reduced orbit lengths is exactly the union of the M_q bins with 2 and 3 removed, at every prime 3 <= q <= 131; and this fails at proper prime powers (4, 9, 25, 128)

families.paper_title: The length spectrum of $q$-discrete Painlev\'e~I over a finite field: an exact form of the bin conjecture at prime $q$, and verification past the published range
families.paper_abstract: Joshi and Roffelsen have shown that the $q$-discrete first Painlev\'e equation, resolved on Sakai's initial value space, defines a bijection of a set of $(q+1)^2$ points over a finite field $\Fq$, and they conjecture on the strength of a Magma computation over every prime power $2\le q\le499$ that every reduced orbit length obeys the Hasse bound $q+2\sqrt q+1$ and in fact lies in one of $\Mq$ explicit disjoint intervals, the \emph{bins}.  We report four things about the set of reduced orbit lengths that is actually realised.  First, for every prime $q$ with $3\le q\le131$ the conjectured containment is an \emph{equality}: every integer in every bin other than $2$ and $3$ occurs as a reduced orbit length, and nothing else does.  This fails at the proper prime powers $q=4,9,25,128$, so the phenomenon is one of prime $q$.  Second, the largest reduced orbit length is exactly $q+1+\max\{d\in\NN:d^2<4q\}$, the largest integer strictly below the Hasse bound, at every prime power $q\le131$ except $q=128$, where it falls one short.  Third and fourth, both conjectures hold for all $3\,534\,638$ orbits over $\FF_{503}$, the first prime power past the published range, and for all $5\,756\,256$ orbits over $\FF_{1009}$ whose parameter $s$ is one of the twelve smallest elements of $\FF_{1009}^\times$, where $\Mq=8$ against $M_{499}=6$.  All statements are formally verified in Lean~4; every search is exhaustive over the range stated and is described.

families.paper_title: Quadratic numerical semigroups of embedding dimension five: two questions of Stamate
families.paper_abstract: Let $H$ be a numerical semigroup, $K[H]$ its semigroup ring and $\gr_\mm K[H]$ its tangent cone; $H$ is called \emph{quadratic} when the defining ideal $I^{*}_{H}$ of $\gr_\mm K[H]$ is generated by quadrics.  Stamate gave a maximal list of twelve $h$-vectors for a quadratic $H$ of embedding dimension five, exhibited an example for each except $(1,4,5)$, and asked whether the list should be reduced further; in the same paper he isolated three artinian ideals $J_1,J_2,J_3$ of $K[x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5]$ arising in his screening, reported that he could find no quadratic numerical semigroup producing them, and observed that if none existed the hypotheses ``$K$ algebraically closed, $\operatorname{char}K\neq2$'' could be removed from his theorem that Koszul and $G$-quadratic agree in embedding dimension five.  We settle both questions.  No numerical semigroup of embedding dimension five whose tangent cone has $h$-vector $(1,4,5)$ is quadratic, so the list of twelve $h$-vectors becomes a list of eleven and the missing entry stays missing.  The second question has a mixed answer: $J_2$ is produced by no quadratic numerical semigroup, for any labelling of the variables, whereas $J_1$ is produced by $\langle 7,23,31,39,40\rangle$ and $J_3$ by $\langle 8,26,35,44,45\rangle$, both quadratic --- so the hypothesis under which the assumptions on $K$ were to be dropped is false.  The proofs turn each question into finite data: the Cohen--Macaulayness of the tangent cone is \emph{derived} from the Hilbert function rather than assumed, the degree-three condition imposed by quadratic generation becomes a connectivity question on twenty vertices, and what survives is killed by a congruence obstruction on Ap\'ery sets.  All finite searches are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.title: The Bremner-Ulas quadrinomial discriminants F_{m,n} are never squarefree when gcd(m,n) >= 3: Conjecture 5.2 of arXiv:1310.5346 = Acta Math. Hungar. 145 (2015) 320-349 is false, and the repair is gcd(F, F') = A_{gcd(m,n)}

Conjecture 5.2 of arXiv:1310.5346v1 is false over an infinite family: for every `m, n` with `n > 2m` and `gcd(m,n) >= 3`, `F_{m,n}` is not squarefree in `Z[X]`; in particular `F_{3,3k}` is not squarefree for every `k >= 3`
The conjecture's literal wording refuted: for every `m, n` with `n > 2m` and `gcd(m,n) >= 3` there is a `z` in `C` with `F_{m,n}(z) = 0` and `F'_{m,n}(z) = 0`, i.e. `F_{m,n}` has a multiple root

The repaired law, verified: for every `(m,n)` with `3 <= n <= 30`, `0 < m`, `2m < n` (all 210 pairs), `gcd(F_{m,n}, F'_{m,n}) = A_{gcd(m,n)}(1,t)` in `Q[t]` up to a nonzero constant -- so `F_{m,n}` is squarefree if and only if `gcd(m,n) <= 2`

families.paper_title: $A_{\gcd(m,n)}^{2}$ always divides $F_{m,n}$:\\ multiple roots of the Bremner--Ulas\\ quadrinomial discriminants
families.paper_abstract: Bremner and Ulas reduce the divisibility of the quadrinomial $x^{n}+x^{n-m}+x^{n-2m}+a$ by a rational quadratic to the rational points of the hyperelliptic curve $s^{2}=F_{m,n}(t)$, where $F_{m,n}=A_{n-m}^{2}-4A_{n-2m}A_{n}$ is built from the sequence $A_{k}=A_{k}(1,t)\in \ZZ[t]$ of their Lemma~3.1, and they conjecture that $F_{m,n}$ has no multiple roots whenever $n>2m$.  We show that this is false and identify the obstruction exactly: $A_{\gcd(m,n)}^{2}$ divides $F_{m,n}$ for \emph{all} $m,n$, over every commutative ring. Since $A_{d}$ is a non-unit precisely for $d\ge 3$, the polynomial $F_{m,n}$ fails to be squarefree, and has a multiple complex root, for every pair with $n>2m$ and $\gcd(m,n)\ge 3$; the smallest is $(m,n)=(3,9)$, where $F_{3,9}=(t-1)^{2}(4t^{3}-27t^{2}+18t-3)$ although $9>2\cdot 3$.  We propose the repaired statement $\gcd(F_{m,n},F_{m,n}')=A_{\gcd(m,n)}$ up to a nonzero constant --- equivalently, $F_{m,n}$ is squarefree if and only if $\gcd(m,n)\le 2$ --- and verify it for all $210$ pairs with $3\le n\le 30$, $0<m$, $2m<n$ by an explicit B\'ezout certificate per pair, in which both exact divisions are checked rather than assumed and no polynomial gcd algorithm is trusted; an independent computation confirms it for all $1560$ pairs with $n\le 80$. Every theorem below is machine-checked in Lean~4; \S\ref{sec:verif} says exactly what the machine checks and names the two steps that remain outside it.  One caveat is stated in full in \S\ref{sub:whichtext}: the published version of the source is closed access, and the refutation is graded against its arXiv e-print.

families.paper_title: Twelve uncertain cardinalities of quantum Latin squares of orders nine and eleven
families.paper_abstract: A \emph{quantum Latin square} of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array of unit vectors of $\CC^n$ every row and every column of which is an orthonormal basis; its \emph{cardinality} is the number of entries once vectors differing by a global phase are identified.  Zhang, Lv and Cao determined the set of attainable cardinalities for every order $v\ge 8$ with $v\notin\{9,11,23\}$ and tabulated what is known at the orders their argument leaves open.  We settle twelve of the entries that table records as uncertain: cardinality $34$ at order nine, the only gap in the otherwise complete attainable interval $[9,59]$ of that row, and $13,\dots,19$, $21$, $48$, $50$ and $54$ at order eleven, among them the three isolated gaps of $[20,53]$ and the first value of the uncertain interval $[54,115]$.  Every witness has integer coordinates.  They are obtained from a classical Latin square by replacing each member of a family of pairwise cell-disjoint subsquares with an orthogonal frame; the content is the packing, not the replacement, and we record the counting ceiling that limits it.  We also delimit the method: a search over order-seven Latin squares never packed more than seven pairwise disjoint intercalates, which puts the uncertain block $[24,27]$ at order seven out of reach of this construction; and for the Fourier matrix at a prime order $p$ the competing Butson mixed-Schur construction has cardinality the size of a sumset of two cosets of one cyclic subgroup, hence only $p$ or $p^2$.  All existence statements below are machine-checked in Lean~4, with no floating point and no square roots entering any certificate.

families.title: Exponents of plane quartics: no reduced curve of degree 4 has exponents (3,3,3,3,4) -- answering the open cell of Dimca-Sticlaru's Example 5.3 (i) by a Koszul-relation lemma on Jacobian syzygies
families.description: **The question.** Dimca and Sticlaru, *On type three complex plane curves* (arXiv:2601.01824v1, math.AG, 2026-01-05), Example 5.3 (i), page 13 of the arXiv PDF, print in italics:

families.paper_title: No plane quartic has exponents $(3,3,3,3,4)$:\\ two Koszul relations force a Koszul syzygy
families.paper_abstract: Let $C : f = 0$ be a reduced plane curve of degree $d$ over $\C$.  Its \emph{exponents} are the degrees of a minimal system of homogeneous generators of the module $D_0(f)$ of Jacobian syzygies $a f_x + b f_y + c f_z = 0$.  Dimca and Sticlaru (arXiv:2601.01824) classify the exponent vectors a quartic of type three can have, up to one cell: ``\emph{We do not know if there is a curve $C$ with $d = 4$ and exponents $(3,3,3,3,4)$}.''  We show that no such quartic exists.  The mechanism is a lemma on the three-variable polynomial ring: if a vector $r$ of polynomials satisfies two Koszul relations $\rho_1 r = \ell^1 \times F$ and $\rho_2 r = \ell^2 \times F$ with $\rho_1, \rho_2$ non-proportional linear forms and $\ell^1, \ell^2$ vectors of linear forms, and no nonzero vector of total degree at most two is annihilated by $\cdot \times F$, then $r = t \times F$ is itself a Koszul syzygy.  For $F = \gr$ the last hypothesis is the standard fact $\gcdop(f_x,f_y,f_z) = 1$ together with a degree count, and the source's own resolution of the Milnor algebra provides the two relations; a quartic with exponents $(3,3,3,3,4)$ would therefore have only three independent syzygies of degree three, a contradiction.  Two explicit quartics with total Tjurina number two --- a new two-nodal one and the source's cuspidal one --- show the relation space is exactly one-dimensional, and two controls show that neither the degree hypothesis on $F$ nor the linearity of the coefficient vectors can be dropped. We also correct a printed formula: equation (2.3) of the source gives the degrees of the second-order syzygies as $d_m - d_j + \epsilon_i$, whereas its own equation (1.2) gives $d_{i+2} - d_j + \epsilon_i$; the source's Example~3.6~(ii) refutes the printed form, both of its minimal second-order syzygies having total degree five, and we exhibit them.  Finally we report two measurements outside the formal development: $3\,920$ quartics with $\tau(C) = 2$ over $\F_{101}$ and $\F_{1009}$ all have $\mu_4 = 0$, that is no fifth generator in degree four, and among $1\,020$ quintics over $\F_{1009}$ the $407$ of type three realise none of the three exponent vectors left open by the source's Remark~5.9~(ii).  The lemma, its corollary, the witnesses, the controls and the correction are checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib; the step from $\gcdop(f_x,f_y,f_z)=1$ to the degree hypothesis is argued in prose.

families.paper_title: Twenty exact minimum distances for generalized $\mathbb{Z}_p$ toric codes on twisted tori
families.paper_abstract: In arXiv:2602.20158, Liang and Chen build qudit CSS low-density parity-check codes from a pair of weight-three Laurent polynomials over a twisted two-dimensional torus, and tabulate sixty-five of them at $p\in\{3,5,7,11\}$.  The distance column of those tables is the output of a randomized information-set algorithm, and its caption states that the printed values are upper bounds on the exact distance which the authors ``believe are tight in practice''.  We prove that twenty of them are exact: for each of the twenty codes of Table~\ref{tab:cells} the minimum weight of a logical operator is exactly the printed~$d$, including $[\![48,4,9]\!]_{3}$, $[\![40,4,9]\!]_{5}$, $[\![32,4,8]\!]_{7}$ and $[\![40,4,10]\!]_{11}$.  All twenty agree with the printed number, so the numbers themselves are not new; what is new is the lower bound, which no source establishes.  Each proof is two-sided: an explicit weight-$d$ logical operator, certified not to be a product of stabilizers by a single pairing, together with a search over every support of size less than $d$ in each of the two directions, of which there are $2\,011\,668\,932$ in all.  The soundness of that search rests on a constructive echelon substitution that replaces the usual rank--nullity argument by an explicit coefficient vector.  Every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The 82-queen cover of $Q_{163}$: minimality, and an obstruction at $Q_{167}$
families.paper_abstract: The queen's graph $Q_n$ has the squares of the $n\times n$ board as vertices, two squares adjacent when they share a row, a column or a diagonal, and $\gamma(Q_n)$ is its domination number.  A recent preprint of Kong prints $82$ squares of the $163\times163$ board and asserts, on the evidence of a short script, that they dominate it; with the Finozhenok--Weakley bound $\gamma(Q_n)\ge\lceil n/2\rceil$ this gives $\gamma(Q_{163})=82$, an exact value beyond the published list, and the type~A structure of the set improves the constant in \OW{}'s amplification theorem to $17/33$.  We first re-establish every printed property of that certificate by exhaustive verified computation over all $163^{2}=26\,569$ squares, in place of the script.  We then prove two statements the source does not make. The certificate is a \emph{minimal} dominating set: each of its $82$ queens owns a square that no other queen of the set covers, so no $81$ of them dominate.  And --- the main result --- it does not extend: with the $82$ squares kept in place, no dominating set of $Q_{167}$ of size at most $84$ contains them, and none of $Q_{165}$ of size at most $83$ does.  The first is a nonexistence statement over all $27\,889^{2}$ ordered pairs of added squares, reduced to $499\times27\,889$ by an anchor argument whose completeness is proved rather than assumed. Since $\gamma(Q_{167})\ge84$ by Finozhenok--Weakley, a new exact value at $167$ needs a new construction and not an extension of this one.  Everything is machine-checked in Lean~4; the two published theorems we rely on --- the Finozhenok--Weakley bound and \OW{}'s amplification theorem --- are cited rather than reproved, and the Finozhenok--Weakley bound appears as an explicit hypothesis of the statements that use it.

families.paper_title: The generating function is algebraic: closed forms and the growth constant $32/3$ for the extension closed subcategories of a uniformly oriented $A_{n+1}$ quiver
families.paper_abstract: Let $R_n$ be the number of full, additive, idempotent split subcategories of $\Aq_{n+1}\text{-mod}$ closed under extensions, for a uniformly oriented quiver of type $A_{n+1}$ --- the OEIS sequence A393920 --- and let $P_n$ be the number of those containing a distinguished point of the associated triangular array; $P_n$ counts the convex topologies on an $(n+1)$-element chain, OEIS A234268.  Mazorchuk proved $9^n<R_n<12.75^n$ for $n\gg0$ and wrote of the true growth rate, which his data put ``probably somewhere around $10.5$'', that finding non-trivial bounds ``is not really easy''.  We show that both generating functions are \emph{algebraic}.  Summing his own interlaced recurrences over their second index produces a polynomial equation with one catalytic variable, and the quadratic method collapses it to the cubic $27u^3-36u^2+8u+1+16xu^2+x\bP=0$, $u=1-x-x^2\bP$, and to the rational parametrisation $x=(Y-1)/(Y^2(3Y-2))$, $\bP=Y^2(3Y-2)(1+Y-Y^2)$, $\bR=Y^2(3Y-2)(5-3Y)$.  Lagrange inversion then gives single binomial sums for both sequences and two-term recurrences with polynomial coefficients --- formulas that neither OEIS entry carries.  The singularity is located exactly: $x=3/32$, a triple root of the discriminant.  Three classical steps of singularity analysis, which we isolate and do not verify formally, then give $\lim R_n^{1/n}=\lim P_n^{1/n}=32/3$, with $R_n\sim\frac{768}{25\sqrt{5\pi}}n^{-5/2}(32/3)^n$ and $R_n/P_n\to 81/64$.  In the effective direction we carry Mazorchuk's truncation scheme to bases $10.3$ and $10.4$ with minimal levels and least integer constants, verify the base-$10$ bound his paper records as unverified, give the first explicit growth bounds for A234268, and explain the scheme's ceiling: its rungs converge to $32/3$ and never reach it.  The algebraic identities and every arithmetic claim are verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Quotient-realizable multisets in a finite group: the classification in $S_3$, counterexamples in $D_8$ and $Q_8$, and the abelianization obstruction in every finite nonabelian group
families.paper_abstract: A multiset $A$ of $|G|$ elements of a finite group $G$ is \emph{quotient-realizable} if $A = \{b(i)c(i)^{-1}\}$ for two enumerations $b, c$ of $G$; equivalently, if $A = \{\varphi(x)x^{-1} : x \in G\}$ for some permutation $\varphi$ of $G$.  Hall proved in 1952 that for abelian $G$ the obvious necessary condition --- that the elements of $A$ have trivial product in $G/[G,G]$ --- is also sufficient, and Aliabadi recently showed that it is not sufficient for $S_3$ and asked a list of questions about the nonabelian case.  We answer four of them outright --- his Problems~7.1, 7.2, 7.3 and 7.6 --- and, with Hall's theorem, a fifth, his Problem~7.5.  First, the obstruction fails to be sufficient in \emph{every} finite nonabelian group: one commutator together with $|G|-1$ copies of the identity is a witness, so the groups in which the abelianization obstruction is the only obstruction are exactly the finite abelian groups.  Second, we classify the quotient-realizable multisets of cardinality $6$ in $S_3$: there are $146$ of them, and they are the two-sided translates of ten explicit representatives.  Third, for $D_8$ and for $Q_8$ we exhibit multisets that pass not only the abelianization test but also the strictly stronger product-one-ordering test that Aliabadi's $S_3$ example was built to pass, and are still not quotient-realizable; each comes with a human proof as well as an exhaustive one.  Finally we count: of the $6435$ multisets of cardinality $8$, exactly $1423$ are quotient-realizable in $D_8$ and exactly $1415$ in $Q_8$, so this count separates two groups that share their order, their abelianization and their character degrees.  The numbered results below are machine-checked in Lean~4 against Mathlib apart from four exceptions; Section~\ref{sec:verif} names those, says which of the remaining statements rest on exhaustive computation and how large each search was, and says which entries of the census are measurements rather than theorems.

families.title: Group representations of the four-atom flexible-atom relation algebras: the least cyclic order of 63_65 is 21, of 57_65 is 46, and 33_65 has none over any small group
families.description: A finite integral relation algebra (FIRA) has an atom structure; an atom `a` is **flexible** when no forbidden diversity cycle involves it. Every FIRA with a flexible atom is representable over a countably infinite set; the **Flexible Atom Conjecture** (Maddux) says it is representable over a finite set. Among the *symmetric* integral relation algebras on four atoms `1', a, b, c` with `a` flexible there are exactly ten (the sixteen subsets of the `b`/`c` cycles `{bbb, bbc, bcc, ccc}`, up to swapping `b` and `c`), and the algebra is fixed by naming which of those four cycles are forbidden. This

families.paper_title: Group representations of the flexible-atom relation algebras $\Asixty$, $\Afifty$ and $\Athirty$: the least cyclic order of $\Asixty$ is $21$
families.paper_abstract: Alm has recently exhibited group representations of the symmetric integral relation algebras $\Afifty$ and $\Asixty$ over the cyclic groups $\Zn{46}$ and $\Zn{29}$, calling the latter the first known cyclic representation of $\Asixty$, and has left $\Athirty$ as the one symmetric integral four-atom algebra with a flexible atom that is not known to be finitely representable. We show that $\Asixty$ has a group representation over $\Zn{21}$, given explicitly, and none over $\Zn{n}$ for $n\le 20$, so that $21$ is its least cyclic order; that $\Afifty$ has none over $\Zn{n}$ for $n\le 22$; and, as a machine-checked fragment of a statement Alm reports for $n\le 100$, that $\Athirty$ has none over $\Zn{n}$ for $n\le 22$.  The non-existence statements rest on an exhaustive enumeration of the $3^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ inverse-closed colourings of $\Zn{n}$, the completeness of which is proved rather than assumed.  These statements, Alm's two published colourings, a calibration against the published cyclic spectrum of the pentagon algebra, and a control showing that a natural weakening of Comer's condition admits spurious representations, have all been verified in Lean~4.  Separately, and without such verification, an exhaustive search reports that $\Afifty$ has no cyclic representation of order below $46$, so that Alm's representation is of least order; that the cyclic spectrum of $\Asixty$ meets $[2,32]$ in $\{21,26,27,28,29,30,31,32\}$; and that $\Athirty$ has no group representation over any of the $92$ groups of order between $2$ and $31$, nor over $38$ of the $51$ groups of order $32$.

families.description: A knot polynomial for a `k`-strand braid is built from R-matrices acting on adjacent strands. For a fixed irreducible representation `Q` occurring `m` times in `T ⊗ T ⊗ T` it is an `m x m` matrix, and it must

statements.label: The Racah matrix U_[[3,1]] printed in equation (34) of arXiv:2603.21688v2, with the seven sign corrections (six asymmetric off-diagonal pairs resolved and the diagonal entry U_44 negated), is symmetric and satisfies U U^T = 1 identically over Q(q)

Equation (34) as printed is not a Racah matrix: the table is not symmetric (its (4,5) and (5,4) entries differ by a sign, for every q > 0), and the symmetric matrix obtained by reading its upper triangle -- so keeping the printed sign of U_44 -- is not orthogonal, its first and fourth rows failing to be perpendicular at q = 2

The sign repair of equation (34) is unique: on the printed magnitudes, the sign repair is unique up to gauge (conjugation by a diagonal sign matrix D: the 64 patterns +-DUD) and overall sign [this label said "exactly two symmetric sign patterns, U and -U" until 2026-09-08 -- literally false with all entries nonzero; the 2^21 search returns exactly the 64-element orbit]; in particular the diagonal signs, which are invariant under the gauge U -> D U D with D diagonal of signs, are determined, so the printed sign of U_44 is wrong under every reading of the table

The 69 literal '?' cells of the v2 e-print of arXiv:2603.21688 lie entirely after \end{document} and do not appear in the paper: they are unfinished author scratch for SO(7), SO(9) and general SO(N), while the SO(5) matrix they were taken to be missing is printed in full as equation (34)

families.paper_title: The two $6\times 6$ Racah matrices for the symmetric representation of $SO(5)$, repaired and certified
families.paper_abstract: A recent preprint of Morozov (arXiv:2603.21688) prints the two $6\times 6$ Racah matrices $U_{\yd{2}}$ and $U_{\yd{3,1}}$ that govern three-strand knot invariants in the symmetric representation $\yd{2}$ of the quantum group $SO(5)$, as its equations (32) and (34).  A Racah matrix is a change between orthonormal bases, hence orthogonal, and symmetric when the three strands carry one and the same representation; and it must solve the Yang--Baxter equation in the form printed there as (11).  Neither matrix has these properties as typeset.  Equation (34) is not symmetric --- six off-diagonal pairs carry opposite signs --- and no symmetric reading of it is orthogonal, because its diagonal entry $U_{44}$ carries the wrong sign; equation (32) is symmetric but not orthogonal, its second row failing to have unit norm.  We give the repairs: seven sign changes in (34), and three amendments to (32) --- $\qn{7}^2\to\qn{7}$ in the $(2,3)$ entry, $x_5=(\sqrt q-1/\sqrt q)^4\to (\sqrt q-1/\sqrt q)^2$ in (33), and a factor $\qn{12}$ missing under the root of the $(2,6)$ entry.  The repaired matrices are symmetric and orthogonal as identities of rational functions of $q$, the repaired (34) carries exactly the printed magnitudes, and the repaired (32) agrees with the printed expressions except at the three amended positions; these statements, and the failure of the printed readings, are proved in Lean~4 through polynomial-identity certificates.  Computations outside the formal development show that both repaired matrices satisfy the Yang--Baxter equation exactly, that the sign repair of (34) is unique up to the gauge $U\mapsto DUD$ and an overall sign, and that the $69$ question marks in the preprint's \LaTeX\ source lie after \verb|\end{document}| and concern $SO(7)$, $SO(9)$ and $SO(N)$, not $SO(5)$.  The mathematics of the preprint is right; its typesetting is not.

families.paper_title: Counting the markings of a graph that realize racks and quandles
families.paper_abstract: A \emph{marking} of a graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $V$ is a map $R\colon V\to\Aut\Gamma$; it makes $V$ into a right quasigroup, and by a theorem of Ta that right quasigroup is a rack exactly when $R_{R_v(w)}=R_vR_wR_v^{-1}$ for all $v,w\in V$.  Let $\murack(\Gamma)$ and $\muqnd(\Gamma)$ be the number of markings realizing a rack, respectively a quandle.  Ta tabulated these numbers for complete graphs, star graphs and cycles on few vertices and left five entries of the table undetermined.  We determine four of them: \[ \mupair(K_5)=(1708,404),\qquad \mupair(K_6)=(36538,6658), \] \[ \mupair(K_{1,5})=(7628,1708),\qquad \mupair(K_{1,6})=(223378,36538), \] where $\mupair=(\murack,\muqnd)$.  The blind sweep over all $|\Aut\Gamma|^{|V|}$ markings is $10^{20}$ maps in the largest of these cases; we replace it by a search that propagates the forcing $R_{R_v(w)}=R_vR_wR_v^{-1}$ and whose tree has at most $2.7\cdot10^{5}$ nodes.  We also record an identity that is visible in Ta's own printed data but is not remarked on there, $\muqnd(K_{1,n-1})=\murack(K_{n-1})$, and explain it: the row of the centre of a star is a \emph{shift}, and racks on a set are in bijection with pairs consisting of a quandle and a compatible shift.  The identity relates two of the previously undetermined entries to two others, so the four new values check each other.  All statements below are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The third-moment Rademacher stability constant\\ is exact on the flat family, on the spike region\\ and on the fourth-moment region $\sum_ia_i^4\ge\tfrac12$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\eps_1,\dots,\eps_n$ be independent Rademacher signs, let $a\in\RR^n$ satisfy $\sum_ia_i^2=1$, write $\Sbar_n=n^{-1/2}(\eps_1+\dots+\eps_n)$ and $\Delta_n(a)=\sum_i(a_i^2-\frac1n)^2$.  Gao and Qian introduce the optimal dimension-free third-moment stability constant $\Copt=\inf\bigl(\E|\Sbar_n|^3-\E|\sum_ia_i\eps_i|^3\bigr)/\Delta_n(a)$, prove $\frac{3(5\sqrt2-7)}{16}\le\Copt\le5\sqrt3-6\sqrt2$ --- a bracket of width a factor just over $13$ --- and conjecture that the upper end $\Cs:=5\sqrt3-6\sqrt2=0.1749726636\ldots$ is the truth.  We prove their conjectured inequality on three explicit regions that hold at \emph{every} dimension.  First, on the flat coefficient vectors: for all integers $1\le k<n$, $\E|\Sbar_n|^3-\E|\Sbar_k|^3\ge\Cs(\frac1k-\frac1n)$, with strict inequality except at $(k,n)=(2,3)$, so $\Cs$ is the unique extremal chord slope of the sequence $\E|\Sbar_n|^3$.  Second, on the vectors in which one coordinate carries at least the $\ell^1$ mass of all the others: there the conjectured inequality holds for every $n\ge2$, and the restricted infimum is \emph{exactly} $\Cs$, attained at Gao and Qian's own dimension-three vector $(a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)=(\frac12,\frac12,0)$ --- so on that region the factor-$13$ bracket collapses to a point.  In dimension four the sharp constant on that region is the new exact value $6-4\sqrt2=0.3431457505\ldots$.  Third, on the fourth-moment region $\sum_ia_i^4\ge\frac12$, which is provably \emph{not} contained in the second: there too the conjectured inequality holds at every $n\ge2$ with the same constant, the restricted infimum is again exactly $\Cs$, and in dimension four it is again exactly $6-4\sqrt2$.  That third region contains the conjectured extremiser, so in dimension four the value of the optimum is in doubt only on the complementary set $\sum_ia_i^4<\frac12$.  The engine is a closed form for $\E|S_n|^3$ coming from two telescoping binomial identities, after which the whole flat family reduces to one sequence of consecutive slopes; on the spike region the extremiser is exhibited by an exact quadratic factorisation rather than by calculus, and on the fourth-moment region a single Cauchy--Schwarz step against $\E S^4=3-2\sum_ia_i^4$ reduces everything to the same chord bound at $k=2$.  Nothing here is an exhaustive computation: $\Copt$ is an infimum over infinitely many dimensions, and all three regions are settled at all of them at once.  Every theorem below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Certified three-colour Rado numbers for $ax+by=cz$ with non-unit coefficients
families.paper_abstract: For positive integers $a,b,c$ and $r\ge 1$, the Rado number $R_r(ax+by=cz)$ is the least $N$ such that every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ admits a monochromatic solution of $ax+by=cz$.  Several hundred values of $R_3$ are in print, and those not covered by a closed form are the output of a satisfiability solver reporting an unaudited verdict; as far as our search reached, no proof log accompanies any of them.  We close that gap for seven equations. For each of \[ 5x+3y=3z,\; 3x+3y=2z,\; 5x+y=z,\; 5x+3y=2z,\; 6x+3y=2z,\; 5x+5y=4z,\; 3x+2y=z \] we determine $R_3$ exactly --- the values are $186$, $243$, $286$, $395$, $648$, $875$ and $1093$ --- and both halves of each determination are machine-checked: the avoiding colouring of $\ints{R_3-1}$ is exhibited and verified, and the non-existence of an avoiding colouring of $\ints{R_3}$ is an LRAT refutation replayed by a formally verified checker against a propositional formula that is constructed, not read from a file.  The bridge between the formula and the colouring problem is a single encoding-fidelity theorem, proved once for all $(a,b,c,r,N)$, and it is proved without any appeal to computation.  The largest instance refutes a formula with $298{,}663$ clauses.  As far as our search reached, these are the first Rado numbers with coefficients other than $a=b=c=1$ to carry a machine-checkable certificate. All statements are verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Rainbow three-term progressions in $\ZZ_n$ with four or more colours
families.paper_abstract: For a surjective $r$-colouring of $\ZZ_n=\ZZ/n\ZZ$, call an ordered solution $(x,y,z)$ of $x+y=2z$ \emph{rainbow} if its three coordinates carry three different colours.  Elvin, Gonzales, Rodriguez and Wilbur determined the largest possible proportion of rainbow solutions for $r=3$ --- it is $2/3$, attained exactly when $3\mid n$ --- and asked what happens for $r\ge 4$, where their counting argument gives only $1-1/r$.  We show that the whole gap at $r=4$ collapses to a single inequality about the colour classes: some pair of classes has size product at most the total \emph{defect} $\sum_i|A_i|^2-M$, where $M$ counts the monochromatic solutions.  That inequality implies the proportion $2/3$ for every odd modulus, and we prove it unconditionally at every odd prime and at the composite moduli $9,15,21,27,33,39,51,57$ and $69$.  The modulus $27$ is the first for which the extension $0\to\Zm 9\to\Zm{27}\to\Zm3\to0$ does not split; we give an exact fibre decomposition of the defect twisted by the $2$-cocycle of that extension and show the twist is not removable and is exactly what makes the modulus $27$ work.  Along the way we record an exact identity for odd $n$ relating the rainbow count to the class sizes, two unconditional bounds strictly below $3/4$, and the exact four-, five-, six- and seven-colour maxima at small moduli, from which the maxima appear to be $1-1/p(r)$ with $p(r)$ the largest odd integer at most $r$ --- so that only an odd number of colours ever helps.  All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.description: An unknown ranking `π⋆` of `n` items is to be identified. Each round the learner proposes a **complete linear order** `π`; the oracle either declares `π` correct — which happens only when `π = π⋆`, and ends the interaction — or returns an **unordered pair `{i,j}` whose relative order in `π` is wrong**. `Q(n)` is the number of proposals a worst-case-optimal learner needs, counting the confirming proposal itself.
