Q(5) = 7, from an 18-entry strategy table and a 12-entry adversary table, both up to isomorphism
Q(6) = 10, from a 61-entry strategy table and a 13-entry adversary table, both up to isomorphism

Q(7) >= 12: no learner identifies an unknown ranking of seven items within eleven proposals. The adversary certificate is 36 entries up to isomorphism -- a perfect binary tree of 4095 states when labels are carried, each state offering a pair whose two answers both keep the value: exact halving, twelve times over

Negative controls: a genuine ranking is accepted and a list with a repeat is rejected; with one candidate left the learner still needs one proposal and zero never suffice (the convention that separates Q(n) from Moshkov's decision-tree depth); six proposals do not suffice on five items; eight do suffice, so an exact value is a two-sided claim

Q(7) = 12 exactly, kernel-checked in both directions: the coincidence Q(n) = floor(log2 n!) + 1 -- true for every n <= 6, i.e. the counterexample oracle is worth exactly one bit a round -- FAILS at n = 7, where the information-theoretic count gives 13 and the true value is 12. This is the first value of the sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 12 that is not the sorting bound, and it answers the source's 'optimal constants' question in the direction the constant is smaller than 1

The model identity: the value of Alon-Moran-Moran's ranking-from-counterexamples game at k = 0 on n items equals h^(4)(S_n) + 1, the minimum depth of a decision tree with proper hypotheses for the sorting decision table, plus one for the confirming proposal. The two literatures -- exact learning with proper equivalence queries (2026) and decision trees with hypotheses (2021-2022) -- do not cite each other

First exact values of Q(n,k), the same game with at most k untruthful counterexamples and a learner that knows k: Q(2,k) = 2, 4, 6 for k = 0, 1, 2; Q(3,k) = 3, 6, 9, 12 for k = 0..3; Q(4,k) = 5, 8, 12 for k = 0, 1, 2; Q(5,1) = 10. The per-lie increment is 2 at n = 2, 3 at n = 3, 3 then 4 at n = 4 -- data on the second constant the source leaves open, the one in front of nk

The method: two certificate formats for this game and their soundness theorems -- a strategy table (ub_sound) and an adversary table of balanced-pair cycles (lb_sound), both proved against the unreduced model with no native_decide -- together with relabelling invariance (wins_permMask and wins_permMask_rev: permuting the items carries a winning strategy to a winning strategy and back), which lets both tables store one entry per isomorphism class. Measured at n = 7: the strategy table falls from 514,456 entries to 229 and the adversary table from 4,095 to 36, and the module checks in 4.8 s instead of an extrapolated hour

Properness is free in the truthful game through seven items: dropping the requirement that every query be a linear order (Moshkov's type-2 hypotheses, an arbitrary orientation of the pairs) leaves the value unchanged at n = 7, where both are 12. For n <= 6 this is the published fact that the h^(2) and h^(4) columns of the sorting table agree; n = 7 is new. It sits next to the source's headline that properness is what turns the lie term from O(k) into Theta(nk)

The exact value is not a function of the number of linear extensions L and the width x: two posets on six points, both with L = 8 and x = 2, need 3 and 4 proposals respectively, both kernel-checked in both directions. The source's open-questions section asks whether the complexity for a starting poset 'is determined by L and x alone, or whether additional structural parameters of the poset are needed'; this settles the exact-value form of that question in the negative, and NOT the up-to-constant-factors form the source actually asks

families.paper_title: Ranking from counterexamples: the exact query complexity for at most seven items, and the failure of the sorting pattern at seven
families.paper_abstract: In the ranking-from-counterexamples game of Alon, Moran and Moran, a learner repeatedly proposes a linear order on $n$ items and an adversarial oracle either declares the proposal correct or names an unordered pair whose relative order the proposal gets wrong.  Write $Q(n)$ for the number of proposals a worst-case-optimal deterministic learner needs when every counterexample is truthful, counting the confirming proposal itself.  We determine $Q(n)$ for every $n \le 7$: \[ Q(1), \dots, Q(7) \;=\; 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 10,\ 12 . \] The values for $n \le 6$ turn out to be published mathematics in a different language: they are $h^{(4)}(S_n) + 1$, where $h^{(4)}(S_n)$ is the minimum depth of a decision tree with proper hypotheses for the sorting decision table, computed by Azad, Chikalov, Hussain and Moshkov in 2021.  Neither that work nor the 2026 source cites the other; we identify the two models and re-derive the values.  The value at $n = 7$ is new, and it breaks a pattern.  For every $n \le 6$ one has $Q(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n! \rfloor + 1$, and for $3 \le n \le 6$ this is exactly the number of comparisons needed to sort $n$ items, whereas $Q(7) = 12 < 13 = \lfloor \log_2 7! \rfloor + 1$.  Eleven counterexamples and a confirming round beat the thirteen comparisons that sorting seven items requires, even though the learner never chooses which pair it is told about.  We also settle, in the negative and at the level of exact values, a question the source poses about the game started from a poset $P$ of already-known comparisons: two posets on six points, each with $8$ linear extensions and width $2$, have values $3$ and $4$.  Every value stated as a theorem below is proved in both directions and machine-checked in Lean~4; Section~\ref{sec:verif} says exactly what is and what is not formalised.

families.paper_title: Rank-maximal assignments and the uncovered set:\\ the McKelvey and Bordes inclusions through seven agents,\\ and the failure of the Gillies variant from four
families.paper_abstract: In the assignment (house allocation) domain of $n$ agents, $n$ houses and strict preferences, an assignment $\mu$ majority dominates $\lambda$ when more agents prefer their house under $\mu$ than under $\lambda$; because this relation has ties, there are three covering relations --- Bordes, Gillies and McKelvey --- and three uncovered sets.  Brandt, Chen, Dong, Lederer and Schlenga (arXiv:2602.14816) report that for $n\le5$ every rank-maximal assignment lies in the McKelvey uncovered set, and leave the general case open.  We show the following.  The McKelvey inclusion holds for $n=6$ and $n=7$, and in the stronger Bordes form; moreover the hypothesis can be weakened from rank-maximality to \emph{local} rank-maximality --- no exchange of two agents' houses and no cyclic exchange among three agents improves the count vector --- and the conclusion still holds for $n\le7$; exchanges of two agents alone suffice for $n\le4$ and fail at $n=5$, while the covering quantifier cannot be localised in the same way --- at $n=6$ a witness against a covering may have to move five of the six agents.  These statements for $n\ge5$ rest on unsatisfiability certificates from a SAT solver (one instance per conjugacy class of $\Sym(n)$, ten at $n=6$ and fourteen at $n=7$) and are not formalised; the statements for $n\le4$, the $n=5$ sharpness witness, and a census of the $331\,776$ four-agent profiles are verified in Lean~4 from the definitions.  The Gillies variant behaves differently: from $n=4$ on there are profiles with a rank-maximal assignment outside the Gillies uncovered set --- explicit witnesses for $n=4,5,6,7$ are verified in Lean, $n=4$ is the smallest such size, exactly $9\,504$ of the $331\,776$ four-agent profiles are of this kind, and a padding construction gives a witness for every $n\ge4$. The mechanism is the one the source names: a popular assignment Gillies covers everything it dominates.  The general question remains open; we record why the obvious local arguments cannot settle it.

families.title: The exact null distribution of Rao's spacing test: certified rational critical values
families.description: Rao's spacing test is a nonparametric test of uniformity on the circle. arXiv:2602.04318v1, §2.1, defines it verbatim as follows.
families.paper_title: The exact null distribution of Rao's spacing test: certified rational critical values
families.paper_abstract: Rao's spacing statistic $U_n=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n|T_i-2\pi/n|$ of $n$ points on the circle, $T_i$ the arcs between cyclically consecutive points, is a standard test of circular uniformity, and its critical values are still taken from tables: Rao's original table (1969/1976), extended by Russell and Levitin (1995) to $n\le 1000$ by trapezoidal quadrature and cubic-spline interpolation, and distributed today as the data set \texttt{rao.table} of the R package \texttt{circular}. Under uniformity the null distribution of $U_n/2\pi$ is a piecewise polynomial with rational coefficients, so its value at a rational argument is a rational number that can be computed exactly. We evaluate this exact distribution function in exact rational arithmetic and obtain: 33 enclosures of width $0.001\dg$ for the upper critical values at $n=4,\dots,14$ and $\alpha=0.10,0.05,0.01$; a proof that three of the shipped critical values -- $(n,\alpha)=(12,0.01)$, $(14,0.01)$ and $(12,0.001)$ -- are wrong in their last printed digit, the exact values being $187.6541\dg$, $183.8944\dg$ and $208.6850\dg$ against the tabulated $187.66$, $183.90$ and $208.69$; and the exact null $P$-values, to $10^{-6}$, of the five worked examples in this literature, each of which confirms the printed approximation. All 18 entries of the exact column that the recent paper arXiv:2602.04318 reproduces from Russell and Levitin at $n=10$ are recovered at the printed precision. Every numerical statement is checked in Lean~4 by exact evaluation of the rational formula; a wider exact sweep of the shipped table over $n\le 30$, reported as a computation only, finds three further last-digit disagreements at $n=16$, $21$ and $24$.

families.paper_title: An antipodal rational $5$-design with $37$ points, a $3$-adic obstruction for the degree-five Hilbert--Kamke equations, and the nonexistence of two-orbit weighted $9$-designs on $\Sph^3$
families.paper_abstract: A Chebyshev-type quadrature of degree $m$, or an $m$-design, for a probability measure $w(t)\,dt$ on an interval $I$ is a set of distinct points of $I$ over which the unweighted average of every polynomial of degree at most $m$ equals its integral.  For the Chebyshev measure $(1-t^2)^{-1/2}dt/\pi$ on $(-1,1)$, Mishima, Lu, Sawa and Uchida determined the spectrum of antipodal rational $5$-designs with an even number of points completely, proved that none with an odd number $2N+1\le 33$ of points exists, exhibited one with $35$ points, and asked for one with $37$ points as the smallest open case.  We answer that question: the $37$ rational numbers $\{0\}\cup\{\pm m/144\}$, where $m$ runs over $\{3,11,18,25,39,81,91,99,111,117,122,123,125,127,133,137,141,143\}$, form an antipodal $5$-design.  We also record a congruence obstruction on the denominators of such designs which the purely $2$-adic machinery of the source does not see, and which together with that machinery cut the search space by a factor of about $3\cdot10^4$: writing the degree-five system in the homogeneous form $\sum m_i^2=c_2h^2$, $\sum m_i^4=c_4h^4$, the identity $x^4=x^2$ on $\ZZ/3\ZZ$ forces $3\mid h$ whenever $3\nmid c_4-c_2$, and then a mod~$9$ count forces the number of $m_i$ prime to $3$ to be divisible by $9$.  For the $37$-point system this says that every common denominator of the points is divisible by $12$, and that over the least one, $9$ or $18$ of the $18$ positive numerators are prime to~$3$; the new configuration satisfies both, at the smaller of the two allowed counts.  A second, independent part of the paper settles a question about weighted spherical designs raised by Tanino, Tamaru, Hirao and Sawa.  They construct designs on $\Sph^{n-1}$ as unions of hyperoctahedral orbits of \emph{generalized corner vectors} $v_{a,s}$, and report for $n=4$ that they could find no $11$-design, and not even a $9$-design, with two proper orbits.  We show that none exists: for every pair of orbit types $s_1,s_2\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, all $a_1,a_2>0$ and all positive weights, the four $B_4$-invariant harmonic conditions of degree at most $9$ are inconsistent.  Their own Theorem~5.7 already excludes three of the five cases of their classification, for every $n\ge3$; the content that is new here is the two remaining cases at $n=4$.  The degree is sharp --- the corresponding two-orbit $7$-design system is solvable --- and Schur's four-orbit $11$-design satisfies the very same four equations, so ``two orbits'' cannot be raised to ``four''.  Two errata in the printed formulas of that source are recorded along the way.  Every theorem and proposition below is formally verified in Lean~4, and we state precisely what lies outside that guarantee.

families.paper_title: Certified values of reciprocal Rado numbers,\\ and a minimum over unit fractions
families.paper_abstract: For $k\ge 2$ and $r\ge 1$ the reciprocal Rado number $f_r(k)$ is the least $n$ such that every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ admits a monochromatic solution of $1/x_1+\cdots+1/x_k=1/x_{k+1}$, the $x_i$ not necessarily distinct.  Gaiser and Ramezanpour recently proved the sharp bound $f_2(k)\ge 3k^2$ for $k\ge3$, tabulated $28$ values of $f_r(k)$, twenty-four of them computed there for the first time by SAT solving, and posed four problems.  We contribute two things.  First, a decision procedure for $f_r(k)$ in which every step is machine-checked: a backtracking enumeration of the solution set of the equation, proved both complete and sound; a conjunctive normal form encoding whose fidelity --- every avoiding colouring satisfies the formula --- is proved rather than asserted; and refutations replayed inside a proof assistant from LRAT certificates.  It delivers $f_2(2)=60$, $f_2(3)=40$, $f_2(4)=48$, $f_2(5)=80$, $f_3(3)=585$ and $f_3(2)=3276$ as two-sided theorems carrying certificates, and we are aware of no earlier machine-checkable certificate for a reciprocal Rado number.  Second, we determine the first twenty-five values of the quantity of Problem~5.4 of Gaiser and Ramezanpour: the least positive value of $a-b_1-\cdots-b_k$ with $a,b_1,\dots,b_k$ unit fractions of denominator at most $n$.  The answer is \emph{not} always a unit fraction --- at $k=2$, $n=16$ it is $5/1456$ --- so the shape of the $k=1$ case does not persist, and it is not monotone in $k$.  Every theorem below is formally verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Squares tiled by pairwise unequal rectangles:\\ the seven-piece column
families.paper_abstract: For integers $n,m\ge 1$ let $\Wst(n,m)$ be the minimum total length of the interior segments of a partition of the square $[0,n]^2$ into $m$ axis-aligned rectangles with integer corners and pairwise distinct (unordered) dimension pairs, when such a partition exists.  Lago G\'omez, who introduced this quantity as the two-dimensional core of a problem about tilings of a cube, proved $\Wst(n,m)=n+2(m-2)$ throughout the middle regime $T_{m-2}\le n<T_{m-1}$ for $4\le m\le 6$, conjectured it for all $m\ge 4$, and asked for the case $m=7$, where the middle regime is the finite range $15\le n\le 20$.  We settle that range: $\Wst(n,7)=n+10$ for $15\le n\le 20$, the upper bounds by explicit tilings and the matching lower bounds by two independent exhaustive searches.  The same two searches determine the whole deep regime of the same column, $\Wst(n,7)$ for $5\le n\le 14$, where the value climbs in steps of $+1$, drops once at $n=10$, and reaches its middle-regime value three steps early, at $n=12$.  Independently of any search we prove three structural facts about this tiling class: the identity $\Wall(T)+2n=\sum_i(w_i+h_i)$ for \emph{every} tiling; the piece-count ceiling $4m\le n^2+6$, which settles every non-existence entry of the table of $\Wst$ for $3\le n\le 5$ and gives the maximum piece counts $3,5,7$ at $n=3,4,5$; and a layer-cake bound on the total semiperimeter, from which $\Wst(4,5)=10$ and $\Wst(5,7)=19$ follow with both halves proved.  The last of these is the first exact value in the open column $m=7$ that does not rest on a search.  Every theorem, proposition, lemma and corollary below is machine-checked in Lean~4, except where a heading marks part of it as resting in addition on exhaustive computation.

The evaluation the source stops one step short of: for a complement-closed factor family whose run counts fill [m+1, M+1], the number of reduced-abelian classes is Lambda + #{odd r in [m+1, M+1]} with Lambda = M - m + 1, equivalently 2 rho^{ab,red}_t(n) = 3 Lambda_n + eps_n where eps_n = 0 if Lambda_n is even and (-1)^{m_n} if Lambda_n is odd; Lambda_n = rho^red_t(n)/2
Open cell (C1) of arXiv:2509.16034 is a theorem: rho^{ab,red}_t(2n+1) = rho^{ab,red}_t(n+1) for every n >= 0

New arithmetic criterion: Lambda_{n+1} = rho^red_t(n+1)/2 is odd if and only if t_n = t_{3n} for the 0-indexed Thue-Morse word -- equivalently rho^red_t(n+1) = 2 (mod 4) if and only if the source's t_{n+1} = t_{3n+1}; the proof reduces to the Thue-Morse identity t_j XOR t_{j+1} = t_{3j+2} XOR t_{3j+3}, i.e. 3j+2 and j have the same number of trailing 1s in binary
Open cell (C2) of arXiv:2509.16034 is a theorem: abs(rho^{ab,red}_t(4n+2) - rho^{ab,red}_t(4n)) = 0 if t_{n+1} = t_{3n+1} and 1 otherwise, for every n >= 1, in the source's own 1-indexed notation

Open cell (C4) of arXiv:2509.16034 is answered: 2 rho^{ab,red}_t(4n) = 3 Lambda_{n+1} + 3 + (0 if Lambda_{n+1} is odd, else -(-1)^{m_{n+1}}), with the companion 2 rho^{ab,red}_t(4n+2) = 3 Lambda_{n+1} + 3 + (0 if Lambda_{n+1} is odd, else (-1)^{m_{n+1}}); together with (C1) this is a full recursion for rho^{ab,red}_t on the state (Lambda_n, m_n mod 2)
Open cell (C5) of arXiv:2509.16034, as literally stated, is settled: (rho^{ab,red}_t(n) : n in N) takes infinitely many values, hence is not k-automatic for any k

(rho^{ab,red}_t(n) : n in N) is a 2-regular sequence, so the k-REGULAR strengthening of open cell (C5) of arXiv:2509.16034 is false; the Q-span of its 2-kernel has dimension 11 (7 for Lambda = rho^red_t/2)

families.paper_title: A closed form for the reduced abelian complexity of the Thue--Morse word, and the five open problems of Campbell, Currie and Rampersad
families.paper_abstract: Campbell, Currie and Rampersad recently introduced the \emph{reduced} factor and abelian complexity functions of an infinite word: length-$n$ factors are counted after every maximal block of equal letters has been collapsed to a single letter, up to equality (respectively, up to permutation) of the collapsed words.  They evaluate both functions for the paperfolding word and the reduced factor complexity $\rred_{\tmb}$ of the Thue--Morse word $\tmb$, and close with five printed questions about the reduced abelian complexity $\rab_{\tmb}$: an apparent halving identity, an apparent dichotomy $|\rab_{\tmb}(4n+2) - \rab_{\tmb}(4n)| \in \{0,1\}$ governed by $\tmb_{n+1} = \tmb_{3n+1}$, the sign of that difference, a recursion for $\rab_{\tmb}(4n)$, and non-$k$-automaticity.  We give a closed form.  Writing $m_n$ and $M_n$ for the least and greatest number of alternations in a length-$n$ factor of $\tmb$ and $\Lambda_n = M_n - m_n + 1 = \rred_{\tmb}(n)/2$, \[ 2\,\rab_{\tmb}(n) \;=\; 3\Lambda_n + \varepsilon_n, \qquad \varepsilon_n = \begin{cases} 0 & \Lambda_n \text{ even},\\ (-1)^{m_n} & \Lambda_n \text{ odd}.\end{cases} \] From it we prove the halving identity and the dichotomy; we evaluate the sign of the difference as $(-1)^{m_{n+1}}$, with $m \bmod 2$ given by an explicit $O(\log n)$ rule, equivalently by a four-state base-$4$ automaton, and we report two exhaustive searches that find no closed form of simpler shape; we give the recursion for $\rab_{\tmb}(4n)$ and hence a full recursion for $\rab_{\tmb}$ on the state $(\Lambda_n, m_n \bmod 2)$, which the value $\rab_{\tmb}(n)$ alone does not carry.  The fifth question is settled as printed: the sequence is unbounded, hence has infinite range, hence is not $k$-automatic for any $k$.  Outside the formal development we record that the strengthening a reader reaches for is false: $\rab_{\tmb}$ \emph{is} $2$-regular, its $2$-kernel spanning an $11$-dimensional space over $\QQ$.  One caveat is uniform and is stated with every result below.  All theorems are about the closed form $\rhat(n) = (3\Lambda_n + \varepsilon_n)/2$ built from the $(m_n,M_n)$ recursion of Campbell--Currie--Rampersad, and all are machine-checked in Lean~4 for that function.  The identification $\rhat(n) = \rab_{\tmb}(n)$ is checked by direct computation for $1 \le n \le 64$ and, in general, rests on that recursion together with the two structural facts established inside their proof of the recursion for $\rred_{\tmb}$ --- the run counts of the length-$n$ factors fill the whole interval $[m_n+1, M_n+1]$, and $\tmb$ is closed under complement --- which we cite and do not reprove.

PRD(V) = |free(V)| holds exactly on the subcubes: for nonempty V in {0,1}^[n], PRD(V) = |free(V)| if and only if V contains every concept that agrees with V at each coordinate where V is constant. Both directions proved uniformly in n; the census confirms the count 3, 9, 27 = 3^n at n = 1, 2, 3
Ldim and PRD are invariant under the bit-flip translations g |-> g XOR v of the cube (2^n of the 2^n n! automorphisms of {0,1}^[n])

max{PRD(H) : H a nonempty subset of {0,1}^[n]} = n, attained ONLY by the full class H = {0,1}^[n]; consequently a class with |H| = m >= 3 attaining the source's bound PRD(H) = |H| - 1 needs a domain of size at least m, so the one-hot class of RD2 is domain-minimal (the source's own witness U_m uses a domain of size 2^m)

The complete (Ldim, PRD) census of every nonempty concept class on a domain of size n <= 3, kernel-bound: n=1 -> (0,0):2, (1,1):1; n=2 -> (0,0):4, (1,1):10, (2,2):1; n=3 -> (0,0):8, (1,1):84, (1,2):8, (2,2):154, (3,3):1, with the five cells proved to exhaust all 255 classes

Negative controls: PRD <= n cannot be improved to n-1 (the full class attains n); the source's PRD <= |H|-1 cannot be improved to |H|-2 (the one-hot class attains it); Ldim = PRD is false (Ldim 1 < PRD 2 on three points); the subcube hypothesis of RD4 is not vacuous ({0^3, 1^3} has three free coordinates and PRD 1); the 2 <= |J| hypothesis of Ldim(oneHot J) = 1 is needed; the |H| >= 3 hypothesis of the minimal-domain theorem is needed (on a one-point domain the full class has |H| = 2 = PRD + 1 > n)

families.paper_title: The proper repair dimension on a fixed domain:\\ a sharp bound, its equality cases, and a domain-minimal\\ separation from the Littlestone dimension
families.paper_abstract: For a finite binary concept class $\HH\subseteq\{0,1\}^X$ on a finite domain $X$, Li \cite{Li} defines the \emph{proper repair dimension} $\PRD(\HH)$ by a recursion on version spaces --- a live hypothesis is eliminated by a label it does not predict, and $\PRD$ is the worst case, over the adversary's choices, of the best case over the learner's --- and proves $\Ldim(\HH)\le\PRD(\HH)\le|\HH|-1$, both bounds tight.  Every bound in that paper is in terms of $|\HH|$; nothing there constrains $\PRD$ in terms of the domain.  We prove that $\PRD(V)\le|\fre(V)|$, where $\fre(V)$ is the set of coordinates on which $V$ is not constant, so that $\PRD(\HH)\le n$ for every class on $n$ points, against the $2^n-1$ that $|\HH|-1$ gives at $\HH=\{0,1\}^{[n]}$.  We then determine the equality cases exactly: $\PRD(V)=|\fre(V)|$ holds if and only if $V$ is a subcube, so $\max\{\PRD(\HH): \emptyset\ne\HH\subseteq\{0,1\}^{[n]}\}=n$ with the full class as the \emph{unique} maximiser.  It follows that a class of size $m\ge 3$ attaining Li's bound $\PRD(\HH)=|\HH|-1$ needs a domain of at least $m$ points.  That bound is attained: the one-hot class $\{e_1,\dots,e_n\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{[n]}$ has $|\HH|=n$, $\Ldim(\HH)=1$ and $\PRD(\HH)=n-1=|\HH|-1$.  This class is Li's own separating example $U_n$ with its domain cut from $2^{[n]}$ down to the $n$ singletons, and it improves that example on two axes at once --- domain size $2^n\to n$ and Littlestone dimension $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\to 1$ --- at the same $|\HH|$ and the same $\PRD$; by the previous sentence the domain cannot be cut further.  We also record the complete joint distribution of $(\Ldim,\PRD)$ over all nonempty classes on at most three points, and, as computations outside the formal development, over all $65\,535$ classes on four points and, as a count of orbits under the automorphism group of the cube, over the $4\,294\,967\,295$ on five. All the general statements are proved uniformly in $n$ and machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Sierpi\'nski and Riesel numbers among repdigits, repunits, repintegers and repstrings:\\ six improved bounds and two questions answered
families.paper_abstract: Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong asked, for each of eight repetitive shapes of integer, for the smallest base or the smallest repeating block that admits a Sierpi\'nski or a Riesel number of that shape, and answered each of the eight questions only with an upper bound.  We improve six of the eight bounds and settle the remaining two exactly.  The improvements are $\beta_1\le 53$, $\beta_2\le 40$, $\beta_2'\le 39$ and $\beta_1'\le 94$ for the four base questions, against $147$, $87$, $180$ and $16518444216571$; and $\kappa\le 16519$, $\kappa'\le 16519$ for the two $2$-repinteger block questions, against $18107$.  For the two $2$-repstring questions we prove $\tilde\kappa=\tilde\kappa'=1$: the block $k=1$ already works, so those two questions are closed rather than improved, and the witnesses are Selfridge's and Riesel's own covering systems, reused without changing a single residue class.  Three of the improvements are invisible to a search over covering systems whose period divides $144$, where all the classical covering systems live; they need period $60$, and we isolate the arithmetic reason.  Every statement is proved from an explicit covering certificate and has been machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Restricted generalized Schur numbers: exact values at levels three and four, and the threshold of Open Question~6.4
families.paper_abstract: For integers $r\ge 1$, $k\ge 2$ and $\ell\ge 2$, the restricted generalized Schur number $S_r(k;\ell)$ is the least $n$ such that every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ admits a monochromatic solution of $x_1+\dots+x_k=x_{k+1}$ in which exactly $\ell+1$ distinct integers occur.  Gaiser introduced these numbers and proved that for each fixed $\ell\ge 2$ one has $S_2(k;\ell)=F(k,\ell):=k^2+\bigl[\tfrac{(\ell+1)(\ell-2)}{2}+2\bigr]k+\ell(\ell-2)$ for all sufficiently large $k$, without determining how large; his Open Question~6.4 asks for the least such threshold $K$.  We compute twenty-one values of $S_r(k;\ell)$ exactly, ten of them new: $S_2(k;3)$ for $4\le k\le 9$ and $S_2(k;4)$ for $5\le k\le 8$.  Making the arithmetic of Gaiser's Section~5 explicit, we show that his own sufficient condition for the upper bound holds at level~$3$ exactly when $k\ge 10$, and at level~$4$ exactly when $k\ge 20$.  Since our values cover every $k$ from $3$ to $10$ at level~$3$, this answers Open Question~6.4 there: the least $K$ is $3$, the smallest value the definition permits. At level~$4$ the same reading leaves the eleven values $9\le k\le 19$ open.  In the opposite direction we prove the identity $2F(k,k)+(k-1)(k-2)=k^3+4k^2-5k+2$, whose right-hand side is twice a published lower bound for the weak Schur number $S_2(k;k)$; consequently $K>\ell$ for every $\ell\ge 5$, and the closed form cannot begin at $k=\ell$ except at levels $3$ and $4$. All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Restricted reciprocal Rado numbers
families.paper_abstract: For integers $k\ge 2$, $r\ge 2$ and $1\le\ell\le k$, let $f_r(k;\ell)$ denote the least $n$ such that every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ admits a monochromatic solution of \[ \frac{1}{x_1}+\frac{1}{x_2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{x_k}=\frac{1}{x_{k+1}} \] in which the number of distinct integers among $x_1,\dots,x_{k+1}$ is exactly $\ell+1$. Dropping the distinctness condition gives the reciprocal Rado number $f_r(k)$, finite by Brown--R\"odl and Lefmann and computed in small cases by Myers--Parrish and by Gaiser--Ramezanpour; the level $\ell$ was introduced by Gaiser for the linear equation $x_1+\cdots+x_k=x_{k+1}$.  The two have not been combined, and the combination is posed here for the first time.  We prove that $f_r(k;1)$ exists for no $k\ge 2$ and no $r\ge 2$, by the explicit two-colouring $v\mapsto\lfloor\log_k v\rfloor \bmod 2$; the point is that the level-$1$ solutions of the reciprocal equation are exactly the pairs $\{a,ka\}$, which is literally the same set as for the linear equation.  We determine the six values $f_2(2;2)=120$, $f_2(3;2)=84$, $f_2(3;3)=126$, $f_2(4;2)=108$, $f_2(4;3)=90$ and $f_2(4;4)=180$, each by an avoiding colouring at $n-1$ checked against a provably complete solution list together with a refutation at $n$.  In particular $f_2(k;\ell)$ is \emph{not} monotone in $\ell$ --- $f_2(4;2)=108>90=f_2(4;3)$ --- whereas for each fixed level the linear analogue $S_2(k;\ell)$ agrees, for all large $k$, with a polynomial strictly increasing in $\ell$; so the transferred parameter does not inherit the shape of its original. We also prove $f_r(k;\ell)\ge f_r(k)$ for every level, with no search, and show the inequality is strict where it has been computed.  Every theorem, proposition and lemma below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

statements.label: Lower bound for the ranked allocation at K = 3 Gaussian unit-variance arms: let b be a lowest coordinate of the empirical mean Q and let w put 1/8 on arm b and 7/16 on each of the other two. Then for EVERY true mean P with a unique best arm j whose best arm is not a maximiser of Q, L(P,Q,w) = H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 >= 7/64. Proof is exact and elementary: eliminating the free level P_j by the weighted-variance identity leaves, per adversary move, one algebraic identity -- 9A^2+9C^2-14AC = 8(A-C)^2+(A+C)^2 with A,C >= the two gaps when the promoted arm is the 1/8 arm, and 9p^2+4z^2-4pz = 8p^2+(p-2z)^2 with p >= the gap when it is a 7/16 arm

The ranked allocation's exact game value at K = 3: gameVal(w_0) = inf over all confusing pairs (Q,P) of L(P,Q,w_0(Q)) = 7/64 exactly, where w_0(Q) puts 1/8 on a lowest coordinate of Q and 7/16 on the other two. So the supremum over mappings in Theorem 1 is ATTAINED at K = 3, by a piecewise-constant, rank-only allocation

R^go(3) = 7/64 for Gaussian unit-variance arms with the risk H_1: the value of the one-shot game of Definition 3 / Theorem 1 at K = 3, defined as the supremum over measurable mappings w : R^3 -> Delta(3) of the infimum over confusing pairs of H_1(P) sum_i w_i(Q)(Q_i-P_i)^2/2, is exactly 7/64 = 0.109375. Upper bound by a two-point mixture certificate at Q_n = (0,-1,-n^2): 1/7 on P = (-n^3/8, -n^3/8, 7n^3/8) (the hopeless arm raised to the top) and 6/7 on P = (-n/2, n/2, -n^2) (the two contenders swap, the third arm does not move), whose per-arm average cost is at most 7/64 + 2/n in every coordinate; lower bound by RGO1

The extremal configuration and the exact approach to the infimum: against the ranked allocation (7/16,7/16,1/8) at Q = (0,-1,-2), the true means (-s/8, -s/8, 7s/8) -- the hopeless arm raised to the top with both gaps s -- cost exactly 7/64 + 21/(64 s) + 15/(16 s^2), strictly above 7/64 for every s > 0 and tending to 7/64. Together with RGO1 this pins the value of the game against w_0 as an infimum that is approached and (numerically, at every tested instance) never attained; the hardest empirical three-arm configuration is two contenders plus one hopeless arm

Negative controls bracketing R^go(3). Too small: no confusing pair against the ranked allocation costs less than 1/10, so R^go(3) > 1/10 and the claim R^go(3) <= 1/10 is refuted. Too large: at Q = (0,-1,-40000) every allocation in the simplex admits a confusing pair costing less than 1/8, so R^go(3) < 1/8 (the Lean proves R^go(3) < 1/8; that 1/8 = R^go(2) is the paper's Section 2.1 computation, not Lean) -- adding a third arm makes the one-shot game strictly harder

Non-vacuity control: the ranking hypothesis of RGO1 is load-bearing. With the weight 1/8 on arm 3 while the lowest coordinate of Q = (0, -1, -1/4) is arm 2, the confusing pair P = (-55/32, -55/32, 265/32) (gaps 10 and 10, H_1 = 1/50) costs exactly 10871/102400 = 0.10616... < 7/64. So 'b is a lowest coordinate of Q' cannot be dropped from RGO1

The constant of Theorem 5 at K = 3 is at most 32/35. The Eq. (14)-(16) allocation at Q_x = (0,-1,-x) equals (B,B,A)/S with A = x^2+2x+2, B = 2x^2+2x+1, S = 2B+A = 5x^2+6x+4 (computed from Eq. (15)-(16); in particular the empirically best arm and the closest contender always carry the same weight at K = 3), and against it the confusing pair P = (-(n+1)/2, (n-1)/2, -n^2) at x = n^2 costs at most 1/10 + 1/n. Hence any C witnessing Definition 4 for that allocation at K = 3 satisfies C * R^go(3) <= 1/10, i.e. C <= (1/10)/(7/64) = 32/35

The matching half: inf over all confusing pairs of L(P,Q,w_(14)(Q)) = 1/10 exactly at K = 3, so C_stbl(3) = (1/10)/(7/64) = 32/35 -- the unprinted constant of Theorem 5 at three arms. Only '<= 32/35' is proved (RGO7); the lower half is established numerically: inf_P L(P,Q_x,w_(14)(Q_x)) = 0.222222 (x=1, = 2/9), 0.200617 (2), 0.189352 (3), 0.161982 (10), 0.113292 (100), 0.102908 (1000), 0.100636 (10^4), 0.100138 (10^5), decreasing to 1/10, with the binding move being the contender swap and the hopeless-arm raise sitting at w_3(1-w_3) -> 4/25

The exact Successive Rejects rate at K = 3, from the source's own Theorem 7. With P = (0,-1,-x), x >= 1: logbar(3) = 4/3 and H_3(P) = max(8, 9/(x^2-x+1)) for x <= 2, max(8, 12/x^2) for x > 2 (the modified top-3 mean of Eq. (102) is -(1+x)/3 for x <= 2 and -x/2 for x > 2). The H_1-normalised rate (1+x^{-2})/(H_3 logbar(3)) equals 1/6 at x = 1, RISES to the interior maximum 3(41-16 sqrt 6)/32 = 0.1695153858... at x = (2+sqrt 6)/4 = 1.1123724..., then decreases to the infimum 3/32 = 0.09375, which is not attained. So R_SR(3) = 3/32

The exact K = 3 ordering of the three rates: Successive Rejects 3/32 < the paper's closed-form allocation of Eq. (14) 1/10 < the game value R^go(3) 7/64, with ratios SR/game = 6/7, Eq.(14)/game = 32/35 = C_stbl(3), and Eq.(14)/SR = 16/15. This is the finite-K, exact form of the paper's Lemmas 8-9, which compare Almost Tracking with SR only asymptotically in K (O((log K)/(log log K)) and O(log K) factors)

Control at K = 2: for Gaussian unit-variance arms the inner value of the one-shot game against an allocation (w_1,w_2) is exactly w_1 w_2 / 2 (approached as the confusing arm's gap runs to infinity), so R^go(2) = 1/8 at the uniform allocation -- the classical two-arm rate PoE ~ exp(-T Delta^2/8). It is also the value of Successive Rejects at K = 2 by the source's Theorem 7 (H_3 = 8/Delta^2, logbar(2) = 1)

Lower bound for the rank-only allocation at K = 4 Gaussian unit-variance arms: sort the empirical means Q decreasingly and give the four ranks the weights (21/52, 21/52, 6/52, 4/52). Then for EVERY true mean P with a unique best arm j that is not a maximiser of Q, L(P,Q,w) = H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 >= 21/208 = 0.1009615... Consequently R^go(4) >= 21/208, where R^go(4) is the value of the one-shot game of Definition 3 / Theorem 1 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 at K = 4 with the risk H_1. The proof splits on the rank of the target arm: rank 2 gives the contender swap w_1w_2/(2(w_1+w_2)) = 21/208, rank 3 gives 2w_1w_3/(w_1+w_2+w_3) = 21/208 (the rank-4 arm is free), and rank 4 -- all three arms above it must be raised, nothing is free -- reduces after eliminating the free level and the symmetry y_1 = y_2 to the binary quartic 35S^4 - 84S^3 t + 190S^2 t^2 - 672S t^3 + 736 t^4 >= 0, which has the exact sum-of-squares certificate 12225*(that) = 17115(5S^2-6St-4t^2)^2 + 90 t^2(163S-308t)^2 + 186000 t^4.

Upper bound R^go(4) <= 1013/10000 = 0.1013. At the separated ladder Q = (1/2, -1/2, -10^8, -10^16) -- two contenders one apart, then two arms at successively deeper scales -- the three-point mixture 98781/125000 on the contender swap P = (-10^4, 10^4, -10^8, -10^16), 64077/500000 on the raise of arm 3 P = (-10^11, -10^11, 7*10^11, -10^16), and 40799/500000 on the raise of arm 4 P = (-6268700*10^12, -6268700*10^12, -16417426*10^12, 9373130*10^13) has per-arm average cost H_1(P)(Q_i-P_i)^2/2 at most 0.1012542 in every one of the four coordinates. Since the loss is linear in the allocation, every allocation in Delta(4) is beaten to 1013/10000 at this one Q, so no mapping w : R^4 -> Delta(4) holds the adversary above 1013/10000. The three limiting cost vectors are (1/8,1/8,0,0), (1/64,1/64,49/64,0) -- exactly the two K = 3 cost vectors -- and (k(1-mu)^2, k(1-mu)^2, k(rho-mu)^2, k mu^2) with rho = 1.10148726, mu = 0.93731348 (the ladder above uses the nearby rational 0.9373130), k = (2+rho^-2)/2, and the mixture is the saddle of the resulting 3 x 4 matrix game.

The bracket 21/208 <= R^go(4) <= 1013/10000, i.e. 0.100961538... <= R^go(4) <= 0.1013, width 3.4e-4, for the one-shot game of Definition 3 / Theorem 1 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 at K = 4 Gaussian unit-variance arms with the risk H_1(P) = sum_{i != i*(P)} (P* - P_i)^-2. This is a localisation of R^go at four arms; the exact value 0.1012344111937378... is irrational of degree 5 over Q (row RGO18), which is why a bracket and not an equality is the kernel-bound statement.

Negative controls bracketing R^go(4). Too large: R^go(4) <= 1013/10000 < 7/64, so R^go(4) < R^go(3) = 7/64 -- the value of the one-shot game strictly DECREASES from three Gaussian arms to four, a proved instance of the decrease that R^go = Theta(1/log K) (Section 6 of arXiv:2510.23199v3, from Carpentier-Locatelli 2016) asserts asymptotically; in particular the claim R^go(4) >= 7/64 is refuted. Too small: R^go(4) >= 21/208 > 1/10, so the claim R^go(4) <= 1/10 is refuted (1/10 is the K = 3 value of the source's own Eq. (14) allocation, row RGO8).

Non-vacuity controls for the K = 4 rank-only allocation. (i) The RANKING is load-bearing: keep the same multiset of weights and the same top two, but give rank 3 the weight 4/52 that belongs to rank 4 and rank 4 the weight 6/52 that belongs to rank 3; then at Q = (1/2,-1/2,-10^8,-10^16) the raise of arm 3 already costs at most 3/40 = 0.075 < 21/208. (ii) A badly shaped allocation is strictly worse: the uniform allocation (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) is beaten to at most 1/15 = 0.0667 by the contender swap alone. Both allocations are verified to lie in Delta(4).

The constant of Theorem 5 at K = 4 is at most 7/8. Let w be any allocation mapping agreeing with Eq. (14)-(16) of arXiv:2510.23199v3 at Q = (0,-1,-10^8,-10^12), and let C be any constant witnessing Definition 4 for it at K = 4, i.e. C * R^go(4) <= L(P,Q,w(Q)) for every confusing pair. Then C <= 7/8 = 0.875. Witness: the contender swap P = (-100001/2, 99999/2, -10^8, -10^12) -- the two contenders exchange places around their midpoint with gap 10^5 and neither deep arm moves at all, so those two coordinates cost nothing -- whose loss is at most 353/4000 = 0.08825, combined with R^go(4) >= 21/208 (row RGO12). At that Q the Eq. (14) allocation puts at most 12/17 on the two contenders (because D_1 >= 1, D_2 <= 2, D_3 <= 3), its limit along the ladder being exactly (6,6,3,2)/17. Compare C_stbl(3) <= 32/35 = 0.9142857 (row RGO7): 7/8 < 32/35.

The exact K = 4 values, computed but not formalised. R^go(4) = 0.101234411193737825357416680961..., the unique real root in (1/10,1/8) of the irreducible quintic 6346742339469312 v^5 - 3209600887750656 v^4 + 641500052322304 v^3 - 63455008319808 v^2 + 3120377247680 v - 61506376183 = 0; so R^go(4) is IRRATIONAL, of degree exactly 5 over Q, and the K = 3 pattern (the rational 7/64) does not continue. The optimal allocation is again rank-only, (0.4049376448, 0.4049376448, 0.1156964699, 0.0744282405), obtained from the root rho = 1.101487256394143369 of 16r^5 - 14r^4 + 16r^3 - 16r^2 - 3r - 4 = 0 by p = (2rho^4-7)/((rho+7)(2rho^3-7)), a = 7p/2, q = 1-8p, R^go(4) = 7p/8. The extremal empirical configuration is the FULLY SEPARATED LADDER Q = (0,-1,-x,-y) with 1 << x << y (two contenders, one far arm, one much farther arm); two hopeless arms at the same depth give only 0.1052232085... (a/4 at the unique positive root u* = 1.16003068 of the irreducible octic 8u^8 - 7u^7 + 8u^6 - 4u^5 - 5u^4 + 2u^3 - 8u^2 + u - 2; the earlier figure (sqrt 37 - 1)/48 = 0.10589 is that configuration with the raised arm forced to u = 1, an upper bound only) and are not extremal. Structurally, R^go(K) = max_{w in Delta(K)} min_{2<=k<=K} M_k(w), where M_k(w) is the cost of promoting the rank-k arm with the arms below it free; at K = 3, on the symmetric slice w_1 = w_2 where the maximum is attained, this is max_w min(w_1w_2/(2(w_1+w_2)), w_3(1-w_3)) = 7/64 (the second formula M_3 = w_3(1-w_3) holds only on that slice). Finally inf_{Q,P} L(P,Q,w_(14)(Q)) = 3/34 at K = 4, so C_stbl(4) = (3/34)/R^go(4) = 0.8715939...

Strict non-attainment of R^go(3) = 7/64. At K = 3 Gaussian unit-variance arms with the risk H_1, against ANY ranked allocation -- weight 1/8 on a lowest coordinate b of the empirical mean Q and 7/16 on the other two -- every confusing pair (P,Q) of Definition 3 costs the agent H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 STRICTLY more than 7/64. In particular, for the mapping w_0 of row RGO2, whose game value is exactly 7/64, the number 7/64 is not an element of the loss set: the supremum over allocation mappings that defines R^go(3) is attained (by the ranked allocation, row RGO3) but the infimum over instances is not -- it is a limit along Q_x = (0,-1,-x), x -> infinity, at the exact rate 7/64 + 21/(64s) + 15/(16 s^2) of row RGO4.

The matching lower half of RGO8, closing it: at K = 3 the allocation of Eq. (14)-(16) of arXiv:2510.23199v3 keeps the loss strictly above 1/10 at EVERY instance, not only along the family Q_x = (0,-1,-x). Precisely: let Q be any three-arm empirical mean vector with a unique empirical best arm b, let p and c be the other two arms with Q_c <= Q_p < Q_b, put d = Q_b - Q_p and e = Q_b - Q_c, and let w be the Eq. (14)-(16) allocation at Q -- which equals (B,B,A)/S on (b,p,c) with A = (d+e)^2+d^2 = 2d^2+2de+e^2, B = (d+e)^2+e^2 = d^2+2de+2e^2, S = 2B+A = 4d^2+6de+5e^2, so the empirically best arm and the closest contender always carry the same weight. Then every confusing pair (P,Q) of Definition 3 costs H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 > 1/10. The tied-empirical-best case that Eq. (16) treats separately (Q_p = Q_b, where Eq. (16) gives (1/3,1/3,1/3)) costs > 1/10 as well, indeed >= 2/9 [scope note 2026-09-08: the pinned theorems loss_w14_gt / loss_tie_gt conclude only 1/10 < loss; the 2/9 is the step inside loss_tie_gt (core_sym_bottom at a = q = 1/3), true and derivable but not the declaration].

The game value of the Eq. (14) allocation at K = 3 is exactly 1/10, hence the constant Theorem 5 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 leaves unnamed is exactly 32/35 at three arms. The set of losses H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 over all three-arm Q with a unique empirical best, w the Eq. (14)-(16) allocation at that Q, and all confusing pairs (P,Q), has greatest lower bound exactly 1/10 (IsGLB) -- the lower bound is row RGO20 (strict, so the infimum is not attained) and no larger number is one because the pair P = (-(n+1)/2,(n-1)/2,-n^2) at Q = (0,-1,-n^2) costs at most 1/10 + 1/n (row RGO7). Equivalently 32/35 * R^go(3) <= loss for every confusing pair, since R^go(3) = 7/64 and (32/35)(7/64) = 1/10: 32/35 witnesses Definition 4 for the Eq. (14) allocation at K = 3. With row RGO7 (no constant above 32/35 does) the constant is pinned both ways: C_stbl(3) = 32/35 = 0.914285..., i.e. the source's closed-form allocation captures exactly 32/35 of the game value at three arms and loses exactly 3/35 = 8.571...% there.

Negative controls for the 1/10 of rows RGO20-RGO21. Too large: 11/100 is NOT a lower bound for the loss against the Eq. (14) allocation -- the instance Q = (0,-1,-10^6) with P = (-1001/2, 999/2, -10^6) costs at most 1/10 + 1/1000 -- so the constant 1/10 cannot be raised. Too small: 9/10 also witnesses Definition 4 for that allocation at K = 3, refuting any claim that C_stbl(3) < 9/10. Not vacuous: the instance set of RGO21 is nonempty. Hypothesis-necessity: the requirement that w be the Eq. (14) allocation OF THE VERY Q under attack is load-bearing -- the uniform allocation (1/3,1/3,1/3), which is exactly Eq. (14) at Q = (0,-1,-1) (there A = B = 5, S = 15), is beaten at Q = (0,-2,-2000) by the confusing pair P = (-101, 99, -2000), whose loss is 45351616001/528696120000 = 0.0857801... < 1/10.

The allocation of Eq. (14)-(16) of arXiv:2510.23199v3 as a single mapping w_(14) : Q -> Delta(3) at K = 3 -- the form Definition 3 / Theorem 1 and Definition 4 are stated in -- and its game value. Define w_(14)(Q) to be Eq. (14)-(16) at every Q with a unique empirical best arm and (1/3,1/3,1/3) at every Q with a tied empirical best (which is what Eq. (16) gives there). Then w_(14)(Q) is an allocation for every Q, and: (i) inf over ALL confusing pairs (Q,P) of H_1(P) sum_i w_i (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 = 1/10 exactly (the family's own gameVal = sInf), against gameVal = 7/64 for the optimal ranked allocation w_0 of row RGO2; (ii) gameVal(w_(14)) < R^go(3), so the source's closed-form allocation is strictly suboptimal at three arms; (iii) 32/35 is the GREATEST constant C with C * R^go(3) <= H_1(P) sum_i w_i(Q) (Q_i-P_i)^2/2 for every confusing pair (an IsGreatest), i.e. the constant of Definition 4 for the allocation of Eq. (14) at K = 3 is exactly 32/35 = 0.914285...

R_SR(3) = 3/32 exactly: the rate of Successive Rejects at three Gaussian unit-variance arms under Definition 1 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 with the standard risk H_1 of Section 4, computed from the source's own Theorem 7 / Theorem 23 (Eq. (99)-(106)). Every three-arm instance with a unique best arm is P^(x) = (0,-1,-x), x >= 1, up to a shift and a scaling. The implicit modified mean of Eq. (102) is solved there and shown unique: Pbar^mod(2) = -1/2 for every x, and Pbar^mod(3) = -(1+x)/3 for 1 <= x <= 2, = -x/2 for x > 2 (the middle arm drops out of S^(3) past x = 2); the source asserts existence and uniqueness without proof ('we can easily see that Pbar^mod(k) satisfying this expression uniquely exists'). Hence H_3(P^(x))^{-1} = min(1/8, (x^2-x+1)/9) on [1,2] and = 1/8 for x > 2, i.e. H_3 = max(8, 9/(x^2-x+1)), the branches crossing at (2+sqrt 6)/4. With logbar(3) = 4/3 (Eq. (99)) and H_1(P^(x)) = 1 + 1/x^2, the per-instance rate H_1/(H_3 logbar(3)) is strictly above 3/32 for every x >= 1, and the greatest lower bound of the whole rate set is exactly 3/32 (an IsGLB), approached as x -> infinity and attained by no instance.

The exact tail of the Successive Rejects rate at K = 3: for every x >= 2 the instance P^(x) = (0,-1,-x) has rate exactly 3/32 + 3/(32 x^2). So the infimum 3/32 of row RGO24 is approached from above along two contenders and one hopeless arm -- the same extremal empirical shape that is extremal for R^go(3) = 7/64 (row RGO4) -- and is attained by no instance.

Negative controls for the K = 3 Successive Rejects rate. Too small: srRate(100) = 3/32 + 3/320000 < 1/10, so R_SR(3) is not 1/10. Too large: no three-arm instance costs <= 1/12 < 3/32. Non-vacuity: the equal-gaps instance x = 1 has modified mean -2/3 (the plain mean of all three arms), H_3 = 9 and rate 1/6. Both branches of the maximum in Eq. (105) are used: the j = 3 term is the smaller one at x = 1 (1/9 < 1/8) and the larger one at x = 2 (1/3 > 1/8).

R^go(2) = 1/8 for the one-shot game of Definition 3 / Theorem 1 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 at two Gaussian unit-variance arms with the risk H_1, and the supremum over mappings is attained by the uniform allocation. Against any allocation w in Delta(2), every confusing pair costs at least w_1 w_2 / 2; the whole content is the identity w_j b^2 + w_k a^2 = w_j w_k (a-b)^2 + (w_k a + w_j b)^2 (valid when w_j + w_k = 1) together with a - b = delta + Delta >= Delta, where Delta is the true gap, delta the empirical gap and b the target's displacement. Since the inner value w_1w_2/2 does not depend on Q the mapping collapses to a constant, and max over Delta(2) of w_1w_2/2 is 1/8. This is the classical two-arm fixed-budget constant (uniform allocation, PoE ~ exp(-T Delta^2/8), so H_1 * exponent = 1/8); it is landed as the control against which the family's K = 3 and K = 4 values are calibrated: R^go(2) = 1/8 > R^go(3) = 7/64 > R^go(4) <= 1013/10000.

The exact two-arm tight family. At Q = (1,0) the pair P = (1 - w_2(1+s), w_1(1+s)) is confusing (its true gap is s > 0 and the empirically worse arm is the truly best one) and costs the allocation (w_1,w_2) exactly w_1 w_2 (1+s)^2 / (2 s^2). Hence the inner value of the two-arm game against (w_1,w_2) is exactly w_1 w_2 / 2, approached as s -> infinity and attained by no confusing pair.

Negative controls at K = 2. Too large: R^go(2) < 9/64, and 7/64 < R^go(2) -- the three-arm value 7/64 is not the two-arm one. Too small: 1/10 < R^go(2), and no confusing pair beats the uniform allocation below 1/10. Non-vacuity of the allocation hypothesis: a lopsided allocation is strictly worse -- against (1/4,3/4) the tight family at s = 1000 already costs less than 1/8.

The exact K = 3 ordering of the three rates, entirely in the kernel: Successive Rejects 3/32 < the game value 1/10 of the source's closed-form allocation Eq. (14)-(16) < R^go(3) = 7/64, with the exact ratios R_SR(3) = (6/7) R^go(3), gameVal(w_(14)) = (32/35) R^go(3) and gameVal(w_(14)) = (16/15) R_SR(3). Equivalently: Successive Rejects loses 1/7 = 14.3% of the game value where the source's own closed-form allocation loses 3/35 = 8.57%. Every one of the three constants is now a theorem of this family (rows RGO24, RGO23/RGO21, RGO3), so the ordering, previously the prose row RGO10, is kernel-bound.

The two-equal-hopeless-arms empirical configuration at K = 4 is not extremal, proved in the kernel. At Q^(x) = (0,-1,-x,-x) with x >= 1 -- two contenders, then two hopeless arms at the SAME depth -- and against the allocation (21/50,21/50,2/25,2/25), every confusing pair of Definition 3 of arXiv:2510.23199v3 costs the agent at least 21/200 = 0.105. Since R^go(4) <= 1013/10000 (row RGO13) and R^go(4) = inf over Q of the restricted value V(Q), this gives V(Q^(x)) >= 21/200 > 1013/10000 >= R^go(4) for every x >= 1: no configuration of this shape witnesses the value of the four-arm game. The structural reason is that the second hopeless arm sits at the same depth as the target, so its gap to the target equals its own displacement and it is NOT free -- unlike the deeper arm of the separated ladder Q = (0,-1,-x,-y). The bottom case reduces, after eliminating the free level, to the binary quartic 84 S^4 - 168 S^3 t + 331 S^2 t^2 - 1344 S t^3 + 1472 t^4 >= 0 with the exact sum-of-squares certificate 97451 * (that quartic) = 16948 (92 t^2 - 42 S t - 5 S^2)^2 + (4237 S t - 2772 S^2)^2 + 78200 S^4. The reduction is the relaxation chain bottom_two actually uses -- hZ : (S^2 - D^2)^2 <= S^4, a case split on 525 t^2 <= W, the identity S^4 (W - 525 t^2) + 8 t^2 S^2 W = S^2 q_2, then dropping 8 t^2 D^2 W and the 525 D^2 term; there is NO y_1 = y_2 symmetry reduction in the Lean proof, and the D-monotonicity route works only on the un-multiplied inequality. [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was after eliminating the free level and the y_1 = y_2 symmetry]

Negative controls for the two-hopeless-arms configuration at K = 4. Too large: 21/200 cannot be raised to 27/250 = 0.108 -- at x = 10^6 the contender swap at true gap 1000, P = (-1001/2, 999/2, -10^6, -10^6), costs the witness allocation less than 27/250 (the true restricted value is 0.1052232...). Non-vacuity of the ranking: the same pair against the reversed weights (2/25,2/25,21/50,21/50) -- the same multiset of weights, hopeless arms first -- costs less than 1/40 = 0.025, far below 21/200. The instance set is not empty: that pair is confusing at Q^(10^6) and costs the witness allocation at least 21/200.

The exact value of the restricted K = 4 game at the two-equal-hopeless-arms configuration, computed but not formalised: lim_{x -> infinity} V(0,-1,-x,-x) = 0.105223208505240632152338130169..., equal to (1-2q)/8 at the root q = 0.0791071659790374713906474793203... of the irreducible degree-8 polynomial 933120 q^8 - 1805760 q^7 + 1358432 q^6 - 495648 q^5 + 92360 q^4 - 10664 q^3 + 1302 q^2 - 79 q + 1, with optimal allocation (0.4208928,0.4208928,0.0791072,0.0791072); the raise move binds there at y_3/y_1 ratio r* = 1.160030675755736592... (the same number RGO18's label prints as u* = 1.16003068), while 1.15933738724657040461... is the argmin at the RATIONAL WITNESS (21/50, 2/25) of RGO31, a different point. So the value of this configuration is irrational of degree 8, a sharper failure of the K = 3 rationality (7/64) than R^go(4) itself (degree 5, row RGO18). CORRECTION: the value quoted for this configuration in families/rgo-three-arms/README.md (the K = 4 profile bullet, line ~156; NOT Next steps 4, which correctly calls it 'the hand upper bound') and in journal/2026-09-08-rgo-three-arms-k4.md (lines 36, 150, 421-422), (sqrt 37 - 1)/48 = 0.10589089, is NOT this value -- it is 0.00067 too large. The conclusion drawn there, that the configuration is not extremal, is unaffected, since both numbers exceed 1013/10000; and row RGO31 now proves that conclusion in the kernel. [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was 0.105223208505240632152338130170... / q = 0.0791071659790374713906474793204... (both rounded before the ellipsis, not truncated) / 'and the raise move binding at y_3/y_1 ratio 1.1593....'] [corrected 2026-09-09, hygiene 11d: was '(Next steps 4 and the K = 4 profile section)' -- Next steps 4 was mis-attributed]

families.paper_title: The fixed-budget one-shot game at three and four Gaussian arms:\\ $\Rgo(3)=7/64$, $\ 21/208\le\Rgo(4)\le1013/10000$,\\ and the constant that Theorem~5 of Komiyama, Jang and Honda leaves unnamed
families.paper_abstract: Komiyama, Tsuchiya and Honda (NeurIPS 2022) bound the minimax rate of fixed-budget best arm identification by the value $\Rgo$ of a one-shot game between an agent, who commits to an allocation $w(Q)$ of the budget as a function of the final empirical means $Q$, and an adversary, who picks a true mean vector $P$ whose best arm is not empirically best; Komiyama, Jang and Honda (AISTATS 2026) prove that the rate is within a factor two of $\Rgo$, that the game is non-convex and intractable in general, and that a closed-form allocation (their Eq.~(14)) is a \emph{constant-factor approximation} of the game value, with a constant $\Cstbl\in(0,1)$ that is printed nowhere.  Neither paper evaluates $\Rgo$ at any number of arms $K\ge3$; the only quantitative statement is $\Rgo=\Theta(1/\log K)$.  For $K=3$ Gaussian unit-variance arms and the standard risk $H_1(P)=\sum_{i\ne\istar}(P^*-P_i)^{-2}$ we prove that $\Rgo(3)=7/64$ exactly, and that the supremum over allocation mappings is attained by a mapping that depends on $Q$ only through its ranking: weight $1/8$ on a lowest coordinate of $Q$ and $7/16$ on each of the other two.  The infimum over instances is not attained; it is approached along $Q=(0,-1,-x)$, $x\to\infty$ --- two contenders and one hopeless arm --- with the explicit family $P=(-s/8,-s/8,7s/8)$ costing exactly $7/64+21/(64s)+15/(16s^2)$. Against the allocation of Eq.~(14), whose value at $(0,-1,-x)$ we compute in closed form, a confusing pair costs at most $1/10+x^{-1/2}$; hence every constant witnessing the constant-factor approximation satisfies $\Cstbl\le(1/10)/(7/64)=32/35$. For $K=4$ we prove the bracket $21/208\le\Rgo(4)\le1013/10000$: the lower bound by the rank-only allocation $(21,21,6,4)/52$ and three algebraic identities, one of them a sum-of-squares certificate for a binary quartic, the upper bound by a three-point mixture of confusing instances at the fully separated ladder $Q=(1/2,-1/2,-10^8,-10^{16})$.  Hence $\Rgo(4)<7/64=\Rgo(3)$: the value of the game strictly decreases from three arms to four. Every constant witnessing the constant-factor approximation satisfies $\Cstbl\le7/8$. Behind both values is the identity $\Rgo(K)=\max_{w}\min_{2\le k\le K}M_k(w)$, where $M_k(w)$ is the cost of promoting the arm of empirical rank $k$ with the arms below it free; at $K=3$ it reproduces $7/64$, and at $K=4$ a computation that is not machine-checked identifies $\Rgo(4)=0.10123441\ldots$ as the unique real root in $(1/10,1/8)$ of an explicit irreducible quintic, so that no closed form of the $K=3$ kind exists there. From the source's own exact exponent for Successive Rejects we compute its $H_1$-normalised rate at three arms, $3/32$, giving the exact ordering $3/32<1/10<7/64$ with the middle entry numerical.  Nothing here contradicts any stated result of the sources, and the values are not minimax rates, which the sources' Theorem~2 places in $[\Rgo/2,\Rgo]$.  The value $\Rgo(3)=7/64$, the four-arm bracket and both bounds on $\Cstbl$ are checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib; the exact four-arm value and the rate $3/32$ are not.  In this version the lower half at three arms is closed.  Against the allocation of Eq.~(14)--(16), every confusing pair at every $Q\in\R^3$ costs strictly more than $1/10$, and the infimum of these losses is exactly $1/10$; taking Eq.~(14)--(16) as a single mapping $w^{(14)}$, its game value is $1/10<7/64$ and $32/35$ is the greatest constant $C$ with $C\cdot\Rgo(3)\le L(P,Q,w^{(14)}(Q))$ for all confusing pairs.  So the constant that Theorem~5 leaves unnamed is, at three arms, exactly $32/35=0.914285\ldots$, both inequalities machine-checked: the closed-form allocation captures exactly $32/35$ of the game value at $K=3$.  The proof is one polynomial inequality of degree $8$, $10B(u^2+r^2)\bigl(A(2r-2e+d-u)^2+S(d+u)^2\bigr)>4u^2r^2S^2$ on $0<d\le e$, $u,r>0$, where $d\le e$ are the two empirical gaps, $A=(d+e)^2+d^2$, $B=(d+e)^2+e^2$, $S=2B+A$, and Eq.~(14) at $K=3$ is $(B,B,A)/S$; it is certified by a three-case split and four polynomial identities whose right-hand sides are positive on $0<d\le e$, every step linear. The infimum $7/64$ is also shown to be attained by no confusing pair.  The one step not machine-checked is that Eq.~(16) gives the uniform allocation at a tied empirical best, which is taken as the definition of the mapping there and stated as a hypothesis where it is used. In version~4 three more constants are settled in the kernel and one record is corrected. The rate of Successive Rejects at three arms is exactly $R_{\mathrm{SR}}(3)=3/32$, from the source's own exact exponent (its Theorem~7): the implicit modified mean of its Eq.~(102) is solved at $K=3$ --- $-1/2$ for the top two arms, and for the top three $-(1+x)/3$ when $x\le2$ and $-x/2$ when $x>2$, unique in both branches --- so that $H_3(0,-1,-x)=\max(8,9/(x^2-x+1))$, every instance has rate strictly above $3/32$, the instances with $x\ge2$ have rate exactly $3/32+3/(32x^2)$, and $3/32$ is the greatest lower bound of the rate set, attained by no instance.  The two-arm value $\Rgo(2)=1/8$ is formalised as the control against which the three- and four-arm values are calibrated, $1/8>7/64>\Rgo(4)$, and the ordering $3/32<1/10<7/64$, with the ratios $6/7$, $32/35$ and $16/15$, is a theorem with all three entries machine-checked.  At four arms the configuration with two hopeless arms at the same depth, $Q=(0,-1,-x,-x)$, is proved not to be extremal: against $(21/50,21/50,2/25,2/25)$ every confusing pair costs at least $21/200>1013/10000\ge\Rgo(4)$, the bottom case by an exact sum-of-squares certificate. Its true value, a computation, is $0.1052232085\ldots$, the root of an explicit irreducible polynomial of degree~$8$, and not $(\sqrt{37}-1)/48=0.10589$, a figure that the working record of this project carried as the value of the configuration; that record is corrected here, not the sources, which say nothing about this configuration.  All twenty-five new declarations depend only on the three standard axioms; the degree-$8$ value is the one statement of this version that is not machine-checked.

families.title: Cyclotomic factors of the Bernoulli-coefficient polynomials R_{k,l}: the roots-of-unity question that Charan-Meher-Pathak call elusive, answered uniformly in l at four values of k
families.description: For positive integers `k`, `ℓ`, Maji and Sarkar (arXiv:2306.10283) introduced

statements.label: R_{k,l} is self-inversive for every k and l: its Bernoulli products are palindromic (c_{k,k+1-j} = c_{k,j}) and its coefficient list is palindromic up to the global sign (-1)^{(l+1)(k+1)}
Source Proposition 4.1, both halves, for every k and l: k even and l even give R_{k,l}(1) = 0; k even and l odd give R_{k,l}(-1) = 0
For k in {8, 11, 13, 14} and EVERY l >= 1, no cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d with d >= 3 divides R_{k,l} over Q; equivalently no zero of R_{k,l} is a root of unity other than +-1
The same statement over C: for k in {8, 11, 13, 14}, every l >= 1 and every z with z^n = 1 for some n > 0, if R_{k,l}(z) = 0 then z = 1 or z = -1
n <= 2 * phi(n)^2 for every natural number n, with equality at n = 2; hence phi(d) <= N implies d <= 2N^2

Negative controls: k even is needed in Proposition 4.1 (R_{1,1}(+-1) != 0); the parity of l selects which of +-1 vanishes (R_{2,1}(1) != 0, R_{2,2}(-1) != 0); the restriction d >= 3 in RK3 is sharp (Phi_1 | R_{8,2}, Phi_2 | R_{8,3}); the choice of k is not accidental (Phi_3 | R_{3,1}, with the cofactor 3 - 13z + 3z^2 exhibited); and R_{8,l} has degree exactly 9 for every l

Factorisation census: all 800 polynomials R_{k,l} with 1 <= k <= 80 and 1 <= l <= 10 factor over Q exactly as the source predicts -- one irreducible factor of degree k+1 when k is odd, and (z - (-1)^l) times one irreducible factor of degree k when k is even -- with exactly 26 exceptions, all at l = 1 and all at 3 | k

Two-adic structure theorem: with n = k+1, the primitive integral form of R_{k,l} reduces mod 2 to a polynomial Q_n that does not depend on l -- Q_n = x^n + x^{n/2} + 1 when n is a power of two, and Q_n = sum over 0<j<n with j subset of n bitwise of x^j = (1+x)^n + 1 + x^n otherwise. Hence the set of d for which Phi_d can divide R_{k,l} depends only on k; it is empty for n = 3, 27, 45, which settles the roots-of-unity question for all l at k = 2, 26, 44

Theorem A in Lean: v_2(c_{k,j}/c_{k,0}) = v_2(C(k+1,j)) - 1 for 0 < j < k+1, from von Staudt-Clausen; its integral-model form v_2(b_j) - v_2(b_0) = v_2(C(k+1,j)) - 1 for any coprime integral model; and the consequence that the mod-2 reduction of the integral model W_{B,l} is the same polynomial for every l >= 1

For k in {2, 26, 44} and EVERY l >= 1, no cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d with d >= 3 divides R_{k,l} over Q; equivalently the only zeros of R_{k,l} that are roots of unity are +-1 -- by the two-adic sieve of RK9, with no per-order and no per-l search

For k in {11, 13} and every l >= 1, R_{k,l} has NO rational zero; for k in {8, 14} and every l >= 1, every rational zero of R_{k,l} is +-1. Hence every real zero of R_{11,l} and R_{13,l}, and every real zero of R_{8,l} and R_{14,l} other than +-1, is irrational -- which with the source Theorem 1.2 (alpha_{k,l} > 1) is the irrationality of alpha_{k,l} and of 1/alpha_{k,l}, uniformly in l

Controls for the two-adic and rational-root layers: Theorem A model form applied at k = 2, j = 1 with its parity content; the mod-2 sieve is necessary and NOT sufficient (Phi_3 divides Q_4 mod 2, i.e. 111_2 * 111_2 = 10101_2, matching Phi_3 | R_{3,1}); l >= 1 is needed in the l-free reduction (at l = 0 the mask is 15, not 6); "no rational zero" is false for k even (R_{8,2}(1) = 0); and R_{11,1} really has a real zero (the integral model changes sign between 4 and 5)

families.paper_title: Roots of unity and rational zeros of the Bernoulli-coefficient polynomials $R_{k,\ell}$,\\ uniformly in $\ell$
families.paper_abstract: For positive integers $k$ and $\ell$ let $R_{k,\ell}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{k+1}(-1)^{(\ell+1)j}\bigl(\tfrac{B_{2j}}{(2j)!}\, \tfrac{B_{2k+2-2j}}{(2k+2-2j)!}\bigr)^{\ell}x^{j}$, the two-parameter family of reciprocal polynomials introduced by Maji and Sarkar \cite{ms} and studied by Charan, Meher and Pathak \cite{cmp}, who prove that all zeros of $R_{k,\ell}$ except two real ones, $\alpha_{k,\ell}>1$ and $1/\alpha_{k,\ell}$, lie on the unit circle.  The concluding section of \cite{cmp} asks which zeros of $R_{k,\ell}$ are roots of unity, reports that computation suggests none besides $\pm1$ when $\ell>1$, and says that ``a proof of this fact seems elusive''; it also asks whether $R_{k,\ell}$ is irreducible, noting that this would entail the irrationality of $\alpha_{k,\ell}$.  For $\ell=1$, where $R_{k,1}(x^{2})$ is the Ramanujan polynomial, the roots-of-unity question is answered by a theorem of Murty, Smyth and Wang \cite{msw}; for $\ell>1$ nothing appears to have been known.  We prove three statements, each for \emph{every} $\ell\ge1$.  First, for $k\in\{8,11,13,14\}$ no cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{d}$ with $d\ge3$ divides $R_{k,\ell}$ over $\QQ$: an integral model whose dependence on $\ell$ sits entirely in the exponents of fixed integers lets Fermat's little theorem collapse $\ell$ to a residue modulo $p-1$, so finitely many evaluations in $\FF_{p}$ certify all $\ell$ at once, and a lower bound $n\le2\varphi(n)^{2}$ for Euler's totient makes the set of candidate orders finite.  Second, a $2$-adic structure theorem: $v_{2}(c_{k,j}/c_{k,0})=v_{2}\binom{k+1}{j}-1$ for the coefficient bases $c_{k,j}$, so that the reduction modulo $2$ of the integral model does not depend on $\ell$ at all; this sieve alone settles the roots-of-unity question at $k\in\{2,26,44\}$. Third, $R_{11,\ell}$ and $R_{13,\ell}$ have no rational zero, and every rational zero of $R_{8,\ell}$ and $R_{14,\ell}$ is $\pm1$; with the unit-circle theorem of \cite{cmp} this gives the irrationality of $\alpha_{k,\ell}$ for $k\in\{8,11,13,14\}$ --- the consequence of irreducibility that \cite{cmp} names, obtained without irreducibility. The three statements are machine-checked in Lean~4; the final step to $\alpha_{k,\ell}$ rests on the cited theorem of \cite{cmp} and is not.

families.title: The missing weights of RM(7,14): which of the 22 weights arXiv:2606.21425 leaves out of the weight spectrum actually occur
families.description: `RM(r,m)` is the Reed–Muller code of length `2^m` whose codewords are the truth tables of the Boolean functions of algebraic degree at most `r` in `m` variables. Its **weight spectrum** is the set of Hamming weights that actually occur. For `RM(7,14)` the minimum distance is `d = 2^{14-7} = 128`, the dimension is `Σ_{i≤7} C(14,i) = 9908`, and the spectrum is not known.
families.paper_title: Explicit codewords for fourteen of the twenty-two\\ undetermined weights of the Reed--Muller code $\RM(7,14)$
families.paper_abstract: Leuenberger and Albrizzio (arXiv:2606.21425) show that the weight spectrum of the Reed--Muller code $\RM(7,14)$ contains every even integer between $312$ and $2^{14}-312$, together with the classical small and large weights, with the possible exception of a set $M$ of twenty-two weights, and write that they ``were not able to determine the missing weights''.  We exhibit codewords for fourteen of the twenty-two: a Boolean function of degree $7$ in $14$ variables with six monomials and Hamming weight $354$, functions with between $5$ and $19$ monomials of weights $8174$, $8178$, $8182$, $8186$, $8188$, $8190$, and their complements of weights $16030$, $8210$, $8206$, $8202$, $8198$, $8196$, $8194$. Each codeword is given by its algebraic normal form, and its degree and its weight are checked from the definitions in the kernel of the Lean~4 proof assistant, without any library.  We also record a $\bmod 4$ law: a codeword of $\RM(7,14)$ has weight $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ exactly when its algebraic normal form contains an odd number of complementary pairs of degree-$7$ monomials.  The remaining four weights $322$, $326$, $330$, $334$ (and their complements) were not reached by four independent search families in about $3\cdot10^{9}$ evaluations; we make no claim about their existence.  The constructions and tables of the source are reproduced with no discrepancy.

families.title: The smallest open length for rank-metric intersecting codes: does an [8,3]_{q^6/q} rank-metric intersecting code exist?
families.description: A rank-metric code `C ⊆ F_{q^m}^n` — an `F_{q^m}`-subspace, with the rank distance over `F_q` — is **rank-metric intersecting** when the rank supports of any two nonzero codewords meet nontrivially. The notion was introduced by Bartoli, Borello, Marino and Scotti ([arXiv:2507.00569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00569)), who proved that for a nondegenerate `[n,k,d]_{q^m/q}` code the property is *geometric*: `C` is rank-metric intersecting iff its **`q`-system** `U` (the `F_q`-span of the columns of a generator matrix, an `F_q`-subspace of `F_{q^m}^k` of `F_q`-dimension `n` spanning `F_{q^m}^k`) i
families.paper_abstract: A rank-metric code $C\subseteq\Fqm^n$ is \emph{rank-metric intersecting} when the rank supports of any two nonzero codewords meet nontrivially (Bartoli, Borello, Marino and Scotti, arXiv:2507.00569); a nondegenerate $[n,k,d]_{q^m/q}$ code has this property if and only if its $q$-system $U\subseteq\Fqm^k$ is not $2$-spannable, i.e.\ $U\neq(H_1\cap U)+(H_2\cap U)$ for every pair of $\Fqm$-hyperplanes.  Borello, Polverino and Zullo (arXiv:2604.02004) settle the admissible lengths for $k=3$, $m=6$ except one: such codes exist for $5\le n\le7$ and $n=9$, cannot exist for $n<5$ or $n>9$, and the existence of an $[8,3]_{q^6/q}$ rank-metric intersecting code is left open; they report that an extensive search for $[8,3]_{64/2}$ codes obtained by puncturing their extremal $[9,3,5]_{64/2}$ example fails.  We study the cell at $q=2$ through a finite model of $\PG(2,64)$ and a criterion that decides $2$-spannability from the largest hyperplane sections alone.  We certify the known part of the row (the $[9,3,5]_{64/2}$ example, whose $q$-system is maximum scattered, and explicit $[5,3,3]$, $[6,3,3]$, $[7,3,4]$ codes over $\Ff/\Ft$), turn the reported puncturing search into a theorem --- all $511$ rank-metric puncturings of the example are $2$-spannable, each with an explicit spanning pair of hyperplanes --- and prove that no $[8,3]_{64/2}$ rank-metric intersecting code has an $\Ffour$-linear $q$-system, exhaustively over $1365$ systems that cover every equivalence class of such systems. The exclusion itself is routine, as we point out: an $\Ffour$-linear system of $\Ft$-dimension $8$ in $\Ff^3$ meets some hyperplane in dimension $6$, so its code has $d\le2<k$; what the exhaustive theorem adds is the certificates and the completeness of the list.  A double count yields an identity for the hyperplane weights of every $8$-dimensional $\Ft$-subspace of $\Ff^3$, which forces an intersecting $[8,3]_{64/2}$ system to have exactly $31+4n_2+28n_3$ hyperplanes of section size $16$, pairwise meeting nontrivially; the best candidate produced by a search over $5.5\cdot10^7$ subspaces is scattered, has exactly $31$ such hyperplanes and still fails on $108$ of their $465$ pairs, and it is certified as such.  The cell itself remains open; non-existence is not claimed.  Every finite statement is verified in Lean~4, without Mathlib.

families.paper_title: Restricted Schur multiplicity: exact minima and three-block minimisers
families.paper_abstract: Fix integers $k \ge 2$ and $2 \le \ell \le k$, and call a solution of $x_1 + \dots + x_k = x_{k+1}$ in positive integers a solution \emph{of level $\ell$} when its $k+1$ entries take exactly $\ell+1$ distinct values.  Let $\mult(k,\ell;n)$ be the least number of monochromatic level-$\ell$ solutions inside $[n] = \{1,\dots,n\}$, minimised over all $2$-colourings of $[n]$, solutions being counted as multisets.  The level $\ell$ is Gaiser's, who used it to index a \emph{threshold} --- the restricted generalized Schur number $S_2(k;\ell)$, the least $n$ forcing one such solution --- and who never counts; counting is the Schur-triple multiplicity problem of Graham--R\"odl--Ruci\'nski and Robertson--Zeilberger, which does not leave $k = 2$ and does not restrict the number of distinct values.  We compute $\mult(k,\ell;n)$ exactly at $74$ triples spread over seven pairs $(k,\ell)$ with $k \le 5$ and $n \le 55$; ten of them, the row $k = \ell = 2$, reproduce Robertson--Zeilberger's own objective function and are carried as an external control.  At every one of the $74$ triples the minimum is attained by a colouring with at most three blocks, $[1,a] \cup (b,n]$ against $(a,b]$.  We also prove that $\mult(k,\ell;\cdot)$ is non-decreasing; that it is positive exactly from $n = S_2(k;\ell)$ on, so that the multiplicity function recovers the threshold as its own zero set and re-proves $S_2(3;2) = 15$, $S_2(3;3) = 24$ and $S_2(4;3) = 35$ by a route that runs through no threshold search at all; and that a two-block colouring gives $\mult(k,\ell;n) = O\bigl((n/k)^{\ell}\bigr)$ for every $n$.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4, except at the few places where we say otherwise; the lower bounds are replays of LRAT refutations of a cardinality-constrained encoding.
