families.paper_title: Root-multiplicity strata of real polynomials: the stratum $\ord{3,1,1,5}$ has homology in two degrees at $d=24$
families.paper_abstract: For a composition $\omega$ and an admissible degree $d$, Shapiro (arXiv:2608.19733) computes the reduced integral homology of the one-point compactification $\Pw_d^{\ord\omega}$ of the closed stratum of monic real polynomials of degree $d$ whose real roots have multiplicities $\omega$, from a finite chain complex $C_*(\omega;d)$ on the compositions obtained from $\omega$ by merging adjacent parts and inserting parts~$2$. That paper proves $\Ht_*(\Pw_{18}^{\ord{3,1,1,3}};\Z)\cong\Z^2$ in degree~$7$, conjectures the value $\Z^{\lfloor(d-10)/4\rfloor}$ in degree $d/2-2$ for every even $d\ge14$, and conjectures that for every admissible pair the reduced homology is free and concentrated in at most one degree (its Conjecture~4) and that it vanishes exactly when the Euler characteristic $\chi_d(\omega)$ does (its Conjecture~5).  We compute these groups by a fill-in-free elimination on the chain complex, each step of which is checked against the original boundary matrix, followed by rank certificates valid over every field, and we verify the results in Lean~4.  The theorem and its stated verified range $d\le22$ are reproduced.  The first conjecture holds at $d=24,26,28,30$ (a computation outside the formal development).  The other two fail: $\Ht_*(\Pw_{24}^{\ord{3,1,1,5}};\Z)$ is $\Z$ in degree~$7$ and $\Z$ in degree~$8$, while $\chi_{24}(3,1,1,5)=0$ --- exactly the cancellation between nonzero Betti numbers in different degrees that Conjecture~5 was formulated to exclude.  Freeness survives at every pair computed.  For the same stratum, whose homological degree the source leaves open, the degrees continue $5,6,7,\{7,8\},\{8,9\},\{9,10\}$ at $d=18,\dots,28$ (machine-checked through $d=24$).  A sweep of the $1{,}866$ admissible pairs with $\abs\omega\le8$ and $d\le20$ finds no smaller counterexample among the $1{,}820$ pairs it resolves.

families.title: The route-chart lift of arXiv:2606.15860v1 verified: its two printed finite conditions kernel-decided over F_3 and F_4, the lift principle formalised at q=3 as a 12-regular SimpleGraph on 34992 vertices of diameter at most 5, and both diameter-5 records N(12,5) >= 34992 and N(16,5) >= 147456 re-derived from independently labelled lifts by exhaustive all-pairs BFS
families.description: The **degree/diameter problem** asks for the largest order `N(Δ, D)` of a simple graph with maximum degree `Δ` and diameter `D`. The Moore bound `MB(Δ,D) = 1 + Δ·Σ_{i<D}(Δ-1)^i` is the trivial upper bound; almost nothing is known exactly, so the field keeps a *table of largest known graphs* and progress means a construction that beats a table cell.

statements.label: Condition (A.0) of arXiv:2606.15860v1: every one of the 864 combinations of an ordered pair of the six base vertices and a voltage in C_4 x C_6 is realised by a nonbacktracking walk of length exactly 5 in the base multigraph B, and the enumeration behind it is the full 6 * 4 * 3^4 = 1944 walks

The 144-vertex controller C = B^gamma is a simple 4-regular graph carrying an explicit inverse-consistent labelling by S = {a, a^-1, b, b^-1}, and is an exact-NB-5 controller: all 20736 ordered pairs of its vertices are joined by a walk of length exactly 5 whose label word is reduced, hence nonbacktracking

The F_3 route chart of Appendix A.6.1 of arXiv:2606.15860v1 is universal: condition (A.1) holds (A_{t^-1} A_t = I and A_{t^-1} b_t = b_{t^-1} for all four symbols), and each of the 324 controllability matrices M_w of (A.2) is invertible -- witnessed twice, by an explicit two-sided inverse and by an independent Gauss-Jordan rank computation giving rank 5

The F_4 route chart of Appendix A.6.2 is universal, in the source's own encoding 0, 1, 2 = alpha, 3 = alpha + 1 with alpha^2 = alpha + 1: condition (A.1) holds and all 324 controllability matrices are invertible, again by an explicit inverse and by an independent rank computation

Negative controls: all 700 non-reduced words of length 5 have a singular controllability matrix over F_3 and over F_4 alike (so no chart can be universal over all 1024 words, and reducedness is exactly the right hypothesis); adding 1 to one entry of A_0 of the F_3 chart makes 18 of the 324 reduced words singular; changing one C_4 voltage of base edge 0 or one C_6 voltage of base edge 7 breaks condition (A.0); corrupting a single label of the 103680-character route table breaks the route certificate; and the orders and degrees are not off by one

The route-chart lift principle at q = 3, s = 5, formalised for the source's own data: the lift on Fin 144 x (Fin 5 -> ZMod 3) is a SimpleGraph whose symmetry is derived from condition (A.1) rather than assumed, has 34992 vertices, is 12-regular, and has every ordered pair of vertices at distance at most 5 -- with the source's key identity x_5 = A_w x + M_w lambda proved in Lean and an explicit length-5 walk constructed for every pair

Orders, degrees and Moore bounds: 144 * 3^5 = 34992 at degree 4 * 3 = 12 and 144 * 4^5 = 147456 at degree 4 * 4 = 16; MB(12,4) = 17569 < 34992 and MB(16,4) = 57857 < 147456, which is what upgrades diameter at most 5 to diameter exactly 5; and both orders lie below MB(12,5) = 193261 and MB(16,5) = 867857

N(12,5) >= 34992 and N(16,5) >= 147456 independently verified: two route-chart lifts built here from the paper's printed data through an inverse-consistent labelling of our own -- a different graph from the paper's, differing in 120960 of 209952 edges at q = 3 and 685440 of 1179648 at q = 4 -- each simple, of the claimed order and regular of the claimed degree, and each of diameter EXACTLY 5 by exhaustive all-pairs breadth-first search

Measurement: an exhaustive all-pairs diameter check on a 147456-vertex 16-regular graph costs 86 s wall and about 300 MB by 4096-source bitset chunks (per-vertex reachability words updated as R'[v] = R[v] | OR over neighbours of R[u]), and 20 s on the 34992-vertex 12-regular graph -- against the 1-3 h the scout priced for per-source BFS

families.paper_title: Two diameter-five degree/diameter records, independently verified:\\ the route-chart lifts on $34\,992$ and $147\,456$ vertices
families.paper_abstract: A preprint of June 2026 by R.~Mizuno constructs a $12$-regular graph on $34\,992$ vertices and a $16$-regular graph on $147\,456$ vertices, both of diameter $5$, and so claims $N(12,5)\ge 34\,992$ and $N(16,5)\ge 147\,456$ in the degree/diameter problem, against the previously recorded $29\,621$ and $132\,496$.  Both values now stand in Comellas's live table of largest known graphs, credited to that preprint; the preprint itself is filed under general mathematics, has no journal version and, at the time of writing, no recorded citation, and its proof rests on two finite conditions that had been checked only by the author's own scripts.  The construction is a \emph{route-chart lift}: a $144$-vertex controller graph, itself a $C_4\times C_6$ voltage lift of a $6$-vertex multigraph, whose directed edges are labelled by a four-letter alphabet, each letter carrying an affine family $x\mapsto A_tx+\lambda b_t$ of maps of $\F_q^5$, with $q=3$ or $q=4$.  We give the first verification independent of the author's own scripts and edge lists.  Both printed conditions --- that every ordered pair of controller vertices is joined by a nonbacktracking walk of length exactly $5$, and that all $324$ controllability matrices of reduced words of length $5$ are invertible --- are decided in the Lean~4 kernel from the paper's printed tables, over $\F_3$ and over $\F_4$, each in two independent ways.  At $q=3$ the lift principle itself is formalised: the lift is constructed as a simple graph on $34\,992$ vertices in Mathlib, its symmetry is derived from the chart's inverse relations, it is proved $12$-regular, and every ordered pair of its vertices is joined by an explicitly constructed walk of length $5$, through the identity $x_5=A_wx+M_w\lambda$.  Negative controls show that reducedness is exactly the right hypothesis (all $700$ non-reduced words have singular matrices) and that the printed voltages and chart entries are load-bearing.  Finally, both lift graphs were rebuilt from the printed data through inverse-consistent labellings of our own, different from the author's, and exhaustive all-pairs breadth-first search gives diameter exactly $5$ for each.  The record claim verifies.

families.paper_title: The Shannon entropy of ranked set and partially rank-ordered set samples\\ of the same size: no ordering relationship for the uniform parent
families.paper_abstract: In partially rank-ordered set (PROS) sampling one fixes a set size $S$ and a design parameter $D=\{d_1,\dots,d_n\}$ splitting the ranks $\{1,\dots,S\}$ into $n$ consecutive blocks, and measures one unit drawn uniformly at random from each block; the measured value from block $d_r$ has the mixture density $f_{(d_r)}=|d_r|^{-1}\sum_{u\in d_r}f^{(u:S)}$.  Ranked set sampling (RSS) of size $n$ is the case $S=n$.  Hatefi and Jafari Jozani, who study the information content of such samples, prove $m^{-1}H_S(X_\rss)\le H_n(X_\pros)\le H_n(X_\srs)$ for the balanced design and then record that they ``were not able to obtain an ordering relationship among the Shannon entropy of RSS and PROS data of the same size''.  We settle that comparison for the $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ parent, and the answer is negative: both orders occur.  For the balanced design $\PROS(2,4)$ one has $H_2(X_\pros)=\tfrac92-2\log 2-\tfrac{27}{8}\log 3<1-2\log 2=H_2(X_\rss)$, while for the design $D=(\{1,2\},\{3\},\dots,\{7\},\{8,9\})$ at set size $S=9$ and sample size $n=7$ one has $H_7(X_\rss)<H_7(X_\pros)$, the gap being $-\tfrac{997119143}{74118870}+\tfrac{79155653}{5764801}\log 2+10\log 3-2\log 5-2\log 7 =-0.06004185\ldots$.  So no ordering relationship between the two entropies can hold. Every entropy here is exact --- a rational number plus a rational combination of $\log 2,\log 3,\log 5,\log 7$ --- and every closed form and every inequality stated as a theorem below is checked by the Lean~4 kernel over Mathlib, with no evaluation axiom and no floating-point step.  Outside the formal development we report two measurements, labelled as such: an exhaustive search over every design of set size $S\le 10$ shows that no reversal occurs for $S\le 8$, so $S=9$ is the smallest set size at which one exists; and over all $34$ balanced designs with $n\ge2$ and $S=mn\le 16$ the inequality $H_n(X_\pros)\le H_n(X_\rss)$ never fails, which locates the obstruction in the general design parameter rather than in the design family as a whole.

families.paper_title: The Chow--Rimani\'c covering number $C_k(2)$: exact values by degree window, and the optimal families
families.paper_abstract: Chow and Rimani\'c introduced a function-field analogue of the lonely runner conjecture: for a finite family $\cF$ of nonzero polynomials over $\Fq$ one sets $\delta(\cF)=\sup_\alpha\min_{f\in\cF}\nm{\alpha f}$ and lets $C_k(q)$ be the least size of a family with $\delta(\cF)<q^{-k}$; they conjectured $C_k(q)=Q_k(q)=1+q+\dots+q^k$.  Hu has recently refuted this at $(q,k)=(2,3)$ with thirteen polynomials over $\Ftwo$ found by a cross-entropy search, giving $9\le C_3(2)\le 13<15$, and asked for the exact value of $C_3(2)$. We settle that question inside the degree window in which the counterexample lives: no twelve nonzero polynomials over $\Ftwo$ of degree at most four have loneliness less than $2^{-3}$, so the thirteen are optimal among all speeds of degree at most four.  We then classify the optimal families in that window: there are exactly three, they carry the same covering-multiplicity distribution, and coefficient reversal carries the published family to the second and fixes the third.  For $k=2$ we compute the value restricted to degrees at most four and at most five and find the conjectured $7$ in both --- past the reach of the Chow--Rimani\'c small-degree theorem, which at $q=2$, $k=2$ reaches only degree two.  Every lower bound is an exhaustive search whose branching rule is proved complete rather than assumed, and every result proved here is machine-checked in Lean~4; the two results taken from the literature are marked as such.

families.paper_title: Corner-vector designs on $\Sph^{3}$:\\ the maximum degree is exactly $13$
families.paper_abstract: For $a>0$ and $s\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ let the \emph{generalized corner vector} $v_{a,s}\in\Sph^{n-1}$ be the unit vector along $(a,1,\dots,1,0,\dots,0)$ with $s$ ones. Its hyperoctahedral orbit $v_{a,s}^{B_n}$ is called \emph{proper} when $a\ne1$; a weighted spherical $t$-design which is a union of such orbits, with one positive weight per orbit, is a \emph{design of type} \eqref{eq:type}.  Tanino, Tamaru, Hirao and Sawa proved that $t\le15$ for every $n\ge4$, exhibited $11$- and $13$-designs on $\Sph^{3}$ numerically, and asked in their Problem~6.1 whether a $15$-design on $\Sph^{3}$ of this type with more than five proper orbits exists.  We answer this negatively and in a stronger form: on $\Sph^{3}$ there is no $15$-design of type \eqref{eq:type} at all, with any number of orbits, proper or not.  Such designs are centrally symmetric, so a $14$-design is a $15$-design; the uniform bound therefore sharpens at $n=4$ from $t\le15$ to $t\le13$.  The value $13$ is attained: we give a $13$-design with nine proper orbits and $656$ points, all of whose parameters and weights are rational and exact, where the examples in the literature have four proper orbits and six printed digits.  Hence the maximum degree of a design of type \eqref{eq:type} on $\Sph^{3}$ is exactly $13$.  The proof is linear-programming duality rather than elimination: in the squared coordinates a design is a point of the convex hull of four explicit moment curves, and the obstruction is a single integer functional on the eleven moment conditions which is strictly positive at every point of every curve.  Its positivity amounts to three degree-$7$ polynomial inequalities, which we prove from exact factorizations; no statement here rests on an exhaustive search.  Every theorem, proposition and lemma below other than the reduction to the moment system and two one-line corollaries has been formally verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}; the remarks, which report how the certificate was found, what was tried and abandoned, and what the published configurations do when recomputed, are labelled as lying outside that development.

families.paper_title: The critical polynomial of a uniform-grid\\ variance-deficit objective: one sign change\\ for $3\le T\le300$, and a closed form at $x=1$
families.paper_abstract: For an integer step count $T\ge1$ put $b_0(x)=T$, $b_j(x)=jx+(T-j)$ for $1\le j\le T$, and \[ H_T(x)\;=\;T^2x\sum_{i=1}^{T}\frac{1}{i\,b_i(x)\,b_{i-1}(x)^2},\qquad x>0 . \] This is the finite-step variance deficit of a Schr\"odinger-bridge sampler on the uniform grid, in the form derived by Fallah and Yang, who prove that $H_T$ has a unique positive critical point for $2\le T\le120$ by exhibiting an integer polynomial with exactly one sign change in its nonzero coefficient sequence, report a numerical scan finding one local minimum for $T\le200$ and for $T\in\{500,1000,5000\}$, and leave the general case open, reducing it to the conjecture that the coefficient sequence has one sign change for every $T$.  Their polynomial is not printed, and the sign-variation count is a property of the polynomial chosen and not of the critical set, so we construct one: an explicit $R_T\in\ZZ[x]$, of degree $3T-3$ for $T\ge2$, given by a quadratic-time integer recurrence, for which we prove --- for every $T\ge1$ and every $x>0$, with no restriction on $T$ --- that $H_T'(x)=0$ if and only if $R_T(x)=0$.  We then prove that the nonzero coefficient sequence of $R_T$ has exactly one sign change for every $3\le T\le300$; that $R_T$ consequently has exactly one positive real root there; and that $H_T$ has exactly one positive critical point for $3\le T\le300$, which is the source's uniqueness statement on $2.5$ times its proved range and $1.5$ times its numerical scan.  Two further results are uniform in $T$ and involve no computation: $H_T'(1)=\bigl((T+2)h_T-3T\bigr)/T^2$ for every $T\ge1$, where $h_T$ is the $T$-th harmonic number, and $H_T'(1)>0$ for every $T\ge3$, so that $T=2$ --- where $R_2=16X^2(X-1)$ and the critical point is exactly $x=1$ --- is the only step count $T\ge2$ at which $x=1$ is critical.  The band results rest on a single exhaustive computation in exact integer arithmetic over the $298$ step counts $T=3,\dots,300$, whose largest instance has degree $897$ and coefficients of up to $9436$ bits.  Every theorem, proposition and lemma below is machine-checked in Lean~4; Section~\ref{sec:verif} records exactly what the kernel checks, and which of the remaining statements are computations outside the formal development.

families.paper_title: Symmetric chain decompositions of the minuscule lattice $M(n)$: twenty-two instances and two exact counts
families.paper_abstract: Let $M(n)$ be the poset of strict integer partitions with largest part at most $n$, ordered by containment of Young diagrams.  Stanley asked in 1980 whether $M(n)$ admits a symmetric chain decomposition; the question is open, and the most recent account, by Dorward, reports that little progress has been made.  We exhibit an explicit symmetric chain decomposition of $M(n)$ for every $n\le 21$; the largest splits the $2\,097\,152$ elements of $M(21)$ into $28\,460$ saturated chains, each symmetric about the middle of the rank range $0,\dots,231$. The decompositions are produced by a middle-out construction in which one outward step is a unit-capacity maximum flow.  We also compute two counts for which only lower bounds were known: $\nscd{M(6)}=1344$, so that the published bound $\ge 1344$ is tight, and $\nscd{M(7)}=295\,069\,056$, about $819$ times the published bound $\ge 360\,036$.  The second count is out of reach of exhaustive enumeration and is obtained from a dynamic program whose state is the bijection between two opposite ranks realised by the chains still under construction.  All statements are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The top two scores of a round-robin tournament: exact distributions, and when the maximum winner's margin is attained
families.paper_abstract: In a round-robin tournament of $n$ equally strong players, let $s_{(n)}$ and $s_{(n-1)}$ be the largest and the second largest score.  Both are named as objects of study in the recent literature, which calls the exact distribution computationally intractable even for small $n$ and derives asymptotics instead.  It is not intractable: carrying only the sorted multiset of scores gives a dynamic program whose state count is the number of realisable score sequences, and we compute the joint law together with the marginals of the runner-up score, of the winner's margin $s_{(n)}-s_{(n-1)}$, and of the number of co-champions, exactly, for the classical model up to $n=13$, the chess model up to $n=9$ and the soccer model ($3$ points for a win, $1$ each for a draw) up to $n=7$.  Two consequences are uniform in $n$.  First, the winner is unique exactly when the margin is positive, so the margin distribution's mass at $0$ is the complement of the unique-winner count in every outcome model.  Second, our main theorem, a characterisation of the largest margin any tournament realises.  Write $M$ for the most one player can take from a single match and $\mu(k)$ for the smallest winner's score over all $k$-player tournaments of the model, the \emph{minimax score}.  On $n\ge2$ players no margin exceeds $M(n-1)-\mu(n-1)$, with no hypothesis on the model whatever; and that bound is the largest realised margin \emph{if and only if} the model contains a total-domination result, one awarding $M$ points to one player and nothing to the other.  If moreover some pair of results splits the smallest match total $m$ as evenly as possible in both orders, then $\mu(k)=\lceil m(k-1)/2\rceil$ and the bound becomes the closed form $M(n-1)-\lceil m(n-2)/2\rceil$, which is $\lfloor kn/2\rfloor$ in the model where a match is worth $k$ points and every split of it is possible --- hence $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ classically and $n$ in the chess model --- and $2n-1$ in the soccer model.  Without that extra hypothesis the closed form can be strictly too large: when a win is worth $g\ge2$ and draws are impossible, the largest margin is $g\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ at every $n\ge2$.  Everything asserted here is machine-checked in Lean~4, the margin results from the definitions with no computation anywhere in their proofs.

families.paper_title: Eight new realizable triples of totally, partially and minimally real common secants to a pair of real twisted cubics
families.paper_abstract:
A general pair of twisted cubic curves in $\PP^{3}(\CC)$ has ten common secant lines. For a real pair each real common secant is \emph{totally}, \emph{partially} or \emph{minimally} real according to whether it meets the two curves in two real points each, in two real points and a conjugate pair, or in a conjugate pair each; the resulting count $(
t,
p,
m)$ takes $161$ admissible values.  Aslam, Faust, Hauenstein, Lopez Garcia, Kagy, Regan, Wampler and Zhang recently realized $128$ of the $161$ by numerical sampling with certification, listed the remaining $33$, asked for the full realizable set, and singled out two families of $21$ admissible $3$-tuples as an open problem.  We realize eight of the $33$: $(4,6,0)$, $(4,5,1)$, $(4,4,2)$, $(3,5,2)$, $(3,7,0)$, $(2,8,0)$, and, in the two families of the open problem, $(0,10,0)$ and $(1,9,0)$.  Each is realized by an explicit pair of \emph{rational} twisted cubics given by a $4	imes4$ integer matrix, and each claim is unconditional: for every one of the nine explicit pairs treated here we also prove that the ten common secants we exhibit are \emph{all} of its common secants over $\CC$.  The certificates are exact rather than numerical, and are of two kinds: elimination reduces the common-secant system of one pair to a single degree-$10$ integer polynomial with a rational univariate representation, from which the ten secants and their types are read off ten integer sign changes and twenty Descartes sign-pattern certificates; and a second, chart-free model in the plane of chords of the first curve, where the common secants are the rank-one locus of a symmetric $3	imes3$ matrix of quadratic forms, supplies the exact count through polynomial identities over $\ZZ$. Every step is checked by the Lean~4 kernel in arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic. We correct one statement of the earlier version of this paper, which asserted that neither the source nor Eisenbud and Harris bounds the number of common secants of a \emph{special} pair: the proof of Proposition~2.2 of the source does bound it, for one explicit special matrix, by a saturation computation returning degree $40$.  We also record an erratum to the printed bisecant system of the source; report what the public data repository of the source now contains, which changes the status of two further cells; and show that no invariant of the ambient isotopy class of the pair of real curves can constrain the $3$-tuple.

families.paper_title: Sum-intersecting families of integers: exact values through $n=15$, and the distinct-sum and $k$-sum variants
families.paper_abstract: A family $\FF$ of subsets of $[n]=\{1,\dots ,n\}$ is \emph{sum-intersecting} if for all $A,B\in\FF$ (the case $A=B$ included) the intersection $A\cap B$ contains elements $x,y,z$, not necessarily distinct, with $x+y=z$; write $f(n)$ for the largest size of such a family.  Berger and Mani conjectured $f(n)=2^{n-2}$ and proved $f(n)\le 0.32\cdot 2^{n}$.  The partition method of Chung, Graham, Frankl and Shearer settles the conjecture only as far as the Schur number $S(3)=13$.  We determine $f(n)$ for every $n\le 15$; in particular $f(14)=4096$ and $f(15)=8192$, the first two values beyond the Schur wall.  The proof runs the Delsarte linear programme of the source paper at a single ground set and exhibits an exact rational optimal certificate there; we prove that the programme's optimum $c_0^{*}(n)$ equals $3$ at $n=14$ and at $n=15$, that $c_0^{*}$ is non-increasing in $n$, and that the whole conjecture reduces to the statement $c_0^{*}(n)=3$ for all $n$.  We also show $f(n)\le \tfrac{5}{16}\cdot 2^{n}$ for $9\le n\le 160$, improving the published constant on that range, and we close two routes to $n=16$: a natural half-splitting lift of certificates is impossible at every even step, and the cyclically consecutive partition bound of Faudree, Schelp and S\'os collapses to a three-part partition and therefore cannot pass $n=13$.  For the distinct-sum variant, where $x,y,z$ must be pairwise different, we determine the maximum $g(n)=2^{n-3}$ for every $n\le 12$ and prove $g(n)\le 2^{n-2}$ for every $n\le 23$.  For the $k$-sum variant we show that any family beating $\tfrac14 2^{n}$ consists entirely of sets of at least three elements, that the extremal cores $\{d,kd\}$ come in $\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ equally good versions, and we compute the maximum for $k=3$, $n\le 12$ and $k=4$, $n\le 8$.  All statements are machine-checked.

families.paper_title: Local stability of Shapiro--Diananda cyclic sums:\\ explicit failures and exact diagonal identities
families.paper_abstract: For $n\ge2$, $1\le k\le n-1$ and positive reals $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with cyclic indices, let $S_{n,k}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i/(x_{i+1}+\dots+x_{i+k})$; $k=2$ is Shapiro's cyclic sum.  At the equal point the sum is $n/k$, and the Diananda inequality at $(n,k)$ asserts $S_{n,k}\ge n/k$.  Sheremet (arXiv:2606.05504) expanded $S_{n,k}(e^u)$ to second order at the equal point, obtaining a circulant quadratic form $Q_{n,k}$ whose minimum $\Cl nk$ over the zero-mean unit sphere decides whether the equal point is a strict local minimum, quadratically degenerate, or a saddle; he classified $k=2,3$ and tabulated $3\le k\le10$ numerically.  We add four things, all of them finite rational arithmetic.  (i) Explicit positive-integer vectors refuting $S_{n,k}\ge n/k$ at the least saddle cell of each $3\le k\le10$; the smallest is $x=(9,5,3,8,8,3,5)$ at $(n,k)=(7,4)$, where $S_{7,4}(x)=961/550<7/4$.  (ii) Five exact identities for $Q_{n,k}$ on the diagonals $n=k+1,k+2,2k+1,2k+2,k+3$, valid for every $k\ge1$: in particular $\Cl{k+1}{k}=(k+1)/k^3$ exactly, the equal point of $S_{2k+1,k}$ is a strict local minimum for every $k$ with $\Cl{2k+1}{k}\ge1/(2k^2)$, and on $n=k+2$ and $n=2k+2$ it is never a saddle.  (iii) A saddle at $(n,k)=(14,11)$, beyond the tabulated range, on the diagonal $n=k+3$ whose symbol factors as $2(k+2)(c+\tfrac1{k+2})(c+\tfrac12)$.  (iv) An erratum: three entries of the source's $k=3$ numerical table are wrong, and the entry $-0.005046$ printed for $n=17$ lies below the infimum of the source's own symbol over the whole interval.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4.  The $k=2$ local analysis is classical (Searcy and Troesch, 1979) and nothing is claimed for it.

families.paper_title: Palindromicity of shifted lower Bruhat intervals: the $(w,x)$ census for $n\le 6$, the $3412/4231$ separation, and the failure of the Carrell--Peterson dictionary
families.paper_abstract: For elements $w,x$ of a Coxeter group $W$, the \emph{shifted lower Bruhat interval} is the right translate $S(w,x)=\{vx^{-1}:v\le w\}$ of the principal order ideal of $w$, carrying the order induced from the ambient Bruhat order.  Dave, Feng, Lesnevich, Oh, Richmond, Wang and Wu introduced it and proved that it has a unique maximum and a unique minimum, that its covering relations are ambient, that it is graded, and that it is EL-shellable.  Gradedness makes its rank generating function $F_{w,x}(q)$ well defined, and at $x=e$ it is the Poincar\'e polynomial of the Schubert variety $X_w$, palindromic exactly when $X_w$ is rationally smooth.  We ask for which pairs $(w,x)$ the polynomial $F_{w,x}$ is palindromic --- a question the source does not raise --- and settle a first round of it in type $A$.  We give the complete census in $\mathfrak{S}_n$ for $n\le 6$: the palindromic pairs number $4$, $36$, $464$, $8228$, $171112$; the permutations palindromic for \emph{every} shift number $2,6,15,38,95$; those palindromic for \emph{no} shift number $0,0,1,4,63$.  We then show that three separate halves of the classical dictionary fail to survive shifting.  The two Lakshmibai--Sandhya patterns, interchangeable in every statement of that dictionary, are separated by shifting: $3412$ is palindromic for none of the $24$ shifts of $\mathfrak{S}_4$ and $4231$ for exactly $8$.  Palindromicity no longer forces unimodality --- the source's own worked example is a witness --- so the Carrell--Peterson factorisation into $q$-integers has no analogue.  And the permutations palindromic for every shift do not form a pattern-avoidance class.  Finally, being palindromic for no shift implies neither containment of $3412$ nor containment of $4231$, although at $n\le 5$ it appears to imply the first.  The counts and witnesses stated below are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Complete solution sets and the extremal product for $\sigma_{n-2}(x)=\sigma_n(x)$ at $n=6$ and $n=7$
families.paper_abstract: For integers $1\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_n$ the equation $\sigma_{n-2}(x)=\sigma_n(x)$ between elementary symmetric polynomials is the decomposition of unity $\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}1/(x_ix_j)=1$; write $f_{n-2}(n)$ for its number of solutions.  Kiss, S\'andor and Zakarczemny introduced the sequence $v_1=1$, $v_2=2$, $v_{n+1}=v_n^2-v_n+1+v_1\cdots v_{n-1}$, observed that $(v_1,\dots,v_{n-1},v_n-1)$ solves the equation, listed all solutions for $n\le 5$, and asked whether $x_1x_2\cdots x_n\le v_1v_2\cdots v_{n-1}(v_n-1)$ holds for every solution. We answer this affirmatively at the two smallest lengths their paper leaves open.  For $n=6$ and $n=7$ we determine the solution set completely --- $f_4(6)=144$ and $f_5(7)=3598$ --- and show that the maximum of $x_1\cdots x_n$ is exactly $1\,257\,813\,360$ and $2\,881\,515\,884\,053\,973\,040$ respectively, attained at $(1,2,4,15,219,47862)$ and $(1,2,4,15,219,47863,2290845186)$.  We also prove, for every $n$, that the tuple $(v_1,\dots,v_{n-1},v_n-1)$ satisfies the equation and has product exactly the proposed bound, so that the question is in substance whether that one family is the product-maximiser; and we replace the majorization estimate through which the source obtains finiteness by an elementary prefix inequality, which is what makes the two exhaustive searches terminate. families.paper_title: Signed difference sets from perfect nonlinear functions
families.paper_abstract: A signed difference set in a finite abelian group $G$ of order $v$ is an element $D=\sum_{g}a_g\,g$ of $\ZZ[G]$ with $a_g\in\{0,\pm1\}$, support size $k$, satisfying $DD^{(-1)}=(k-\lambda)\,0_G+\lambda G$.  He and Wu recently produced a $(125,28,3)$ signed difference set in $C_5^3$ out of quartic multiplicative characters of $\FF_{25}$ and $\FF_5$, together with quartic Jacobi sums.  We show that their signed set is, verbatim, the graph of the norm map $\Nm\colon\FF_{25}\to\FF_5$ with the subgroup $\{0\}\times\FF_5$ subtracted, so that no character theory is needed to see it.  What that identity uses is only perfect nonlinearity: if $f\colon A\to B$ is a map of finite abelian groups with $|A|=n^2$, $|B|=n$ and every nonzero derivative of $f$ balanced, then $\Gam_f-(\{0\}\times B)$ is an $(n^3,\,n^2+n-2,\,n-2)$ signed difference set.  Binary quadratic forms of nonzero discriminant supply such an $f$ over every finite field and in every characteristic, so there is a signed difference set with parameters $(q^3,\,q^2+q-2,\,q-2)$ in the elementary abelian group of order $q^3$, for every prime power~$q$; the He--Wu example is the case $q=5$.  Three members of the family --- at $(27,10,1)$ in $C_3^3$, $(64,18,2)$ in $C_2^6$ and $(343,54,5)$ in $C_7^3$ --- occupy cells recorded as open in Gordon's signed difference set database, and two further members are beyond its parameter range.  We also exhibit two inequivalent $(125,28,3)$ signed difference sets in $C_5^3$, separated by an affine-covariant invariant, so the He--Wu set is one of at least two classes there.  All statements are formally verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The six-vertex model with N\'eel boundary: the printed table audited, the boundary convention pinned down, and the counts extended to $N=26$
families.paper_abstract: Tavares, Ribeiro and Korepin (J.~Stat.~Mech.\ 2015, P06016) introduced the \emph{N\'eel}, or anti-ferroelectric, fixed boundary condition for the six-vertex model on an $N\times N$ grid, tabulated the number $\Om_{\NE}(N)$ of configurations for $N\le 20$, and remarked that, unlike the domain-wall boundary, this boundary seems to admit no product formula.  Their definition of the boundary is a figure drawn at $N=4$.  We show that the figure has two natural readings --- the perimeter arrows alternate in and out all the way round, or the two ends of every row and of every column carry the same arrow --- which coincide for even $N$ and differ for odd $N$, and that only the alternating reading reproduces the table: the literal reading counts $4$ and $593$ at $N=3,5$ where the table prints $7$ and $1322$.  The printed numbers are correct; the readable definition is what needed pinning down, and the literal reading is a second sequence --- $1, 2, 4, 64, 593, 64914, 2964632, 2033739170, 474833620053, \dots$, equal to the table at even $N$ --- that the source does not print and that we found neither in the OEIS nor in any paper citing the source.  We audit all twenty printed integers with four independent counters, extend the table by six terms, $21\le N\le 26$ (the last has $118$ digits), and check the authors' remark that the counts agree with the alternating-sign-matrix numbers up to $N=3$ and part at $N=4$ ($64$ against $42$). A row-transfer dynamic programme is proved, for every $N$ and every fixed boundary, to equal the length of a duplicate-free list of exactly the configurations; the values of the table for $N\le 6$, those of the literal reading for $3\le N\le 6$, and the alternating-sign-matrix comparison are then kernel evaluations in Lean~4 with Mathlib, without \lean{native\_decide}.  Everything beyond $N=6$ is a computation outside the formal development and is labelled as such.

families.paper_title: Skirting sets and the inverse football pool problem, with $f(8,4)\le36$
families.paper_abstract: A tuple $x\in\ZZ_q^n$ \emph{skirts} $y\in\ZZ_q^n$ if $x_i\neq y_i$ for every coordinate $i$, and $S\subseteq\ZZ_q^n$ is a \emph{skirting set} if every tuple is skirted by some element of $S$; $f(n,q)$ denotes the least size of a skirting set.  This is the \emph{inverse football pool number} $T(n,q)$ of \"Osterg\aa rd and Riihonen and of Brink, studied since the 1950s.  It was reintroduced in 2026 by Adriaensen, Ihringer, Martin and Villagr\'an, who named skirting sets and identified $f(n,q)$ with the total domination number of a direct power of a complete graph, and by Kuang and Wang as the number of binary subcubes needed to cover the ternary cube; neither 2026 paper cites the older work, and every interval in the tables they print is superseded by it.  Already known are $f(7,3)=29$ and $f(8,3)=44$ (Brink), and $f(6,4)=15$ and $f(7,4)\le23$ (Ashik Mathew and \"Osterg\aa rd, under the name of blocking sets in a discrete torus).  One cell is improved here: $f(8,4)\le36$, against the published $40$, so that the record for that cell becomes $[27,36]$.  We also give explicit machine-checked witnesses at every cell of the 2026 tables --- among them $44$ tuples of $\ZZ_3^8$, $29$ of $\ZZ_3^7$ and $15$ of $\ZZ_4^6$ realising three of the known values above --- each verified by complete evaluation from the definition, and three of them irredundant.  We record besides that the growth constant $C_q=\inf_{n\ge1}f(n,q)^{1/n}$ equals $q/(q-1)$ for every $q\ge2$, granted the Johnson--Lov\'asz--Stein covering estimate as it has been printed for general $q$; the matching lower bound is a counting argument, and for $q=3$ no unproved estimate is needed.  Every theorem below has been machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The smoothest average at half-width one:\\ the four open cells of Gait\'an, Garz\'on and Madrid
families.paper_abstract: For a symmetric kernel $u$ on $\{-n,\dots,n\}$ with $\sum u = 1$, Gait\'an, Garz\'on and Madrid (arXiv:2604.25074) study the smallest possible operator norm of $f \mapsto \nabla^k(u * f)$ on $\ell^2(\Z)$, written $C_{k,n,1}$ over all such kernels and $C_{k,n,2}$ over those with a non-negative Fourier transform.  Their Table~2 prints the word ``Open'' in four cells: $C_{1,n,2}$, $C_{3,n,2}$, $C_{4,n,1}$ and $C_{6,n,1}$.  We settle all four at half-width $n = 1$, in both directions: $C_{1,1,2} = 4\sqrt3/9$ and $C_{3,1,2} = 48\sqrt{15}/125$, both attained only at the Fej\'er kernel $(1/4,1/2,1/4)$; $C_{4,1,1} = 16t^2/3$ with $t^3 + 3t = 2$, and $C_{6,1,1} = 16t^3$ with $t^4 + 4t = 3$, $t > 0$, each attained at a unique kernel with a two-point equioscillation.  The route is the Plancherel reduction the source itself uses, which turns each cell into a weighted Chebyshev problem $\min \max_{[-1,1]} (1-x)^{k/2}|q(x)|$ over $q(1)=1$, $\deg q \le n$; we check the reduction by recovering the source's Theorems~1.4 and 1.7 from its Propositions~1.6 and 1.9.  The same elementary method reproduces the source's own two restricted cells at $n = 1$ as $16/27$ and $27/32$, the latter being the value of its elliptic (Zolotarev) constant at modulus $k^2 = 8/9$, a closed form the source does not print. A one-parameter law $t^{m+1} + (m+1)t = m \Rightarrow \min = t^m/(m+1)$ (unrestricted) and $\min = m^m/(m+1)^{m+1}$ (restricted) explains all six numbers and is proved on paper. We state the caveat plainly: at $n = 1$ each cell is a one-parameter minimax problem and the proofs are elementary.  For the two unrestricted cells the source's own Lemma~5.2 already supplies existence, uniqueness and the two-point equioscillation, so what is added there is the solution of the resulting $2\times2$ system; in the two restricted cells the optimum sits on the boundary of the sign constraint and the value is a maximum of $y^m(1-y)$.  What is new is the \emph{value} in a cell the source declares open, and the classical monograph literature on Chebyshev--Zolotarev problems was not searched.  The four polynomial inequalities, the controls and the two reproduced cells are checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib; the passage from $C_{k,n,j}$ to them, and every uniqueness assertion, is on paper and is marked as such.

families.paper_title: A counting formula for linear\\ self-orthogonal cellular automata
families.paper_abstract: A bipermutive local rule of diameter $d$ over $\FF$ generates, through its no-boundary cellular automaton, a Latin square of order $2^{d-1}$; Mariot and Mazzone call the automaton \emph{self-orthogonal} when that square is orthogonal to its transpose.  They determined the number $\LIN(d)$ of linear self-orthogonal cellular automata for $3\le d\le 16$, observed that the values follow $2^{d-3}$ until they stop doing so at $d=7$, reported that the sequence is not indexed in the OEIS, and asked for a counting formula. We give one.  We show that $\LIN(d)$ is the number of invertible circulant matrices of order $d-1$ over $\FF$ with zero diagonal, and that \[ \LIN(d)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\Psii(d-1)+\mu(X^{d-1}-1)\bigr), \] where $\Psii(n)$ is the number of invertible circulants of order $n$ over $\FF$ (OEIS A003473) and $\mu$ is the M\"obius function of $\FF[X]$, so that $\mu(X^n-1)$ is $0$ for even $n$ and $(-1)^{r(n)}$ for odd $n$, with $r(n)$ the number of distinct irreducible factors of $X^n-1$.  Both halves of the identity are proved, together with the classical product formula for $\Psii$.  The closed form reproduces all fourteen published values and extends them to $d=30$; it also settles the shape of the data exactly, in that $\LIN(d)=2^{d-3}$ holds precisely when $d-1$ is a power of two or an odd prime having $2$ as a primitive root, the first failure being $d=7$.  All statements below are machine-checked in Lean~4, with one explicitly labelled exception.

families.paper_title: Over-learning forces instability for at most five agents:\\ trace bounds for $\rho(A-\Efrak)$ and a quartic threshold
families.paper_abstract: In the averaging-plus-learning dynamics $X_{t+1}=AX_t+\Efrak(\bar\sigma-X_t)$ of Popescu and Vaidya, $n$ agents average their neighbours' opinions with the weights of a row-stochastic matrix $A$ while each is pulled towards an external ground truth $\bar\sigma$ at its own \emph{learning rate} $\Efrak(i)\ge 0$.  The error obeys $X_{t+1}-\bar\sigma=(A-\Efrak)(X_t-\bar\sigma)$, so it dies from every initial condition exactly when $\rho(A-\Efrak)<1$.  Popescu, Syatriadi and Vaidya ask whether a single agent learning at rate at least $3$ already destroys that: is $\rho(A-\Efrak)\ge1$ as soon as $\Efrak(i)\ge3$ for some $i$?  They settle $n=1$ and $n=2$, and settle every $n$ only under an extra hypothesis (a symmetric $A$, or a Gershgorin isolation condition on the remaining agents).  We prove the answer is yes for every $n\le5$, for the wider class of row-substochastic $A$ and with no sign condition on the other learning rates.  The instruments are the second and the fourth moment of the spectrum: writing $d_i=\Efrak(i)-A(i,i)$, and $r_i$ for the total averaging weight agent $i$ sends to the other agents, \[ \rho(A-\Efrak)^2\ge\frac1n\sum_i d_i^2, \qquad \tr\bigl((A-\Efrak)^4\bigr)\ge\sum_i d_i^4-4\sum_i\max(d_i,0)\,r_i , \] and the two are joined by a constraint peculiar to the problem: a fast learner pays for its outgoing weight out of its own diagonal, so that $\Efrak(i_0)\ge3$ forces $d_{i_0}\ge2$ \emph{and} $r_{i_0}\le d_{i_0}-2$.  Four consequences hold at every $n$.  The extremal function $f_n$ of Popescu, Syatriadi and Vaidya satisfies $f_n(R)\ge(R-1)^+/\sqrt n$, and also $f_n(R)\ge1$ as soon as $R\ge3$ and $(R-1)^4\ge5n$, where the threshold they obtain from an $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ Ostrowski--Elsner spectral variation bound is $(n2^n+3n-1)/2$ --- and their bound is vacuous at $R=3$ for every $n\ge2$.  If a quarter of the agents learn at rate at least $3$, then $\rho(A-\Efrak)\ge1$; and so it is if the set of agents reachable from one fast learner is closed under the influence relation and has at most four members.  We also prove $f_3(3)<2$, so that the exact formula $f_n(R)=(R-1)^+$ of Popescu, Syatriadi and Vaidya stops at $n=2$; the certificate is an explicit quadratic Lyapunov form, the characteristic polynomial being irreducible with a near-double root.  Finally we show where the method stops: an explicit $7\times7$ instance satisfying the hypotheses has both trace powers below $n$ while $\rho(A-\Efrak)\ge2$, and on it the fourth-moment estimate is an equality.  Every theorem and proposition below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The split locus of superelliptic curves: determination for small fields, and members that are neither maximal nor Hermitian quotients
families.paper_abstract: Let $X\colon y^{n}=f(x)$ be a superelliptic curve over $\F_q$ with $f$ separable of degree $d\ge 3$ splitting into distinct linear factors and with $n\mid q-1$.  Say that the pair $(n,f)$ lies in the \emph{split locus} when every value of $f$ outside its roots is an $n$-th power in $\Fs$, so that every unramified fibre of $x$ splits into $n$ rational points.  A recent preprint isolated this locus, exhibited one family inside it --- a family of quotients of the Hermitian curve, all of them maximal --- wrote that it did not know how far the list extends, and asked whether every member of the locus is a maximal Hermitian quotient.  We answer both halves in the negative and determine the locus over small fields.  Over $\F_{16}$ the pair $n=3$, $f=\Tr_{\F_{16}/\F_2}$ lies in the locus, and its curve has $33$ rational points against a maximality bound of $73$ and genus $7$ against the Hermitian genus $6$; this is proved with no appeal to any axiom.  It is not an accident of one field: for every even $m=2e\ge 4$, $q=2^{m}$, and every $n\ge 3$ dividing $q-1$, the curve $y^{n}=\Tr_{\Fq/\F_2}(x)$ lies in the locus and is neither maximal nor a quotient of the Hermitian curve, and at $e=1$ both inequalities degenerate into equalities --- which is exactly the Hermitian case.  We further determine the locus completely, by exhaustive search over all $2^{q}$ root sets: for nine fields $q\le 19$ inside a formal development, and, outside it, for six further fields, up to $q=32$.  Over $\F_{16}$ the locus consists of $2101$ pairs $(n,R)$, of which the previously known Hermitian family is a single cell of $48$.  Finally, Weil's character-sum bound yields $d\ge\sqrt{q}$, sharper than the pigeonhole bound of the source for small $n$, and over the square fields $q=9,16,25$ the minimum $d=\sqrt q$ is attained exactly by the Hermitian quotients.  The answer to the source's question is therefore yes at minimal degree and no above it.  Every numbered statement of Sections~\ref{sec:witness}--\ref{sec:census} is machine-checked in Lean~4, with one documented gap: the finite-field input to the infinite family is verified in three concrete field models rather than uniformly in $m$.  The computations that lie outside the formal development are labelled as such where they appear.

families.paper_title: Square-free words with square-free arithmetic subsequences: a correction at $(3,9)$, and the first data on shifted triples
families.paper_abstract: For an infinite word $w=w_0w_1w_2\cdots$ over $\A$ and integers $p\ge 1$, $s\ge 0$, write $\sh{w}{p}{s}$ for the subsequence of letters at positions congruent to $s$ modulo $p$, and $\su{w}{p}=\sh{w}{p}{0}$. Call a triple $(p,q,s)$ \emph{positive} when some infinite square-free ternary word $w$ has both $\su{w}{p}$ and $\sh{w}{q}{s}$ square-free, and a pair $(p,q)$ positive when $(p,q,0)$ is. Delépine, Ochem and Rosenfeld (arXiv:2605.29853v1) determine every pair with $p,q\le 20$ except $(5,8)$, and ask which triples are positive.  We prove that $(3,9)$ is a positive pair, correcting the list of negative pairs printed in Proposition~28 of that preprint --- its Table~1, its companion code and the argument here all agree that $(3,9)$ is positive. We then give the first values for the shifted problem: the shifts reachable from $s=0$ by translation are exactly the multiples of $\gcd(p,q)$; $129$ triples coming from the six cells $(3,9)$, $(3,12)$, $(3,18)$, $(3,24)$, $(3,30)$, $(4,36)$ are positive, settling each of those cells at every shift; $(4,12,s)$ is positive if and only if $4\mid s$, which is the first witness for the assertion that for non-coprime pairs the starting positions matter; and $36$ further triples are negative, each with its exact maximum admissible length. We also record $34$ positive pairs with $q>20$ whose verdict follows from morphisms published in the companion code of the same preprint but which its own counting script classifies as unresolved. Every result proved below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

statements.label: h_0^{(l)}, the reference height function of the source, is exactly the l^1 distance from (x,y) to the central crease {(k,-k) : 0 <= k < l}: it equals |x-k| + |y+k| for some k < l and is <= |x-k| + |y+k| for every k < l, at every site and every width l >= 1

The reference configuration h_0^{(l)} itself satisfies the ice rule |h_0(u) - h_0(v)| = 1 at every pair of adjacent sites of Z^2, for every width l >= 1, so the volume-zero configuration set is a singleton rather than empty

With h = h_0^{(l)} + 2r, the ice rule |h(u) - h(v)| = 1 across an edge u ~ v with h_0(v) = h_0(u) + 1 holds if and only if r(u) - r(v) is 0 or 1: the source's Proposition 2.1 is the forward implication only, and the converse is what makes the reduction to reduced height functions a bijection

Every site at positive distance from the central crease has a neighbour one step closer, so from any site v there is a set of h_0(v) + 1 distinct sites, all at distance at most h_0(v), on each of which the reduced height is at least r(v)
A site carrying reduced height r(v) >= 1 at distance d = h_0(v) from the crease forces total volume >= d + 1; equivalently, a configuration of volume n vanishes at every site with h_0 >= n

Correction to arXiv:1607.01890v1, Section 2.1: the printed eastern crease '(x+l-1, l-1) for x > 0' is not a crease for l >= 2, since h_0 strictly decreases from (x+l-1, l-1) to (x+l-1, l-2), whereas (x+l-1, 1-l) is strictly below both its vertical neighbours, as the source's own Figure 2 shows
The zero level set of h_0^{(l)} is exactly the central crease {(k,-k) : 0 <= k < l}, and the unit spike at any crease site is an admissible configuration
a_l(1) = l for every width l >= 1: the configurations of volume one are exactly the l unit spikes at the sites of the central crease

Negative controls: a unit spike at a site off the crease is not a configuration, because its inward neighbour carries 0; and a height-two spike on the crease is not one either, because the drop to its outward neighbours is 2

The sub-level sets of h_0^{(l)} are finite, hence the set of width-l configurations of volume n is finite and a_l(n) is a genuine finite count, for every l >= 1 and every n -- which the source never establishes
C(l,n) <= a_l(n) for every width l >= 1 and every volume n, unconditionally and with no restriction l >= ceil(n/2): the 0/1 indicator of any n-subset of the central crease is a configuration

families.paper_title: The square-ice analogue of plane partitions: a finite count, the volume-two formula for every width, and ten closed forms beyond the printed table
families.paper_abstract: Govindarajan, Guttmann and Subramanyan (arXiv:1607.01890; Ann.\ Inst.\ Henri Poincar\'e D \textbf{6} (2019) 123--154) count the ways $a_\ell(n)$ of removing $n$ oranges from an infinite stack whose $k$-th layer is a $k\times(k+\ell-1)$ rectangle, as height functions on $\Z^2$ above a reference $\hz$ subject to the ice rule.  They print closed forms for $a_\ell(2),\dots,a_\ell(9)$, attribute proofs of those for $n\le 4$ to a 2016 IIT Madras thesis whose text gives counting explanations for $n\le3$ only, tabulate $a_\ell(n)$ for $\ell\le 20$, $n\le 15$, and conjecture that for $\ell\ge\lceil n/2\rceil$ the count is a polynomial $\sum_k g_k(n)\binom{\ell}{n-k}$ with $\deg g_k=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, of which they determine $g_0,\dots,g_6$.  We first make the object well posed: $\hz$ is the $\ell^1$ distance to the segment $\{(k,-k):0\le k<\ell\}$, the ice rule is \emph{equivalent} to a step condition on the reduced height, a site at distance $d$ carrying anything costs volume $d+1$, and so $a_\ell(n)$ is a finite number --- which the source never shows.  We prove $a_\ell(0)=1$, $a_\ell(1)=\ell$ and $a_\ell(2)=\binom{\ell}{2}+4$ for every width, the last by a classification whose ``$+4$'' is the four sites at distance one from the segment with a single neighbour on it; the source's width-monotonicity conjecture is thereby a theorem for $n\le 2$, and $\binom{\ell}{n}+4\binom{\ell-1}{n-2}\le a_\ell(n)$ holds for all $\ell\ge1$, $n\ge2$.  A sign error in the printed description of the eastern crease is recorded; no result depends on it.  An independent enumeration reproduces every printed cell of the source's two tables that it reaches --- all $320$ of Table~2 and all $114$ of Table~3 with $n\le19$, $344$ distinct cells --- and extends them to $\ell\le 36$, $n\le 19$; on that table we read off the ten closed forms $a_\ell(10),\dots,a_\ell(19)$ the source does not print, find the threshold $\ell\ge\lceil n/2\rceil$ exactly sharp for every $n\le 19$, determine six further coefficient polynomials $g_7,\dots,g_{12}$ of the predicted degrees with data to spare, and confirm both monotonicity conjectures at every cell.  The general theorems, the small-volume formulas and every identity between a closed form and the enumerated table are checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib, without \lean{native\_decide}; the table itself is a computation outside the formal development and is labelled as such throughout.

families.paper_title: Additive complexity of small linear codes:\\ a corrected cell, two exact values in dimension five,\\ and the extended ternary Golay code
families.paper_abstract: For a prime power $q$, write $\sslp_q(r,k,d)$ for the least number of additions and scalar multiplications needed to compute $Lv$, where $L^{\mathsf T}$ generates an $[r,k,d]_q$ code: the \emph{additive} complexity of the best code with the given parameters.  The quantity was introduced by Dumas, Lia and Sheekey, who tabulate eleven of its values and ask for precise results at more small parameters.  We settle one of their cells against the published value, improve four others, and add a cell their table does not have.  For $q\in\{2,3\}$ we prove $\sslp_q(10,4,4)=3$, not the $4$ that appears in their table: three additions produce a $[10,4,4]_q$ code, and no two do.  The witness computes two of the four standard basis vectors as intermediates and never outputs them, which is what the published lower bound overlooks; putting the generator matrix in systematic form is not available here, because a change of basis preserves the code but not the length of a program computing it.  Over $\FF_3$ in dimension five we prove $\sslp_3(13,5,5)\le 7$, $\sslp_3(12,5,5)\le 8$, $\sslp_3(11,5,5)\le 9$ and $\sslp_3(10,5,5)\le 10$, against the printed $\le 11$, $\le 12$, $\le 12$ and $\in[5,12]$; for the first of these we also record that $\le 8$ already follows from a binary program in the same paper, so the improvement there is from $8$ to $7$.  In dimension six we prove $\sslp_3(12,6,6)\le 14$, for the extended ternary Golay code --- a cell the published table does not contain, and one that paper needs.  Exhaustive searches reported separately, outside the machine-checked development, close two of these cells: $\sslp_3(13,5,5)=7$, and $\sslp_3(10,5,5)=10$ against a published bracket of $[5,12]$; they also bracket the new cell as $\sslp_3(12,6,6)\in[10,14]$.  Substituted into a lemma of Dumas, Lia and Sheekey, the values bound from below the cost of multiplication in algebras of order $3^5$ and $3^6$, and cap what that lemma can ever give.  Every statement below that is labelled as a theorem, proposition or corollary is machine-checked in Lean~4, with no \texttt{sorry} and in a development that imports no mathematical library, with one exception that is marked as such in its own statement and proved on paper; the exhaustive searches that are not checked in the kernel are clearly marked and are stated as remarks, not results.

families.title: The SS-RS-GD inequalities at n = 2: the eta_{2,K} = 1 belief is false at d = 4, the RS-GD half holds at eta = 1, and the d = 2 case for every K
families.description: Yun, Sra and Jadbabaie (arXiv:2103.07079v1, COLT 2021 open problem, *Can Single-Shuffle SGD be Better than Reshuffling SGD and GD?*) study the expected iterate of stochastic gradient descent on a quadratic finite sum under three sampling schemes: **single shuffle** (SS, one permutation drawn once and reused), **random reshuffling** (RS, a fresh permutation each epoch), and plain **gradient descent** (GD). For real symmetric `A_1, …, A_n` (the `A_i = I − ηM_i` of a quadratic problem) and `K` epochs they define, with `P_σ = A_{σ(1)} A_{σ(2)} ⋯ A_{σ(n)}`,

statements.label: the SS-RS inequality of Yun-Sra-Jadbabaie's Conjecture 1 FAILS at n = 2, eta = 1: for the symmetric positive definite integer matrices A = diag(1, 100, 10^4, 10^6) and B = [[10^7, 1.1*10^6, 10^4, 0], [1.1*10^6, 2*10^5, -6000, 100], [10^4, -6000, 2100, 110], [0, 100, 110, 10]] at K = 2, d = 4, one has ||W_ss|| > rho^2 = 11263576900000000 >= ||W_rs||, with a four-part exact integer certificate; this refutes the belief 'for n = 2, we believe that the conjecture itself is likely true for any d and K, with step-size constants eta_{2,K} = 1' stated verbatim in arXiv:2103.07079v1 section 4.1

the RS-GD half of Conjecture 1 holds at n = 2 with eta = 1 and no conditioning hypothesis: for all real symmetric PSD A, B and all c >= 0 with A + B <= (2c)*I, one has -c^2*I <= (AB+BA)/2 <= c^2*I, hence ||W_rs|| <= ||W_gd|| for every K and every d; the constant c^2 is attained at A = B = c*I, and eta = 1 is sharp -- for every eta > 1 a 1x1 witness has W_gd = 0 while W_rs != 0

the d = 2 SS-RS inequality for every K and every real spectrum: if N is a real 2x2 matrix whose two eigenvalues are real ((tr N)^2 >= 4 det N) and -c*I <= sym N <= c*I, then -c^K*I <= sym(N^K) <= c^K*I; equivalently w_R(N^K) <= w_R(N)^K for the real numerical radius w_R(X) = ||sym X||. At N = AB with A, B PSD this is Yun-Sra-Jadbabaie's Theorem 4 (thm:ss-3), here with the PSD hypothesis weakened to 'N has real spectrum'. The real-spectrum hypothesis is not removable: a rotation has w_R(N^2) = 1 > 0 = w_R(N)^2

the optimal step-size constant eta_{2,2} of Conjecture 1 satisfies 1/4 <= eta_{2,2} < 1 - 1/84375000 = 1 - 1.1851852e-8, the upper half KERNEL-BOUND: the SSRS1 witness rescaled by 10^-6 and 10125000^-1 satisfies Conjecture 1's own hypothesis (1-eta) I <= A, B <= I with 1-eta = 1/84375000 and still violates ||W_ss|| <= ||W_rs||. A sharper witness, found by a homotopy in the conditioning cap and certified in exact rational arithmetic, gives eta_{2,2} < 1 - 3.9591821e-7; that one is not yet formalised

the infimum over N = AB with A, B PSD of the margin lambda_min(sym(N^2))/||sym N||^2 -- which is >= -1 exactly when the K = 2 SS-RS inequality holds -- is -1/3 at d = 2, numerically -0.999999998 at d = 3, and at most -1.0356 at d = 4 (exact witness); so d = 3 is the open dimension and, if the d = 3 numeric is right, d = 4 is the minimal dimension of any eta = 1 counterexample

Conjecture 1 of Yun-Sra-Jadbabaie (arXiv:2103.07079v1) FAILS at n = 2, K = 2, d = 4 for every step-size constant eta > 1 - 1/389765: for the symmetric positive definite integer matrices A = diag(1, 49, 3844, 389376) and B = [[5074956432, 841928256, 7921368, 0], [841928256, 280642752, -13956696, 74958], [7921368, -13956696, 3066336, 126945], [0, 74958, 126945, 26908]], the rescaled pair A' = A/389376, B' = B/5220000000 satisfies the conjecture's own hypothesis (1/389765) I <= A', B' <= I and still has ||W_ss|| > rho^2 >= ||W_rs|| at K = 2, with rho = 42869796155, rho^2 = 1837819422371252784025, the violating vector v = (-8, 4, -4, 8) and certified ratio 1.0482812150 (true ratio 1.0489088162). Hence eta_{2,2} < 1 - 1/389765 = 1 - 2.5656485e-6, a factor 216.5 sharper than conjecture_one_fails (1 - 1.1851852e-8) and 6.5 sharper than the exact-arithmetic witness of journal/2026-09-03-ssrs-n2-founding.md section 7.1 (1 - 3.9591821e-7). The bracket on the optimal step-size constant is now 1/4 <= eta_{2,2} < 1 - 2.5656485e-6

the conditioning of the SSRS6 witness, kernel-bound on BOTH sides. Upper: 1*I <= A <= 389376*I and (5220000000/389765)*I <= B <= 5220000000*I, by four cleared-LDL^T integer certificates, so cond(A) = 389376 exactly and cond(B) <= 389765; conditioning_rayleigh records the Rayleigh-quotient reading that makes 'condition number' the right word. Lower: every Loewner sandwich m*I <= A <= M*I has M >= 389376*m (cond_A_ge) and every m*I <= B <= M*I has M >= 380791*m (cond_B_ge), so ANY normalisation (1-eta) I <= A/s_A, B/s_B <= I of this pair has 1 - eta <= 1/389376 (normalisation_floor). The cap 1/389765 used in SSRS6 is 0.0999% above that floor: the remaining about five and a half orders of magnitude (log10(0.75 / 2.5656485e-6) = 5.47; "seven" was v1's figure -- v2 referee 2026-09-03) down to eta_{2,2} >= 1/4 are a gap in the WITNESS, not in its bookkeeping. Exact rational bisection on LDL^T: lambda_min(B) = 13704.3865656996, lambda_max(B) = 5218514684.2663055854, cond(B) = 380791.556

controls for the SSRS6 witness: (i) 10^21 is NOT a Loewner bound for W_rs, witnessed by u = (1,1,1,1), so with ||W_rs|| <= rho^2 = 1.8378e21 the bound rho^2 is bracketed in (10^21, rho^2] and not vacuously large; (ii) at the wrong vector w = (1,0,0,0) the Rayleigh quotient of W_ss is 6.073e19 and does NOT escape [-rho^2, rho^2], so the refutation depends on the violating vector and is not an artefact of the shape of the statement; (iii) the claim cannot be weakened upward: (1/380800) I <= B/5220000000 is FALSE, refuted by the same integer vector that realises lambda_min(B); (iv) non-vacuity: A - 1*I and 389765*B - 5220000000*I are both PSD, so A and B are positive DEFINITE and the hypothesis of conjecture_one_fails_sharp is satisfiable strictly inside the cone, not on its boundary

families.paper_title: The constant $\eta_{2,K}=1$ is impossible:\\ an exact counterexample to the single-shuffle\\ inequality at $n=2$, $K=2$, $d=4$
families.paper_abstract: Yun, Sra and Jadbabaie compare the expected iterate of stochastic gradient descent on a quadratic finite sum under single shuffling, random reshuffling and plain gradient descent, and conjecture that for every number of components $n$, every epoch count $K$ and every dimension $d$ there is a step-size constant $\eta_{n,K}\in(0,1]$ for which $(1-\eta_{n,K})I\preceq A_i\preceq I$ forces $\|\Wss\|\le\|\Wrs\|\le\|\Wgd\|$.  About the first component of their conjecture at $n=2$ they write: \emph{``Nevertheless, for $n=2$, we believe that the conjecture itself is likely true for any $d$ and $K$, with step-size constants $\eta_{2,K}=1$.''}  We refute that belief, with two explicit witnesses.  For the symmetric positive definite \emph{integer} matrices $A=\mathrm{diag}(1,10^2,10^4,10^6)$ and an explicit $B$ with entries at most $10^7$, at $K=2$ and $d=4$, we have $\|\Wss\|>\rho^2\ge\|\Wrs\|$ with $\rho=106130000$; the true ratio is $\|\Wss\|/\|\Wrs\|=1.035608302215\ldots$.  Rescaled into the conjecture's own normalisation the pair satisfies $\tfrac{1}{84375000}I\preceq A',B'\preceq I$ and still violates the inequality.  A second, far better conditioned pair --- $A=\mathrm{diag}(1,7^2,62^2,624^2)$ and an explicit $B$ with entries of at most ten digits --- does the same at $\tfrac{1}{389765}I\preceq A',B'\preceq I$, a factor $216.5$ sharper, with true ratio $1.048908816189\ldots$; and we prove that \emph{no} renormalisation of that pair can reach past $\tfrac1{389376}$, so its bookkeeping is within $0.1\ witness rather than of the accounting.  Hence no admissible constant reaches $1-2.5656\ldots\times10^{-6}$, while $\eta=\tfrac14$ is admissible, by the authors' own Theorem~3 together with the $n=2$ case of the Recht--R\'e inequality.  The conjecture itself survives at $n=2$; what dies is the value of the constant, and a stated belief becomes a quantitative question whose answer, the supremum $\eta^{*}_{2,2}$ of the admissible constants, is bracketed by $\tfrac14\le\eta^{*}_{2,2}\le1-2.5656\ldots\times10^{-6}$ --- about five and a half orders of magnitude in $1-\eta$, and no better.  Each certificate is four denominator-cleared $LDL^\top$ identities and two Rayleigh quotients, all in exact integer arithmetic, so the refutations are checked by kernel reduction alone, with no compiled evaluation and no floating point anywhere in the proofs.  We also record, with credit, the two halves of the $n=2$ picture that do hold --- the reshuffling-versus-gradient-descent inequality for all positive semidefinite $A,B$ at $\eta=1$, and the single-shuffle inequality at $d=2$ for every $K$ --- and we explain why the counterexample is invisible to the searches that look for it: the violating eigenvalue is the \emph{negative} one, and the largest eigenvalue can never violate the inequality.  Every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.title: The sharp output cardinality k* of a full-support, unique-Bayes, disjoint-argmax counterexample to Fisher consistency of the structured-SVM margin-rescaling surrogate among common-geodesic (modular) metrics: the source brackets 5 <= k* <= 8 and calls the value open; a new six-output witness on K_{3,3} at q = (1,1,2,2,3,3)/12 gives k* <= 6, an exhaustive exact decision over all rational q and v kills every five-point modular metric that arises from a graph and every one with integer distances at most four, and a tie-broken K_{m,n} family gives witnesses at every cardinality >= 6
families.description: `Y` is a finite output set with `k = |Y|` and `L : Y × Y → ℝ_{≥0}` is a metric. The **margin-rescaling structured-SVM surrogate** is

statements.label: k* <= 6: a modular metric on six outputs (the shortest-path metric of K_{3,3}), a full-support q = (1,1,2,2,3,3)/12 whose Bayes set is the single output a_3, and an exactly optimal score vector v = (-1,-1,-1,0,0,0) -- optimality certified by an explicit self-coupling through weak duality -- whose maximisers {b_1,b_2,b_3} are all non-Bayes; this improves the source's own bound k* <= 8. The metric is modular but not median

A second six-output witness on the same K_{3,3} metric, q = (1,1,1,2,1,1)/7 and v = (1,1,1,0,0,0), whose single Bayes output b_1 lies in the HEAVY part and whose argmax is the whole light part -- so the failure is not a knife-edge choice of q and the Bayes output may sit on either side

The source's four-output unit star (its Corollary 3.4) re-certified: v = (-1,0,0,0) is exactly optimal by a three-cycle self-coupling, Bayes = {o}, argmax = {a,b,c}, disjoint -- and its q has a zero, so it does not bear on the full-support question

The source's five-output K_{2,3} witness (its Theorem 5.1 at m = 2, n = 3) re-certified, together with the proof that its Bayes set {a_1,a_2} has two elements and therefore equals no singleton -- the exact defect that leaves k* open
The source's three-dimensional Hamming-cube witness (its Theorem 5.4) re-certified, giving k* <= 8, and the cube metric proved median over all 512 triples -- the only known median witness

Negative controls: no witness on 0 or 1 outputs; the three-point equilateral metric is a metric that fails the common-geodesic condition; at the witness distribution the embedded report of the Bayes output is ALSO an exact minimiser and IS decoded correctly (so the witness is about some minimiser, not all of them); the embedded report of a non-Bayes output is not optimal; and at the uniform q on K_{3,3} every output is Bayes

The certificate layer for the self-coupling dual, for an arbitrary finite metric: weak duality (the easy half of the source's Proposition 2.1), the optimality certificate, complementary slackness (its equation (4)), the embedded-report identity S_M(phi(y),x) = 2 L(y,x) (its Lemma 2.2), and the diagonal criterion -- a positive diagonal entry in any optimal self-coupling forces argmax v = {y} with y Bayes

Exhaustive decision over ALL rational q and ALL score vectors v: no five-point modular metric among the five arising from the 21 connected graphs on five vertices, and none among the seventeen with integer distances at most four (from 228,502 labelled metrics), admits a full-support unique-Bayes disjoint-argmax witness -- so k* = 6 conditional on the five-point classification

The counts of connected graphs on n vertices whose shortest-path metric is modular / median, n = 1..8: 1,1,1,3,5,16,41,156 and 1,1,1,3,4,11,23,69; the median row is OEIS A292623 and the modular row is absent from OEIS. Plus the engineering fact that `decide` cannot evaluate rational arithmetic in the Lean kernel (Rat addition normalises through Nat.gcd), while the identical table over the integers decides fine -- the reason this family carries integer certificates

A seven-output witness: K_{3,4} with the tie broken at a_1, q = (2,1,1,1,1,1,1)/8 and v = (0,0,0,1,1,1,1), single Bayes output a_1 and argmax the whole four-element part -- so witnesses are now kernel-certified at cardinalities 6, 7 and 8

The general tie-broken complete-bipartite family: for every m >= 3 and n >= m, K_{m,n} with q(a_1) = 2/(m+n+1), all other weights 1/(m+n+1), and v = 0 on the light part and 1 on the heavy part, is a witness -- hence there is a witness on k outputs for EVERY k >= 6, and m = 2 (the source's own case) is exactly where the construction fails

families.paper_title: Six outputs suffice: unique-Bayes counterexamples\\ to Fisher consistency of the structured-SVM\\ surrogate on modular metrics
families.paper_abstract: Let $\YY$ be a finite output set and let $L$ be a metric on it.  The margin-rescaling structured-SVM surrogate is $\SM(v,y)=\max_{y'\in\YY}\{L(y,y')+v_{y'}-v_y\}$, and the question is whether the canonical decoder $v\mapsto\amax_y v_y$ is Fisher consistent for $L$. Nowak-Vila, Rudi and Bach showed that it is necessary that every triple of outputs have a common geodesic point --- that $L$ be a \emph{modular} metric --- and left sufficiency open. Fei and Luo have recently shown that the condition is not sufficient, and that five outputs are necessary and sufficient for a counterexample at a fully supported conditional distribution. Their discussion isolates a strictly harder quantity: the least number $k^{*}$ of outputs carrying a counterexample that is at once fully supported, has a \emph{single} Bayes output, and whose score maximisers all miss that output.  They bracket $5\le k^{*}\le 8$ and call the value open.  We prove $k^{*}\le 6$.  On the shortest-path metric of $K_{3,3}$ the distribution $q=(1,1,2,2,3,3)/12$ has the single Bayes output $a_3$, the score vector $v=(-1,-1,-1,0,0,0)$ minimises the conditional surrogate risk exactly --- certified by an explicit self-coupling through weak duality --- and its maximisers are the whole opposite part.  A second witness on the same metric, $q=(1,1,1,2,1,1)/7$, puts the single Bayes output in the heavy part instead, and a seven-output witness on $K_{3,4}$ certifies the cardinality $7$ as well, so witnesses now exist at $6$, $7$ and $8$.  Two further results are proved on the page rather than machine-checked: a tie-broken complete-bipartite family gives a witness at \emph{every} cardinality $k\ge6$ and fails exactly at $m=2$, the case the source itself treats; and an exact decision procedure over all rational distributions and all score vectors, run to completion on every five-point modular metric arising from a graph and on all seventeen with integer distances at most $4$, returns no witness, so $k^{*}=6$ conditional on that enumeration.  The witnesses, the source's three counterexamples and the certificate layer are formally verified in Lean~4 against \emph{Mathlib}.

families.paper_title: An asserted inequality, proved and sharpened:\\ the exact minimum of the threshold-rounding ratio\\ of Elbassioni and Ray
families.paper_abstract: In their analysis of a threshold-rounding algorithm for stabbing axis-parallel segments, Elbassioni and Ray exhibit a family of fractional solutions of the standard LP relaxation whose rounding cost ratio tends to an explicit two-variable function $\gamma(\tx,\ty)$ of the two rounding thresholds, and assert that $\gamma\ge1.89$ everywhere, with the sentence: \emph{``We skip the technical proof since it does not yield much insight and since this can be easily checked numerically.''}  The assertion stands unproved in the 2021 preprint, and Appendix~B of the 2024 journal version repeats it word for word, with the thresholds renamed.  We prove it, and we determine the constant it approximates.  The minimum of $\gamma$ over $[0,1)^2$ is attained at $(t^{*},\tfrac12)$ and at $(\tfrac12,t^{*})$, where $t^{*}$ is the unique root in $[\tfrac{7}{20},\tfrac25]$ of the integer quartic $q(t)=6000t^4-16040t^3+14600t^2-5080t+577$; and that minimum lies between $1.891152196075811250$ and $1.891152196075811251$.  So the published $1.89$ is true, and short of the truth by $1.152\ldots\times10^{-3}$.  The proof of the inequality is a twenty-five-box Bernstein certificate in exact integer arithmetic, with the certified coefficient arrays computed from the source's own density rather than stored.  The exact minimum needs neither a derivative nor any arithmetic in the quartic field: two divided differences turn it into polynomial identities and a handful of further rational positivity certificates, and one of those identities makes the resulting bracket for the minimum quadratically accurate, which is where the eighteen decimal places come from.  Every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Counting amplitude moduli: $\chi(\ket{H}^{\otimes m})\ge 4$ and $\chi(\ket{T}^{\otimes m})\ge 4$ for every $m\ge 31$
families.paper_abstract: The stabilizer rank $\chi(\psi)$ of an $n$-qubit state $\psi$ is the least number of stabilizer states whose complex span contains $\psi$.  For the two Clifford-inequivalent single-qubit magic-state orbits --- the octahedron-edge state $\ket{H}=\cos\frac{\pi}{8}\ket{0}+\sin\frac{\pi}{8}\ket{1}$ and the octahedron-face state $\ket{T}=\cos\beta\ket{0}+e^{i\pi/4}\sin\beta\ket{1}$, $\cos2\beta=1/\sqrt3$ --- we prove that $\chi(\ket{H}^{\otimes m})\ge4$ and $\chi(\ket{T}^{\otimes m})\ge4$ for every $m\ge31$.  The proof counts moduli.  Every amplitude of a stabilizer state is $0$ or $\gamma\, i^{e}$ for one fixed scale $\gamma$, so an amplitude of a state in the span of three stabilizer states is determined by a \emph{type} in a $5^{3}=125$-element set; multiplying all three symbols of a type by $i$ multiplies the amplitude by $i$ and leaves its modulus alone, so at most $(125-1)/4=31$ distinct nonzero moduli can occur.  The $m+1$ Hamming-weight classes of a magic state carry $m+1$ pairwise distinct moduli, and $32$ of them do not fit.  Both statements quantify over every finite set of stabilizer states: no dictionary of stabilizer states is enumerated, and no floating-point search enters.  For comparison, the published lower bounds carrying explicit constants first reach $4$ at $m=40$ for the $H$ orbit and at $m=148$ for the $T$ orbit; asymptotically they all dominate the count used here, and the improvement is in the constant, not the rate.  Every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4 by kernel reduction alone.

families.paper_title: Unextendible product bases of Pauli eigenstates: an orthogonality layer over total domination in $K_q^{\times n}$
families.paper_abstract: Call a set $S\subseteq[q]^{n}$ of words \emph{unextendible} if every word of $[q]^{n}$ disagrees with some member of $S$ in every coordinate.  The minimum size of such a set carries two names in two literatures that do not cite each other: it is the minimum skirting set $f(n,q)$ of Adriaensen, Ihringer, Martin and Villagr\'an, and it is the total domination number $\gamt(K_{q}^{\times n})$ of the direct power of a complete graph, studied since Meki\v{s} through Defant--Iyer and Vemuri.  Reading the six letters of $[6]$ as the six single-qubit Pauli eigenstates turns a word into a stabilizer product state, and a \emph{pairwise orthogonal} unextendible set into an unextendible product basis.  Neither literature imposes orthogonality, and the unextendible-product-basis literature never fixes the local alphabet; this paper works at that intersection.  We prove that the minimum size $\sstab(5)$ of a Pauli-eigenstate unextendible product basis on five qubits is exactly $6$, attained by an explicit six-state example in which every one of the six letters occurs exactly once at every coordinate --- it is the GenShifts basis of DiVincenzo, Mor, Shor, Smolin and Terhal with its two free local bases taken to be the $X$- and $Y$-eigenbases, and five is the largest number of qubits at which that specialisation is available --- and we prove $9\le\gamt(K_{6}^{\times 6})\le 10$, whose upper half improves the published bound $f(q,q)\le 2q-1$ at $q=6$.  Along the way we record, with their sources, the covering bounds that are already in print, give a short self-contained proof of $\gamt(K_{q}^{\times n})\ge n+3$ for $4\le q\le n$ (a bound implied by two published theorems), and separate $\sstab(n)$ from the unrestricted qubit minimum $f(n)$ for every $n\ge 6$ not divisible by $4$.  Every combinatorial statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: The Bessel constant behind the sharp Khinchin inequality\\ for Steinhaus sums at negative moments:\\ $\sup_{3\le t\le 12}\,3J_0(t)^2\,|J_1(t)|<\tfrac1{10}$, proved from the power series
families.paper_abstract: Rapaport, Tkocz and Wu (arXiv:2512.09077) determine the sharp constant $A_p$ in the Khinchin-type inequality $A_p\|S\|_2\le\|S\|_p$ for Steinhaus sums $S=\sum_j z_j\xi_j$ in the last open range $-1<p<0$.  The technical core of their proof, their Lemma~10, bounds $\int_0^\infty|J_0(t)|^3t^{p-1}\dd t$ for the Bessel function $J_0$ by splitting the integral at $t=1,3,12$, and two steps of that bound are asserted rather than proved: the constant $L=\sup_{3\le t\le 12}\bigl|\tfrac{d}{dt}|J_0(t)|^3\bigr|=\sup_{3\le t\le12}3J_0(t)^2|J_1(t)|$ is stated to be less than $0.1$ on the strength of a numerical check, and on $[1,3]$ the supremum of $|J_0|$ over a subinterval is stated to be attained at an endpoint on the strength of the shape of $|J_0|$.  We prove both statements from the power series of $J_0$ and $J_1$ in exact rational arithmetic.  The obstacle is that on $[3,12]$ the series cancels catastrophically, so neither interval evaluation of the truncated series nor a grid with a Lipschitz constant obtained from a bound on $|J_0|,|J_1|$ (which is what one is trying to prove) is available.  The classical monotonicity of the energy $J_0^2+J_1^2$, whose derivative is $-2J_1^2/t$, removes the circularity: one exact enclosure at the single point $t=3$ bounds $|J_0|$ and $|J_1|$ by $0.428$ on all of $[3,12]$, hence $|(3J_0^2J_1)'|\le0.79$ there, and a $289$-point dyadic grid of step $1/32$ closes the argument with $\sup_{[3,12]}3J_0^2|J_1|\le0.0805+0.79/64<0.093$.  The same certificate shows that $0.08$ is not an upper bound and that the bound fails at $t=1$, so the interval $[3,12]$ cannot be widened to $[1,12]$.  Every statement is checked by the kernel of the Lean~4 proof assistant over Mathlib, which contains no Bessel function; the numerical part is discharged by kernel evaluation over $\QQ$ with the three standard axioms only.  The third numerical step of the same proof, a six-node tangent-line table, is not treated here: it requires rigorous enclosures of $\Gamma$ and its logarithmic derivative, which we price.
