Kominers, *Prisoners, rooms, and light switches*, Electron. J. Combin. **28** (2021) #P1.27 (36 pp., open a

statements.label: Soundness of the winning certificate: a finite closed table of core states carrying a must-have-visited set and a rank with one progress label per rank value proves that a finite-memory profile is SAFE (no declaration is ever wrong, after any finite schedule prefix) and LIVE (every fair schedule reaches a declaration)

Soundness of the losing certificate: a lasso -- a finite schedule prefix reaching a core state c, plus a finite declaration-free cycle at c that plays every (prisoner, room) pair -- proves that the profile does NOT win, by exhibiting a fair schedule under which no declaration ever happens
Soundness of the unsafe-declaration certificate: a schedule prefix after which a prisoner declares although a named (prisoner, room) pair has not occurred proves the profile is not safe

Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.19488v1 formalized at r = 3,4,5,6: Alice's, Bob's, Charles' and Deborah's protocols (Algorithms 2-5) are a winning profile for n = 4 prisoners with q = 3 states, and the source's n = 3 and n = 2 adaptations win at r = 3

Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.19488v1 formalized at r = 4,5,6: Algorithms 2-4 together with two copies of Deborah-and-Eve's protocol (Algorithm 6) are a winning profile for n = 5 prisoners with q = 3 states

In the cell left open by Question D (n = 5, r = 3, q = 3) the source's own Algorithm 6 profile does not merely resist proof, it DEADLOCKS: there are exactly six reachable configurations in which all fifteen (prisoner, room) moves are self-loops, and a fair schedule parks the game in one of them for ever
Negative control (too-large claim): Theorem 4's four protocols do NOT win at r = 2, so the source's 'we may assume that r >= 3' restricts the protocol and not merely its proof

Negative control (too-small claim): truncating Deborah's protocol so that she declares one Repeat block early is UNSAFE -- there is a reachable schedule prefix after which she declares although a named prisoner has not visited a named room
Non-vacuity control: the certified winning profiles really do live in three switch states -- no reachable configuration puts a room in a state >= q

The obvious extension of Theorem 5 to six prisoners fails for a reason extra rooms cannot repair: Alice, Bob, Charles and THREE copies of Algorithm 6 are already UNSAFE at r = 3 and r = 4 (and, in C, at r = 5..8)

Bounded search in the open cell: no single-entry rewrite of Algorithm 6 wins at n = 5, r = 3, q = 3 -- all 3612 profiles obtained by changing one of the 42 table entries of Deborah's or Eve's copy (padded with three spare memory states) to any of the 43 alternatives lose, each with a refutation certificate

Cost of the open cell n = 5, r = q = 3: an exhaustive distance-2 sweep around Algorithm 6 (6,152,832 profiles, 4,727.6 CPU-s) and stochastic searches over Deborah's and Eve's tables found no winning profile; and the obvious search fitness was MEASURED to be broken, scoring the inert protocol best, so every earlier plateau was the do-nothing corner and not a near miss

Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.19488v1, and KK21's q = 2 loss, reproduced by exhaustion at a memory bound: over all 390,625 profiles in which each of two prisoners runs a protocol with at most two memory states, none wins with two switch states -- at r = 2 (the source's Theorem 1) and at r = 3 (KK21)

families.title: Walk posets of vertex-transitive graphs: the finite truncation obstruction Phi_H, the Petersen negative, and a new multiplicable instance at T(6)
families.description: **Source.** Ryunosuke Matsuoka, *A Non-Multiplicable Upho Poset Constructed from the Petersen Graph*, arXiv:2606.17549v3 (math.CO, 16 Jun 2026, revised 19 Jun 2026).

statements.label: The encoding: Matsuoka's Phi_H as a labelling problem, decidable, with the word form proved equivalent
Headline negative: Phi_4 of the Petersen walk poset is unsatisfiable, and Phi_3 is not
Infrastructure: a complete pruned depth-first search whose 'false' is a theorem
The positive engine: a rank-periodic transport model satisfies Phi_H at every height; the eight Cayley instances
Matsuoka's Theorem 4.1 reproved: L(Petersen) from one regular subgroup of Aut(L(Petersen) x K2), not a Z3 table
New: every truncation of the walk poset of T(6) = L(K6) = J(6,2) is satisfiable -- an instance of Matsuoka's open Question 4.9
Negative controls, including the calibration that a satisfiable truncation proves nothing
The catalogue: sixteen graphs identified, with rank sequences and vertex-transitivity witnesses
Two-fold automorphisms: the group `Γ` of the dodecahedron is exactly the automorphism group of its distance-2 graph, and has 240 elements
The dodecahedron has no twisted regular representation — the finite obstruction that decides its cell
Corollaries: the positive engine is dead at the dodecahedron at every period, and the dodecahedron is not a Cayley graph
Every Cayley graph's walk poset is multiplicable — Matsuoka Example 3.6, and the non-vacuity control for Order.Mult
The walk poset as a poset: WP, its order, Matsuoka's multiplicable, and the additivity of the rank
The criterion as a graph-generic pair of complete searches, with both prunes proved
The bridge: a multiplication on the walk poset forces a twisted regular representation
P(Dodecahedron, v₀) is not multiplicable, and Remark 3.10 provably cannot say so
Four more catalogue cells decided about the poset: Petersen, T(5), KG(6,2), Coxeter are not multiplicable
The control that the criterion is not non-Cayleyness: L(Petersen) carries a twisted regular representation ten of whose fifteen rows are not automorphisms
P(T(6),v₀) and P(L(Petersen),v₀) are multiplicable — the positive engine upgraded from Φ_H to a monoid

families.paper_title: Multiplicable walk posets: a two-fold automorphism criterion, the dodecahedron, and the triangular graph $T(6)$
families.paper_abstract: The \emph{walk poset} $\Pw$ of a finite graph $G$ with base point $\vo$ has as elements the pairs $(v,m)$ joined to $\vo$ by a walk of length $m$, ordered by the existence of a walk realising the rank difference.  For vertex-transitive $G$ it is a finite-type $\NN$-graded upho poset, and Matsuoka used it to refute the conjecture of Fu, Peng and Zhang that every finitary upho poset is \emph{multiplicable}: $P(\text{Petersen},\vo)$ is not.  He then asked for which finite vertex-transitive graphs $\Pw$ is multiplicable. Matsuoka's negative machinery rests on a spectral rigidity lemma, which forces every pair of bijections $(\varphi,\psi)$ with $u\sim w \iff \varphi u\sim\psi w$ to be diagonal and therefore applies only to graphs whose spectrum contains no pair $\pm\lambda$.  We remove that hypothesis.  Our main theorem shows that a multiplication on $\Pw$ produces a \emph{twisted regular representation}: a regular section of the group $\Gr$ of two-fold automorphisms of $G$ whose partner family is conjugate back into it.  Only symmetry of the adjacency relation, twin-freeness, and stabilisation of the rank sets are used---neither vertex-transitivity nor connectivity.  Since a twisted regular representation is a finite object, non-multiplicability becomes decidable by a finite search whose completeness is proved rather than assumed.  We apply this to the dodecahedron, where $\Gr$ has $240$ elements against $|\Aut| = 120$: $P(\text{Dodecahedron},\vo)$ is not multiplicable, and it is a cell that Matsuoka's spectral criterion provably cannot reach, the adjacency matrix being singular.  On the positive side we show that $P(T(6),\vo)$ is multiplicable for the triangular graph $T(6)=L(K_6)=J(6,2)$, which is neither a Cayley graph nor spectrally accessible, and we reprove Matsuoka's positive result for $L(\text{Petersen})$ from a single regular subgroup instead of a solver-found table.  Fifteen of the sixteen graphs of a reference catalogue are thereby decided.  Every statement is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.title: Wastlund's zero-free disk conjecture at k = 4: the first open case of arXiv:2602.07563, closed for the explicit numerator by an effective Janson comparison plus a 235-cell certificate table
families.description: `K_{m,n}` carries `mn` independent mean-one exponential edge costs. For `k ≤ min(m,n)`, `C_{k,m,n}` is the minimum total cost of a `k`-matching (a set of `k` pairwise vertex-disjoint edges); `C_{n,n,n}` is the random assignment problem. Wästlund (arXiv:2602.07563v1, math.PR, 7 Feb 2026) studies the moment generating function

statements.label: Dominance lemma over the complex numbers: if sum_j |b_j| R^j < |p0| prod_i (1 - R/|rho_i|) then p0 prod_i (1 - t/rho_i) + B has no zero on the CLOSED disk |t| <= R; the comparison factors are given as rational linear factors and conjugate-pair quadratics 1 - b t + a t^2 with the side conditions b^2 <= 4a, a <= u^2, uR < 1

Wastlund's P:zeroFree3 re-proved from the same dominance lemma: Phat_{3,m,n} has no zero on the closed disk |t| <= mn/3 for all real m, n >= 3, kernel-clean

Sharpness at the worst cell: Phat_{4,4,4} has a real zero strictly between 43/10 and 431/100, while the conjectured radius there is mn/4 = 4, so the closed-disk radius cannot be widened past 1.0776 mn/4 at k = 4; and the (4,4) certificate itself fails when the radius is widened by 10%

The E-coefficient closed forms at k = 4, derived by running the source's recursion with m and n both symbolic in exact Q(m,n): E = Phat_4 - D_3 has e0 = e1 = e6 = 0, each Delta*e_j is an integer polynomial symmetric in m<->n of bidegree (7,7), (6,6), (5,5), (4,4), and e5 = 22 / prod_{i+j<3} (m-i)(n-j)

Conjecture C:zeroFree of arXiv:2602.07563v1 holds for k = 4: identifying Phat_4 with the numerator of the moment generating function F_{4,m,n} (the source's T:matchingRecursion and P:polynomialDegrees) turns WZ2 into the conjecture's first open case

Two printing errata in the source's proof of P:zeroFree3: both cubic coefficients are printed +2t^3 and should be -2t^3, and the printed P/Q equals F divided by mn(m-1)(n-1)(m-2)(n-2); the proposition and its proof are unaffected

Measured degradation of the Janson comparison for k >= 5: the dominance ratio sum_j |e_j| R^j / D_{k-1}(R) at (m,n) = (k,k) is 87.3, 1.013e5, 7.143e8, 3.531e13 for k = 4,5,6,7, decaying like 1/n along a strip, which gives k = 5 a residual box of about 7e4 ordered cells and prices it at >= 10 CPU-h and ~85 MB of certificates -- parked

tailOK is exactly the positivity region of W on the integer quadrant: for all integers m, n >= 4, 0 < W(m,n) if and only if tailOK m n. Equivalently the Janson comparison fails at EVERY one of the 235 residual pairs, not only at (4,4); the residual set has exactly 235 members with row profile (58,28,18,13,10,8,7) for m = 4..10

The k = 4 tail is a real staircase, not seven integer strips: for each a in 4..10 the two-variable shift W(a + u, n0(a) + v) has all 121 coefficients >= 0 with positive constant term, so W > 0 on the whole real quadrant [a, inf) x [n0(a), inf) and its transpose; the union of the fourteen quadrants contains the entire integer tail region tailOK (the quadrant m, n >= 11 included, as it sits inside [10,inf) x [11,inf)), and each corner is sharp in both coordinates

Wastlund's P:zeroFree3 for real parameters: Phat_{3,m,n} has no zero on the closed disk |t| <= mn/3 for all REAL m, n >= 3, proved from a real-coefficient dominance lemma lemD_real; identified with the rational statement WZ5 by phat3R_qcast, phat3R (m:R) (n:R) z = cev (phat3 m n) z

The k = 4 zero-free closed disk for REAL parameters: Phat_{4,m,n} has no complex zero with |t| <= mn/4 for all real (m,n) in the staircase region of WZ13 -- in particular for all real m, n >= 11 and for all real m >= 4, n >= 62 -- identified with the integer/rational statement WZ2 by phat4R_qcast, phat4R (m:R) (n:R) z = cev (phat4 m n) z

families.paper_title: The zero-free disk conjecture for bipartite matching at $k=4$:\\ an effective Janson comparison and a finite certificate table
families.paper_abstract: Let the $mn$ edges of $K_{m,n}$ carry independent mean-one exponential costs and let $C_{k,m,n}$ be the minimum cost of a $k$-matching.  \Wa{} showed that the moment generating function $F_{k,m,n}(t)=\E e^{tC_{k,m,n}}$ is a rational function of $t$ whose first pole sits at $t=mn/k$, and conjectured that it has no complex zero in the open disk $|t|<mn/k$; the conjecture would give a Gaussian scaling limit for the random assignment problem.  He proved it for $k\le3$ by comparison with a real-rooted function of Janson, remarked that there ``seems to be no hope of generalizing this argument to higher values of $k$'', and proved --- non-effectively, with no bound on the exceptions --- that for each $k$ only finitely many pairs $(m,n)$ can fail.  We settle the first open case, $k=4$, for the explicit numerator: for all integers $m,n\ge4$ the degree-six polynomial $\Ph_{4,m,n}$ has no zero in the \emph{closed} disk $|t|\le mn/4$.  Modulo \Wa's identification of $\Ph_{4,m,n}$ with the numerator of $F_{4,m,n}$, which we quote from his paper and do not reprove, this is his conjecture at $k=4$.  The proof makes his own comparison effective.  We compute the discrepancy $E=\Ph_4-D_3$ between the numerator and Janson's in closed form over $\QQ(m,n)$ --- four coefficients, one of them the clean $e_5=22\big/\prod_{i+j<3}(m-i)(n-j)$ --- and reduce the comparison to the positivity of an explicit integer polynomial $W$ of bidegree $(10,10)$.  We then determine the positivity region of $W$ exactly.  On the integer quadrant it is precisely the region the comparison covers, so the comparison fails at every one of the $235$ residual pairs and at no other pair; each of those pairs is closed instead by an exactly verified dominance certificate, and the failure region of the comparison and the certificate table coincide.  Over the reals the region the certificates cover is a staircase of fourteen closed quadrants, no corner of which can be moved inwards inside the domain $m,n\ge4$, and on it the zero-free disk holds for real parameters --- in particular for all real $m,n\ge11$ and all real $m\ge4$, $n\ge62$, real parameters being the generality in which \Wa{} states his own $k\le3$ result. The radius is close to sharp: $\Ph_{4,4,4}$ has a real zero below $1.0776\cdot mn/4$, so the statement has about $7.5\ of slack at its tightest pair.  The results below are machine-checked in Lean~4; the last section says exactly what that covers and what it does not.

statements.label: There are at least 95 weakly contractible non-contractible finite T_0-spaces on eleven points: 95 explicit posets on Fin 11, each with no up-beat and no down-beat point (hence a minimal finite space, hence non-contractible by Stong) and each carrying a checked elementary-collapse sequence taking its order complex to a single vertex (hence weakly contractible by McCord + Whitehead)

The number of minimal finite spaces (beat-point-free posets) on n points is 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 11, 36, 160, 954, 7929, 92092, 1493102 for n = 1..12; the number in which every element covers 0 or >= 2 elements is 1, 1, 2, 4, 11, 38, 173, 1056, 8772, 99391, 1529466, 31696602; and the number of weakly contractible non-contractible ones is 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 10, 95, 792 for n = 1..12. None of the three sequences is in OEIS

families.paper_title: Weakly contractible non-contractible finite $T_0$-spaces on eleven points: the classification, and where height three begins
families.paper_abstract: A finite $T_0$-space is weakly contractible but not contractible when it has no beat points (so it is its own core, and is not contractible by Stong's theorem) and its order complex is contractible (so it is weakly contractible by McCord's theorem). Cianci and Ottina showed that the smallest such spaces have nine points and that there are exactly two of them; Das and Mawiong classified the ten-point case, finding ten spaces, all of height two with an antichain of middle elements, and asked whether this uniformity persists at larger cardinalities.  We exhibit 95 such spaces on eleven points and show that the uniformity breaks exactly there: 17 of the 95 have height three and a middle set that is not an antichain, and the number of middle elements reaches six.  On twelve points we exhibit fourteen spaces with seven middle elements and only two minimal or only two maximal elements.  Each exhibited space is certified in the Lean~4 kernel twice over: it has no up-beat and no down-beat point, and an explicit sequence of elementary collapses takes its order complex to a vertex.  An exhaustive census of the $46{,}749{,}427$ posets on eleven points (and of the $31{,}696{,}602$ twelve-point posets in which every element covers zero or at least two elements), reported separately from the certified part, says that the 95 are all of them, and that there are exactly 792 such spaces on twelve points.  Every order complex encountered is collapsible, so the classification does not depend on the freeness of fundamental groups of small finite spaces.

families.title: The enumeration table of rectangular weighing designs W(m,z,k): the starred cells settled exactly, and four printed values corrected
families.description: A **weighing design** `W(m, z, k)` is, in the sense of arXiv:2608.04814v1 §2 (verbatim), "a matrix of size `m × z` with entries from `{0, ±1}`, in which each column contains exactly `k` non-zero entries and **each row contains at most `m − k` zeros**"; its columns are mutually orthogonal, `WᵀW = k I_z`. families.paper_title: The enumeration table of rectangular weighing designs $\W{m}{z}{k}$:\\ the starred cells settled exactly, and four printed values corrected
families.paper_abstract: A weighing design $\W{m}{z}{k}$ in the sense of Lejeune Herman and Goos (arXiv:2608.04814) is an $m\times z$ matrix over $\{0,\pm1\}$ with exactly $k$ non-zero entries in every column, at most $m-k$ zeros in every row, and $W^{\mathsf T}W=kI_z$. Their Table~1 counts the isomorphism classes (row and column permutations, row and column sign changes) for $4\le m\le24$ with two zeros per column when $m$ is even and three when $m$ is odd; the entries marked $\star$ were obtained by a partial enumeration and are lower bounds.  We re-enumerate the whole table by canonical augmentation with a canonical form in place of the pairwise isomorphism tests of the source, at a total cost of $2.8$ processor-hours against the $9.6$ days the source reports for one extension step.  Of the $111$ completely enumerated cells, $106$ reproduce exactly.  The other five are corrections: the cell $\cell53$ holds one class, not three; the $m=23$ row is $5,22,119$ at $z=3,4,5$, not $2,4,59$, and it does not terminate at $z=5$ but continues with $459$ and $1834$ classes at $z=6,7$; and $\cell{24}{4}$ holds $77$ classes, not $72$.  All $25$ starred cells of the rows $m=16$ and $m=18$ and of the cells $z\le7$ ($m=20$), $z\le6$ ($m=22$), $z=5$ ($m=24$) are settled exactly; every exact value exceeds the printed bound, by a factor of up to $1806$, and the $m=18$ row runs four columns further than the table prints.  Two of the exact values --- at the square cells $\cell{16}{16}$ and, past the printed row, $\cell{18}{18}$, which are the classical $W(16,14)$ and $W(18,16)$ --- agree with counts announced by Lampio and Ganzhinov in $2025$ and are replications; for the rest we found no prior enumeration.  For $26$ cells a refuting statement is verified in Lean~4: an explicit list of designs, each checked against the definition, pairwise separated by a proved isomorphism invariant, and longer than the printed entry --- at $\cell{23}6$ and $\cell{23}7$, where the table prints nothing, the list refutes the termination mark instead; at $\cell53$ the exhaustive half is verified as well.

families.paper_title: First-order model counting over a linear order with the successor relation of another linear order: closed forms for two benchmark sentences
families.paper_abstract: T\'oth, Kuang, Zou, K\r{u}la, Wang, Wang and Ku\v{z}elka (arXiv:2608.10877) study weighted first-order model counting over a domain carrying a linear order $\le$ together with a relation $S$ constrained to be the successor relation of a second linear order.  Among their five benchmark sentences, three are identified with entries of the OEIS; for the remaining two, $\Phi_5$ and $\Phi_6$, the paper reports ``no matching entry in the OEIS'' and gives no formula.  With $\le$ fixed to the standard order of $[n]$ and $S$ ranging over all $n!$ successor relations---the convention under which the paper's own identifications are stated---we show that $\FOMC(\Phi_5,n) = 2\,(n-1)!\,(n+1)\,(2^n-1)$ and that \[ \FOMC(\Phi_6,n) \;=\; (n-1)!\sum_{m=0}^{n} 2^{m(m-1)}\,(2^m+1)^{\,n-m}\,\bigl(m + n\,2^m\bigr), \] a formula with $n+1$ terms in place of a search over $n!\,4^n\,2^{n^2}$ structures.  The first sequence is twice a shift of OEIS entry A052840, whose formula line has carried the equivalent expression since 2019, so the $\Phi_5$ formula is not new mathematics; the $\Phi_6$ formula and its first values $5, 63, 4190, 1804770, 4298378184$ appear to be unrecorded.  Both formulas, the first values, the faithfulness of the encoding of the successor axiom, and a set of negative controls are machine-checked in Lean~4.

The `s = 0` row is Erdős–Ko–Rado: `IsSWitnessFamily d 0` is "uniform and intersecting", so `W_{d,0}(n) = binom(n-1,d)` for `n ≥ 2(d+1)` — and the two edges of the table do not squeeze its interior

The `s = d-1` fibres, exactly: a fibre of the trace map is an intersecting family of `2`-sets, so at most `max(n-d,3)` members and `n-d` is attained — giving `W_{d,d-1}(n) ≤ max(n-d,3)·binom(n,d-1)` at every `n`, which first beats the trivial bound at `n = d²+2d` and brackets `W_{2,1}(9)` in `[28,63]`

The `s = d-1` column has no `binom(n-1,d)` bound, the fibre route's ceiling is exactly `d·binom(n-1,d)`, and the extremal family at `(8,3,2)` is not a star — arXiv:2602.17459's non-star construction, kernel-verified

families.paper_title: The thin problem for uniform witnesses: $\W_{3,2}(8)=\bin{7}{3}$ and $\W_{5,3}(12)>\bin{11}{5}$
families.paper_abstract: A family $\cF$ of $(d+1)$-element subsets of $[n]$ is an \emph{$s$-witness family} if every member $F$ carries a set $B_F\subseteq F$ with $|B_F|=s$ that no member of the family cuts out of $F$, i.e.\ $F\cap F'\neq B_F$ for all $F'\in\cF$; $\W_{d,s}(n)$ denotes the largest size of such a family.  Chao, Xu, Yip and Zhang conjectured $\W_{d,s}(n)\le\bin{n-1}{d}$ for $n\ge 2(d+1)$ and $0\le s\le d$, and in June~2026 Xu disproved it for $d\ge4$ and $\lceil (d+2)/2\rceil\le s\le d-1$, leaving open exactly one shape: whether $\W_{2s-1,s}(n)>\bin{n-1}{2s-1}$ can hold for a fixed $s\ge2$ and infinitely many $n$.  We settle the first in-range cell of each of the first two branches of that question, and they disagree. At $s=2$ the inequality fails at its first in-range $n$: $\W_{3,2}(8)=35=\bin73$, the star being optimal.  At $s=3$ it holds: $\W_{5,3}(12)\ge471>462=\bin{11}{5}$, exhibited by a family with no point common to all its members.  The latter is in particular a counterexample to the conjecture at a parameter set the published disproof does not reach.  Around these we give the first table of $\W_{d,s}(n)$ --- all $48$ cells with $n\le7$, all $27$ with $n=8$, and $36$ of the $44$ with $n=9$ --- prove that the whole space $\bin{[n]}{d+1}$ is an $s$-witness family exactly when $n+s<2(d+1)$, close the two edges $s=0$ and $s=d$ of the table by argument at every $n$, bound the column $s=d-1$ through the fibres of the trace map, and show that the colouring certificate an exact maximum-clique solver emits can never close the next open cell $\W_{3,2}(9)$.  Every statement below is machine-checked in Lean~4 except the exhaustive computations, which are named as such.

At g = 2 these are the source's own Remark (C(0^6,10) < C(4) and C(2^3) < C(0,0,6)); the genus-14 pair C(0^6,46) < C(40) and C(2^{39}) < C(0,0,42) is computed here and shows the hypothesis is not an artefact of small genus.

Negative control, a too-small claim refuted: neither bound of Conjecture 1 can be narrowed. Replacing C(3g-2) by the next value up, or C(2^{3g-3}) by the next value down, breaks the statement already at g = 3 -- C(7) < C(2,6) and C(2,2,2,2,3) < C(2^6). The uniqueness of the two extremisers, asserted at every genus in WN4 and WN5-WN10, is the same statement in general.

Negative control, a natural strengthening refuted: C is monotone in NEITHER direction of the dominance order on lambda = d - 1. lambda = (4,2) dominates (3,3) yet C(3,5) > C(4,4), while the global minimum sits at the dominance-largest partition (3g-3) and the global maximum at the dominance-smallest 1^{3g-3} (C(7) < C(2^6) at g = 3). So dominance is not the order behind Conjecture 1; refinement, a proper suborder of reverse dominance, is.

The dilaton reduction: because C(1,d) = C(d) exactly (the source's Eq. (32)) and a part d_j = 1 contributes 0 to sum_j (d_j - 1), deleting all the 1s preserves the genus and, for g >= 2, leaves a non-empty tuple with all parts >= 2. Hence Conjecture 1 for d_j >= 1 is EQUIVALENT, genus by genus, to Conjecture 1 for primitive d -- so the source's primitive checks at g <= 13, and rows WN5-WN10 here, already carry the full d_j >= 1 statement at those genera.

families.paper_title: Refinement monotonicity of normalized Witten intersection numbers,\\ and the nesting conjecture at genus $14$--$18$
families.paper_abstract: Guo, Yang and Zagier (arXiv:2603.15233) normalise Witten's $\psi$-class intersection numbers as $C(\dd)=2^{2g}\prod_j(2d_j+1)!!\,/\,(3^{2g-2+n}(2g-3+n)!)\int_{\Mbar_{g,n}}\psi_1^{d_1}\cdots\psi_n^{d_n}$ and conjecture (their Conjecture~1) that for $g\ge2$ and $d_1,\dots,d_n\ge1$ of genus $g$ one has $C(3g-2)\le C(\dd)\le C(2^{3g-3})$.  Their Lemma~2 proves the lower inequality, and they report the upper one checked for $d_j\ge2$ and $g\le13$.  We verify the upper inequality, in exact rational arithmetic and over the complete set of tuples with all $d_j\ge2$, at genus $14$ to $18$ ($560\,709$ further tuples), with $2^{3g-3}$ the unique maximiser at each genus.  We then observe a stronger statement that the source does not make: indexing the tuples of genus $g$ with all $d_j\ge2$ by the partitions $\lambda=\dd-1$ of $3g-3$, the value $C$ increases strictly whenever one part of $\lambda$ is split into two.  We verify this at every genus $2\le g\le18$, over $11\,514\,074$ single-split steps.  Since $(3g-3)$ and $1^{3g-3}$ are the two extremes of the refinement order, refinement monotonicity implies the nesting inequalities, with strict inequalities off the extremes and uniqueness of both extremisers; and it is the only one of the natural orders left standing, since the length-then-lexicographic order of Guo, Norbury, Yang and Zagier, weak monotonicity in the length, and the dominance order all fail for these numbers, by examples printed in the source or read off its Table~1.  All values are computed through the Dijkgraaf--Verlinde--Verlinde recursion in an integer normalisation, controlled against the one-point formula, Zograf's two-point formula and the dilaton relation, and the whole check is verified in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Explicit kernel elements for multiplication by a general linear form\\ on $\kk[x_1,\dots,x_m]/(x_1^2,\dots,x_m^2,e^2)$,\\ and spanning sets for the kernel on the lines $m=3d-3-k$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\kk$ have characteristic zero, let $E=\kk[x_1,\dots,x_m]/(x_1^2,\dots,x_m^2)$, let $e=x_1+\dots+x_m$, and let $A=E/(e^2)$, so that $A_j=E_j/e^2E_{j-2}$.  Crispin Qui\~nonez, Lundqvist and Nenashev conjectured that the Hilbert function of $\kk[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(x_1^2,\dots,x_n^2,\ell_1^2,\ell_2^2)$, for general linear forms $\ell_1,\ell_2$, is a lattice-path count $a(n,d)$; Booth, Singh and Vraciu translated the conjecture at $(n,d)$ into the assertion $\dim\ker\varphi_{n+1,d}=\Dl(n,d)$, where $\varphi_{m,d}\colon A_{d-1}\to A_d$ is multiplication by a general linear form and $\Dl$ is the excess of $a$ over its binomial approximation, and they exhibited exactly one element of that kernel.  Boij and Lundqvist have since proved the conjecture for all $n$ and all degrees, by a Hilbert-series computation that produces no element of the kernel at all. The dimension is therefore known; the elements are not.  We construct them.  For every subset $L_0\subseteq[m]$ of size $k$ and every integer $s\ge0$ we write down a pair $\Rel{L_0}{s}\in E_{d-1}$, $\Cel{L_0}{s}\in E_{d-2}$ with $L\cdot\Rel{L_0}{s}=e^2\cdot\Cel{L_0}{s}$ identically in $\ZZ[a_1,\dots,a_m]$, so that $\Rel{L_0}{s}$ lies in $\ker\varphi_{m,d}$ for a general linear form $L=\sum a_ix_i$; the member $k=0$, $s=m-2d+2$ is the element of Booth, Singh and Vraciu, and the range of validity is sharp at its lower end.  On the diagonal line $m=3d-3-k$, where the parameter $s=d-1-k$ is forced, the resulting $\binom{m}{k}$ elements span the \emph{whole} of $\ker\varphi_{m,d}$; we prove this at eight parameter sets on the lines $k=0,1,2,3$, and in particular the $m$ elements attached to the singletons span the $n$-dimensional kernel on the line $n=3d-5$, for $d=3,4,5,6$ --- the case Booth, Singh and Vraciu named as the next one.  The identities are verified as polynomial identities over $\ZZ[a]$, and the independence at one integer specialisation --- an asymmetry forced by the problem, since a rank at a point bounds the generic rank only from below.  We record why no single numerical specialisation can decide the conjecture in either direction, and one transcription correction to the literature.  Every computation reported below is machine-checked in Lean~4; the two places where such a computation is combined with a published upper bound to give an equality are marked as such.

families.paper_title: The borderline case of the Migliore--Mir\'o-Roig--Nagel conjecture\\ for level monomial almost complete intersections:\\ complete integer eliminations up to $a=13$
families.paper_abstract: Let $\kk$ have characteristic zero, let $R=\kk[x,y,z]$, and let $I$ be generated by $x^{a_1+t}$, $y^{a_2+t}$, $z^{a_3+t}$ and $x^{a_1}y^{a_2}z^{a_3}$, so that $R/I$ is a level monomial almost complete intersection.  Migliore, Mir\'o-Roig and Nagel conjectured a characterisation of when such an algebra fails the weak Lefschetz property; in the form Cook and Nagel restated it, failure occurs --- apart from the two quadruples $(2,9,13,9)$ and $(3,7,14,9)$, which are exceptions --- exactly when $t$ is even, $a_1+a_2+a_3$ is odd and $a_1,a_2,a_3$ are not all distinct.  One implication is a theorem and the other is open.  Booth and Vraciu reduce the first unresolved value $t=(a_1+a_2+a_3)/3+1$ to the integer zeros of an explicit polynomial $\Fg_a(a_1,a_2)$, where $a$ is defined by $a_3=2(a_1+a_2)-3a$.  They settle $a\le3$, report a \textsl{Macaulay2} verification for $a\le6$ under the extra hypothesis $a_1\ge a$, and stop: for $a\ge7$, ``the list of values that need to be checked is too large to be practical.''  We determine the zero set of $\Fg_a$ on the admissible region $0<a_1\le a_2\le a_3$ completely, for $2\le a\le13$ and in both regimes.  In the regime $a\le a_1$ the zeros are the diagonal $a_1=a_2$ for odd $a$ and none for even $a$, apart from the single triple $(3,7,14)$ at $a=2$; the levels $7\le a\le13$ are new.  In the regime $a_1=r<a$ --- which the published \textsl{Macaulay2} code excludes by construction --- the zeros are $a_2=a_3=3a-2r$ for odd $r$ and none for even $r$, apart from the single triple $(2,9,13)$ at $a=3$; this is new for $4\le a\le13$, and all $78$ pairs $(a,r)$ are settled without any appeal to compiled evaluation.  The two exceptions are exactly the two quadruples the conjecture already excepts, and every remaining zero is a triple on which failure of the weak Lefschetz property is already a theorem: no analogue of the exceptional quadruples appears at any level above $a=3$ in this range.  Granting Booth and Vraciu's reduction, the conjecture therefore holds at $t=(a_1+a_2+a_3)/3+1$ for every admissible triple with $2\le a\le13$, and no exceptional quadruple beyond the two known ones occurs at that $t$ in that range.  Up to $a=8$ the method replaces divisor lists by a scan reaching only $\sqrt{N(a)}$ together with one modulus certificate per surviving value of $S=a_1+a_2$; past $a=8$ the scan is itself the obstruction --- it would need $1.5\cdot10^{10}$ trial divisions at $a=12$ --- and is replaced by a divisor list \emph{built} from the factorisation of $N(a)$, with each certificate evaluated at $S$ reduced modulo its own modulus.  Two small corrections to the source are recorded.  Every theorem below about the polynomials $\Fg_a$ is machine-checked in Lean~4; the consequence for the conjecture, being a statement about Lefschetz properties, is not.

families.paper_title: The minimal truncation weight of a block-staggered\\ Haar-doped Clifford circuit:\\ Table~I of Kim, Kim and Lee recomputed with explicit return cycles,\\ corrected at $k=7$, and extended to $k=9$
families.paper_abstract: Kim, Kim and Lee (arXiv:2602.03234) bound the Liouvillian gap of a dissipative Floquet circuit --- a two-layer brickwork of the fixed Clifford gate $u=\iSWAP\,(H\otimes H)$, doped with Haar-random single-qubit rotations on every $(k+1)$-st site and followed by on-site depolarization --- by the least Pauli-weight cutoff $\wstar(k)$ at which the weight-truncated Floquet dynamics still carries a return cycle of localized Pauli strings.  A smaller $\wstar$ is a sharper, system-size-independent upper bound on the gap at doping density $1/(k+1)$.  Their Table~I prints $\wstar(k)=2,5,5,7,8,7,9,11$ for $k=1,\dots,8$.  The truncated dynamics is a finite directed graph on Pauli strings, so every cell is an exact combinatorial fact.  We recompute the table from the gate alone. Seven cells reproduce; the eighth does not: $\wstar(7)=8$, not $9$, witnessed by the weight-$8$ cycle $\str{XXYZYYIXZ}\to\str{YZYXXZYIX}\to\str{ZIYXZXYXY}\to\str{XZIYYXYXZ}\to$ back, which the paper's contiguous-support seeding cannot find.  We add the first cell past the table, $\wstar(9)=11$, so the sequence reads $2,5,5,7,8,7,8,11,11$: still non-monotone and still at most linear in $k$.  Every upper bound $\wstar(k)\le v$ is an explicit return cycle on a periodic chain, checked by evaluation inside Lean~4 with no axiom beyond propositional extensionality; every matching lower bound is an exhaustive search over all strings of weight $<v$ confined to a stated span, so each equality asserted here is a computation within that span, not a formal theorem.  We also show that the $k=4$ representative cycle printed in the paper's Appendix~G does not close (one doped-site label is wrong, and one label change repairs it), that Section~III\,A's depolarizing factor $e^{-2\gamma\wt}$ contradicts the paper's own Appendix~A ($e^{-\gamma\wt}$), and that the $N$-independence of $\wstar$ reported there is a consequence of its definition.  \emph{Added in version~2.}  The same finite object carries a second invariant that the paper never names but prints implicitly: the \emph{support width} $\sstar(k)$, the least number of consecutive sites inside which every string of some return cycle fits.  We determine it exactly for $k\le9$ --- $3,5,5,7,9,9,9,13,13$ --- and observe that for $k=2,\dots,8$ these are precisely the widths of the representative strings of Appendix~G, so those seven values are the paper's own data; new are their minimality, the two cells $\sstar(1)=3$ and $\sstar(9)=13$, and the fact that for every $k\le9$ one cycle attains $\wstar(k)$ and $\sstar(k)$ simultaneously.  Unlike $\wstar$, the measured $\sstar$ is non-decreasing, and it jumps exactly where Table~I stops: an exhaustive sweep with no weight cutoff at all finds no return cycle inside $14$ consecutive sites for any $k\in\{10,11,12,13\}$ (nor inside $15$ for $k=11,13$), which is the wall the enumeration the paper describes meets at $k=10$.  Past the wall we use a SAT encoding of the cycle condition on a ring: it yields a kernel-checked $13$-step return cycle at cutoff $19$ on $26$ qubits for $k=12$, which we verify lifts to a localized cycle on the chain ($\wstar(12)\le19$, $\sstar(12)\le21$, neither claimed tight), and an $11$-step return cycle at cutoff $12$ on $22$ qubits for $k=10$, which we show does \emph{not} lift --- it wraps the ring --- so that $\wstar(10)$ remains open.  The periodic-chain certificate for $\wstar(5)\le8$, missing in version~1, is supplied.  \emph{Added in version~3.}  The $k=10$ cell is settled from above.  Re-running the propositional search under a localization constraint that is actually sufficient --- one window of $18=n-4$ sites whose position advances by two sites per Floquet step; a fixed window is sufficient but empty, because the localized cycles exhibited here translate --- returns an $11$-step return cycle at cutoff $14$ on $22$ qubits, and this one does lift to the chain: cut at its unique long run of identities it drives the chain for all $11$ steps with support width $17$ at every step and closes as an exact translate by $22=2k+2$ sites, the rule the paper's Table~III states for even $k$.  Hence $\wstar(10)\le14$ and $\sstar(10)\le17$ --- the ring cycle and its width kernel-checked, the lift a computation --- so that the corrected and extended sequence reads $2,5,5,7,8,7,8,11,11,\le14$ and, with the wall of version~2, $\sstar(10)\in\{15,16,17\}$. The same search was reported unsatisfiable at cutoffs $12$ and $13$ by one solver run that we attribute and have not reproduced; it constrains only cycles of length $11$ inside such a window, so $\wstar(10)=14$ is not claimed and no lower bound on $\wstar(10)$ is asserted here.

families.title: Minimum depth of open-boundary Yang-Baxter integrable quantum circuits: the exact formula ceil((N+1)/(min(k,N-k)+1)) and the refutation of arXiv:2607.02093 Conjectures 1 and 2
families.description: **Source.** *Open-boundary integrable quantum circuits with different geometries*, [arXiv:2607.02093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02093) **v1** (submitted 2 Jul 2026, single version as of 2026-09-07; primary **math-ph**, cross-listed cond-mat.stat-mech, hep-th, nlin.SI, quant-ph). All section, equation and figure numbers below are read off the **compiled PDF** of v1 (`arxiv.org/pdf/2607.02093v1`), not the raw LaTeX.

statements.label: Circuit depth is the height of the heap of pieces and equals the minimum number of gate layers: the ASAP fold is a layering of the word, and no layering uses fewer layers. Kernel-clean, no native_decide.

Exhaustive minimum circuit depth over all 2^N placements n-vec in {1,...,N}, for 2 <= N <= 10 and every kappa_-; agrees with the source's Conjecture 1 on all odd N <= 9 and with Conjecture 2 for N = 2, 4, 6.
Exhaustive minimum circuit depth for 11 <= N <= 16 over all 2^N placements, equal to ceil((N+1)/(min(kappa_-, N-kappa_-)+1)) at every kappa_-.
Exhaustive minimum circuit depth for 17 <= N <= 19 (2^19 = 524288 placements at N = 19), equal to the same closed form.

Conjecture 1 of arXiv:2607.02093v1 (odd N, d = (N+3)/2 - kappa_-) is FALSE. First counterexample N = 11, kappa_- = 2, n-vec = (8,4), depth 4 against the conjectured 5, with its explicit four-layer schedule and the exhaustive proof that three layers are impossible; the failure recurs at every odd N in 11..19.

Conjecture 2 of arXiv:2607.02093v1 (even N, d = (N+4)/2 - kappa_-) is FALSE. First counterexample N = 8, kappa_- = 2, n-vec = (6,3), depth 3 against the conjectured 4 -- inside the range N = 2,...,10 the source names -- with its explicit three-layer schedule; the failure recurs at every even N in 8..18.

For the (+kappa, rho) circuits the minimum depth over all 2^(N-1) placements n-vec^rho in {1,...,N-1} is exactly N+1, for every 3 <= N <= 20; this settles exhaustively the three sizes N = 11, 13, 15 for which the source sampled only.

An explicit placement attaining ceil((N+1)/(min(kappa_-, N-kappa_-)+1)) for every N <= 120 and every kappa_- <= N: kappa_-+1 staircases with gap profile (g_0,...,g_{kappa_--1}, d-2), replacing the source's Eqs. (61) and (63).

Controls for the model and the sweeps: every (kappa,-kappa) word has exactly N+1 gates; the maximum depth is N+1; the sign-flip duality kappa_- <-> N-kappa_- holds configuration by configuration; the kappa_- = 0 staircase has depth N+1; no table entry is the sentinel; the too-small claims are refuted at N = 8 and N = 11 and the witnesses exhibited; the twelve gates of the N = 11 witness cannot share one layer.

THEOREM (proved in the record, not yet formalized): for every N >= 2 and every 0 <= kappa_- <= N, the minimum depth over all placements with |n-vec| = kappa_- is exactly ceil((N+1)/(min(kappa_-, N-kappa_-)+1)).

The source's Eq. (73) prints the left product of the (+kappa, rho) circuit as a rightward (increasing) product where its own Lemma 1 (Eq. (35)) and Theorem 1 (Eq. (42)) give a leftward (decreasing) one; the two are not interchangeable, and only the leftward reading reproduces the source's own d = 2N value in its Fig. 14.

families.paper_title: The minimum depth of open-boundary Yang--Baxter integrable circuits: an exact formula and two errata for arXiv:2607.02093
families.paper_abstract: An open-boundary integrable circuit in the construction of Garc\'{\i}a Fern\'andez, Paletta and Retore (arXiv:2607.02093) is a fixed word in two-site gates and two boundary gates, determined by the set $\vn\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ of sites carrying the inhomogeneity $-\kappa$.  They ask for the minimum depth of the circuit over all $\vn$ with $|\vn|=\km$ and conjecture $\tfrac12(N+3)-\km$ for odd $N$ and $\tfrac12(N+4)-\km$ for even $N$.  Both conjectures are false: at $N=8$, $\km=2$ the placement $\vn=(6,3)$ has depth $3$ against the conjectured $4$, and at $N=11$, $\km=2$ the placement $\vn=(8,4)$ has depth $4$ against $5$; $N=8$ lies inside the range $N=2,\dots,10$ the source says it studied, and both lie well inside the $N\le51$ (odd), $N\le50$ (even) to which it reports having checked the conjectures.  The minimum is $\lceil (N+1)/(\min(\km,N-\km)+1)\rceil$ for every $N\ge2$ and $0\le\km\le N$: the lower bound is a chain argument on the word, the upper bound an explicit placement whose $+\kappa$ sites are spread over $\km+1$ staircases rather than the two of the conjectured placements.  The minimum was also computed exhaustively over all $2^{N}$ placements for $2\le N\le19$, and the explicit placement was checked to attain the formula for every $N\le120$.  For the circuits with inhomogeneities $+\kappa$ and $\rho$ only, the inequality $d\ge N+1$ that the source verified exhaustively for $N=5,6,7,9$ and by sampling for $N=11,13,15$ has a one-line proof for every $N$, and the minimum is verified here to be exactly $N+1$, exhaustively over all $2^{N-1}$ placements, for every $3\le N\le20$; a product in the source's Eq.~(73) is printed in the wrong order.  Every finite statement here --- the depth semantics, the tables, the two counterexamples, the placements to $N=120$, the $(+\kappa,\rho)$ sweeps and the product-order check --- is verified in Lean~4 without Mathlib; the closed form for all $N$ is proved on paper.

families.paper_title: Twenty-two improved lower bounds for the Zarankiewicz numbers $z(m,n;3,3)$
families.paper_abstract: The Zarankiewicz number $z(m,n;s,t)$ is the largest number of ones in an $m\times n$ zero--one matrix with no all-ones $s\times t$ submatrix.  For $s=t=3$ the exact values are known only in a small range, and the state of the art is a table of lower and upper bounds that several groups have been improving through 2026.  We give twenty-two new lower bounds in the window $11\le m\le 16$, $18\le n\le 23$, each certified by an explicit $K_{3,3}$-free matrix, with gains of $+1$ to $+8$ over the best previously recorded value; among them are improvements at all five cells treated in the most recent paper on the subject.  We also machine-check, for all $s$ and $t$, the two structural lemmas the area runs on --- monotone padding $z(m,n;s,t)\le z(m,n+1;s,t)$ and minimum-line deletion $z(m,n;s,t)\le k\Rightarrow z(m,n+1;s,t)\le k+\lfloor k/n\rfloor$, both of them published at this generality --- and record the three upper bounds the second of these gives. Everything is verified by the Lean~4 kernel: no statement in the development delegates any step to compiled evaluation, and the reduction that makes this affordable, from a $2^m\cdot 2^n$ subset enumeration to an $n^3m$ scan over column triples, is itself proved rather than assumed.  Two cells are now bracketed within three, $120\le z(13,19;3,3)\le 122$ and $137\le z(16,18;3,3)\le 140$, and we argue that closing either needs an upper-bound argument rather than more search.

families.paper_title: The constant in Lemma~4 of ``Better-than-KL PAC-Bayes Bounds'':\\ a lower bound of $3.66$, an improvement of $8$ to $5.687$,\\ and the Cauchy--Schwarz residue
families.paper_abstract: \sloppy The Zhang--Cutkosky--Paschalidis divergence $\Dz(P,Q;c)=\int|r-1|\sqrt{\ln(1+c^2(r-1)^2)}\,dQ$, $r=dP/dQ$, is the complexity term of the PAC-Bayes bounds of Kuzborskij, Jun, Wu, Jang and Orabona (COLT 2024), and the comparison with the Kullback--Leibler divergence that gives that paper its title rests on its Lemma~4, $\Dz(P,Q;1)\le\sqrt{8\,\Dtv(P,Q)\,\Dkl(P,Q)}$, whose constant $8$ is the product of three factors of $2$ and is not claimed sharp; the paper's conclusion asks ``whether our bounds can be further improved''.  We settle the constant half of that question in three parts.  (i)~No constant below $3.66$ can replace the $8$: at $P=\Bern(129/500)$, $Q=\Bern(91/100)$ the ratio $\Dz^2/(\Dtv\Dkl)$ equals $3.66030952\ldots$, and the two-point supremum is $\Cstar=3.660310847\ldots$. (ii)~The $8$ can be replaced by $2\cg=5.686636\ldots$ today: applying Cauchy--Schwarz directly to the ZCP integrand, before the step $\ln(1+x^2)\le2\ln(1+|x|)$ of the source's proof, gives $\Dz(P,Q;1)\le\sqrt{2\cg\,\Dtv\Dkl}$ with $\cg=\sup_{r\ge0}g(r)/k(r)$, $g(r)=|r-1|\ln(1+(r-1)^2)$, $k(r)=r\ln r-r+1$; the source's two composed steps are each sharp, but in different regimes, which is why their product $4$ exceeds $\cg=2.8433\ldots$.  (iii)~The Cauchy--Schwarz route cannot go below $2\cdot2.843$: any constant $c$ with $\Dg\le c\,\Dkl$ for the post-Cauchy--Schwarz functional $\Dg$ satisfies $c>2.843$, so the remaining factor $2\cg/\Cstar=1.5536$ between the route's floor and the two-point value cannot be recovered by sharpening any step other than the Cauchy--Schwarz one.  We also show that the ``better-than-KL'' divergence exceeds $\Dkl$ pointwise by up to $\kappa=\sup_{r}z(r)/k(r)=2.189094761\ldots$, $z(r)=|r-1|\sqrt{\ln(1+(r-1)^2)}$, with the supremum approached on two-point alphabets, and we state as a conjecture, with search evidence, that $\Cstar$ is the supremum over all alphabets.  The three lower bounds ($3.66$, $2.189$, $2.843$), Lemma~4 at the first witness, and the negative controls are checked in Lean~4 with Mathlib from rigorous rational enclosures of eight logarithms; the improved constant is proved on paper, and the one-variable formula for $\kappa$ is the instance $(\fz,\fk)$ of a theorem of Sason and Verd\'u, whose convexity hypothesis on $\fz$ we verify.  No statement of the source is contradicted. \par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Added in version~2.}  The improvement is now machine-checked, at the slightly larger constant $5.7$ in place of $2\cg$. The pointwise inequality $g(r)\le2.85\,k(r)$ holds for every real $r\ge0$, hence $\cg\le2.85$, by an interval certificate --- thirteen cells on $[13/10,32]$, each closed by the tangent of the convex $k$ at an interior point of the cell against the tangent of the concave logarithm, two Mercator-series regions on $[1/4,1]$ and $[1,13/10]$, one tangent cell on $[0,1/4]$ and an elementary tail on $[32,\infty)$ from $\ln r\ge5\ln2$ --- built from $26$ rigorous rational enclosures of logarithms; and Lemma~4 holds with $5.7$ in place of $8$, $\Dz(P,Q;1)^2\le5.7\,\Dtv(P,Q)\,\Dkl(P,Q)$, for all finitely supported $P,Q$ with $Q$ strictly positive, both in Lean~4 with Mathlib.  The matching kernel lower bound --- every $c$ with $g\le c\,k$ on $[0,\infty)$ has $c>2.843$ --- brackets the constant of the improved lemma as $2.843<\cg\le2.85$, so the certified $5.7$ is within $0.25\ kept unchanged. \par\smallskip\noindent\emph{Added in version~3.}  The additive constant of the source's Lemma~3, $\Dz(P,Q;c)\le\Dz(P,Q;1)+2\sqrt{\ln(2+2c)}\,\Dtv$, is false: its proof applies a correct auxiliary lemma with $c$ where $c^2$ is called for, and the lemma fails in the kernel at $Q=(\frac12,\frac12)$, $P=(\frac38,\frac58)$, $c=10^4$ --- the source's own Theorem~6 parameter at $n=5000$, $\delta=0.01$ --- as do both printed versions of its Theorem~2.  The same proof gives $2\sqrt{\ln(2+2c^2)}$; the sharp constant, proved on paper, is $K^*(c)=G(c)+G_1(c)$, $G(c)=\sup_{t>0}[\sqrt{\ln(1+c^2t^2)}-\sqrt{\ln(1+t^2)}]$, attained on two points, with $4.662<K^*(100)\le4.70$ in the kernel against the printed $4.608$; and Theorem~2 is restated with both constants machine-checked.  Versions~1 and~2 are kept unchanged.

families.title: The state complexity a(n) of the linear relation Y = nX in Zeckendorf representation (OEIS A372846) -- the sequence arXiv:2603.21645 says it cannot prove the growth of
families.description: Fibonacci (Zeckendorf) representation writes `n` as a sum of distinct `F_i`, `i ≥ 2`, with no two consecutive Fibonacci numbers used; the coefficient word `e_t ⋯ e_2` is read **most-significant digit first**, and `[x] = Σ e_i F_i` evaluates an arbitrary binary word (`[01001] = 6`). A pair of integers is read on **two tapes in parallel** over the alphabet `Σ₂ × Σ₂`, the shorter representation padded with leading zeros. All of this is verbatim from the source, arXiv:2603.21645v1 §2.2 (`:241`, `:257`).
families.paper_title: The state complexity of $Y=nX$ in Zeckendorf representation: exact values, the OEIS A372846 bound, and the reachable states of the Moradi--Rampersad--Shallit automaton
families.paper_abstract: Let $a(n)$ be the number of states of the smallest deterministic finite automaton that reads two Zeckendorf representations in parallel and accepts exactly the pairs $(x,y)$ with $\val{y}=n\val{x}$, the dead state not counted; this is sequence A372846 of the OEIS.  Moradi, Rampersad and Shallit build an automaton $\Mnc$ with $36n^2$ states for the relation $Y=nX+c$, print $a(1),\dots,a(10)$ as computed by \texttt{Walnut}, write that the quantity ``is roughly $2n^2+\alpha^2n$, but we do not know how to prove this'', and close the remark with ``A better understanding of the reachable states of $\Mnc$ might help reduce the bound.''  The OEIS entry sharpens the guess to the conjecture $a(n)\le 2n^2+\varphi^2n+1$.  We prove $a(n)$ exactly for $1\le n\le16$ and $a(32)=2132$ --- to our knowledge the first proofs of any term --- by an explicit automaton whose correctness is certified by integer arithmetic alone (two forward-closed half-planes in the plane of two consecutive differences replace the irrational estimate of the source) together with a Myhill--Nerode table for partial acceptors, in which liveness of the prefixes is an essential hypothesis.  We show that the OEIS inequality, stated over the reals with $\sqrt5$, is equivalent to an integer inequality, and prove it at the nineteen values $n\in\{1,\dots,16,32,49,50\}$; outside the formal development it is verified for every $n\le601$, where the smallest slack is $0.652476$ at $n=14$ --- not at $n=32$, as the $48$ published terms suggest --- exactly two $n$ have slack below $1$, both proved here one state from the edge, and beyond $n\approx40$ the slack grows like $0.10\,n$.  We answer the closing sentence: the part of $\Mnc$ reachable from the initial state has exactly $6n^2+6n-4$ states for every $c$, certified for $n\le100$ and computed to $n=601$, a factor $6$ below the printed count.  Past the $48$ terms of the OEIS entry we certify $a(49)\le4926$ and $a(50)\le5128$, and two independent implementations agree on $a(49),\dots,a(60)$ and continue to $a(601)=723916$.  All theorems are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Consecutive Zeckendorf--Niven terms in a $2$-AP: a two-parameter family of five-term runs, and six-term runs confined to two Fibonacci shapes
families.paper_abstract: A positive integer $n$ is \emph{Zeckendorf--Niven} when the number $\sZ(n)$ of summands in its Zeckendorf representation divides $n$.  Lao, Miller, Rosa, Shiliaev, Tresch, Wong and Zhang recently studied how many consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression of common difference two can be Zeckendorf--Niven.  They proved that the only runs of eight or more terms are subsequences of $2,4,\dots,18$, and constructed a five-term run starting at $27+F_{120j+17}$ for every $j$; between five and seven the maximum outside that block is left undetermined.  We prove three things.  First, their construction is one line of a two-parameter family: for $8\le a$, $a+2\le b$, $11\le b$ and $F_a+F_b\equiv 58 \pmod{60}$, the number $n=6+F_a+F_b$ starts a run of five, and the run is exactly five on both sides.  Second, every $n\ge 21$ that starts a run of six satisfies $n+3=F_G$ or $n+5=F_G$ for some $G\ge 21$; beyond $n\ge 21$ there is no hypothesis at all --- none on the size of $n$, none on the position of its Zeckendorf digits.  Third, neither of the two surviving one-parameter families produces a run of six for $G\le 501$, so no $n$ with $21\le n<F_{500}\approx 1.39\cdot 10^{104}$ starts a run of six: throughout that range a run beginning outside $2,4,\dots,18$ has at most five terms, and five occurs.  What is left of the question is a single Fibonacci-index divisibility problem, stated in Question~\ref{q:residue}.  All three results, and every lemma they rest on, are machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Runs of consecutive outer vertices in generalized Petersen graphs, and two erroneous published values of the zero forcing number
families.paper_abstract: Let $\GP{n}{k}$ be the generalized Petersen graph and $\Zf$ the zero forcing number.  The standard upper bound $\Zf(\GP{n}{k})\le 2k+2$ is witnessed by a run of $2k+2$ consecutive vertices of the outer cycle.  We prove that this witness cannot be shortened inside its own shape: for every $k\ge 1$, every $n\ge\max(2k+3,\,5k-1)$ and every starting index $j$, the shortest run of consecutive outer vertices that is a zero forcing set of $\GP{n}{k}$ has length exactly $2k+2$.  The lower half of that statement is proved by exhibiting, for each $k$, an explicit set of $6k-2$ vertices --- a number independent of $n$ --- which contains the run of length $2k+1$, misses the next outer vertex, and is closed under the colour-change rule.  At $k=3$ this turns the negative half of a computation Krishnan reports for $10\le n\le 300$ --- that seven consecutive outer vertices do not force --- into a theorem for every $n\ge13$, and gives the first statement we are aware of that rules out a family of candidate $7$-element sets uniformly in $n$, which is the shape of the open half of his Conjecture~5.  Alongside these we record a lower bound $\Zf(\GP{n}{k})\ge 4$ valid for all $n$ with $2k<n$ and $n\ne 3k$, the resulting exact value $\Zf(\GP{n}{1})=4$ for all $n\ge 5$, and two published values of $\Zf$ that are wrong: the claim $\Zf(\GP{n}{3})=8$ for $n\ge 12$ of Rashidi, Shajareh Poursalavati and Tavakkoli, whose failure at $n=12$ was found by Krishnan and is confirmed here, and the entry $\Zf(\GP{7}{2})=5$ printed in the $\ell=0$ column of Table~1 of arXiv:2508.02564v1, whose true value is $6$.  Every theorem here is machine-checked in Lean~4, and each one quantified over all $n$ is proved without computation.

families.paper_title: Two-neighborly simplicial 0/1-polytopes
families.paper_abstract: A $0/1$-polytope is the convex hull of a subset of the vertices of the unit cube.  Ziegler proved that a simplicial $0/1$-polytope of dimension $d$ has at most $2d$ vertices and asked whether the equality case is always a cross polytope; Kaibel and Pokutta recently answered this in the negative with an explicit example in dimension $7$, and asked in turn whether a simplicial $0/1$-polytope can be $2$-neighborly at all.  We answer their question affirmatively by exhibiting simplicial $2$-neighborly $0/1$-polytopes in dimensions $4,5,6,7$, with $6,8,10,12$ vertices respectively; the three of dimension at least $5$ have, in addition, no cube-antipodal pair of vertices, which is the stronger form in which the question is posed.  Each example is certified twice and independently: through a complete facet enumeration, and through an explicit integer separating functional for every pair of vertices.  We complement this with complete censuses of every subset of $\{0,1\}^3$ and of $\{0,1\}^4$, which show that in those dimensions the largest $2$-neighborly simplicial example has $2d-2$ vertices and that none of the $2d$-vertex examples is $2$-neighborly, and we recompute the invariants of Kaibel and Pokutta's dimension-$7$ examples from their definitions rather than from their tables.  Every theorem and proposition below is machine-checked in Lean~4.

families.paper_title: Zero patterns and unitary similarity:\\ the cell An and \DJ okovi\'c could not compute,\\ and their Conjecture 3.6 through $n = 12$
families.paper_abstract: For a zero pattern $I$ inside $\ZZ_n\times\ZZ_n$ put $\chi_I=\prod_{(i,j)\in I}(x_i-x_j)$, and pair it with the Vandermonde $\chi_n$ in the inner product for which the Laurent monomials are orthonormal.  An and \Dj{} showed that for a pattern of maximal size the single integer $\ip{\chi_I}{\chi_n}$ decides whether every traceless complex $n\times n$ matrix is unitarily similar to one vanishing on $I$, and conjectured that for their Hessenberg-shaped patterns $J_{k,n}$ this integer is $(-1)^{n-1}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n-2}{k-1}$.  They report the conjecture verified for $n\le 10$ with one exception: at $(n,k)=(10,5)$ their program ran out of memory.  We compute that cell, $\ip{\chi_{J_{5,10}}}{\chi_{10}} = -17640$, so the conjecture holds at all $45$ cells with $n\le 10$ and the pattern $J_{5,10}$ is $10$-universal.  We then compute the two rows past their range: the conjecture holds at $n=11$ and at $n=12$, so every $J_{k,11}$ is $11$-universal and every $J_{k,12}$ is $12$-universal.
